Osama bin Laden wanted to attack India years before 9/11, CIA file reveals
The US' Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has released 71 declassified reports related to the 9/11 attacks.
Terrorist leader Osama bin Laden intended to attack India and several other countries years ago, a newly declassified CIA intelligence brief has revealed.
Bin Laden’s al-Qaeda network identified India and Pakistan as possible targets for terrorist strikes before the September 11, 2001 attacks in America, per the top secret document prepared for US president Bill Clinton in 1998.
The revelation is part of a major CIA release which came on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. On September 11, the CIA made 71 intelligence reports public. It was the largest release of 9/11-related records.
Deep Dive
One brief, titled “Bin Ladin Terrorist Network Still a Threat” and dated August 28, 1998, said bin Laden intended to attack several countries, including India and Pakistan.
It said he planned attacks in “Egypt, the Arabian Peninsula—especially Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen—India, Pakistan, Uganda, and possibly Nigeria.” The brief also said US officials had helped arrest bin Laden operatives preparing attacks in Tirana, Albania, and possibly Baku, Azerbaijan.
What the 1998 CIA assessment means
The document does not detail any specific attack plan for India. It shows that US intelligence assessed India and Pakistan as countries where bin Laden’s network intended to carry out attacks, more than three years before 9/11.
The warning came weeks after the August 7, 1998, US embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, which killed 224 people and brought bin Laden and al-Qaeda firmly into the focus of US counterterrorism officials.
ALSO READ | What CIA warned about before 9/11 attacks: 5 key takeaways from newly declassified intelligence files
India would face a major terror attack three years later. On December 13, 2001, terrorists from Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed stormed the Parliament complex in New Delhi.
Nine people, including security personnel and a gardener, were killed in the attack; all five attackers were also killed.
The Parliament attack came three months after the September 11 attacks in the US.
Osama bin Laden was killed in Pakistan
Pakistan later became deeply intertwined with the US hunt for bin Laden and the al-Qaeda network. The CIA’s 9/11 records show that US intelligence continued to monitor bin Laden’s activities and his relationship with the Taliban. A later CIA assessment in June 2000 was specifically titled “Pakistan pressing Bin Ladin network.”
Bin Laden ultimately spent his final years hiding in Pakistan. In 2010, intelligence linked one of his couriers to a compound in Abbottabad, near Islamabad.
US forces killed bin Laden there in a raid on May 2, 2011.
Warnings about 9/11 came later
The CIA records include a July 1998 brief on possible US attacks, a December 1998 warning about aircraft hijackings, and the August 6, 2001 brief titled “Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US.”
ALSO READ | 25 years after 9/11: The warnings, ‘muscle hijackers’ and details you may not know
On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four US passenger planes. American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the World Trade Center’s North Tower, followed by United Airlines Flight 175 hitting the South Tower. Both towers later collapsed.
American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon. Passengers on United Airlines Flight 93 fought back against the hijackers before the plane crashed in Pennsylvania.
A total of 2,977 people, excluding the 19 hijackers, were killed.
What was Osama bin Laden’s role?
Osama bin Laden, al-Qaeda’s founder and leader, directed the organisation behind the attacks. He was not one of the hijackers. The plot developed over several years.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, whom the 9/11 Commission called the attack’s “principal architect”, worked with bin Laden and other al-Qaeda leaders on the plan.

Céline Dion moved to tears on stage as sellout Paris residency begins
Thousands of fans crowd into Europe's largest indoor venue for Canadian singer's comeback
Eleven minutes before 9 p.m. local time, the lights went down and screams erupted as Céline Dion took the stage in a Parisian suburb for her first concert in six years.
Dion, 58, opened the show at at Europe's largest indoor concert venue with a rendition of 1998's On Ne Change Pas, stopping partway through as she was moved to tears.
"I promised not to cry," she told the crowd in Nanterre, wearing a black gown and diamond necklace.
"Tonight I want to sing for you, for me, for life."
Thousands of devoted fans packed Plenitude Arena on Saturday to watch Dion's return to the stage, opening a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined the singer's career.
"Finally. It’s amazing we’re all together. I made a promise. I made a promise to come back and be back on stage," Dion said, speaking in French and then English.
“Thank you so much for your support, your patience and, if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me," she continued, quoting her own 1996 song.
Concertgoers, who made their way through thousands of feet of barricades to get inside the venue, were wearing anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns.
One woman wore her wedding dress.
"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.
"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."
Inside, special edition Céline champagne glasses sold out within minutes and the lines for champagne itself stretched more than 30 metres. Even the men's washroom had snaking line ups.
"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, heading into the arena with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees. "With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."
One of the best-selling artists of all time, she announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.
Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light has buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées or along the famed river Seine.

Indonesian passenger ship overturns, sparking search for about 130 missing
BANJARMASIN, Indonesia — Indonesian rescuers say about 130 passengers and crew are missing after a ferry carrying more than 240 people sank in bad weather in the Java Sea on Sunday. At least 107 people were rescued and the bodies of six passengers were recovered as the search operation expanded in waters around the vessel's last known position.
The ferry was traveling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, officials said.
The vessel's captain had earlier reported rough seas with waves up to 3 meters (10 feet) before issuing a distress message, saying the ship was listing, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned and then sunk.
The rescue agency in Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2 a.m. Sunday. The ship had departed from Surabaya, Indonesia's second largest city, en route to Banjarmasin, a city on Borneo Island.
"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in a video briefing.
In response, a rescue ship was headed to the Virgo Transport 8's estimated last known position, he said, and authorities were deploying rescue teams supported by four vessels, including a navy ship, and a helicopter as the ferry was carrying a large number of passengers and crew.
Survivors are rescued and dead bodies recovered
Initial information indicated the vessel's last known position was in the Java Sea, about 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin. The ship's manifest said it was carrying 243 people — 213 passengers and 30 crew members — although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest.
Sudayana, who is coordinating the search, said the agency was working with maritime authorities and other relevant agencies while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area.
Search teams, assisted by nearby tugboats and other passing vessels, had rescued 107 people and recovered six bodies by Sunday afternoon, he said.
The Japanese-built Virgo Transport 8 is designed to transport both passengers and vehicles.
Distraught relatives wait for news at a port
Hundreds of relatives gathered at a command center in Banjarmasin's Trisakti port on Sunday, awaiting word on family members believed to be aboard the ferry. Many anxiously checked passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued searching for survivors.
"I was shocked when I saw my uncle's name on the passenger list," said a woman who goes by a single name, Bunga. "But I felt relieved after officials told me he had been rescued."
Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.
Last month, at least 211 people were rescued from an Indonesian ferry that caught fire in rough seas near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, while one person was found dead and four others remain missing. The incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.
Sunday's accident comes just four days after a fire that gutted a passenger ferry in the Philippines killed at least 76 people, with at least 10 others still missing.

What was the PSX? The souped-up PS2 rarely sold outside of Japan
The PSX was one of Sony's flops that tried to do too much.
When looking back at the history of video games, the odd console curio is always fun to examine. Long before the Meta Quest cracked the VR market, Nintendo dipped its toes into virtual reality waters with the Virtual Boy. Then there was Sega, who tried to cash in on the success of the Genesis with its bizarre 32X add-on. And who could forget the Nintendo 64DD? Oh, that's right: everyone.
Speaking of weird machines that were never released outside of Japan, enter Sony's PSX: a hybrid PS2 that was also a DVR, among other functionality. Not to be confused with the internal codename for the original PlayStation, there are several reasons the PSX never got a worldwide release (which we'll get to).
If you've never heard of Sony's niche machine, we don't blame you. Released at the height of the PS2's era but a couple of years before the PS3, the PSX was a confusing offering. It was a clumsy beast that failed to capture the imagination of either gamers or DVD enthusiasts. Let's get into exactly what the PSX was and why it failed so badly.
What is the PSX console?
The Sony PSX was an all-in-one entertainment system that launched in Japan in December 2003 and never came to other regions. Not only was it a fully functional PlayStation 2, it was also a DVR (remember those?) and a DVD burner. On top of that impressive job roster, the PSX could play PS1 games, sported a built-in TV tuner and eventually boasted broadband compatibility following a post-launch patch.
Unlike the PS2, which didn't natively support a hard drive — though you could optionally install one via the PS2's expansion bay — the PSX shipped with either a 160GB or 250GB HDD. With the company apparently seeing it more as a digital video recorder/entertainment player than an actual console, the PSX was promoted under the Sony brand, not PlayStation.
The doomed machine's greatest legacy was it being the first Sony system to showcase the XrossMediaBar (XMB) home menu that the PS3 would later make famous... or should that be infamous?
Why was the PSX never released outside Japan?
"It was a big sales dud" is the short answer. Despite initially selling 100,000 units during its launch week back in late 2003, sales quickly tapered off — even after an updated model released in 2004 (which Engadget covered at the time). Though Japanese reports from back then suggest Sony shipped several hundred thousand units by March 2004, the company was reluctant to publish concrete sales data. Over 20 years later, there still aren't reliable lifetime sales figures for the PSX.
Why did the PSX bomb as hard as it did? The somewhat niche selling point of the system didn't help: a hybrid video recorder/DVD player that's also a PS2 is hard to market succinctly. In the spring of 2004, GameSpot reported internal conflicts at Sony might have hindered any potential success the PSX would've had. An unnamed source "close to Sony" told the site, "A lot of things have been said about the failure of the PSX inside the company, but it was probably due to the unrealistic way that its development was conducted." Said source would then claim that Sony's games division and its Blu-ray disc department (who were both handling production of the PSX) "couldn't work too well together," ending up with "a machine that's neither a game console nor a DVD recorder." Cue the machine being phased out in early 2005.
A couple of additional factors sealed the early demise of the PSX. In particular, it cost a heck of a lot more than a PS2. The 160GB model cost ¥79,800, while the 250GB PSX was priced at ¥99,800 (roughly $730 and $910 respectively, circa 2003). By contrast, the PS2 had dropped to around ¥19,800 in Japan the month before the PSX launched, with the colossally successful console costing around $179 in the US by that time.
There were also broadcasting rights issues that made a full-scale international release tricky to pull off. Because the PSX was a DVR designed around Japanese TV, an overseas version of the machine would have required the additional overheard of Sony coordinating with US and European broadcasting regulators.
Is PSX the same as PS1?
This is a pretty easy mistake to make, but no, these consoles are distinct. "PSX" was a codename Sony used internally during the original PlayStation's development, which video game journalists and eventually gamers adapted as a short way of referring to it. Back then, "PS1" wouldn't have been used since there was no second console yet, and "PS one" was eventually used as the official name for the system's slim redesign. Sony never actually marketed the first PlayStation as the PSX.
There's understandably a big difference between one of the most successful consoles of all time and a super-niche hybrid system that was never sold outside of Japan. For context, the PS1 sold an eye-watering 102m units over its lifespan, whereas the PSX was discontinued not even two years after it launched. So don't mistake Sony's iconic 32-bit system for weird digital recorder-meets-console.
But hey, at least the corporation learned its lesson and never made another such misstep again, like when PlayStation struck a hammer blow to game preservation. Wait a minute...

New study reveals which Americans are the most tired
Fatigue is defined as a ‘physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest’
Pretty much everyone is tired, and now there's proof to back that claim up.
A new study, conducted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Health Statistics, found that approximately 71.5 percent of adults in the U.S. say they experience fatigue on multiple days over the past three months.
The report's author, Natalie A.E. Young, said that fatigue is “one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S.” The study surveyed approximately 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024, NBC News reports.
According to the report, women and younger adults are more likely to report that they're experiencing frequent fatigue than men.
Young said that people who report regular fatigue “are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn’t been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population."
Everyone gets tired, but fatigue is not the same as feeling sleepy. According to the study, fatigue is defined as “physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest.”
General fatigue — not to be confused with chronic fatigue syndrome — can be a symptom of other health problems. It can arise as a side effect of some medications.
People who reported experiencing fatigue were found to be more likely to experience “co-occurring functioning difficulties,” like cognitive difficulties, depression, and anxiety, according to Young.
The report found that adults experiencing fatigue are more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and approximately twice as likely to report having cognitive difficulties or anxiety compared to those who did not report experiencing regular fatigue.
One in six adults said that they experience fatigue almost daily — "most days" or "every day" per the study's language — and that fatigue was highest in the 18-34 response bracket, with nearly 20 percent saying they experienced regular fatigue.
The lowest group to report regular fatigue was seniors aged 65 and older. Of that group, only 12.9 percent said they experienced regular fatigue.
Twenty percent of women said they experienced regular fatigue, while only 13 percent of men reported the same.
The CDC survey did not look at the underlying causes of frequent fatigue, and it does not compare the responses to any previous years.

A Bengaluru commercial court has temporarily restrained hyperlocal news startup Way2News from using confidential information and intellectual property belonging to AppsForBharat, the operator of spiritual tech platform Sri Mandir. The court passed the ad-interim ex parte injunction on Thursday (September 10) in a commercial suit filed by AppsForBharat against Way2News and its former employee Shivam Kumar Singh. The order restrains Way2News, its directors, employees, agents, and others acting on its behalf from using AppsForBharat’s confidential information, intellectual property, and other data allegedly received from Singh until the next hearing. Since the order was passed ex parte, Way2News and Singh were not heard before the interim relief was granted. Inc42 has reached out to AppsForBharat and Way2News for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response. What AppsForBharat Has Alleged According to court filings accessed by Inc42, Singh worked as a senior operations associate at AppsForBharat and was involved in coordinating with priests and temples and managing on-ground pooja operations. He resigned on August 3, 2026, citing “personal exigencies”, and his last working day was August 7. AppsForBharat alleged that one of its employees received a request from Singh on August 25 seeking access to the startup’s Google Drive. The request was allegedly sent using a Way2News email address, prompting AppsForBharat to launch an internal investigation. The startup claimed the drive contained videos, marketing material, operational information, financial data, and details of suppliers and customers. AppsForBharat further alleged that Singh joined Way2News in violation of the non-compete provision in his employment agreement and shared its confidential information with the platform. It also accused Way2News’ spiritual tech platform Veda Mandir of publishing promotional videos identical to marketing material created by Sri Mandir. AppsForBharat also accused Way2News of approaching its employees and customers and sought separate ex parte injunctions against such solicitation. However, the court declined to grant these two injunctions without hearing the defendants and issued notices to them instead. The current injunction is limited to Way2News’ alleged use of AppsForBharat’s confidential information. The interim order does not constitute a final finding of data theft or copyright infringement. AppsForBharat Seeks ₹1 Cr AppsForBharat has sought ₹1 Cr in compensation for alleged losses and contractual breaches. It has also sought the return of its confidential material, permanent injunctions against its misuse and the solicitation of employees and customers, and an account of revenue generated through its alleged unauthorised use. Founded in 2020 by Prashant Sachan, AppsForBharat’s Sri Mandir app enables users to book online pujas and offerings, receive prasad, and access devotional content. In July 2025, AppsForBharat raised ₹175 Cr in a Series C round led by Susquehanna Asia VC. It has raised about $65 Mn to date. Meanwhile, Way2News was founded in 2015 by Raju Vanapala. It primarily offers short-format hyperlocal news in vernacular languages. It later entered spiritual tech with Veda Mandir, which facilitates pooja, chadhava, and daan offerings at temples. The startup raised $14 Mn in a WestBridge Capital-led Series B round in 2024 and has raised nearly $30 Mn to date.

Ending speculation that former West Bengal Chief Minister and Trinamool Congress chairperson Mamata Banerjee may contest the upcoming Assembly bypolls, the Trinamool Congress on Sunday (September 13, 2026) announced candidates for Nandigram and Rejinagar constituencies.
The Mamata-led faction has fielded Sanchita Pradhan (Dey) from Nandigram and Rabiul Alam Chowdhury from Rejinagar. Elections to the two constituencies in south Bengal are scheduled for October 6.
The party had also announced that Adbul Salam will be contesting polls from the Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency in Assam. The Mamata-led faction decided to announce candidates a day after the other faction of the party led by Ritabrata Banerjee said it would not field candidates if Ms. Banerjee decided to contest from Nandigram.
Ms. Banerjee had contested and lost the Nandigram Assembly polls in 2021 to Suvendu Adhikari with a narrow margin. The by-polls will be held at a time when the Mamata faction and Ritabrata Banerjee faction are contesting over the the party symbol of grass and twin flowers. Leaders from both the factions met Election Commission (EC) officials in Delhi staking claim over the symbol. The leaders of the Ritabrata Banerjee faction have said that if the EC does not give the group Trinamool symbol the party will field candidates as independents.
The by-polls have also come as a setback to Opposition unity as almost every opposition party has fielded candidates. The CPI(M)-led Left Front has nominated Sayeed Asad Aliu from Rejinagar and Shanti Gopal Giri from Nandigram. The Congress has nominated Mohd Abdullahil Kafi from Rejinagar and Milan Pradhan from Nandigram. After the defeat of the Trinamool Congress in the 2026 Assembly polls, the party was left with 80 MLAs, more than 65 of whom have sided with Mr. Ritabrata Banerjee.
The bypolls are being held as Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who won from both Nandigram and Bhabanipur, subsequently gave up the Nandigram seat. The byelection is also scheduled in Rejinagar following the decision of Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AJUP) leader Humayun Kabir to vacate the seat. Mr. Kabir, who had won from both Naoda and Rejinagar, decided to give up Rejinagar. His son Golam Nabi Azad is the AJUP candidate from Rejinagar. The bypolls to Nandigram and Rejinagar are scheduled for October 6. The last date for filing nominations is September 16.

My oldest son was my only child for three years. I think that built a bond that doesn't exist with any of his four siblings who had to share me from day one with an expanding brood of children.
I can honestly say, I do not have a favorite child, but it was this oldest one who taught me how to be a mother. That included how to let go when the time came.
At the age of 19 after an inauspicious start to college, he moved cross-country to San Francisco, a frequent transition for kids who grow up in Boston.
Since he was the first of my five to depart home, it hit me pretty hard; but it was clear he needed a change and I willingly co-signed his decision.
I did the same thing at the same age
My son informed me of his impending move on a Monday. He left that Thursday. I didn't discourage him. I'd done the same thing at the same age. Like him, I'd notified my mother that I was leaving home just four days before I actually did. My destination was Phoenix, where I was joining my brother who'd just moved west to accept a job in the desert and had invited me to join him.
I packed my most important worldly possessions in a camp trunk, shipped it out first and then flew to our new home.
My son was riding across the country in a van with three other 19-year-olds. He packed even less than me. I don't remember crying as I watched them depart. I was already thinking about the mess he'd left behind and how it was up to me to clean it up.
I braced myself for what I was about to find
Our house was small and with so many children, we'd converted almost every inch of living space into a bedroom. My son's room had been our basement playroom, but when he hit puberty, I wanted him to have privacy away from his younger siblings so sent him downstairs to his own personal lair.
His brother, who still shared a room with two siblings, coveted the space and didn't take long to box up his belongings in anticipation of a move downstairs. Before he could haul his things down, though, I wanted to clear out whatever might have been left behind.
I was nervous about what I might find and didn't want any of the other kids to uncover something illicit or illegal.
Fortunately, I didn't find any contraband although I wondered what might be in the small safe in the closet. When I asked him, my son said it was empty and since he'd lost the key and we couldn't open it I decided to accept that answer.
There were a few books and some out-of-date electronics, but most of what he left behind were clothes he'd outgrown. I wasn't surprised when I found a Playboy magazine hidden under a pile of old sweaters. In fact, it made me laugh as I recalled my parents finding an issue when my brother left home.
It's what he took with him that surprised me the most
The clear-out didn't take long. If he could be unsentimental about what he'd left behind, so could I. By the end of the day, his brother had taken over the space, made it his own, and settled in.
The intrepid travelers arrived safely on the West Coast five days later. They easily found jobs and a place to live. My son's first job in the Bay Area was on an assembly line in an electronics factory. It was an enlightening experience for him that empowered his next decision — registering for college and setting forth on the path towards the career he has today.
When he moved into his own apartment, I went out to help him set it up. He gave me a tour of the space and proudly commented on how he wanted to fix it up. As I stepped into his bedroom, I saw something familiar propped up on his mattress. It was his Christmas bear that had sat under our tree each year since toddlerhood. I hadn't realized he'd taken this childhood treasure with him.
My oldest moving out was the first monumental shift in our family dynamic. When I looked at that stuffed bear, I knew that even though he now lived 3000 miles away from me, my son really wasn't that far from home.

Bangladesh on Sunday (September 13, 2026) said it wants to “reset” its relationship with India and build a new bilateral engagement based on mutual interests, while describing ties during the tenure of deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina as “uncomfortable”.
The remarks by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir came two days after Bangladesh said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would not participate in the BRICS Summit hosted by India as he was not invited to the event, with the invitation instead extended to the BIMSTEC chair.
The two-day BRICS Summit concluded on Sunday (September 13, 2026). India had invited Mr. Rahman to attend the summit as chairperson of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), while a separate bilateral invitation had been in place since February.
Bangladesh wants to “reset” its bilateral relationship with India, Mr. Kobir told reporters. “We want to move towards a new relationship, which should be done through bilateral discussions, not through a multilateral forum,” he said.
India-Bangladesh ties have been strained over New Delhi providing refuge to Hasina, who fled to India following her ouster in a youth-led agitation in August 2024.
Mr. Kobir said Bangladesh needs to move beyond what he described as an “excessive preoccupation” with India and approach its relationship with New Delhi in a balanced manner, focusing on mutual interests and treating it as part of its broader engagement with other countries.
“We have to get out of the India fascination. India is just another country, and Bangladesh wants good bilateral relations with it,” he said.
Responding to a question, the Minister said, “Breakfast in India, lunch in India, dinner in India — then when will you eat your own food?” Mr. Kobir also said Prime Minister Rahman is scheduled to leave for New York on September 21 to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly and stay there until September 26.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting between Mr. Rahman and U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UNGA, he said such meetings are often decided at the last moment during major international conferences.
“The primary focus of the Prime Minister’s visit is to address the UN General Assembly,” Mr. Kobir said, adding that details of the sideline meetings would be known in due course.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Trump’s Secret Points System for Cabinet Members
The White House held a summer contest to see who could appear in the most congressional districts and states with competitive midterm elections.
Nearly every day, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles meets with Meghan Bauer, a presidential assistant who coordinates with Cabinet members, to review who’s recently traveled where, who’s heading out into the country, and—perhaps most important—who’s in a swing district at that very moment. The debrief is part of the administration’s unofficial Cabinet Travel Competition, overseen by Bauer, in which the White House encourages Cabinet secretaries to traverse the country to promote President Trump’s agenda and tracks their visits to politically competitive congressional districts or states ahead of the midterm elections.
We first found out about the competition when chatting with a Cabinet secretary about an event that person had declined to attend in Manhattan, in part for fear of being docked points in the White House contest for going to a solidly blue area. (Several White House officials said that no one ever loses points, and two added that a trip to New York for a cable-news hit praising the administration’s policies, for instance, would still count toward the contest.)
When we talked with Karoline Leavitt late last month, in her final days as White House press secretary, she marveled: “I think we have seven or eight of them out on the road in targeted districts just today.” The formal competition ran from Memorial Day to Labor Day, although secretaries will likely be encouraged to keep going through November. There were rumors of a prize—possibly a dinner with the president for the winning Cabinet secretary, plus their family—but several White House officials insisted that the competition is simply for bragging rights. They all spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were discussing internal matters.
These officials said that contestants are encouraged to travel to key congressional districts or competitive states, appear with members of Congress, and participate in local media interviews. The thinking, in part, is that local press coverage is more valuable than talking with national outlets in Washington, and that Cabinet officials can help drive Trump’s message by highlighting how his actions and policies have improved the lives of voters. Any midterm-related travel must be flagged for White House approval—and everyone is instructed to comply with federal rules that forbid certain forms of partisan politicking. As in previous administrations, taxpayers foot the bill for travel related to the secretaries’ official duties, and the top officials are expected to pay for any personal political travel themselves. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. got approval to use a more costly military jet for some of his trips, The Washington Post reported.
In February, Wiles told agency heads they should limit their international travel so that they could focus on helping Republicans win the midterm elections. The president would do the same, she said at the time, and he would spend every other week stumping through the country, ramping up to at least once a week as the November elections neared. Punishment for those who disobeyed was swift; among the various reasons Kristi Noem was pushed out as Homeland Security secretary were images of her atop a camel in Bahrain and well-documented horseback-riding jaunts in Argentina’s Campo de Mayo and near South Dakota’s Mount Rushmore, where there are no competitive federal midterm races. “They know not to take 10-day-long vacations in Wyoming,” Leavitt said of the Cabinet members. “The president is working all the time, and he expects them to as well.”
The White House declined to provide us with its tally of each Cabinet member’s political travel, but it did send us a list of the numbers of visits made to at least 13 states over the summer. In the lead with 46 visits was Texas, where Republicans are spending millions to try to hold on to a Senate seat. Following close behind was Pennsylvania with 42, and New York with 40. (Manhattan may not be MAGA country, but New York has several competitive House districts.) On the lower end of the most-visited states were New Jersey and North Carolina (both 10), Alaska (five), and Nevada (four). In a little more than three months, the White House said, Cabinet members made a total of 265 visits to those 13 states.
We made our own list, searching through publicly documented domestic travel by members of Trump’s Cabinet starting on Memorial Day and ending on August 31. To try to emulate the White House’s tracking system, we gave each person a point for traveling to a competitive congressional district or a state with a close Senate race. We used the Cook Political Report ratings to determine competitiveness, focusing on the 37 districts with races that Cook rated as a toss-up or leaning toward one political party, as well as any states with a similarly competitive Senate contest. (Though the White House might reward someone who went to Manhattan for a media interview, we did not. We also awarded only one point for multiple stops in one state during a single trip.)
According to our tally, the winner is likely Small Business Administration head Kelly Loeffler, who took at least 18 trips to competitive states, including more than one stop each in Georgia, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia. She is followed closely by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins (at least 17), Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling (at least 15), and Kennedy and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (at least 10 each). In certain ways, the competition is really just among the handful of members whose job lends itself to regular national travel; folks such as the U.S. trade representative, the CIA director, and the director of the Office of Management and Budget seem to have each taken only one trip to a competitive area since Memorial Day. We could not find any midterm-related trips for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who since his confirmation has clocked thousands of miles overseas. And though Duffy tied for fourth place during this period, we were nonetheless surprised his travel wasn’t a bit more robust, given that he previously spent several months traversing the country with his family for his six-episode reality series, The Great American Road Trip. Perhaps he was just recovering from his long joyride across the United States.
The White House spokesperson Olivia Wales praised both Trump’s Cabinet and his policy achievements in an emailed statement. “Cabinet officials will continue to meet with everyday Americans across our country to inform future policymaking and tout these victories, drawing a strong contrast to the record of failure by radical Democrats on the border, inflation, and crime,” she wrote. Since Trump’s first term, Democrats and watchdog groups have accused Trump officials of violating the Hatch Act—a 1939 federal law that, to minimize partisanship in government, limits federal employees from engaging in certain political activities. And in the run-up to these midterms, at least one Cabinet member—Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—has come under intense criticism for seemingly blurring the line between personal and government travel.
Two decades ago, President George W. Bush’s staff similarly tracked Cabinet travel before the 2006 midterms, and offered incentives to federal employees who volunteered in battleground races. The Office of Special Counsel condemned the operation years later, objecting to the use of federal funds for political purposes. Back then, the Republican National Committee kept an “Administration Tracker” spreadsheet to log the travel of political appointees to targeted races, and the White House kept its own list of Cabinet “assets” and where they had deployed. The investigation found that the Bush tracking system spurred a “friendly competition” between White House liaisons that, ultimately, was part of the “type of electioneering proscribed by the Hatch Act.”
The partisan travel of federal officials has long been legally and politically fraught. During the Biden administration, in 2024, House and Senate Republicans investigated trips that top officials from the Small Business Administration, including the administrator, took to crucial battleground states. Federal watchdogs found in 2021 that members of the Trump administration had shown “willful disregard” for the law by pushing for Trump’s reelection in their official capacities.
Whether the White House is violating the law now would depend on what internal safeguards have been created to prevent federal funds from being spent on political purposes, Donald Sherman, the president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, told us. “The details do matter,” he said. “But it is also hard to imagine that that compliance is being prioritized in a competition-like scenario, particularly in an administration that has been hostile to the Hatch Act in pretty much every other instance.”
Trump fired the head of the Office of Special Counsel when he returned to office, and the Hatch Act has not been enforced against senior Trump-administration officials since then, despite complaints from watchdog groups about apparent violations. A White House official told us that the administration has implemented a process in which the White House and agency ethics officials review political appearances by Trump’s appointees. “All Administration officials who chose to participate in political activity and travel have been encouraged to work with their respective agency counsels and the White House to ensure that they are in full compliance,” the official wrote in an emailed statement.
In the run-up to the 2010 midterms, then-President Obama and his team invented the “Recovery Summer,” a six-week push—featuring, yes, Cabinet secretaries and other senior officials—to spotlight infrastructure investments from their stimulus bill. In 2022, the Biden administration deployed its top messengers across the country to highlight his policies as well. Then–Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg proved the most in-demand Cabinet surrogate, and his position allowed him to tout the administration’s roughly $1 trillion infrastructure bill.
But those administrations were more diligent than Trump’s in distinguishing between personal and government travel, and took pains not to mix the two. And despite the Trump administration’s alleged disregard for the Hatch Act, many of the Cabinet members we’ve tracked have similarly avoided blurring political and government trips, albeit with (at least) one notable exception. In May, before the official competition began, Hegseth appeared in Kentucky alongside the former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, who successfully challenged Representative Thomas Massie, a Trump irritant, in the Republican primary. Hegseth’s star turn on the stump raised questions about whether he’d violated the Hatch Act; though a Pentagon spokesperson said Hegseth had attended in his “personal capacity,” he appeared the same day at Fort Campbell in Kentucky in his official capacity to award Purple Hearts. Past Pentagon chiefs and other top Defense Department officials have avoided even a whiff of partisanship. Then, in August, Hegseth appeared at the Iowa State Fair alongside Representative Zach Nunn, where he endorsed Nunn’s reelection bid and praised him as an ally of both the Pentagon and the president.
Perhaps emboldened by his previous campaign-trail appearance—which prompted much griping but no meaningful consequences—Hegseth declared, “According to the lawyers, I’m only here in a personal capacity.”
Agriculture Secretary Rollins—a frequent traveler, by our count—journeyed in early June to a farm in North Carolina, where she walked between rows of tobacco and stood in front of John Deere tractors, touting the Trump administration’s labor reforms, which she said had reduced costs for the state’s farmers. In July, she joined a radio interview in Georgia with Representative Brian Jack—a Republican expected to win his reelection campaign—and described a new program for shipping meat as “so exciting” and “so important” for the state. And in late August, she appeared at the Iowa State Fair, where she defended Trump’s controversial decision to ease restrictions on imported beef, which she said was necessary to lower prices for struggling families. All three states have competitive Senate races that are essential to Republicans maintaining control of the chamber.
Her fellow Cabinet members traveled to other key states to spread similar enthusiasm. Energy Secretary Chris Wright—with nine trips to competitive areas, by our count—traveled to Alaska to deliver “a giant thank-you” for the state’s copious oil exports. And Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins tied with him, including travel to a military event in Virginia Beach with Vice President Vance and a day of stops in central Michigan to meet with local veterans, alongside the district’s Republican representative.
The agency chiefs tailor their messages to their specific audiences. But if the competition is any indication—and mere mention of it elicited knowing nods and smiles from agency staff and White House officials—the Cabinet officials understand their singular mission: to spread the Trump doctrine far and wide, but especially to purple battlegrounds. They are eager to comply.
Madison Hahamy, Jack Rodriquez-Vars, and Marie-Rose Sheinerman contributed to this report.

Mental health conditions that may develop following a traumatic incident could contribute to a higher risk of future cardiovascular issues such as non-fatal heart attack and stroke or a fatal cardiac event, according to new research.
"Traumatic events are common experiences and can include serious fires or explosions, physical assault, transportation accidents, the suicide or death of a loved one, and severe medical illnesses or injuries," lead author Jennifer A Sumner, an associate professor in the department of psychology at the University of California Los Angeles, said.
"Experiencing traumatic events can significantly affect mental health as well as cardiovascular health. Although most work to date has focused on PTSD and cardiovascular health, our research suggests that we should think about a wide range of mental health consequences when looking at cardiovascular disease risk after trauma," Sumner said.
The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, examined national health registries in Denmark, looking at 2,19,866 adults who did and did not develop major heart or brain conditions following a traumatic event.
About 44,000 of the 2,19,866 participants experienced a non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death between 1995 and 2019.
Researchers compared 1,75,872 people who experienced a trauma but not a cardiovascular event to peers who experienced a heart attack, stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death during the 24-year period.
A wide range of mental health conditions were considered as possible cardiovascular predictors, and machine learning was used to identify the 15 most important mental health disorder predictors of heart and brain outcomes.
Alcohol abuse was found to be the most important mental health risk linked to serious heart or brain conditions for men and women.
"For men and women, the most important psychiatric predictor of MACCE (major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events) was alcohol use disorders," the authors wrote.
"After a traumatic life experience, individuals may turn to alcohol to cope and help manage their emotions. Over time, this new behaviour might develop into alcohol abuse, thus increasing their risk of a serious heart or brain condition," Sumner said.
Mood disorders, including depression, were found to be strong indicators of post-traumatic psychiatric issues associated with cardiovascular outcomes for both men and women. However, mood disorders were a more prominent predictor for women, compared to men.
Psychological conditions that can arise after a traumatic event connected to a higher risk of heart and brain conditions in the future included PTSD, mental disorders caused by brain or physical issues, non-substance-induced confusion, different substance use disorders, personality disorders, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and anxiety disorders.

For decades, Britain played a key role in training India’s military during the colonial era. Now, in a striking reversal, Indian Air Force (IAF) pilots are training Britain’s Royal Air Force (RAF) pilots. For the first time, three IAF pilots have joined the RAF as qualified flying instructors (QFIs) at RAF Valley in Wales, UK. The Indian instructors will train young British pilots on the BAE Hawk T2 aircraft, which is also used by the IAF for the final stage of training its combat fighter pilots. The three-member Indian team, led by a Squadron Leader-level officer, will initially be deployed in the UK for two years. The development has an interesting historical link with India’s colonial past. The British established an auxiliary air force in India on October 8, 1932. During World War II, the force was designated the Royal Indian Air Force (RIAF) in 1945 in recognition of its service during the war. When India became a republic in January 1950, the force dropped the ‘Royal’ prefix and became the Indian Air Force. More than seven decades later, Indian pilots have taken on a different role in Britain — training pilots of the RAF itself. The deployment is part of efforts by India and the UK to deepen military training and defence cooperation. The decision to send IAF instructors to Britain was taken in February this year after the two countries agreed to expand military training engagements. The IAF described the deployment as “a historic first in India–UK defence cooperation”. In a post on X on Friday, the force said: “Three Indian Air Force Qualified Flying Instructors (QFIs) have joined RAF Valley, Wales, to instruct Royal Air Force pilots — marking the first deployment of Indian QFIs to the UK.” The IAF said the move was a “landmark step” towards strengthening professional excellence, interoperability and long-term India-UK ties. The three IAF instructors will train RAF pilots on the BAE Hawk T2, a jet trainer used by the British Air Force. The aircraft also has an important role in India’s fighter pilot training programme, where it is used as the final training platform before pilots move towards operational combat aircraft. The Indian QFIs will therefore bring experience from the IAF’s own advanced flying training system to RAF Valley. Their initial deployment is planned for two years. The deployment comes amid efforts by New Delhi and London to strengthen their wider defence partnership. In April this year, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh held talks with Jonathan Nicholas Powell, the UK’s National Security Adviser, on regional security developments. The two sides also reviewed the progress of existing India-UK defence cooperation frameworks. The push for closer military cooperation had also featured in discussions between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer during Starmer’s official visit to India in October last year. According to the joint statement issued after their meeting, the two countries agreed to expand exchanges between their armed forces through joint exercises, training and capacity building. NEW DELHI: A day after Iranian President 
Masoud Pezeshkian
 met UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi, Tehran signalled a push to move past the conflict and strengthen ties with its Gulf neighbour.
Pezeshkian said Iran had no problems with the UAE or other regional countries, drawing a distinction between Tehran's relations with its neighbours and its opposition to US military bases in the region. His remarks came after the meeting with the UAE leadership at a time when the West Asia conflict has strained relations across the region.
“We have no problems with the UAE. We have no problem with any of the regional countries. We have a problem with the American bases located in these countries and from which they are attacking our country,” Pezeshkian said.
Pezeshkian said Iran considered the UAE and other Gulf states to be “brothers” and expressed a desire to expand relations with them. “The UAE, the Emiratis and other countries of the region are our brothers. We have been living together for a long time and we have had trade. We have supported each other,” he said.
Iran draws line between UAE and US bases
Pezeshkian on Sunday said Tehran's objection was directed at the use of territory in neighbouring countries by the United States rather than at the Gulf states themselves.
“So this is the US that has come here and established bases, and from those bases they martyr our children, they attack our infrastructure and bomb, and they target our leaders, commanders and people,” he said.
“In fact, the problem is that the friendly and neighbouring countries should not allow enemies to utilise their soil to attack our country,” the Iranian President added.
He said Tehran wanted to strengthen ties with the UAE and other neighbouring countries. “Right now, we have a good relation with the UAE and we can expand it, and with other countries, the same happened. So we would like to have a sincere relation with all of them,” Pezeshkian said.
The Iranian President also accused the United States of seeking to exploit the region's energy resources while using arms sales to deepen divisions among regional countries.
“However, it is the US which does not want this to happen,” he said, alleging that Washington wanted to "utilise our petroleum reservoirs of the region” while selling weapons and missiles to regional countries “in order to scare us from each other and pit us against each other.”
“It is actually exploiting the capital of the region and also it is destroying the peace and stability,” Pezeshkian said.
Iran, UAE leaders meet in Delhi
Pezeshkian's comments came a day after his meeting with UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi.
The meeting brought the Iranian and Emirati leadership together as the expanded Brics grouping discussed the escalating conflict in West Asia. Details of the talks were not immediately made public.
The meeting was significant against the backdrop of tensions between Iran and several Gulf states over the wider regional conflict. The UAE has also maintained security partnerships with Western powers, a point repeatedly criticised by Tehran.
The New Delhi Summit nevertheless provided a platform for direct engagement between regional powers that have differed over the conflict.
Pezeshkian calls for regional cooperation
Pezeshkian said Iran wanted neighbouring countries to pool their capabilities to improve regional security and promote economic and cultural ties.
“We, with the neighbouring and regional countries, can share our powers in order to help each other and establish security and help our people in order to promote our culture and economy again,” he said.
His remarks came as the Brics Summit sought to build consensus on the escalating West Asia crisis, with the conflict emerging as a major issue during discussions in New Delhi.
Brics declaration calls for restraint
Brics leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, expressing serious concern over the escalation in West Asia and calling for maximum restraint, dialogue and diplomacy.
The declaration called for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure and stressed the importance of maintaining global trade, supply chains and energy flows amid the conflict.
It also expressed concern over attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, stressing that nuclear safety and security must be maintained even during armed conflicts.
The declaration called for the implementation of relevant UN General Assembly and Security Council resolutions and urged all parties to maintain a ceasefire and ensure full and unhindered humanitarian access to the Gaza Strip.
The Iran-UAE engagement in New Delhi, followed by Pezeshkian's comments on closer regional ties, came as the Brics platform sought to position itself as a forum for dialogue and diplomacy amid the continuing West Asia crisis.

For China, H-6N bomber enhances nuclear deterrence and second-strike capability
Country’s nuclear triad complete as airborne leg supplements intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles

Last month, the People’s Liberation Army released footage showing its H-6N bomber flying with a nuclear-capable Jing Lei-1 (JL-1) air-launched ballistic missile (ALBM), offering a rare look at China’s airborne nuclear strike capability.
The H-6N is one of the latest modernised variants of the H-6, the country’s only strategic bomber. Its flight carrying the ALBM during a joint anti-ship exercise was featured in a documentary by state broadcaster CCTV for the PLA’s 99th anniversary.

Brazil is in fashion, as Brazilians like to say. Here's why
Brazil is experiencing a cultural surge as celebrities and tourists embrace its vibrant culture
RIO DE JANEIRO -- RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazil is having a moment. Celebrities and record numbers of tourists donning green, yellow and blue are flooding into the country. Brazilian culture — from its Oscar-nominated films to funk music — is taking the world by storm. Global fashion brands and influencers are leaning into the hype.
For decades, Brazilians have lamented that the country and its cultural makeup and output have long gone under-appreciated in what has become known as the “mongrel complex.”
But as attention from abroad pours in and consolidates itself in 2026, some say a shift may be underway with the rise of “caramelo pride” — a ubiquitous celebration by Brazilians of caramel-colored street mutts that have come to represent the country.
Here’s a look at the phenomenon.
Brazil has captured the world’s attention and admiration before, and Brazilians cyclically observe that “Brasil está na moda,” or Brazil is in fashion.
Many trace the current popularity of the phase to 2023, when Brazilcore, a fashion trend featuring the colors of the Brazilian flag and inspired by Brazilian culture, gained widespread global traction. Celebrities including Bad Bunny, Emily Ratajkowski, Hailey Bieber, Tina Kunakey, Sabrina Carpenter, Alex Consani and Addison Rae have all participated in the trend.
Fashion was “very rigid, with many uniformized clothes. Suddenly came this wave from Brazil showing more skin, using more color,” said Néli Pereira, a PhD candidate at the University of Sao Paulo in cultural studies who specializes in Brazil. The spontaneity and vivid color palettes resonated amid a craving for more light-heartedness.
Recently, the popularity of Brazilcore has morphed into a massive, multi-faceted global phenomenon that celebrates “brasilidade,” or Brazilianness, moving beyond fashion to include music, dance, cinema and sport.
Brazilcore can be spotted on high streets around the world and takes the forms of bikinis, micro-shorts, crochet pieces, soccer shirts and accessories. Brands including fast fashion giants, such as Zara and H&M, have put out tops in green and yellow or emblazoned with Rio de Janeiro, while Chanel, Jil Sander and Schiaparelli have all made references to Brazil’s national colors.
The hype around Brazil has also translated into record numbers of tourists visiting the country. More than 9 million tourists came to Brazil last year, a 37% increase compared with 2024. Jokes on the internet abound about the CPF — an individual’s fiscal identity in Brazil — being the new sought-after green card.
In Rio, visitors head to Rocinha favela, kitted out in Brazilcore, and pay for footage of themselves striding out onto a terrace, plonking themselves down as a drone captures the scene before panning out to capture Rio’s stunning urban landscape. These videos have gone viral in recent months.
“If you don’t do the video with the drone, it’s as if you didn’t come to the favela,” said Eduardo Maristany, a 30-year-old tourist from Barcelona, who recently partook in a tour of Rocinha. Like many others, he chose the country as a destination after seeing an influx of videos on social media about Brazil’s famed favelas, beaches and parties.
It’s not just tourists who are engaging with Brazil. Madonna, Lady Gaga and Shakira performed free shows on Copacabana Beach in 2024, 2025 and 2026 respectively, drawing at least a million concert-goers each time, according to Rio City Hall numbers.
And in 2024, Bruno Mars posted a video of himself dancing to funk music, seemingly getting a Christ the Redeemer tattoo on his chest and posing with a caramelo dog. With more than 13 million likes on Instagram, the video ends with the words: “I love you Brazil.” Rosalia and Dua Lipa have also professed their love for Brazil online.
Meanwhile, Brazilian culture — from Anitta’s funk music to Academy Award-nominated films such as ‘I’m Still Here’ and ‘The Secret Agent’ — is being celebrated on the world’s biggest stages and across the internet, turbocharging Brazil’s soft power.
It's frequently said about the country that “Brazil is not for amateurs.” The oft-repeated phrase taps into the complexity of the continental-sized country, where exuberant celebrations of life – epitomized by Carnival — coexist alongside violence, poverty and political scandals reminiscent of telenovelas.
Brazil’s ambiguities “make sense in a world filled with conflicts, inequalities and scarcity,” said Bruno Pompeu, a professor at the University of Sao Paulo’s school of communications and arts.
The country’s formidable presence online is also contributing to the current wave of interest in Brazil. Brazil — with a population of over 200 million — is one of the most connected countries in the world and social media users are showcasing the country’s seemingly infinitely multilayered culture.
“Brazil pulsates creativity and has this very particular characteristic of interacting on the internet in a collective manner. It’s common for content to be quickly transformed into memes and cultural references,” said Eduardo Lorenzi, general director of operations for Latin America at TikTok.
Brazilians are known for their high engagement, a much-sought-after characteristic in the attention economy.
Courtney Henning Novak, a Californian and prolific reader and writer, developed an online community composed mostly of Brazilian followers after her rave review of a 1881 book by Brazilian author Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis went viral.
“Brazilians love to comment. I get more messages than I can keep up with, and there’s a lot of positive energy,” she said.
For the global entertainment industry, brands, event organizers, businesses and influencers, Brazil represents a key market and an exceptionally valuable fan base.
Vitor Oliveira, a 36-year-old tour guide from Rocinha, credits social networks for the explosion of tourism in his neighborhood. “Influencers coming here were a game changer and primordial to the increase of tourism in Rio and especially in Rocinha,” he said.
Beyond digital engagement, Brazil’s current moment in the spotlight is the result of a confluence of factors involving politics, diplomacy, culture and economics, said Pereira, pointing to policies that support the showcasing of Brazilian culture and a huge effort to attract tourists by Embratur, Brazil’s government tourism agency.
Like all trends, this one is likely to fade, experts say, predicting that the upcoming election and the return of political polarization may diminish the association of yellow and green with joy.
French comedian Paul Cabannes, who is based in Sao Paulo and has millions of followers across different platforms, posts humorous content about Brazil and has watched as the number of foreigners producing content almost exclusively about Brazil soared.
“It’s a formula that’s getting a bit tired. I think it’s harder to succeed doing this than before,” he said.
In an increasingly multipolar world, many Brazilians believe that the country’s soft power is here to stay. But Pereira predicts that Brazil’s “mongrel complex” will resurface if the current attention from abroad fades. “Once people stop giving us those little pats on the head, it’ll all come back," she said.
