Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings.
Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally.
Springshot powered Spirit’s technology stack for the last three years, right up to the “very last flight,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. Yet his company got no notice when Spirit prepared to auction off a massive dataset that he thinks likely improperly includes a substantial amount of data and intellectual property (IP) that Springshot owns—not Spirit.
In a limited objection filed last month, Springshot argued that Spirit’s sale agreement does not make it clear what data is being sold. It only vaguely references categories of data that would possibly rope in Springshot data, including “productivity and collaboration data,” “core business systems and business application data,” and “workflow and process data.”
“This expansive definition does nothing to differentiate between Springshot’s intellectual property that exists within Spirit’s data repositories and systems, but Spirit does not own, and Spirit data that it actually owns and has the capacity to sell,” Springshot argued.
Springshot urged the court to pause Spirit’s data sale until a transparent forensic process establishes that none of the data Google is grabbing is actually owned by third parties.
If the bankruptcy court does not “pump the brakes,” it risks sanctioning an “unauthorized acquisition and use of trade secrets” that could doom startups, Springshot alleged. In an email to Ars, Springshot summarized its fears as the court possibly creating “a precedent where startups see massive amounts of IP transferred to the world’s richest and most monopolistic companies via bankruptcy courts.”
“Bankruptcy cannot become the new land grab for AI,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “The possession of IP is not ownership.”
Asked for comment, Google’s spokesperson declined to discuss mounting objections and repeated a prior statement provided to Ars that did not address any of the concerns raised.
“We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google’s spokesperson said. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset.”
Google may use Springshot data to make AI rival
It seems likely that a wide range of Spirit vendors could be in the same spot as Springshot, Kreuzkamp suspects, and his firm is not the only one complaining.
Citing Springshot’s concerns in a separate objection, the International Aero Engines LLC and the IAE International Aero Engines AG alleged that the dataset might also include its proprietary commercial information, technical data, and financial data. Both vendors cited confidentiality provisions in Spirit agreements that appear to have been completely ignored in the push to get the data sale approved.
Top concerns are that proprietary data could be transferred to Google without consent, giving firms no chance to guard against Google—or a third party later gaining access to the data—infringing ownership rights and exposing trade secrets. Both vendors said they risked irreparable harm through the sale to Google and then again through possible resales to future third parties.
For Springshot, it also seems possible that Google could use its valuable IP to create a rival product. In August, just a week before the controversial Spirit auction, Europe’s largest airline, Ryanair, announced a five-year partnership with Google. Under the deal, Ryanair will share operational data to improve Gemini Enterprise tools. That “is precisely the function Springshot served for Spirit,” the startup said in a footnote in its objection, while alleging that “Springshot’s data may be among the most AI-relevant assets to be purchased.” As Springshot argued:
“Should the sale proceed without such safeguards, and should Google obtain Springshot’s intellectual property and ingest that data, Springshot would forfeit the value of its technology it has spent 15 years developing. That existential threat is only amplified by the fact that Google has recently announced its desire to operationalize its own AI platform for airline operations, placing it in direct competition with Springshot.”
Adam Schwartz, a privacy litigation director for a digital rights nonprofit called the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Ars that allowing Google to buy this dataset via bankruptcy proceedings is unusual.
“This is the first time I am aware of so public a bankruptcy proceeding regarding whether a bankrupt company may sell off the personal data it has amassed as an asset in bankruptcy,” Schwartz said. “It is also the first time I am aware of a company seeking to sell its employees’ data (as opposed to its customers’ data) as an asset in bankruptcy.”
Kreuzkamp is worried that because bankruptcy courts have not deeply considered this issue before, the system is just not set up to protect vendors like his company. In the past, it was straightforward to determine who owned an asset. Consider how Spirit is selling airplanes, which bills of sale clearly demonstrate that it owns, he said. His experience suggests that when it comes to digital assets, courts don’t have the proper notice provisions that are necessary to ensure vendors can advocate for IP to be segregated from sales, should purchases like Google’s become the norm.
“Our main concern with everything is if you want startups to continue building, you need to protect what they built,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “If they spent 15 years building IP, that IP should not be misappropriated because their customer went bankrupt.”
Springshot and the IAE objectors both want the court to require Spirit to segregate any proprietary vendor data before approving the sale to Google. Springshot argued that it should include any data or information generated by its service or software, including data “likely commingled with much of Spirit’s own operational data (like its employees’ emails, chat histories, etc.).”
“To ensure Springshot’s intellectual property is not among the data acquired by Google (or any other potential buyer) a forensic process is necessary to first identify, and then segregate, Springshot’s intellectual property from that actually owned by Spirit,” Springshot argued.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that Springshot engaged with Spirit every day before it shut down.
“We were very tightly coupled with them, did a lot of great work helping that airline,” he said. “And so, I know there are tens of thousands of emails and documents that I’m sure are in their servers.”
Pilots warn of public harms from sale
If Spirit is forced to segregate a large chunk of data, the value of the dataset may substantially depreciate for Google. In its sale agreement, Google stipulated that Spirit ensure that “no portion of the Assets has been deleted, modified, or removed,” other than through planned processes like the deidentification of customers’ personal data and “de minimis” removals preserving privileged materials.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that prior to reading the Spirit-Google sale agreement, he assumed that if one of the companies he partnered with became insolvent, that either vendor data would be destroyed or that agreements would be honored to prevent transfers to third parties.
On September 16, there will be a hearing where the court will mull objections to the sale. Along with vendors, unions and groups representing many former Spirit employees have joined flight attendants who quickly opposed the sale out of fears that Google or a third party could possibly link them to scrubbed data.
Troublingly, the sale agreement only required de-identification of customer personal data, and former Spirit workers worried that Google’s AI system may combine confidential worker data in ways that may expose information that they might not want public. As groups representing machinists, aerospace workers, and transport workers noted, workers aren’t even aware of all the risks, since “the proposed sale raises novel technological and legal concerns on very short notice.” Seemingly, not even Spirit knows the “ultimate uses” to which the data “may be put after it is sold and processed through artificial intelligence,” they warned.
Schwartz told Ars that Spirit should have gotten consent from workers before selling 80,000 email accounts, 100 million emails, 20 million SharePoint documents, and 500 million Teams messages.
“My top concern is that data privacy is a fundamental human right, enjoyed for example by employees in relation to their employers,” Schwartz said. “This includes the norm that data collected from a person for one reason should not be used or disclosed for another reason without first getting their opt-in consent. Therefore, it is the Spirit Airline employees themselves who should be making the decision whether they want to bear the risk to their privacy of their emails being turned into AI training data.”
Some former workers are alarmed that the data sale could possibly harm the public.
Most ominously, the Air Line Pilots Association, International warned that if Google’s AI system re-identifies pilots in the data set, airways could become more dangerous.
Flight safety programs depend on pilots feeling comfortable sharing in-depth incident reports without fear that confidential information may become public, the Federal Aviation Administration has found. Therefore, any “disclosure of confidential flight operations data through the Sale Agreement can be expected to chill voluntary compliance by pilots across the industry as it becomes known that such data can be sold to third parties with no expertise or interest in aviation safety and presumably included in databases accessible by the public using artificial intelligence software,” the association warned.
Late Google rival vows to resolve objections
Last week, an AI training data lab, Micro1, put in a last-minute competing bid that it claims resolves all objections to the data sale. Outbidding Google by 25 percent, Micro1 offered $12.5 million in cash, while promising that if debtors pick Micro1 over Google, the bankruptcy proceedings can avoid any further delays.
However, Micro1’s plan notably includes de-identifying the data in-house, which Spirit debtors were opposed to in the auction process. Spirit even chose a lower second bid should the Google sale fall through because the de-identification was completed by independent third parties. It seems, then, that even if the late bid is considered, it’s less likely to tempt debtors. Additionally, Micro1’s claims to resolve all objections may be somewhat exaggerated. In Springshot’s case, Micro1 does not promise to segregate IP, trade secrets, or proprietary data. Instead, Micro1 only says that it will not use Springshot data to create a rival product or ever sell the data to a would-be rival.
Ars could not reach Micro1’s lawyers for comment, but the data lab said it plans to attend the upcoming hearing to entice debtors to take their offer.
Kreuzkamp told Ars that he appreciates that Micro1 acknowledges Springshot’s concerns, but his objective remains scrubbing Spirit’s dataset of any data that Springshot owns.
His company’s lawyers have been in contact with Spirit debtors’ legal team and plan to defend Springshot’s proprietary data at the upcoming hearing. They feel confident the court will take their concerns seriously. But there are no guarantees, as the bankruptcy court prepares to approve this unusual sale. Kreuzkamp said it remains unclear what process a bankrupt company like Spirit should be taking to “ensure that it extricates everything that is proprietary from a dataset.”
“I just think it’s a very complex issue when it comes to extricating the data that’s owned by somebody else,” Kreuzkamp said. However, now’s the time to do it, he suggested, since “once you throw data into an AI model, it’s impossible to trace what the model did with that.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Jalna (Maharashtra) [India], September 13 (ANI): Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange Patil on Sunday issued an eight-day ultimatum to the Maharashtra government, warning that he will launch an indefinite fast unto death at Mumbai's Azad Maidan on September 19 if the community's reservation demands are not fulfilled.
Speaking to ANI in Jalna, the activist asserted that the battle for Maratha reservation will now shift to the state capital if the administration fails to act within the stipulated timeframe.
"The government has eight days left. If the Maratha community's demands are not met within this period, I will sit on a fast unto death at Mumbai's Azad Maidan at 10 AM on September 19. Whatever happens next will take place in Mumbai. The government shows no regard for the issues faced by poor Marathas," Jarange Patil said.
The quota campaigner also alleged that the state machinery is actively intimidating his supporters and targeting his associates under the guise of legal inquiries.
"My close associates were being harassed under the pretext of investigations. Attempts are being made to exert pressure by issuing notices to those standing with him in the movement, but this will not halt the agitation," he stated.
Striking an uncompromising note, Jarange Patil declared that pressure tactics would not deter him from taking the stir forward.
"I will not surrender to the government out of fear of an investigation. If the time comes, I am ready to face death, but I will not kneel before the government," he affirmed.
Earlier, on September 4, a state government delegation met Patil on the sixth day of his indefinite hunger strike at Antarwali Sarati in Jalna district to appeal to him to call off his agitation, even as the activist remained firm on his demands.
The government delegation comprised Maharashtra Ministers Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil, Uday Samant, Makarand Aaba Patil, and BJP MLA Prasad Lad.
During the meeting, the ministers held detailed discussions with Jarange regarding various key demands of the Maratha community.
Addressing the media, Maharashtra Minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil said, "Efforts are being made to complete the process of making Kunbi records available to Gram Panchayats by September 5. Action will also be taken to issue certificates to the Maratha community based on the Hyderabad Gazette."
He further appealed to the public, saying, "Maratha community members in Marathwada should apply for certificates starting tomorrow. If any issues arise, individuals should apply directly to the respective District Collector. Nodal officers will be appointed in every district, and individuals can contact them in case of any problems."
The minister assured that official orders regarding OBC concessions would be issued soon. "Orders regarding OBC concessions will be issued on September 8," Vikhe Patil noted, adding that "the Shinde Committee has discovered 58 lakh Kunbi records so far, and the government is working on processing them."
He also announced that "a Maratha Reservation Cell will be set up, and 300 crore rupees will be allocated for the Annasaheb Patil Economic Development Corporation," reaffirming that "the government stands with the movement initiated by Manoj Jarange to bring justice to the Maratha community."
In a direct appeal to the activist, Vikhe Patil folded his hands and stated, "I request with folded hands to end the fast."
Concurring with the delegation's concerns, Maharashtra Minister Uday Samant and BJP MLA Prasad Lad emphasised that "Manoj Jarange should get admitted to a hospital for treatment and suspend his indefinite hunger strike due to deteriorating health."
However, Manoj Jarange remained steadfast, stating, "I will not end the indefinite hunger strike until demands are met." Setting a firm timeline, he insisted, "Fulfil all demands by September 11."
Outlining the next steps of the agitation, Jarange added, "If the government accepts all demands, the Maratha community will bring gulal to Mumbai. The date to head to Mumbai for the agitation will be announced during the meeting on September 12."
Reiterating his commitment, Jarange concluded, "This is my final agitation. If all demands are implemented, I will not need to protest again."
Despite lengthy deliberations and major assurances from the state representatives, the government delegation's attempt to persuade Jarange proved unsuccessful, and the team departed Antarwali Sarati as the activist firmly maintained his stance to continue the hunger strike until all demands are fully implemented. Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate’s Mar-a-Lago dinner with Donald Trump under spotlight
In short:
Earlier this year, Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate declared he had dinner with US President Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago.
The mayor told a Gold Coast radio show he and Mr Trump shared tomahawk steaks and "expensive wine".
But the ABC has uncovered conflicting recollections about the dinner.
Tom Tate, mayor of Australia's glitziest city the Gold Coast, was in the middle of expensive ratepayer-backed trip around the world, the icing of which would be dinner with US President Donald Trump.
"He knew who I was, and he came up and called me Mr Mayor," Mr Tate later recalled.
The February dinner, he said in interviews, had taken place at Mar-a-Lago, the president's famed Florida holiday retreat, following signing of a deal with a Queensland developer for a proposed Trump Tower on the Gold Coast.
They shared tomahawk steaks and "expensive wine". "Mate, I had dinner with him," Mr Tate told Triple M Gold radio about meeting the president.
But the ABC has uncovered conflicting recollections and questions about openness for the headline-making trip.
The White House has told the ABC that the US president and First Lady Melania Trump "did not have dinner with that group" including the mayor.
And an ABC right to information request for documents turned up next to no documents about a moment the mayor described as the Gold Coast getting a "guernsey to meet the leader of the free world".
World trip
The Gold Coast is Australia's sixth-biggest city, a tourism mecca of glamour and surf with a population swelling past 647,000.
Mr Tate, 67, is its controversial four-term mayor, selling the city with a message of being "open for business" and camera-friendly stunts such as wielding a golden sledgehammer.
He had been busy overseas throughout February. In cold Milan, he was clad in a white, pink and orange windproof jacket and a white Olympic beanie as he grasped the silver torch as an official Games torchbearer. He posted a picture on Instagram.
That day started jam-packed. An itinerary released under right to information laws shows Mr Tate, on the Brisbane 2032 Olympic committee, was instructed to wear neutral or white shoes, leave the hotel at 6:45am, not forget his identification, and start his 200m-torch walk at 10:13am.
Other days were similarly hectic. That included multiple meetings with infrastructure officials in Dubai, interspersed with lunch at the high-class Sexy Fish restaurant. Mr Tate posted on Instagram too there: the mayor meeting a Dubai official in traditional Arab robes; the mayor in a hard hat on a building site.
The council itinerary includes separate briefing packs, outlining who Mr Tate was meeting or details about their background. Even Mr Tate's meeting with the Dubai Future Foundation's boss recommended the mayor wear business attire.
It all contrasted with a dearth of information about what happened when Mr Tate, after Dubai, arrived in Florida and pulled into 20 acres of landscaped gardens that constitute the Mar-a-Lago Club, founded by Mr Trump in 1995.
Mr Tate said he was there for the signing of an ultimately doomed deal between the Trump Organization, run by Mr Trump's son Eric, and Queensland developer Altus to construct a Trump Tower on the Gold Coast. The plan was for a $1.5 billion deal for a 340-metre tall, six-star luxury complex on the beach at Surfers Paradise.
Altus was headed by David Young, a former bankrupt developer who had come back to construct housing near Rockhampton and successfully secured a long-sought deal with the Trump Organization. Mr Young posted online a photo shaking hands with Eric Trump in Florida that February.
The dinner
Yet all that is listed in council documents for the mayor's three days at Mar-a-Lago is a four-word entry for a Friday: "Meeting with Trump Organization".
Mr Tate would later tell media about the signing and then having dinner with the president. He talked of his wife marvelling at how beautiful the first lady was "in real life".
During a Triple M Gold radio interview (which started by playing the lyrics "Tom Tate, he's our mayor and he is great" to the tune of English pop band Madness's Our House), he twice noted dining with the president.
Triple M: Tom, so you have had, you had dinner with Donald?
Mayor: Yeah, yeah, and Eric [Trump] and Lara [Eric's wife].
He added: "We were drinking expensive wine and a couple of tomahawks."
The White House, asked about the dinner and Australians that night, told the ABC: "The President and the First Lady did not have dinner with that group."
Another perception of the dinner, which has been told to the ABC, is the two politicians did meet briefly, when the president came to where his son Eric and the Australians were sitting, but the US leader was seated at another table at Mar-a-Lago that evening.
Mr Tate had insisted he had flown to Florida following an "invitation" from the Trump Organization.
"I was there as mayor of the city. So that's the gift to the city," he told the ABC in an earlier interview.
No record of an invitation exists, according to the right to information search of Gold Coast council records. Mr Tate's office since said: "The invitation was issued verbally."
Mr Tate had also initially listed on his council register of interests that the Trump Organization had paid for his accommodation and meals, along with transfers.
It caused a stir, with questions about the mayor potentially having a conflict of interest with a Gold Coast Trump Tower proposal, which had attracted almost 100,000 petitioners objecting. Also, local Gold Coast media was hammering council about official overseas travel.
The invoice
But Mr Tate's office since changed the register declaration to say he had personally paid for the accommodation and transfers.
"My intention was always to personally fund any hospitality provided to me at Mar-a-Lago," he said in a statement.
"Pending receipt of the invoice, and in an abundance of caution, I disclosed the hospitality on my register of interests to ensure my disclosures remained consistent with my reporting obligations.
"Once the invoice was received, I promptly paid the amount personally and immediately updated my register."
He did declare receiving a red hat, along with the meals.
The mayor has declined to answer many questions, only issuing statements. He will not supply the Mar-a-Lago invoice, even after a right to information request from the ABC.
Mr Tate's office said the trip was "private".
The whole council trip was book-ended. Mr Tate had work events in Los Angeles in late February. Again, the council itinerary indicates Los Angeles was full of meetings, such as Mr Tate attending Amazon MGM Studios, which worked with Gold Coast-linked contractors.
Still, the ABC can reveal, in between Florida and Los Angeles, Mr Tate took a week-long private holiday, flying in and out of Barbados, allowed under council rules.
Flights involving Barbados were paid personally. Council records show the cost to ratepayers of flights from Australia to Italy and Dubai and Florida, and then to Los Angeles and home, was almost $33,000, the ABC can reveal. (He was entitled to a business class flight and paid personally to upgrade to first-class).
Mr Tate's office insisted that the Barbados side-trip was economical given his Los Angeles events.
"Doing so avoided the need for two separate trips to the United States and ensured no additional airfare costs were incurred by the city," it said.
The Gold Coast Trump Tower proposal fell over in less three months.

Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.
Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”
The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles which reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.
When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”
The news, first reported by Uganda Pulse news website, will undoubtedly be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multi-sport event for wounded service personnel.
At the time, Kiwanuka credited President Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our teams entry” adding their support “marks a new chapter for our service men and women.”
The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by head of the royal household , the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, and clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.
The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity,” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024, and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife Beyoncé so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

The Indian Motion Picture Producers’ Association (IMPPA) has issued a clarification regarding what it described as incorrect interpretations of a recent order passed by the Bombay High Court in connection with a dispute between Saffron Magicworks Private Limited (owned by Nikhil Dwivedi) and Andolan Films Private Limited (owned by Vikramaditya Motwane). IMPPA has also been impleaded in the proceedings.
IMPPA issues clarification over ‘incorrect’ interpretation of Bombay High Court order
According to the association, certain communications and news reports currently in circulation have presented an inaccurate understanding of the scope and effect of the High Court’s order. IMPPA stated that its involvement in the matter was limited to carrying out its institutional responsibilities under its Memorandum and Articles of Association.
The association explained that the dispute between Saffron Magicworks Private Limited and Andolan Films Private Limited had been placed before IMPPA’s Dispute Resolution Committee. Any determination or direction issued by the committee, it clarified, was related to the parties involved in the dispute and the specific issues that had been brought before it.
IMPPA further stressed that it has no independent commercial claim or interest in the underlying dispute between the two companies. The association also urged that the High Court’s order should be understood strictly on the basis of its express terms.
Addressing reports suggesting restrictions on its functioning, IMPPA clarified, “No blanket restraining order has been passed against IMPPA restraining the discharge of its institutional functions.” The association said that some reports presently being circulated do not accurately reflect the order’s scope or its implications for IMPPA.
IMPPA also stated that it does not accept any characterization of the court order that goes beyond what has been expressly stated by the High Court. The association maintained that it will continue to carry out its responsibilities in accordance with applicable law, its governing framework and the directions issued by the court.
The clarification comes amid reports and communications surrounding the legal dispute involving Saffron Magicworks and Andolan Films. Through its statement, IMPPA has sought to distinguish its institutional role from the commercial dispute between the two parties and clarify the extent of the court’s directions concerning the association.

An Israeli soldier shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupied West Bank.
Eyewitnesses said that a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.
Reached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.
“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”
Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.
“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”
Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.
The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man, apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.
Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.
The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.
On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.
Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.
After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.
It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.
Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.
East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.
On 4 September, two Palestinian teenagers were shot dead in al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.
The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.

The Bengaluru City Police have launched ‘Project Khushi’, a structured health and wellness programme aimed at supporting the long-term physical and mental well-being of police personnel, Home Minister Priyank Kharge said on Tuesday.
The programme will initially be implemented in the Electronics City police division, covering around 600 police personnel. Each batch will undergo a three-month programme comprising health check-ups, expert-led guidance sessions, and digital engagement activities.
The initiative will focus on preventive healthcare, nutrition, physical activity, quality sleep, and stress management, besides other lifestyle factors crucial for the long-term well-being of police personnel.
Pilot programme shows encouraging results
According to the Home Minister, an earlier pilot programme conducted as part of Project Khushi produced encouraging results. Around 61% of participants recorded a reduction in blood sugar levels, while 70% corrected Vitamin B12 deficiencies. In addition, 59% of participants reduced their body weight.
Mr. Kharge said that the results demonstrate that sustained and scientifically designed health interventions can have a positive impact on the well-being of police personnel.
Partnership with health and corporate organisations
“Our police personnel work every day in challenging and stressful conditions to ensure the safety of our communities. It is essential to pay continuous attention to their health. Healthy police personnel are the backbone of an effective and resilient policing system,” Mr Kharge said.
He added that equal importance must be given to mental well-being, a healthy lifestyle, and stress management, along with physical health.

A motorcyclist has died after hitting a pothole on the Western Highway in Victoria's south-west this afternoon.
Victoria Police said emergency services were called to the Western Highway in Trawalla after reports that a motorcycle had struck a pothole and lost control at around 12:50pm. 
The rider, a 71-year-old Ballarat man, died at the scene.
"The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are yet to be determined and will be investigated," a Victoria Police spokesperson said. 
All westbound lanes were closed on the Western Freeway between Windermere and Beaufort. 
It comes just days after a new report from Victoria's auditor-general found almost half of Victoria's road network is in poor condition and crumbling faster than the government can repair it.
Victoria Police has urged anyone with dashcam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

iOS 27 adds a native Custom EQ for compatible AirPods with an H2 chip or later. Go to AirPods settings > Audio and Routing > Equalizer > Custom, then adjust lows, mids, and highs to tune bass, vocals, and treble to your taste.
Apple has officially started rolling out iOS 27 for eligible devices, and it brings a lot of useful additions. If you are using any Apple audio product, iOS 27 gets a new native custom equalizer to fine-tune the music from your AirPods and other Apple audio products (requires Apple’s H2 chip; you can see full compatibility here).
In this guide, you will learn how to use the new custom EQ for your AirPods and other Apple devices.
Table of Contents
How to Use the New AirPods Custom EQ in iOS 27
The new native equalizer is only available in the latest iOS 27. If your iPhone is eligible for the latest iOS 27, you can go to General > Software Update and update to the latest iOS 27.
Custom EQ Supported Device List:
Custom EQ for Apple iOS 27 is only available for audio devices with an H2 chip or later. Here is the official compatibility list.
- AirPods Pro 2
- AirPods Pro 3
- AirPods 4
- AirPods Max 2
Now, if your device supports it, follow the steps below.
First, Update Your iPhone to the Latest iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down.
Step 3: Tap on General.
Step 4: Tap on Software Update.
Step 5: Tap on Update Now (if the update is available).
Please ensure that your iPhone is on the iOS 27 eligible device list.
Next, Update Your AirPods Firmware
Step 1: Connect your AirPods to your iPhone.
Step 2: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 3: Tap on your AirPods (you will see this option if your AirPods are connected to your device) and next go to Step 5.
Step 4: If you don’t see it, open Bluetooth.
Tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 5: Now, scroll down and tap on AirPods Beta Updates.
Step 6: Enable the option that says AirPods Beta Updates.
Ensure your iPhone is connected to the internet and your AirPods are connected to your iPhone. Your AirPods will automatically update to the latest software.
How to Use the Custom Equalizer on iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on your AirPods.
Or else, you can go to Bluetooth and tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on Audio and Routing.
Step 4: From here, scroll down and tap on Equalizer.
Step 5: Select the Custom option.
Step 6: Now you can adjust lows, mids, and highs based on your preference. You can move the slider to the top and bottom. The line above refers to high, and the line below refers to low.
1. Lows: Increase or decrease bass.
2. Mids: Meant for vocals, where you can increase or decrease the vocal presence, especially if the music has singer vocals.
3. Highs: Treble, which AirPods are mainly known for. You can adjust treble sound using high settings.
Step 7: If you want to reset, tap on the Reset option.
Step 8: If you don’t want custom controls, you can tap on “Recommended,” and it will use Apple’s default recommended sound signature.
Currently, the iOS 27 custom equalizer is very basic. Even though Apple has the best ecosystem, Apple only decided to give you basic controls to customize the sound output from your audio devices.
I know most people are fine with the default settings on the AirPods, but sometimes even I prefer more control over the music.
Adding custom equalizer settings natively on your iPhone eliminates the need to download third-party apps, which sometimes have compatibility issues. However, Apple’s basic equalizer still leaves room for third-party options. Apple also offers you the option to reset the changes you have made.
This is a good start. Hopefully, in iOS 28, Apple will bring more features to this custom equalizer to fine-tune the sound signature of the AirPods. Using EQ does bring a noticeable sound difference. If you don’t see this option or are facing any issues, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.
FAQs about iOS 27 AirPods Custom EQ
1. Does AirPods Custom EQ Work on iPad and Mac?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ is also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27
2. Can You Save Multiple Custom EQ Presets for AirPods?
As I said before, current EQ settings are basic. As of now, you can only have one custom EQ profile
3. Does Custom EQ Work With Spatial Audio and Adaptive Audio?
Yes, it works with spatial audio and adaptive audio, but those settings are different from custom EQ. Currently, custom EQ only allows you to adjust lows, highs, and mids.
4. Does Custom EQ Affect Calls and Videos or Only Music?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ applies to all media playing on your iPhone, including videos, music, TV shows, and much more.
5. Why Is the Custom EQ Option Missing on Supported AirPods?
If you don’t see the custom EQ option on your iPhone, make sure that you update to iOS 27. Custom EQ options are available for AirPods that have an H2 processor. At the time of writing this article, current supported models include AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

What Is the Good Life?
The philosophy professor Meghan Sullivan doesn’t just want to teach her students about virtue; she wants to make them better human beings.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
David Brooks: Hi, I’m David Brooks. If you are listening to or watching this, you’ve stumbled across the first episode of a new podcast called The Permanent Questions.
The idea of the podcast is that there are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life. How do you find your purpose? How do you confront death? How do you save a relationship that’s going through a rough patch? How do you build a just society?
Now, you may be asking yourself, “How the hell did a political pundit get into these deep waters?”
When I was 18, an incredibly lucky thing happened to me: The admissions officers at Columbia University, Wesleyan, and Brown decided I should go to the University of Chicago. I didn’t know anything about Chicago. I’d never visited. I never knew anybody who went there, but it was the only school I got into.
It turned out to be the perfect school for me. My favorite joke about Chicago: It’s a Baptist school where atheist professors teach Jewish students Saint Thomas Aquinas. And I fit right in.
There’s a saying, “If you catch fire with enthusiasm, people will come for miles to watch you burn.” My professors had caught fire with enthusiasm.
Those teachers were filled with a certain conviction. The conviction was, if you read important books, had important conversations, and addressed big questions, you would have the keys to the kingdom.
They gave us new things to love: new ideas, new heroes, new activities, new subjects. They tried to teach us how to see, not only to see with your preconceptions and the things you think you see, but to see with the clarity of a Tolstoy, the moral depth of George Eliot, the empathetic outrage of James Baldwin.
Mostly, they introduced us to the Great Conversation. The Great Conversation is a tradition of debate that goes back for thousands of years. It’s a collective attempt to find a workable balance between the inevitable tensions of life—the tension between autonomy and belonging, between freedom and order, between diversity and cohesion, safety and exploration, tenderness and strength, intellect and passion. The Great Conversation never ends, because there is no permanent solution to these tensions, just a temporary resting spot that works in this or that circumstance.
I never wanted to leave the Great Conversation, and I never have. I went off and became a journalist and a political pundit, and that was a worthwhile thing to do, and I still do it. A lot of the big questions in life are political questions. Who should lead us? What does a just society even look like? But none of my six books are about politics. They’re about the kind of questions my teachers asked me back in Chicago: How do you educate your emotions? How do you survive a setback?
As my career has gone on, I came to the conclusion that we as a society are over-politicized and under-moralized. That is to say, we pay attention to every little political scandal, but many people have been given no instruction on the basic questions of how to live, of how they should find their calling, what they should really want.
And over the last 15 years or so, this sensation has taken a deeper urgency. Like a lot of countries, America seems to be going through some sort of spiritual, relational, and social, and maybe moral crisis. You know all the stats: rising loneliness, rising despair, rising distrust, rising polarization.
We’re living through a period of great technological advance, but we’re losing our humanistic core. Because of technological improvements and social deterioration, our lives are objectively better, but subjectively worse. The elements of civilization that lift the spirit and nurture the affections are playing a smaller and smaller role in our national life. Religion, literature, art, theology, history, philosophy, friendship, even conversation.
In previous periods of technological advance, there was a humanistic counterreaction. Humanists said, “Okay, bring us your science. Bring us your machines. Bring us your efficiency. Bring us your technology. That’s fine. But don’t turn us into machines ourselves.” And the humanists made an aggressive counter-push to say, “We will preserve our humanistic core. We will preserve what is essentially human. ”
This podcast is an attempt to be a small part of that kind of humanistic reaction.
We asked Meghan Sullivan to be the first guest on the show because she’s the kind of great teacher I’m talking about. Meghan teaches one of the most beloved courses at Notre Dame University, which is called “God and the Good Life.” She’s won Notre Dame’s Joyce Award for Excellence in Teaching, and as you’ll see, she’s got a dynamic personality. She co-authored a book based on the course, called The Good Life Method: Reasoning Through the Big Questions of Happiness, Faith, and Meaning.
Meghan doesn’t just do education, providing students with facts they can regurgitate on a test. Meghan does formation. She helps students become better versions of themselves. And so it’s a great pleasure to welcome Meghan Sullivan to this table.
Brooks: Welcome, Meghan Sullivan. You are the first guest on The Permanent Questions. You are the founding figure of our podcast. So thank you for being here.
Meghan Sullivan: Heavy is the crown. This is a tremendous responsibility, David.
Brooks: I know. All future guests will be measured by your exemplary example.
Sullivan: Exactly. I’m hopefully gonna create a large ceiling for this podcast.
Brooks: So, you grew up in North Carolina, and I assume you had a moderately normal childhood. And then you became a philosopher. So how the hell did that happen?
Sullivan: I did not grow up in an academic family. My mom was a receptionist in a dental office, and my dad worked a bunch of different jobs, but for most of high school he worked at this company called Replacements. They basically replaced, like, broken plates. My dad was in the plate-replacement business. My mom was in the dental-billing business. So that was not particularly academic background, but very, very loving. And if you would’ve told me when I was a high-school student that I would end up a philosophy professor, I would have asked you to throw me off a bridge.
Most of my students have never met a professional philosopher before they take my class. But in high school, actually, one of my best friends, her dad was a philosophy professor at our local university, and we were very, very judgy, snotty teenage girls, and we devoted probably two years of high school to thinking, “We cannot understand this guy’s job.”
So in high school, I had a well-considered, extremely negative opinion of the profession of philosophy that was based on nothing but vibes about my friend’s dad’s books.
I got a scholarship and went to the University of Virginia, so this big public school where, as a freshman, you’re just sort of fed into the meat grinder. You just get whatever classes are left over after all of the big kids register for their classes. And my academic adviser was talking to me, and I was so stressed because I couldn’t get any of the pre-law classes that I desperately wanted, or econ classes. And he’s like, “I think that you would really love this ethics class called ‘Issues of Life and Death’ in the philosophy department. It’s really debate-y, and I just think given your background, you’re gonna have a blast in there. ”
So I was like, “Okay, fine. Philosophy. ” And I enrolled in that class, and I was hooked by the second week. The exact moment—I remember this really vividly—I was sitting in Alderman Library, in the library at UVA, and we’d just gotten our first assignment for all of our classes, our first writing assignment, and I was writing all these boring book reports for my other classes.
In “Issues of Life and Death,” the question we were assigned is: “Should you end your life?” And I remember talking to the TA being like, “Do you want me to write about what, you know, David Hume says about suicide?” And he’s like, “Absolutely not. I want the strongest possible argument about whether you should continue living.”
And I was like, “Are you allowed to ask me that? Like, is that allowed?” And he’s like, “Not only is it allowed, but there are better and worse answers, and if you don’t have a really tight, really well-argued position, you’re gonna get a bad grade in this class.” And I just remember sitting in the library, the kind of blinking cursor on Microsoft Word staring at me, thinking, Ah, we’re firing live ammunition here. Like, this is real. And that just totally got me hooked.
Brooks: Now, a lot of philosophers write abstruse academic articles with a lot of notations and numbers and diagrams. You actually teach this class, and you’ve written this book, on how to live. Why’d you become that kind of philosopher?
Sullivan: I had an epiphany my third year at Notre Dame. I was getting ready to go up for tenure, and I’d been teaching our big intro philosophy class. And when you go through the tenure process, at first, you’re only focused on keeping your job, and then you start to hit a point where you imagine a future where you’re just a professor and you’re not worried about getting fired all the time. And I was in that kind of mindset of thinking, What do I wanna do with the rest of my career after I hopefully survive this tenure vote?
And I felt very, very strongly that I wanted to focus the next chapter on my teaching. That’s what really I loved about my job. And I’d been teaching Aristotle. And we inflict Aristotle on every single freshman at the University of Notre Dame. And Aristotle has this line in the second chapter of his book about the good life that I’ve always loved, and I always assign students to write essays about.
He says, “We conduct this examination not so that we can know what virtue is, but so that we might be good.” We do all this not so we can know what dead people said about virtue and philosophy, but so that we can become happier people. Otherwise, there’s no benefit of it, he says. This whole enterprise is pointless if it doesn’t find some way to make us better.
Brooks: Now, you’re in the business of helping people become, as you said, happy and good. And this podcast is in the same business. I’m joining your team.
Sullivan: Yeah, all right.
Brooks: And so, as we enter this conversation, I thought I’d raise some objections to the life we have chosen.
Sullivan: Bring it. Objections are the love language of philosophy.
Brooks: So the first one is what’s—why is this necessary? I get up in the morning; I have my Frappuccino; I surf my media feed; I go to work, which is good, I like my work; I go home; I watch Netflix. Why should I read a bunch of complicated books and have hard conversations?
Sullivan: So one assumption I think we should challenge is that there are some people who do philosophy, a small number of people, like my friend’s dad, and then everybody else doesn’t do philosophy.
That’s like saying there are some people who exercise, and everybody else doesn’t exercise. I get why you’d make that assumption if you think that exercise or philosophy is this really, really narrow prescribed activity. But that’s just not true.

Go think about, instead, the ways that you can use your time to earn to give under this capitalist system.
And it’s a kind of radical idea, but also one that has a really logical deductive argument that gets you to that conclusion. Now it’s just taken as ethics in certain quarters, especially in the tech industry. Some of my colleagues in the econ department would say this just is ethics, doing a really rigorous cost-benefit analysis and opting for the option within your control that’s going to have the greatest possible impact.
I vehemently reject this worldview. And Aristotle and the philosophers from this virtue ethics tradition of the last 2,500 years that I deeply admire, they have considered this idea, and they have also vehemently rejected it. So you might ask: What’s wrong with trying to save people’s lives? What’s wrong with trying to use reason and skill to have the greatest impact in the world?
Well, one of the points that you made in your essay about this Princeton class that I thought was spot-on is: There is this foundational question about what a human being is. Is a human just a mechanism for redistribution in a society? So are you just an earner, somebody who receives money and then spits it out towards, hopefully, the best causes? Or do you have a rich inner life? Do you have a telos? Do you have a purpose that has to be cultivated and tended?
If you believe the latter, then you’re gonna have some serious questions about this effective-altruist strategy. One: What happens to you if you leave college and you go work in that high-frequency trading firm, and you’re around people that all day long only talk about making money? Like, what is that gonna do to the type of character you have, the type of person that you believe yourself to be? Maybe the first year you’re gonna be pretty tough. You’re gonna be living in your cheap apartment, you’re gonna be writing your checks to fighting malaria, and you’re gonna be able to tough it out.
But over time, you are gonna come to worship money. Because you’re gonna be thinking about it 24/7 all day at your job. And every minute that you’re not working, you’re gonna be thinking about what your money could be spent on curing out in the world. Money is going to be the sole focus of your life, and that is unethical. You have made yourself into something that’s less than what a human is called to be.
I think that’s gonna be one of the big tensions. Another big tension with effective altruism as a movement is, I think I would’ve been—I was more sympathetic with the movement maybe 10, 15 years ago, when the focus was on immediately relieving extreme suffering because of preventable diseases.
Like, they used to tell you, “Go earn a lot of money, and then use it to buy bed nets to stop kids from getting malaria tomorrow. ” So, all right, I can kinda feel the urgency of that. But this calculative system says you must devote your life to whatever is going to have the greatest possible causal impact. And one of the shifts that they’ve made in the last 10 years is realizing those kids with malaria, they’re a pretty good investment, but actually, right now, your dollars would be better spent building really well-aligned artificial intelligence that’s gonna help people 100 years from now in vastly greater numbers flourish much better than any human being could right now.
