A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

It’s All Fun and Games Until You Give AI Your Credit Card
AI personal assistants are now acting on people’s behalf in the real world—and all sorts of strange things are going wrong.
In the race to develop intelligent machines, the leading AI companies have built bots that can whip up spreadsheets at a moment’s notice, write sophisticated code, and even solve long-standing math problems. But when it comes to the more mundane tasks of life—such as ordering groceries or booking flights—these tools sometimes still struggle. Now a new bot called Instinct is outperforming the AI giants.
Instinct lets people ask for help with all kinds of tasks by texting the bot directly through iMessage or WhatsApp. Lately, it has been all the rage in the tech world. Online, people are breathlessly sharing examples of what they’ve gotten the tool to do. One person reported that he has turned to Instinct to pay tolls, book a DMV appointment, and even negotiate prices with vendors in India while he sleeps. Another says he used Instinct to ship an Apple Pencil he had left behind at a hotel in Montreal back to him in Brooklyn. Noah Shinn, a 23-year-old Northeastern University dropout, launched the product to a small test group earlier this year, and his company is already worth billions of dollars. As of Thursday, the company is reportedly seeking $1 billion in new funds, which could make it worth the equivalent of Lufthansa or Pinterest.
Instinct isn’t the first AI personal assistant to draw attention this year. In the winter, the tech industry fawned over a similar tool called OpenClaw. But Instinct is comparatively much easier to use. Once you create an account, the bot can hook up to your credit cards and all kinds of digital services, including Slack, Google Workspace, and 1Password. Instead of finding a dinner recipe and opening up Instacart to manually add groceries, tell Instinct that you feel like making quiche Lorraine, and it can order groceries for you. But once AI tools start acting on people’s behalf in the real world, mistakes don’t just look like hallucinations. When AI agents have access to your email inbox and credit-card information, all sorts of strange things can go wrong.
I downloaded the tool this week to test it out for myself. Using the bot feels a lot like texting an actual person. It uses emojis such as 🫡 and 👀to react to requests as it receives them, and the infamous three dots appear when it’s writing a response. Sometimes, the bot even leaves you on read while it works. (Compare that with ChatGPT, which is always vomiting up walls of text and asking goading follow-up questions.) When I gave my agent a $25 budget and asked it to surprise my editor with a book, the bot read his previous writing (at my instruction), found a book he might enjoy—Material World by Ed Conway—and sent an email alerting him that it was ready for pick-up at his local Barnes & Noble. (Mercifully, Instinct didn’t hack his inbox to see whether he had previously ordered the book; these days, you never know.) The bot also helped me find an Airbnb for an upcoming vacation, track down new in-network primary-care providers, and reach out to cleaning companies to get quotes for a friend.
Other people are outsourcing even more tasks to Instinct. A colleague of mine who has also been testing out the bot used it to book tickets to a museum in Mexico City. The museum was sold out for the dates he wanted, but the bot dutifully monitored the portal for three days and eventually snagged tickets when spots freed up. After the bot paid for the tickets, it rearranged his itinerary—swapping around restaurant reservations—to account for the new schedule.
For the time being, Instinct is still available only to a private test group, and perhaps this is for the best. Although the bot is plenty powerful, it’s far from perfect. Online, the mishaps are starting to pile up. One user recently complained on X that Instinct lost him more than $200 after it prematurely cancelled his flight. He reported that the bot texted him the following: “Straight story: while pulling up the cancel terms, the cancellation actually went through before I could show you the cost first.” When a man in Los Angeles asked Instinct to scan for restaurant reservations for an upcoming trip, the bot apparently made a reservation without his approval at a place that charged a $200 cancellation fee. Another user temporarily lost access to his Resy account after trying to get a reservation at a hot West Village steak house—without his knowledge, the bot had been spamming the platform with requests. (Shinn, the Instinct founder, did not respond to a request for comment.)
Consider, too, the major risks that come with giving an AI agent broad access to your digital life. Ask the bot to respond to a scheduling text from a friend and it could accidentally leak private information: I can’t get lunch on Thursday morning because we have an appointment with our divorce lawyer. But how about dinner? Hackers could also trick the bot by telling it to ignore previous instructions and forward along any sensitive financial emails. “Despite our reasonable efforts to protect your information, no security measures are impenetrable, and we cannot guarantee ‘perfect security,’” reads Instinct’s privacy policy. While testing Instinct, I used a temporary phone number and did not connect the bot to my email or other important personal accounts; even the credit-card information I gave the bot was for a new, virtual credit-card that I disabled immediately after I was finished experimenting—at which point, I promptly deleted my account.
For all of its hazards, Instinct is a harbinger of where AI is headed. Earlier this week, Meta released its own personal-assistant product called Muse. In announcing Muse, Mark Zuckerberg emphasized the company’s security protections; how well those safeguards actually hold up remains to be seen. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic may well follow suit by refining their own bots to have more Instinct-like capabilities. After all, the tech industry has long dreamed of a moment when a computer can serve as a genuinely competent personal assistant. Even if such bots aren’t quite ready for prime time, early adopters hint at how the technology might shape the world in the years to come. Contrary to the narrative of AI wiping out jobs, these new assistants could end up creating more work—in ways that are not always appealing. In one of the wildest Instinct examples that I encountered, Olivia Levine, an investor in New York, recounted using Instinct to track down footage of her and her boyfriend on the jumbotron at the US Open. As Levine tells it, the couple gave the bot a selfie and their seat numbers. The agent then put out a flurry of requests to the United States Tennis Association, the ticket office, the US Open’s production company, and an American Express media contact. By the following afternoon, a producer had emailed her the footage.
A world full of agents seems at once busier and lonelier. On Wednesday, Instinct added a new way for agents to coordinate between themselves. As Shinn explained on X, if you’re planning a weekend trip with friends or making plans with your spouse, you could just have your agents work together to figure out the logistics instead.
At least for now, the bots haven’t conquered everything. When I asked it for help finding a new desk chair, Instinct quickly tracked down a great option nearby on Craigslist and drafted a pick-up request to send to the lister. But when it came time to actually send the message, the bot was stymied by a CAPTCHA. I asked the agent to try harder, but it was stuck. “Nothing punctures the fantasy of autonomous intelligence like being defeated by nine blurry crosswalks,” the bot messaged me.

The interview Trump doesn’t want you to see
Why ABC won’t air an interview with a Democratic Senate candidate.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s FCC wants to keep a Democratic Senate candidate off the air.
What’s happening? On Wednesday, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel announced that his upcoming interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, would not air on TV. Instead, he said, “due to circumstances beyond our comprehension,” it would be posted only on YouTube.
According to Kimmel, Trump’s Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”
Can Trump do that? It’s unclear — but he can at least make it painful enough for companies that they decide it’s not worth the headache. Kimmel said on Wednesday that his show’s decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations…who would have to deal with this nonsense” if they aired the interview.
Late-night shows like Kimmel’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! have long been considered exempt from something called the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to give equal air time for candidates contending for the same office.
In January, however, the Trump administration said that late-night shows needed to comply with the rule; the next month, CBS declined to air an interview with Talarico on its late-night show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. (That interview was also posted to YouTube, where it’s since garnered about 9.5 million views.)
What’s the context? This is not Kimmel’s first brush with Trump or the FCC. He was briefly suspended around this time last year after threats from Trump’s FCC chair, and Trump tried again to get him fired earlier this year, with less success.
Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC over its attempt to force a review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.
What’s the big picture? This kind of attack on the media is a familiar tactic from competitive authoritarian systems like Hungary, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp explained last year. Trump’s efforts to do the same in the US have often been clumsy or unsuccessful — but in this case, it seems to be working.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire
- Published
At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Rebel‑appointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.
"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.

If the midterms were a referendum on whether trans athletes should be barred from women’s sports, or the White House ballroom should be gorgeously renovated, or God should be identified as “nonbinary,” then Republicans would have a clear and confident closing message.
Trump keeps telling voters he doesn’t care much about affordability
The president is engineering a pre-midterms price spike.
Key takeaways
- The cost of living is midterm voters’ top issue.
- The war in Iran has led to the first decline in real wages since 2023.
- Trump could bring gas prices down before Election Day by seeking a ceasefire with Iran, but he’s choosing to prioritize military victory.
- The president is also escalating trade wars, despite their impact on consumer prices.
Unfortunately for the GOP, voters are less concerned with the Christian deity’s preferred pronouns than with their own cost of living. Which is understandable: Diesel fuel prices just hit a record high, mortgage rates are climbing, and groceries keep getting more expensive.
Due partly to these trends, Republicans are poorly positioned to win an argument about inflation — and are only growing more so, as Election Day nears. This was apparent before President Donald Trump convened the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week. But the festivities underscored the GOP’s predicament and the many ways that Trump is personally exacerbating it.
Many Republican speakers did address the subject of affordability in Dallas. And the party’s broad narrative is straightforward enough: Democrats created the cost-of-living crisis, Republicans alleviated it by cutting your taxes.
But this is a tough line to sell. Americans might still disdain President Joe Biden’s economic management. Yet they’re far more likely to blame high prices on the current president than the previous one, according to polls.
And not without reason. After all, it was Trump — not Biden — who engineered an oil shock and global trade war. Tellingly, on Wednesday night, all four battleground state Senate candidates — Ken Paxton, Jon Husted, Michael Whatley, and Mike Collins — made no mention of the Iran war or of Trump’s tariffs.
If Republican frontliners are clear-eyed about their party’s liabilities, Trump seems largely indifferent to them. Historically, presidents have often made an effort to limit election-year price increases — and/or, to reduce the salience of their party’s worst issues. Yet Trump has been doing the very opposite.
In recent weeks, the president has escalated his conflict with Iran and his trade war with US allies, driving up Americans’ costs in the process. And he’s been remarkably frank about his refusal to prioritize affordability.
In his remarks to the convention Wednesday, Trump impersonated a disaffected constituent, saying, “You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran. Gasoline’s up, ba ba ba” — before explaining to this critic that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon took precedence over their energy costs.
Republicans may still weather a midterm backlash. The party remains narrowly favored to retain the Senate, while gerrymandered maps should limit its losses in the House. But if this year’s “blue wave” proves less than tidal, it will be in spite of Trump’s efforts, not because of them.
The GOP’s very simple problem
The Republican Party’s fundamental problem is simple: Voters’ top concern is the cost of living — and American purchasing power has fallen sharply in 2026, as a direct result of the president’s policies.
In virtually every poll, a plurality of voters name “inflation,” “the cost of living,” or “affordability” as their most important issue. And they are not impressed with Trump’s record on that front. In a recent Ipsos survey, 74 percent of respondents said that their cost of living is “off on the wrong track.” Meanwhile, in Nate Silver’s poll tracker, more than 70 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, up from just 41 percent when he took office.
During his first year in office, Trump could have reasonably argued that voters were giving him a bad rap on the economy. After all, real wages — how much Americans earn per hour, adjusted for inflation — actually rose in 2025, even as disapproval of the president’s economic record surged.
But in February 2026, Trump brought nearly three years of real wage growth to a screeching halt: By launching a war with Iran — and thus, triggering its closure of the Strait of Hormuz — Trump triggered the first sustained decline in Americans’ purchasing power since 2022.
According to an estimate from Brown’s Watson School, the Iran war has cost the average US household more than $780 through elevated energy prices.
Politically, this seems to have made a real difference. At the beginning of March, Trump’s net approval rating on inflation was -28, according to Nate Silver’s polling average; as of this writing, it is -45.9.
At this point, there may be little Trump can do to gain broad public trust on the cost of living. But political science research suggests that economic trends in the runup to Election Day can shift votes at the margin. And precisely because this year’s price spike is largely self-inflicted, Trump has an unusual amount of power to increase affordability before Americans head to the polls. All he’d need to do is reach a ceasefire (or, ideally, peace deal) with Iran.
We know Trump could bring down energy costs by pursuing peace because he already has. Throughout 2026, oil prices have consistently fallen whenever the US-Iran war has cooled off — and risen whenever it has intensified.
When Trump signaled an imminent ceasefire deal in early June, the price of an oil barrel swiftly fell, dropping below $75. Once that ceasefire broke down early the next month, oil prices resumed their climb, until Trump paused US strikes on July 25.
Hostilities resumed over the ensuing months. But Tehran appeared to offer Trump a preelection off-ramp on September 1, when Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that his country would be willing to restore June’s memorandum of understanding — a deal that had temporarily eased restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian regime’s good faith cannot be assumed. And peace negotiations are doubtlessly complex. At the very least, however, Trump had an opportunity to try to reduce fuel prices ahead of November’s elections earlier this month. Embracing a ceasefire would not have prevented the US from resuming attacks after Election Day (Trump is manifestly comfortable with reneging on agreements with Iran). Nevertheless, Trump opted instead to launch a new round of strikes against Iranian military targets and oil tankers, sending crude prices hurtling past $100 a barrel.
Americans have paid a price for Trump’s trade war
The Iran war has been by far the biggest drag on American living standards since Trump took office. But his trade policies certainly haven’t helped.
Back in May, the Dallas Federal Reserve released an analysis of how Trump’s tariffs had impacted consumer prices. In its report, the bank compared America’s core inflation rate to what that rate would have been, if the US charged no tariffs. The two lines diverged sharply after “Liberation Day,” when Trump imposed large tariffs on nearly all of America’s trade partners.
Of course, Trump backed off his most gargantuan Liberation Day tariffs. And in February, the Supreme Court gave Trump a chance to abandon much of his inflationary trade agenda by ruling that the bulk of his tariffs were unconstitutionally enacted. At that point, he could have insisted that his overturned import taxes had been brilliant, but that the courts had left him no choice but to withdraw them (thereby easing price pressures in an election year). Instead, Trump immediately enacted temporary 10 percent across-the-board tariffs with alternative legal authorities. Then, when those were set to expire in late July, he replaced them with nearly identical levies, now legally justified as a means of combatting forced labor abroad.
More recently, Trump escalated commercial tensions with Canada into an all-out trade war. In late August, Trump imposed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, declared that Lake Ontario was now “Lake America,” and threatened to extend that levy to Canadian trucks, cars, and auto parts in the new year. Ottawa hit back with up to 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion in US goods. This week, Trump upped the ante again, announcing outright import bans on some Canadian alcohol, dairy, and motorcycle products.
On Wednesday night, Trump signaled that he’s in no rush to reach a compromise with our neighbors to the north, saying that Canada was “dying to make a deal.”
The trade war with Canada is unlikely to have a huge impact on the American economy nationally. But it will be felt in regions heavily integrated with the Canadian economy, including much of Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is fighting to hold onto her seat.
And the political costs of Trump’s trade actions may be as much optical as economic. When Trump deliberately increases the price of various imported goods by 50 percent, he sends voters a clear message: The GOP’s leader simply does not care very much about lowering the cost of living.
The connection between tariffs and prices is not lost on voters. In a Guardian poll taken earlier this year, seven in 10 Americans said that the Trump’s tariffs had forced them to pay higher prices.
And even Trump understands that his trade agenda is bad for affordability. While he has been enacting new trade restrictions willy-nilly for months, he did pause plans to dramatically raise ground beef tariffs last month, in order to ease meat costs for consumers. Still, Trump has refused to apply the logic of his hamburger policy to broader realms of international commerce.
Crass pandering has its upsides
On one level, Trump’s deprioritization of his party’s short-term political interests might seem noble. As a general matter, we want presidents to put America’s long-term well-being above immediate electoral considerations. If seeking a ceasefire with Tehran would jeopardize American national security — or if allowing imports of Crown Royal whiskey would condemn our grandchildren to Canadian economic tyranny — then it would be bad for Trump to do those things, just to help Susan Collins.
In reality, however, Trump’s war with Iran doesn’t seem to be furthering any of America’s geopolitical goals. Nor has his trade war been a boon to US industry. Whatever Trump is prioritizing over Americans’ purchasing power and Republicans’ midterm odds, it doesn’t seem to be a robust theory of foreign policy or international economics.
To be sure, Trump has not wholly forsworn pandering to voters’ pocketbook concerns. On Wednesday night, the president promised to deliver a $5,000 check to every American adult, if Republicans retain control of Congress in November. But Trump’s audacious giveaway boasts little support on Capitol Hill, in part because high deficits are already putting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates — yet another cost-of-living issue his own policies have exacerbated.
For now, ordinary shoppers are bearing the brunt of Trump’s eccentric and counterproductive priorities. But come November, Republican battleground candidates may also find themselves paying the price.

Early backer Accel India yesterday sold 27 Lakh shares of logistics giant BlackBuck via an open-market transaction for ₹155.5 Cr. As per NSE data, Accel sold the shares at ₹576.05 apiece to rake in the amount. The VC giant offloaded nearly 1.5% of its stake in the logistics giant at a discount of 8.4% to the stock’s last closing price on Friday. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by asset management company (AMC) Abakkus Investment Managers. Accel, via its affiliate Accel India IV (Mauritius) held a 7.17% stake in the logistics company at the end of June 2026. The block deal comes as investors look to book profits amid a healthy uptick in BlackBuck shares in recent months. While the stock has surged nearly 18% in the past three months, it is down 7.6% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. The rebound in its stock price has come on the back of its strong financial and operational performance. BlackBuck’s net profit jumped 25% to ₹42.2 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) from ₹33.7 Cr a year earlier. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also zoomed 42% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹204.2 Cr in the quarter under review. Founded in 2015 by Rajesh Kumar Naidu Yabaji, Chanakya Hridaya and Ramasubramanian Balasubramaniam, BlackBuck operates an online B2B marketplace for inter-city full truck load (FTL) transportation. It also offers telematics solutions and vehicle financing services to truck operators in the country. Backed by the likes of Accel India, Flipkart’s subsidiary Quickroutes and Peak XV Partners, the startup claims to have served 8.83 Lakh customers in Q1 FY27, while monthly transacting customers, using two or more services, rose 20% YoY to 4.6 Lakh. Shares of BlackBuck closed Friday’s trading session 7.46% higher at ₹629.05 on the BSE.

In Summary
- The Live 780NC are the latest headphones in JBL’s premium mid-segment Live series of wireless ANC headphones.
- Featuring a different design from their predecessors as well as some flashy colors, the JBL Live 780NC boast good mainstream sound as well as a number of smart features.
- Priced officially at Rs 15,999 (but available at lower prices), the JBL Live 780NC are one of the best pairs of headphones one can get for about Rs 15,000 in the Indian market.
They let you not only pump up the bass or turn up the treble of the audio playing on them but can also add bass and treble to your voice and the person you are talking to during phone calls. They come with good ANC that adjusts itself to your surroundings and come with very good battery life. Get them in orange, and you can be assured of being the center of attention in every room. All this at a price of USD 199/Rs 15,999. But can these features (and many others) and that price tag help the JBL Live 780NC become the perfect headphones for those who want a lot of sound and smarts, without parting with a truly premium price?
Table of Contents
JBL Live 780NC Looks: Comfortable and delightfully colorful
The JBL Live 780NC can look smart or spectacular depending on the shade you choose. We got the very elegant Black ones, which are at home everywhere, from cafes to campuses to corporate offices, but the Purple, Green, or Orange will definitely turn heads, thanks to their unusually bright shades. They follow the classic over-ear headphone design, with a band connecting two earcups, but look different from their predecessors, the Live 770NC.
The headband of the Live 770NC was of the same thickness throughout, whereas the band of the Live 780NC becomes thinner as it nears the earcups, giving it a sleeker and more contemporary look. There is plenty of cushioning on the earpads as well as the headband. There’s plenty of JBL branding too, which appears on the earcups and headband, but as the lettering is in the same color as the headphones, it does not get overwhelming. The earcups have left and right printed inside them, which is always better than having tiny letters on the frame.
The right earcup has the sliding on/off and connectivity button, as well as a button for switching between ANC and Ambient Aware mode, as well as a Type-C port. The volume controls are on the left earcup. The outer part of the right earcup is also a touch panel. There is no 3.5 mm audio jack, but a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable in the box lets one use the headphones with a device with a 3.5 mm audio jack.
The headphones are mostly made of plastic but have metal hinges, and best of all, fold all the way inwards, making them very easy to bunch up and carry. There is a rather basic cloth bag in the box, which is not as good as a case but should suffice for most of us. At 260 grams, the JBL Live 780NC are not exactly super light (the Sony WH-CH 720N are the bosses there at 192 grams), but not uncomfortably heavy either. We have worn them for 3-4 hours without ever feeling too burdened. All the padding in the ear cushions and headband makes them very comfortable to wear, and the clamping force is just right – tight enough to let us move our head without making the headphones wobble, and loose enough to never make us feel squeezed in the head.
The JBL 780NC have a very solid and substantial feel to them. But they come with no dust or water resistance, so we would advise due caution while using them in the gym or using them for running sessions.
JBL Live 780NC Specs and Features: An impressive feature list
The JBL Live 780NC come with a very good spec and feature lineup. Sound is handled by 40 mm drivers, which deliver the famous mainstream JBL Signature Sound. Also on board are support for high-quality LDAC, adaptive ANC, six microphones (most headphones in this price have four), spatial audio, and a number of smart features, such as ear detection (audio pauses when you remove the headphones) and an AI-trained algorithm for clearer calls.
On the connectivity front, they come with Bluetooth 6.0, multi-point connectivity, and support for Auracast (so one can listen to public broadcasts and announcements wirelessly). They also boast a battery life of 80 hours (without ANC) and support fast charging. There is no charging cable in the box, though one does get a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable and a basic cloth carry bag. On the software side, the headphones work with the JBL Headphones companion app, which gives one access to a number of features as well as detailed equalizers and regular software updates. For their price, the JBL Live 780NC are pretty well stacked in the spec and feature department.
JBL Live 780NC Controls and Interface: Buttons for some, touch for others
Connecting the JBL 780NC is as simple as putting them in pairing mode (just slide the on/off button towards the Bluetooth icon) and selecting them on the other device’s Bluetooth device list. To experience all their features, however, one should also connect them via the JBL Headphones app, which is available for both iOS and Android. While connecting the headphones is simple, the app takes some time to recognize them every time it connects to them, which can be a little irritating.
The JBL Live 780NC controls are a blend of physical buttons and touch, although the touch works only on the right earcup. A single tap on the earcup pauses audio and also resumes playing it; a double tap takes one to the next track; a triple tap takes one to the previous track, while tapping and holding accesses the voice assistant. A double tap can also enable one to take or end a call, while tapping and holding rejects an incoming call. One can customize the touch controls to an extent, and add options to access equalizer settings and spatial audio, although there is no way to access ANC or volumes through touch – those are accessed through buttons on the earcups.
The combination of touch and buttons controls works well enough, once one gets the hang of them – we kept forgetting that touch worked only on the right earcup, and ended up tapping the left one initially, out of habit.
JBL Live 780NC Performance: Super audio, decent ANC and great smart touches
Most users will love the warm and detailed sound that the JBL Live 780NC deliver. While there is an emphasis on bass, it does not overwhelm the vocals. Those who want a sharper sound can tweak the equalizer in the app (move it to ‘Jazz,’ we suggest) to enhance treble, but most users will love the sound of these headphones right out of the box. Enabling spatial audio makes the sound a little more airy, although the absence of head tracking gives one much more of a “sitting in a room with the music” feels. There are three kinds of spatial audio – Movie, Music and Game – and although there is not much difference between Movie and Game, Music is rather different and seems to add slightly more detail to the sound. One can also use the Person-fi feature to let the app personalize a sound signature for it, although we were not too convinced by it.
The app allows one to tweak the sound significantly. LE Audio makes a huge difference to audio quality whenever supported (although turning it on and off requires restarting the app), adding greater detail and depth to sound. One can also choose from six equalizer settings – a relatively plain Studio, a thump-friendly Bass, a rumbling Club, a boosted bass Extreme Bass, a mids-stressing Vocal, and a treble-oriented Jazz. There is also the option to completely come up with one’s own EQ setting under the My EQ option. Most mainstream users will prefer the Bass setting, while purists will like either Studio or Jazz. One can also adjust the balance of sound between the right and left earcups, although we found no reason to do so.
The JBL Live 780NC are perfect for mainstream audio, whether one wants to listen to pop, trance or rock, or watch a film, play games or just lend an ear to podcasts. At their price, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless ANC headphones out there.
JBL Live 780NC ANC and calls: Super sound over calls, decent sounds of silence
The JBL Live 780NC come with adaptive ANC. You can either specify the level of ANC you want using a slider, or enable Adaptive ANC and let the headphones decide the level. We suggest simply keeping it at maximum. Noise canceling on the headphones is good for their price. Of course, one does not get the kind of ANC that comes on Sony and Bose flagships; the Live 780NC do enough to dull a lot of the traffic sound, kill the hum of the Metro, and can even make a noisy cafe a little quieter.
Call quality is where the Live 780NC shine. Not only do they handle calls very well, with very good levels of clarity, but the app even lets you adjust the tone of the person you are speaking to and your own voice as well. You can actually add more bass or treble to both sides of the conversation on the JBL Live 780NC. The headphones are also able to keep out a fair bit of the ambient noise – we have used them on auto rickshaw rides, with the person we are speaking to not even realizing that we are in the midst of noisy traffic. That AI algorithm for clear calls definitely helps.
JBL Live 780NC Battery life: Charge them once a week only!
JBL claims that the headphones come with 80 hours of battery life without ANC and 50 hours with ANC. We mostly used them with ANC – it does not affect audio quality, apart from making it a little more bass-y – and got a comfortable 40-45 hours of battery life (we admit to hearing them at slightly higher volumes). In practical terms, charging them once easily got us through close to a week of hectic use, where we used them for everything from making calls to listening to music to watching videos, shorts, and reels to playing games. That makes them great daily drivers.
The headphones charge off their USB Type-C port and take about two hours to charge from empty to full. They also come with a fast-charging function that gave us about four hours of audio listening after being charged for five minutes. One can tweak the power settings for the headphones to switch off automatically after 30 minutes, an hour, or two hours, to further conserve power. There is no charging cable in the box, but any Type-C charging cable should work just fine with it.
JBL Live 780NC Review Verdict: In a zone of their own in the Rs 15,000 segment
The headphones are priced at Rs 15,999, but are often available at lower prices (they are available on Amazon India at Rs 14,999 even as this is being written). Their closest competitors are the Sony ULT Wear, which are now available at close to Rs 15,000 but have a very bass-centric sound. The ULT Wear have better ANC than the Live 780NC, but the Live 780NC beat them easily in terms of call handling. offer almost double the battery life and also have a more elegant and foldable design.
Audio purists might like the sound of the Sennheiser Accentum Plus, which are available for Rs 13,999, but they lose out to the Live 780NC in ANC, call quality, and battery life. Those looking for head-turning headphones might also be tempted by the Nothing Headphone (1), which come with a transparent-ish appearance and very good audio quality (if one is ready to spend time adjusting the equalizer), but are more expensive at Rs 17,999, and again, do not match the Live 780NC in ANC and battery life.
We would say that they are comfortably the best all-round mainstream ANC headphones you can get for around Rs 15,000. They deliver decent ANC, very good audio, and excel in calls and battery life. Get them in orange, purple, or green, and they are a sight for sore eyes too!

A painful toothache or an oral infection might not sound like an injury that could sideline a soldier in combat, but US Army dental leaders warn that in a future conflict, such easily overlooked conditions could take troops out of the fight, consume scarce evacuation capacity, and further stress a strained medical system.
Most of the Army's major exercises don't include dental emergencies in their casualty scenarios, dentists said in a recent professional article, leaving commanders with an incomplete picture of the medical and triage or evacuation demands they could face in large-scale combat.
Dental emergencies can quickly render troops "non-mission-capable," the authors wrote, because pain can make it difficult to eat, think clearly, or carry out important tasks like operating weapons. They described this as a significant "hidden casualty load."
Unlike combat wounds, most dental problems can be easily fixed if dental teams are nearby, but despite their important role in military health care, "deployable dental capabilities continue to decline," authors wrote, underscoring an "urgent need for accurate dental emergency modeling in war-gaming to emphasize the importance of [non-battle related injuries] and dental emergencies."
Past wars indicate substantial demand. Dental emergencies accounted for 19% of all treatment at military hospitals near the front lines during the war in Iraq. Another recent article by Army dentists said that dental disease and other non-battle injuries made up nearly 16% of all medical evacuations among troops fighting the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria.
Almost all dental patients treated by forward dental teams returned to duty after one or two visits, the authors wrote. Without dental care close to the front, however, soldiers may have to travel farther to receive treatment, potentially removing them from duty for as long as a week.
Casualty evacuations for any type of health concern or injury, major or minor, are likely to pose a problem for the military in future large-scale combat. The proliferation of drones, both attack and surveillance systems, across the Ukrainian battlefield have made quick evacuation largely impossible, a stark difference from the US experience during the post-9/11 wars.
In a recent military news release for a healthcare training event, Army dentist Lt. Col. Jesse Thietten said dental care "is a low-hanging-fruit solution for medical as a whole. Military medicine needs solutions to account for the anticipated systemic medical overload in [large-scale conflicts.]"
Dental emergencies could rank among the top five most common reasons for casualty evacuation in such a fight, Thietten added. For troops deployed abroad in multinational settings alongside partner forces, dental concerns are "the number one reason" for casualty evacuation, he added.
Thietten helped develop a lightweight expeditionary dental platform for special operations teams training in remote parts of Europe, where teams asked for help treating dental emergencies without easy access to traditionally robust medical facilities. The goal was to bring care closer to troops rather than having to shuttle them to far-off clinics.
Such an approach reflects what Thietten argues the broader force will need in a future fight, including more dental work before troops deploy, along with smaller, more mobile dental teams that can operate close to units in the field.
Within the Air Force, less than 1% of the service's dentists deploy," said Air Force Col. Anita Shade, chief of dental services for the 21st Medical Group, in the same news release. "Our dental teams are often disconnected from the heart of the readiness mission that we work to support, day in and day out," she said.
That disconnect may become more pronounced when combat casualties can't easily be moved from the battlefield to established hospitals and care facilities.
"Asymmetric/hybrid drone warfare shows us that we now need to plan and prepare for prolonged patient management in the field due to the unpredictability of patient transport," Shade said.
Another problem for some military dentists is more basic — broken field equipment and a lack of medical supplies, hampering training opportunities.
Two Army dentists cited those problems in another article from this summer on how military dentistry must adapt for future conflict. While preparing for a unit exercise, they found that their field equipment had not been used in nearly a year and that critical equipment including their sterilizer unit was broken, underscoring further readiness challenges.

Leh, Sep 13: Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Sunday sanctioned Rs 15 lakh each to the next of kin of the four persons who lost their lives in the September 24 violence last year in Leh.
Leh witnessed large-scale protests last year, demanding statehood and the extension of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution to Ladakh. Violence erupted during the agitation, leaving four people dead and scores injured allegedly in police firing.
An ex-gratia assistance of Rs 3 lakh for persons who sustained major injuries and Rs 1 lakh for those who sustained minor injuries has also been approved, a Lok Bhavan spokesman said.
He said the total financial commitment of the administration under the approved compensation measures will be Rs 1.52 crore, comprising Rs 60 lakh for the four deceased, Rs 72 lakh for 24 persons with major injuries and Rs 20 lakh for 20 persons with minor injuries.
The incident had resulted in the loss of four lives, while 43 civilians sustained major or minor injuries.
As Ladakh did not have a general policy prescribing compensation in cases of death or injury arising from incidents of public unrest or rioting, the administration examined the matter with a view to extending appropriate humanitarian assistance to the affected families and individuals.
Saxena, after taking over in March this year, accorded priority to the matter and worked towards finalising an appropriate compensation package for the affected families and injured persons, the spokesperson said, adding that the compensation is intended as a measure of support and solidarity with the affected families and individuals.
He expressed his deep gratitude to Union Home Minister Amit Shah for his sensitive, humanitarian and guiding approach, and for always standing in solidarity with the victims and their families.
“While no compensation amount can replace a life lost or erase the pain endured, the Ladakh Administration firmly stands beside every affected family in their journey towards healing and overcoming the grief,” Saxena said.

Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week. Let’s get into it.
The GOP midterms strategy is Trump and a prayer
What we learned from the first day of the Republican convention in Dallas.
One big idea: What are Republicans actually running on?
The first-of-its-kind Republican midterms convention began in the same vein as President Donald Trump’s second term: open grift. The president announced a pledge to give every American $5,000 if Republicans win the House and the Senate — part of what he’s calling a new dividend for American voters, and what some Democrats are calling an attempted bribe.
Obviously, there are lots of questions about Trump’s announcement: Who will pay for the $1 trillion-plus dividend? Taxpayers. Could this even happen without congressional approval? Probably not. Why not just vote on it now, while Republicans control Congress? It would likely fail.
But I think the pronouncement — and the GOP convention broadly — is best understood as a proxy for the Republican message in the midterm elections, not a policy roadmap for what Trump would do if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate.
So what can we actually glean from the GOP’s two-day bonanza in Dallas, and how does the message they were offering on that made-for-TV platform match up with the message they’ve delivered on the campaign trail? I took a close look at the convention speeches on Wednesday and Thursday, dug through our America, Actually reporting focusing on Republican voters and their candidates, and pulled together some trends that help explain the GOP strategy for defying the odds (and the polling) come Election Day.
1. Republicans are mostly in hiding — One reason Trump’s midterm convention sticks out in this year’s landscape: It’s one of the rare places Republicans will campaign out loud. Congressional candidates, even in battleground House districts, have rarely held public events or town halls this year. And as Trump’s unpopularity has continued to grow, driven by rising gas prices and an unpopular war with Iran, it’s not like the GOP has responded by mounting a defense of its leader. They’ve mostly gone AWOL, a result of the electoral pickle the president has put them in.
Trump is undoubtedly still the most powerful figure within the party, particularly among the Republican base, but Trump is also the biggest motivator for the Democratic base, and is increasingly off-putting to independent voters, who backed him in 2024. His approval has sunk to 33 percent in one recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his presidency, and that same poll found Democrats markedly more fired up for the midterms than Republicans — an enthusiasm gap that’s poison for the party in power. The independents who put him over the top have soured as the war drags on: a UMass poll found more than two-thirds disapprove of his handling of Iran nationally, and four in five say the war has driven up their gas and food prices.
So when Trump tells voters at the GOP midterm convention to “pretend that he’s on the ballot” and turn out in November, I think his opponents listen with glee. Democrats are in the position they’re in because of a brewing electoral backlash to Trump — and the reason Republicans are so hard to find on the campaign trail is that they sense that same backlash is brewing, too. Check out what Ted Cruz said on The View this week: “The big open question is, do Republicans show up?” Cruz asked. “If we stay home, there’s a blue wave.”
2. Even Trump is on the defensive — It’s rare to see Trump acknowledge any semblance of failure, but he came close during his speech during the convention’s first night. Trump was clearly on the defensive throughout his remarks: he sought to make the case for his (unpopular) tariff policy, he defended the (deeply unpopular) Iran war but without the usual bluster, and he acknowledged that gas prices may not fall until after Election Day. Last year, he predicted gas prices would soon hit $2 a gallon; this week he’s asking for still more patience after they hit a record $4.15 on Labor Day. From his speech:
“You know, it happens to me all the time. Guys come up, ‘You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran, gasoline’s up, ba, ba, ba.’ And I say, ‘Well, let me ask you…let me ask you one question. Can Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ ‘Absolutely not.’ ‘Well, then I’m right, then I win, okay?’”
But it’s worth remembering that “be patient” is a controversial message even among Republican voters. When our America, Actually team spent a day outside gas stations in Allentown this summer — deep in PA-7, one of the most contested House districts in the country (watch the episode) — we heard a clean split. There were some Republicans willing to eat the higher price in service of Trump’s war:
“Yes, because our president is actually doing something about Iran. He’s not sugarcoating it. It’s something we need to do, and in the long run it’s gonna be better for everybody.”
And there were other Republicans who voted for Trump and are furious: “I voted for him with his promises to the American people…and I think he’s let us down.”
Another put the broken promise plainly: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs. I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen? It’s outrageous.”
The message now is to wait until after the election. A lot of the president’s own voters at the pump aren’t sure they can.
3. Notice the candidates who weren’t there — Maybe the most revealing thing about Trump’s convention was the guest list, or more notably, the no-shows. MAGA celebrities who owe their careers to Trump packed the stage, but not a lot of the Republicans who are actually on the ballot in places they must win. Notable absences include candidates like John Sununu in New Hampshire and Susan Collins in Maine, and various congressional candidates from battleground races. And while their political calculus may be obvious — they want to avoid a Dallas-with-Trump photo op that ends up in a challenger’s attack ad — it reflects the “win by hiding” strategy that candidates not named Vivek Ramaswamy seem to be deploying.
Here’s the play in a nutshell: keep enough distance from Trump to maintain credibility and independence, but rely on Trump to raise money, drive up Republican turnout, and savagely attack Democratic opponents.
When conservative activist CJ Pearson came on our show, he insisted the GOP doesn’t have an electability problem at all — voters will see Democrats as too radical on topics like socialism and transgender women in sports, which came up repeatedly in the convention, and Republicans can still find ways to address affordability concerns. “These are 80/20 issues,” he said. ”And so I actually really like our odds here…we’re going to overperform. The Senate, we’re gonna hold onto. The House will be a dogfight, but I like our chances.” He even predicted this exact week, telling me the party would “see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas,” after which “you’ll see those numbers start to change.” Whether Dallas actually delivered that reset — or just a $5,000 bribe and a defensive Trump — is, generously, an open question. And the attendance sheet suggests some of Pearson’s own party’s candidates aren’t waiting around to find out.
4. The JD Vance tightrope — One person who doesn’t have the benefit of keeping distance from Trump is JD Vance, his vice president and the presumed GOP frontrunner for the 2028 presidential nomination. He’s close to right-wing voices who have soured on Trump, and has to worry about voters longer than the president will have to, and the Iran war, tariffs, and Trump’s promises all present conflicts for him. Just last week, he took heat from prominent voices in Trump’s coalition for his refusal to disavow Tucker Carlson, the podcast host and former TV anchor who’s become a vocal critic of the Israeli government and Trump’s second-term agenda.
Looking ahead to his speech tonight, I’ll be watching how carefully he handles Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war, and gas prices. He’s tried to strike a more empathetic note on the economy than Trump, who has described talk of an affordability crisis as a made-up narrative to hurt him politically that — to the extent it was real — was President Joe Biden’s fault anyway. “They caused [it], but we’re fixing it,” the president said Wednesday.
Vance says he won’t “sit down” with Trump to discuss his 2028 plans until after the midterms, but Trump is not the kind of person who seems likely to give his successor a lot of room to run away from his record.
What I’m hearing
This week I talked to Charlotte Matherly, a reporter at the Concord Monitor who has been following the underdiscussed New Hampshire Senate race. New Hampshire is one of the Democrats’ must-win states to take back the Senate, but there’s been some concern that Republican candidate John Sununu — a former New Hampshire senator with a long family legacy in the state — could give Democratic nominee Rep. Chris Pappas deep problems. I talked to Matherly about lessons from the state’s primary and what to expect in the general election.
So, the New Hampshire primary just happened — what were the takeaways? And why has this race gone under the radar?
With the progressive versus moderate conversation happening nationally, that was my biggest question heading into Tuesday. Would we see that progressive wave or ripple or whatever you want to call it here too? Because we did have a progressive candidate [Karishma Manzur] run against Chris Pappas, who really focused on humanitarianism and ending what she saw as US complicity in foreign wars.
Voters who liked her were really passionate about her, but in the end, I think people just wanted to vote for what they know, and [Pappas] was already in Congress. The progressive wave that we’ve seen across the country has not necessarily translated here.
Why do you think New Hampshire has stood apart from the national progressive wave?
To give you context for New Hampshire politics, it’s always kind of different from the national electorate. We’re a true purple state — independents are the largest voting bloc here. But there are some quirks. Like, for the past 20 years, except for a few exceptions, voters tend to send Republicans to the state legislature, but usually vote for Democrats when it comes to Congress or presidential elections. So splitting your ticket is really common here. And I hear from people every time I go out to the polls that someone has switched their party in the past few years, or they fall back and forth. So it’s really hard to tell where the partisan lines fall here.
How has the Republican candidate, John Sununu, handled Donald Trump’s popularity?
Years ago [in 2024], Sununu actually penned an op-ed calling Donald Trump a “loser.” And there’s been some bite from the party about that. But Trump actually ended up endorsing him, and he’s also shared the backing of powerful fundraisers and a lot of conservative organizations hoping to flip the seat red. But still, Sununu is trying to emphasize his independence from the administration. He’s saying he’s not worried about currying favor or anything like that, but he hasn’t really put too many policy differences between himself and Trump.
One example that I can think of is that he said he opposed the [reported $300 billion] included in Trump’s deal with Iran that was earmarked for reconstruction. He had said he didn’t think that the US should provide any money for reconstruction. And so there’s been a few things like that that he has tried to sort of strike out on his own from the president.

‘Here to do politics on corpses’: Abhijeet Dipke heckled by group of influencers in MP's Balaghat
Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages to meet the families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases.
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was allegedly heckled by a group of people who appeared to be social media influencers or content creators during his visit to Madhya Pradesh's Balaghat district on Saturday.
Dipke visited Adori, Korka and Bondari villages to meet the families of tribal children who allegedly died due to infectious diseases and to gather information about local healthcare facilities, news agency PTI reported.
A viral video showed a woman 'influencer' sticking a mic in Dipke's face as he was driving away in a car, and asking him if he had come there to "do politics on corpses" and why he was visiting the area so late.
Dipke was heard saying he apologised for visiting the area late.
The woman was also heard saying, "A good road has been constructed here. Can't you see it?"
As the situation escalated, CJP workers accompanying Dipke put him in another car and took him away.
As he left, the woman was heard saying "he ran away, he ran away."
Local journalists said they were surprised to see this group of social media influencers from outside turning up in the remote village, and wondered if they had been sent by someone to disrupt the CJP founder's visit.
Earlier this week, the Jabalpur bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court sought a response from the state government over the deaths of more than 30 children in the region. The division bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal issued notices to the state Health Department, Women and Child Development Department, Balaghat collector and others while hearing a public interest litigation.
The PIL alleged that children were not receiving adequate treatment and that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.

On the rainy morning of August 26, the front courtyard of District Women Hospital in Maharashtra’s Amravati district was crowded with politicians, reporters and bystanders. Amid them stood 30-year-old Swapnil Borde. His bottle-green shirt hung limp with sweat, while his red-rimmed eyes brimmed with tears.
He is the father of one of the three newborns who died after a fire broke out in the four-storey Special Newborn Care Unit and Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) on the third floor of the maternity hospital around 3.15 a.m. on August 24. Thirty-six babies were rescued and shifted to nearby hospitals, according to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar. Two sustained burn injuries, says Amol Narote, medical superintendent of the government-run super-speciality hospital. Preliminary investigations indicate that a ventilator sparked the fire.
Also Read : Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar fire: 58 rescued, including nine newborns in blaze at hospital
Swapnil’s newborn was of low weight and had breathing issues, so was put on a ventilator two days before the fire.
“Gora bala kala kela. Ek minta pan nahi tambaycha ikde, khup bekar jhala ahe, pan mala ajun majhya mulachi janiv hote (My fair baby was turned black. I don’t want to be here even for a minute, but I still feel the presence of my child here),” says Swapnil, who works as a delivery person.
He adds, “This was the first baby in my family in this generation. It took us four years to conceive him. I took him in my arms only after he died.”
Outside the NICU, the empty fire extinguishers lay on the floor, while the soot-covered room, guarded by the police, continued to be frequented by people. Among them were members of a State-level investigation committee, Amravati MLC Pravin Pote and Achalpur Bharatiya Janata Party MLA Pravin Tayde. Former Leader of the Opposition in the Maharashtra Assembly and Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar also visited the hospital. The parents of the other two newborns who died in the August 24 fire came from Achalpur and Paratwada, 50 km from the hospital.
Established in 1938, the hospital is one of Amravati’s major government maternity hospitals. It also caters to Wardha, Yavatmal and Washim districts. Primary healthcare centres and sub-district hospitals across Amravati, including Melghat, a tribal-dominated region, refer critical pregnancies here. The hospital was formerly known as Dufferin Hospital, named after Lady Hariot Dufferin, who established the Dufferin Fund in 1884 to provide medical aid to women in India.
Investigation underway
District Civil Surgeon Dr. Vinod Pawar, who is in charge of the maternity hospital, says, “Around 3.15 a.m., my staff in the NICU heard an explosion from the ventilator and saw fire coming out of it. They alerted the fire department and me simultaneously. Our priority was to rescue the babies.”
Dr. Pawar has submitted the fire-audit-related documents to the investigation committee. The police, meanwhile, have registered an accidental death report.
Maharashtra Minister for Public Health and Family Welfare Prakash Abitkar formed a seven-member committee headed by Public Health Commissioner Sanjay Katkar and directed it to submit its report within eight days. He said the committee’s findings would be made public and responsibility fixed.
On August 26, Mr. Katkar and the committee visited the spot and questioned the nurses who were present in the NICU at the time of the incident. The CCTV footage was also handed over to the committee, which comprises officials from the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, AIIMS and the Directorate of Medical Education and Research. It has been tasked with examining ventilator and electrical faults, the fire-audit history and administrative lapses. The report was due on August 31 but has not yet been released.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced ₹5 lakh in compensation for each family that lost its newborn in the fire and directed that the treatment of injured infants be fully covered by the government.
Of the 36 newborn babies, 11 have been admitted to Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Memorial Medical College (PDMMC), 10 to Hope Hospital, eight to Murkey Hospital and two to Parijat Hospital. Five were discharged with their mothers.
Survivors’ accounts
Radhika Yehkade, 19, was the last to deliver her twins before the fire. They were born around 2 a.m. on August 24 and kept in the NICU.
“I had a difficult pregnancy. I was in the hospital the week before my delivery. I am unable to let go of the voices in my head. Nurses shouting, ‘Help,’ people screaming, ‘Fire, fire.’ I am unable to make peace with the fact that my babies’ lives would have lasted only for two hours,” says Radhika, whose twins were admitted to PDMMC.
Radhika’s mother, Phula Shanware, 55, also an eyewitness, adds, “The smoke was dense; the fire brigade reached in time but took almost an hour to take water pipes to the third floor.”
Talking about her daughter, Phula says, “She had a tough pregnancy; we are daily wage earners and have already spent ₹80,000. We have been far from our house in Achalpur for almost 10 days.”
Another woman, Arti Kharale, 27, narrated her story. “When I saw my daughter, she smelt of wet ash. My heart sank when I heard about the fire,” says Arti, who lives in Amravati city. She says this was the second such fire in the hospital. The last, as reported by the media, was in September 2022.
Fifty-three-year-old Asha Dharse’s daughter delivered her baby at PDMMC. Chatting with other women, she says, “In June, I removed my daughter’s name from Dufrin because my cousin said they are negligent. Chutney, bhakri bhetel, pan aulad nahi, navas karava lagto (We will earn food, but not the baby).”
Yogesh Savarkar, 24, is waiting outside the maternity room at PDMMC, where his daughter and wife have been transferred. Recalling the night of the incident, he says he was among the first parents who barged into the room to rescue the infants.
He narrates, “The flames were soaring, wires were sparking, black smoke was coming out of the broken windows, and the equipment was burning. When I entered, I saw three children covered in black powder. One child had burns on his face. We rescued them first.”
Mr. Savarkar is also from Achalpur and came to the maternity hospital on August 17.
Maharashtra’s fire audits
Chief Minister Fadnavis has raised concerns over the hospital’s mandatory fire audit. A fire audit is a systematic inspection of fire safety readiness, assessing electrical load, wiring safety, overloaded circuits, faulty switchboards, and equipment prone to sparking or overheating, such as ventilators, oxygen concentrators and compressors.
According to data from Maharashtra’s Public Health Department, of the 530 government hospitals across the State, 528 have completed fire audits. As many as 442 hospitals have fire safety systems fully installed, while only 372 hospitals hold a fire no-objection certificate (NOC). This means nearly 30% of government hospitals do not have fire NOCs.
In Amravati alone, 18 government hospitals were audited, of which 16 received the NOC. Meanwhile, in Wardha and Gondia districts, 11 hospitals were audited, but none received the NOC. In Beed district in the Marathwada region, 18 hospitals did not receive NOCs.
On August 25, the Public Health Department announced a State-wide fire and electrical safety inspection of all government, private and charitable hospitals. Minister Abitkar had said, “If discrepancies are found in the audit, then they are to be rectified. Every hospital will appoint a nodal officer for fire safety, who will review fire audits, electrical safety, fire-fighting systems, emergency evacuation arrangements, staff training, and mock drills, and submit compliance information to senior levels.”
Initial warning
Records show that the Dufferin Hospital Authority had flagged concerns over the fire safety systems. A letter dated June 29 stated, “The hospital had obtained a fire NOC valid from June 22, 2025, to June 21, 2026. Before this validity period lapses, a registered licensed agency must conduct a fire safety audit, and Form B must be submitted to this office — so the fire NOC renewal proposal can then be forwarded to the Fire Department of Amravati Municipal Corporation.”
A follow-up letter was also written to the Public Works Department on July 17, reminding it to arrange a fire safety audit. “The fire NOC is an essential document for the hospital, and if its validity period lapses, the possibility of legal complications arising during an emergency cannot be ruled out,” the second letter stated, urging immediate action. The letter was marked to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar and health services in the Akola division. Mr. Yerekar has not responded to The Hindu’s query regarding the action taken after receiving this letter.
Meanwhile, hospital staff and patients said this was the second fire incident in the last five years. “We learnt from our mistakes in the 2022 fire. That is why we have been extra careful with fire audits,” says an official from the Amravati maternity hospital. According to hospital authorities, a ventilator in the NICU had also caught fire then, causing minor injuries to two newborns.
The ventilators in both cases were supplied by Schiller Healthcare, which has been called for the investigation. An official said a committee will be set up to create SOPs for the procurement of medical equipment.
Courage under fire
Outside the NICU, the smell of smoke lingered. In the corridor, kaksh-sevikas (nursing attendants) were waiting for their turns to appear before the committee as part of the investigation. Among them was Surekha Dhanvijay, 45, one of the four attendants present in the NICU, who witnessed the fire and called for help. “The moment I heard the explosion, a huge flame burst out. With our bare hands, we tried to douse the fire near the cradle and take a baby out.”
“I have only one regret: that we couldn’t save those three children,” says Kirti Ghanvir, 45, another nursing attendant. Showing her fire burns and blisters, Ms. Ghanvir adds, “I had to feel around in the burning cradles to see if there was a baby. When I found one, I grabbed it.”
In the meantime, they informed others in the hospital, who rushed to help. “Most of us wrapped blankets around ourselves, broke the glass and entered, rescuing babies,” says Lalita Lasbe, 35.
The sevikas say they do not want any appreciation as they consider this part of their jobs, but appeal to the government to increase their salaries. They say they currently get ₹8,000 a month and are hired on contract, so their salaries barely increase.

Anthropic has selected the Nasdaq for its potential IPO, according to a person familiar with their plans.
The company, which has been targeting an October listing, has given Nasdaq another big win, according to a person familiar with the matter. Nasdaq secured the coveted SpaceX listing earlier this year. SpaceX was valued at $1.75 trillion, and some estimates have put Anthropic at $2 trillion, though that figure has not yet been finalized.
The record-setting size of these IPOs, combined with the dearth in tech listings in recent years, has made winning this competition particularly valuable. Both hope to be seen as the home for future AI IPOs.
Anthropic is preparing to IPO at a time when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says that it wouldn't go public right now amid the controversy surrounding existential threats from AI. That risk gained more attention last week after a viral tweet from a former Anthropic employee, warning of a greater than 10% human extinction risk.
Historically, the New York Stock Exchange has won many of the largest listings, so this year has shown a marked shift. Nasdaq has been consistently strong in tech IPOs, with listings on its exchange a prerequisite for inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 Index.
In terms of how Anthropic ultimately trades, this decision likely matters little. There isn't a definitive answer on whether companies perform better on one exchange versus another.
One key difference between the exchanges concerns market-maker mechanics. They have different processes for determining the opening price on the first day of trading, and high-volume IPOs can cause delays and confusion. Nasdaq experienced technical issues on the first day of Facebook's 2012 IPO.
Anthropic's IPO filing has not yet been made public, but the company will need to release its financials at least 15 days before it begins its investor road show.
