As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability
The worst measles resurgence in the U.S. in decades keeps growing. Vaccination rates keep falling. Flu, COVID-19, and RSV keep coming back. Against this backdrop, many public health experts are worried about the reliability of health information coming from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Red flag. Red alert," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.
Daskalakis and other independent public health authorities around the country are alarmed by how the CDC handled two deaths that Pennsylvania state officials recently blamed on measles. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took the unprecedented step of questioning the deaths, and the CDC removed them from the agency's website.
"When they raise doubt on the adjudication that a state may have made around a death, that is highly problematic," says Daskalakis. "This is dangerous."
Usually, when someone dies from measles, the state where the tragedy happened determines the cause of death and reports the death to the CDC so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country. The CDC usually defers to the state's determination.
So Kennedy's public dispute with the state and the CDC's response is concerning for what it may mean for the relationship between states and federal health officials, who have to work closely to protect the public, Daskalakis and others say. That relationship has already become strained under the Trump administration.
"What we have been seeing, that got amplified even more with these measles cases, is a breakdown in the coordination and trust between states and the federal government," says Dr. Anne Zink, a senior fellow at the Yale School of Public Health who previously served as Alaska's chief medical officer and president of the Association for State and Territorial Health Officers. "That to me is a significant concern. These partnerships are critical and essential to making us healthy and well."
Zink and others also worry about whether the public, state and local health officials, doctors and others will be able to trust federal health data about measles as well as other diseases, such as flu, COVID-19 and RSV. Could CDC succumb to pressure to suppress information to minimize concerns about those diseases and the impact of falling immunization rates? Kennedy has long questioned vaccines.
"We need to have good solid evidence-based national data. And I'm obviously concerned that it will happen again for other infectious diseases," says Dr. Georges Benjamin, who heads the American Public Health Association. "If it happens with flu and with COVID, the question is: Who can we rely on for the data on a national level. More people will get sick and more people because they won't know what to do. They won't know who to trust. And that is the problem here."
Many also worry about what this means for the effectiveness of the new CDC director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, who recently took over after a tumultuous year that has left the CDC demoralized and diminished. Many hoped Schultz, a well-respected physician and attorney with solid public health experience, would restore the CDC's morale and credibility by pushing back against political pressure. But many say the way the CDC handled the Pennsylvania measles cases don't bode well for Schultz pushing back against political pressure.
"We are seeing a pretty compromised CDC and a director who is at best facilitating non-scientific behavior and at worst colluding with non-scientific behavior," says Daskalakis.
Others agree.
"What the director should be doing instead of looking into these disease counts is responding to the outbreak itself," says Dr. Debra Houry, who resigned as the CDC's chief medical officer at the same time as Daskalakis for the same reasons. "I haven't heard from her talking about the importance of getting kindergarteners vaccinated when we're seeing declining rates. It's back to school time around the United States. We need her to step up publicly to talk about what can be done."
Neither the CDC nor the Department of Health and Human Services responded to NPR's repeated requests for comment.

England chasing the rainbow with more questions than answers
- Published
It is 2026 and Joe Root is again England Test captain and Kevin Pietersen is back in the fold.
For those two things to be the new normal says plenty about the upheaval in one of the most turbulent summers in English cricket's recent history.
The debate as to whether there should have been alterations to the leadership after the Ashes has become a moot point, because England have nevertheless ended in a post-Bazball era.
Has the lack of change in the spring led to a wasted summer? Try telling any of Jordan Cox, Emilio Gay or Dan Lawrence that the summer has been wasted. Or a resurgent Ollie Robinson. Or Root, who had to rummage around his garage to dig out his old captain's blazer.
Are England a better team in September than they were in June? It is hard to argue that a team that has lost Ben Stokes has improved, though that should take nothing away from all the good things England have done in the 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan.
It is not a criticism of Stokes to say his personality dominated the England team he led. By the end of his reign, England were characterised by what Stokes said and did.
Naturally, England are different under Root, a different personality to Stokes.
Until the third evening of the third Test at Edgbaston, most of those differences seemed positive. There had been a calmness about England's demeanour, perhaps because they had not been tested to that point.
That calmness eroded with every swing of Razaullah's blade. Two hours of chaos frazzled England and exposed old doubts from Root's first spell as captain. The skipper himself felt it necessary to duck off the field. Stokes rarely lost control in such a fashion.
Even after such a bruising session, there were some small positives. Stand-in coach Marcus Trescothick was happy to admit his disappointment at what had transpired, a shift in tone from the Kool Aid messaging of the Bazball boys.
In reality, we are ending the summer with no clear knowledge of how good this England team is, following a pattern of years gone by: the drawn Ashes in 2023, a shock defeat by Sri Lanka at The Oval at the end of 2024 and the failure to win the final Test against India last year.
And that is the ultimate frustration of England's Test performances in the four-plus years that Rob Key has been director of cricket.
When the defining series have rolled around, England have not won them. In between those big challenges there have been more questions than answers. The brass ring always remains just out of reach, always searching for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.
- England in better place than start of summer - Root 
  - Published1 hour ago
- Who has given selectors food for thought? England-Pakistan player ratings 
  - Published3 hours ago
For now, England have a blossoming four-man pace quartet that has drawn comparisons with the famous Ashes winners of 2005.
Robinson has ruled England's summer, taking his 28 wickets at an average of 9.32; the sort of statistics in keeping with Test cricket from before World War I.
With Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson bringing the pace, England have a Swiss army knife of an attack, albeit lacking a left-armer.
Still, England are only one injury away from some inexperienced reserves. Sam Cook, Sonny Baker, Matthew Fisher and Henry Crocombe have four caps between them. Brydon Carse is available, though it remains to be seen if England will take him on tour while the Derby incident is still under investigation. Perhaps the in-form Olly Stone is due a recall.
The challenge for England is to find the right blend to suit the winter. The four seamers could operate in South Africa and the one-off pink-ball 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne, but the two matches in Bangladesh in February will demand a change in formation.
Despite the burning summer, spin has become a redundant weapon. The list of candidates to play in Bangladesh is long because there is no outstanding one among them.
Shoaib Bashir, Jack Leach, Dom Bess, Will Jacks, James Coles, Mason Crane, Liam Patterson-White, Calvin Harrison and Jack Carson may all think they have a shout of being on the plane.
The incumbent is Dan Lawrence, who has not had many opportunities to show the value of his part-time off-breaks.
Lawrence's bowling gives him an advantage when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, probably leaving a choice between Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay for the first Test in South Africa in December.
Both men have made three half-centuries in their first summers as Test batters. Cox is extremely highly rated by the England management, who must decide how much weight to put on Gay's skill as a specialist opener.
The top of the order has emerged as England's biggest batting concern. Ben Duckett made the only century of the summer, yet averages 23 since the beginning of the Ashes.
Gay's average in his six Tests is below 25 and his frustration at his second-innings dismissal against Pakistan came out with a swish of his bat towards the stumps. His running between the wickets is jittery and he is rarely placed in an important position in the field.
Of all the issues around the batting, England need Root to rediscover his best. The captain ends the summer without a hundred for the first time since 2019 and with his lowest average in a home season since the same year.
This time last year, it was full steam ahead in the pursuit of India great Sachin Tendulkar. Now, the 1,643 runs to catch the Little Master look a little further away. The smart money will be on Root to come out of his funk, rather than this being the start of a late-career decline.
Root will meet incoming coach Stephen Fleming in the coming days to plot the route forward.
Along with Key - the great survivor of England's chaotic summer - the trio will look for a way to win the marquee series, to claim the major prizes on offer in the months ahead: in South Africa this winter, the Ashes next summer, in India in early 2028.
And this is where England find themselves yet again, with judgement reserved until biggest challenges.
Still grasping for the brass ring, still chasing the pot of gold.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on how it proposed to determine whether packaged foods were “high” in sugar, salt or fat as part of its proposed front-of-pack warning labels, as it underlined that food safety was a cause of “national interest”.
The FSSAI had last month proposed prominent red warning labels on packaged foods high in added fat, added sugar or salt, marking a regulatory pivot after the top court questioned its reluctance to introduce such warnings.
In an affidavit filed before the court, the food regulator said the labels would take the form of a red hexagonal warning on the front of packages where a product was found to be high in two or more specified nutrients of concern — fat, sugar or salt. The thresholds would be based on those prescribed under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while examining the FSSAI’s affidavit, however, questioned how the regulator would determine the threshold beyond which a packaged food would be classified as “high” in sugar, salt or fat.
“If you ask them to put a label, say high in salt, high in sugar, high in sodium, high in potassium, how will you determine it? Have you laid down any guidelines?” the Bench asked.
Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, said the regulator was adhering to the guidelines issued by the ICMR-NIN.
The Bench was hearing a public interest litigation petition filed by non-profit organisations 3S and Our Health seeking warning labels on packaged foods to indicate high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fats. On Thursday, it indicated that it would soon pass a detailed order seeking further information from the stakeholders.
“We have done some homework and undertaken some study. We propose to pass an order calling for some further information from you. Study the order and come back with an appropriate further report,” Justice Pardiwala told Mr. Chahar.
‘Take orders seriously’
The top court also asked the regulator to take its directions “seriously”, stressing its concern over the impact of food safety standards on public health, particularly that of growing children.
“We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously... We expect one and all to extend cooperation in a cause which is in national interest,” Justice Pardiwala said.
‘Two-phase rollout’
The FSSAI had told the court that it intended to introduce the front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPNL) system in two phases to give consumers time to adapt to the new labels and the food industry time to reformulate its products. Under the first phase, the warning would apply to products high in two or more of the three specified nutrients, added fat, added sugar and salt, besides certain sweetened beverages. The second phase would extend it to products high in even one of these nutrients.
The Bench, however, questioned why a product would initially have to be high in more than one nutrient to attract the warning.
“It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?” Justice Pardiwala asked.
Taking the court’s suggestion into account, Mr. Chahar told the Bench that the regulator could consider introducing the warning labels “in one go”, rather than in two phases. This would effectively bring products high in even one of the three nutrients within the warning-label regime from the outset.
Senior advocate Devadatt Kamat, appearing for an intervenor, meanwhile argued that ultra-processed foods could not be placed on the same footing as other packaged foods, citing the example of snacks such as Kurkure on the one hand and eggs or salted cashews on the other. He urged the court to consider a more prominent warning for ultra-processed products.
“Ultra-processed food and packaged food... both cannot be equated,” Mr. Kamat submitted. Pointing out that red and green marks are already used to distinguish non-vegetarian and vegetarian products, respectively, he suggested that a different colour could be prescribed as a warning for ultra-processed foods.
The Bench said it would consider the suggestion and pass an order, which would be uploaded within a day or two.
Earlier, the court had questioned the FSSAI’s reluctance to adopt warning labels for foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat and asked whether pressure from food manufacturers was influencing the regulator.
“You don’t want people of this country to remain healthy? More particularly growing children?” the Bench had asked, warning the authorities that it was their “last chance” to rollout the warning labels.
The court had made clear that its concern was not about banning any particular food but ensuring that consumers, particularly children, knew what they were consuming before making a choice.

Earlier this year, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) which affects one in eight women worldwide, was renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) by the Endocrine Society.
A global consensus article published in the Lancet in May, led by Professor Helena J. Teede, argued that the name reduced a long-term hormonal and endocrine disorder to focus on ovaries and cysts, leading to inadequate treatment, or fewer people getting diagnosed with the condition.
Professor Terhi Piltonen, president of International Androgen Excess and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Society (AE-PCOS Society), and also one of the co-leads of the Lancet publication, from Oulu University Hospital, Finland, in conversation with The Hindu speaks about the name change, and its implications on patients, treatment plans, and research.
Excerpts from the interview:
Can you tell me about the process of renaming the syndrome from PCOS to PMOS?
It was sustained work over 14 years that eventually led to the name change. Earlier, there were some individual opinion papers. There were fifty-six societies were invited to be part of the whole process. And about one hundred persons represented these organisations, the patient organisations, and healthcare professionals.
We had meetings where we narrowed down on the different opinions, and we had to take into consideration many different aspects; cultural aspects, acceptability, and adaptability to understand how is it that we want it to change the life of these women. It's been a long process, but the last bit of the process took around two years.
How would the name change impact existing treatment protocol?
We are now thinking about it in a more holistic way; not only looking at the ovary, but also looking at how it affects the mood, the psychological profile, the metabolic profile and also the menstrual cycles. And I think I'm hoping that with the new name, we will now understand that this is a whole-body syndrome.
We know how to manage it, but the name change emphasises how we need to listen to the patients and take a more holistic view and invite other disciplines to play their part.
The women need the opportunity to be asked about their mental health issues, weight management, their skin, their quality of life, how they manage at work, and when they would like to conceive so that we can anticipate how they can have overall good health.
Does the name change impact the research that is being conducted?
There is a three-year overlap period where we are going to put in the codes for PCOS and PMOS while researching and eventually we will transition to using PMOS.
But of course, I am hoping that we'll see more diverse studies, for example my colleague who is an endocrinologist or in internal medicine, or a dermatologist, might take an interest in researching certain parts of the condition. So far, it was only OB-GYNs who were diagnosing it. But I think that others might acknowledge their work in seeing PMOS.
Is it also monetarily challenging to conduct research in an area that impacts women, and not men?
Yes, it is. This is only a fraction of the money that goes into erectile problems or diabetes. , In terms of funding, I think it is not proportional to the prevalence. I'm hoping that there will be more grants and that the industry would get involved as they now know that it is a condition that needs a lot of different approaches.
PMOS is often seen as a ‘modern’ condition. How true or untrue would you say that is?
When we think about nutrition, our bodies haven't been developed to be capable of dealing with very high energy foods. In our evolution, there has been a problem of not having enough food, and we had been moving around and collecting things, and having low-calorie food for thousands and millions of years. And now in a very short time, we have entered a period where food is available, that too, food with high-energy content. So, I think it kind of became a disadvantage for this type of genotype that women have.
And in society now, we have lots of pressure with hectic work lives, and with social media, and other stress factors. This sort of environment does not really serve any of the people who are sensitive to stress. And women are especially sensitive to stress altogether. I think it is linked to modern society in one way, but it does not mean that it's not relevant or that it is not meaningful.

F1 Spanish Grand Prix: Oscar Piastri eighth, Kimi Antonelli wins in Madrid
In short:
Oscar Piastri has finished eighth at the F1 Spanish Grand Prix, racing with a damaged front wing after being hit twice on the first lap.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli won the race for Mercedes, pitting under a virtual safety car while then-leader Lando Norris missed out.
What's next?
Antonelli leads the drivers' championship by 81 points ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Saturday, September 26.
Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner, as Kimi Antonelli took full advantage of a fortunate safety car to win the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix.
Piastri finished eighth in the maiden grand prix at the brand-new Madring circuit, driving most of the race with a damaged front wing.
The Australian started seventh on the grid and got a fair start off the line. Russell, starting sixth, cut across Piastri and made contact with the Australian's front wing.
The pair made contact again while braking for the first corner, with Piastri's front left colliding with the rear of Russell's car.
Part of Piastri's damaged wing flapped in the breeze as the Australian tried to finish as high as he could.
Piastri went deep into the race before pitting, emerging back on track in 11th.
The Australian battled back in the final laps to climb back up to eighth.
Norris cruelled by safety car, Antonelli tightens grip on title with win
An ill-timed safety car cost reigning world champion Lando Norris the chance of victory in Spain, as Kimi Antonelli's win gave the young Italian an 81-point lead in the drivers' championship.
Norris, who started on pole, had a healthy lead over Antonelli on lap 14 of 57 when misfortune struck the McLaren driver.
Aston Martin's Lance Stroll went off the track, leading to a virtual safety car being called.
Norris had passed the entrance to the pit lane moments before the VSC was deployed, meaning he had to drive at 40 per cent speed while others behind him, including Antoenlli and Max Verstappen, took a cheap pit stop.
As Norris approached the pit entrance on lap 15 the VSC ended and he pitted while his rivals were able to race at full speed.
McLaren also had a slow stop thanks to an issue with changing the front right tyre, meaning he dropped from first to sixth.
"Tough race, one that just got away from us," Norris said.
"I felt like we deserved it today, but that's racing. We'll take it on the chin and try again next time."
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc did not pit and led the race from Antonelli.
Leclerc stayed out until lap 48 of 57, and with the Madring proving hard to pass on, Antonelli, Max Verstappen and Norris were bunched up behind him, setting up a tense finish.
Once Leclerc pitted, Antonelli was able to drive in clean air and pulled away from Verstappen, who was able to hold off Norris for second place.
"It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all," Antonelli said post-race.
"It's good to win, but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando deserved the win."
While Antonelli claimed his eighth grand prix win of the season, his nearest rivals in the championship were off the podium.
Mercedes teammate Russell placed fifth, while Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton retired early with a brake failure.
Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship is a big 81 to Russell, and 101 points to Hamilton with either eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East at the end of the year.

The Global Fintech Festival (GFF) 2026 came to a close today with three days of conversations, launches, and partnerships. Following a day focused on partnership announcements between traditional financial institutions and fintech and AI startups, the ecosystem continued to capitalise on the momentum to roll out another wave of new developments. Here are some of the top launches from the final day of GFF 2026… BharatPeX Launches Enterprise Payment Gateway with Dynamic Routing BharatPe’s enterprise payments division BharatPeX launched a payment gateway targeting ecommerce and fintechs enterprises. The platform offers a single integration supporting over 100 payment options, including UPI, cards, net banking, and bank transfers via IMPS, NEFT, or RTGS. It consolidates checkout, settlements, refunds, payouts, and automated reconciliation into a unified operational dashboard. It also features a dynamic routing engine that directs transactions to acquiring bank partners based on real-time success rates, card BIN performance as well as service availability. Additionally, the BharatPeX Payment Gateway offers capabilities like native OTP, tokenisation and CVV-less payment experiences, as well as EMI options, recurring payments, and virtual account tracking. PayU Rolls Out Agent HQ for SMB Merchants Prosus-owned fintech startup PayU launched Agent HQ, an AI agent storefront designed to help small and medium business (SMB) merchants deploy autonomous agents across sales, marketing, and operations. As search traffic transitions toward GenAI platforms, Agent HQ enables merchants to make their product catalogs discoverable and transactable directly on AI search systems like ChatGPT and Claude. The no-code tool integrates directly into existing PayU dashboard without requiring additional developer integration. It is built on historical platform data from PayU’s network of over 4.5 Lakh merchants. “By putting a personalized team of AI agents to work across the business - from improving discoverability and driving growth to managing chargebacks, reconciliations, refunds, settlements, etc. - we want to put control back in merchants' hands, enabling them to focus on their growth,” said PayU’s CPO Manas Mishra. Union Minister Nitin Gadkari Launches OneTag To Enable FASTag Portability Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari launched OneTag, a portability solution for FASTags jointly developed by the Indian Highways Management Company (IHMCL) and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). As it currently stands, vehicle owners looking to switch their issuer bank must replace the physical windshield tag and undergo onboarding again. OneTag reduces this friction by enabling users retain the same tag, bringing down reissuance costs. NPCI provides the underlying central architecture to update issuer records across the toll network. Meanwhile, users can avail the service through NHAI’s Rajmargyatra mobile app. Existing issuer banks manage customer verification, wallet closures, refunds, and pending settlements, while the user’s selected new bank will complete the onboarding and provide services after the tag is ported. The new tag will retain the same Tag ID linked to the same vehicle registration number.

Throughout 2026, an image circulated online purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump's Fordham University transcript featuring a grade point average of 1.28.
The alleged report card suggests Trump got D, C and F grades across five classes.
One Facebook user who shared the supposed university record in January wrote (archived), "Is this a surprise to anyone?"
(Brian Little, accessed via Facebook)
The image also spread on X (archived, archived) and Instagram (archived) throughout the summer of 2026. Snopes readers wrote in asking if the transcript is real.
In short, the report card is fake. In March 2019, Fordham University posted (archived) about the image on X, calling it a "forgery."
The image is a forgery, not an actual Fordham University transcript. Fordham University respects the privacy of its students and alumni, and follows federal law regarding the handling and release of academic records https://t.co/gJ0qfpR4nB pic.twitter.com/CXCQ90kG76
— Fordham University (@FordhamNYC) March 8, 2019
Additionally, the fake document lists an address — 85-15 Wareham Place, Jamaica, New York — for Trump that he reportedly last lived at when he was four years old, meaning he did not live there when he attended Fordham University from 1964 to 1966 (PDF Page 89), aged around 18-20 years old.
It was not possible to find any evidence that Fordham had released an authentic copy of Trump's transcript regarding his years at the school, as of this writing.
Trump's former "fixer" and lawyer Michael Cohen, who testified against Trump in the trial that eventually found the now-president guilty of falsifying business records in connection with payments to a porn star, told Congress in 2019 that Trump asked him to send letters to his former schools that "threatened" them not to release his grades (PDF Page 14).
PBS reported in February 2019 that Fordham University spokesperson Bob Howe said the school had received a letter from Trump's legal team threatening legal action if it released his grades. That same year, Howe also told Snopes, when we previously investigated this claim, that the transcript is fake.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Actor Tatyana Ali is advocating for Black and Indigenous maternal health
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Actor and singer Tatyana Ali has become an important voice in a growing movement to improve maternity health outcomes for Black and Indigenous mothers and babies by addressing systemic racism and inequity in maternity care. Ali has been calling for reproductive justice since experiencing what she calls "obstetric violence" during the delivery of her first-born son Aszi in 2016.
Ali, 47, says being a mother is the most important role of her life, as she embarks on the latest chapter of her Hollywood career. She will compete on the new season of Dancing with the Stars on ABC, starting Tuesday, September 15. Ali is perhaps best known for her role as the lovable Ashley Banks on the NBC sitcom The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air in the 1990s. Since then, she has acted in TV and digital series, movies and released an album.
Ali and her husband Vaughn Rasberry are raising two sons, Alejandro and Aszi. In an interview with NPR, she said it was the birth of her oldest, Aszi, that eventually made her want to speak out for Black and Indigenous mothers.
Ali described having a normal pregnancy with Aszi and the days of waiting for his birth as filled with joy.
"So excited and just waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting. My mother's song when she was waiting for me was 'cuando, cuando, cuando – when when, when? When are you coming?' I sang that song. I thought we were prepared," she said.
But during the delivery at the hospital, Ali says her birth plan was immediately ignored. And she was physically restrained.
"It went from a small group of people in the room to many people in the room screaming, yelling at me," she said. "I was held down by about four people."
Ali described chaos and aggressive and dismissive behavior by the doctor and nurses.
"Faces, screaming, terror, panic. I needed somebody to help me," she said.
Ali says her hospital records detail the doctor using a high-risk emergency procedure that is rarely used. The Zavanelli maneuver is a last-resort procedure performed when a baby is stuck inside the birth canal. Ali says in her case, her son was already crowning when the doctor pushed him back inside of her. "After they pushed him inside me, and I remember roaring. I convulsed after that. Like my body – I can hear the bed just go buh-buh-buh-buh," she said, describing the sound of the bed shaking. "And I was out."
The doctor then performed an emergency c-section to deliver her son.
Aszi became strong enough to go home after several days in the neonatal intensive care unit. Ali says at the time, the hospital's head urologist told her the infant was in shock from his traumatic birth. Ali says it took some time for her to realize she had experienced "obstetric violence." She blames systemic racism in healthcare, after hearing similar stories from other women of color.
"It wasn't just me. I was just one tiny drop in a very, very large bucket that has been overflowing for a very, very long time," she said.
Black maternal health in America
The United States is arguably the most dangerous country in the developed world to give birth to a baby, with a much higher rate of maternal deaths compared to other wealthy nations. 649 women in the U.S. died of maternal causes in 2024, according to federal data.
But there is a huge disparity in the numbers: Black mothers were more than three times as likely to lose their lives from pregnancy-related causes than white women.
Many in the maternity care field are concerned by stories like Ali's and the statistics. Dr. Tamika Auguste is chair of women's and infants' services at MedStar Washington Hospital Center.
"I can't tell you how many Black women have said to me: 'Hey Doc, don't let me die,'" she said in an interview. "The poor rates in outcomes of Black maternity patients is something that rocked us to our core."
Auguste says important work has been done in the maternal healthcare field to improve protocols and guidelines to address conditions like cardiac issues, hemorrhaging and hypertension, which are more prevalent among Black women. But she says there's still the problem of bias.
Auguste points to the dangerous misconception among some in medicine that Black patients have a higher threshold for pain. She believes it's key for medical teams to acknowledge that disparities exist and communicate intentionally about bias to prevent it from affecting patient care.
"We are very purposeful in looking at outcomes with a lens of demographics of different racial breakdown of different types of data," said Auguste.
She says those discussions are moving the needle slightly. Her hospital in Washington, D.C., employs about a dozen midwives.
"Physician, midwife, doula, nurse, anesthesiologist, working together as a team. That is critical," said Auguste.
But access to maternity care is a barrier. Dr. Auguste's own hospital recently closed one of two postpartum units, citing financial pressure. More than 500 hospitals closed maternity wards between 2010 and 2022, according to a study published in the medical research journal JAMA.
Nationwide, more than half of counties don't have hospital-based labor and delivery services, according to the non-profit organization March of Dimes. The group calls these maternity care deserts.
In the South, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to live in areas without adequate access to maternity care providers, according to KFF Health News. People of color are also more likely to be uninsured.
Healing journey
Ali says, through her own healing, she has found beautiful relationships and support in the Black and Indigenous maternal health community. She travels the country speaking at conferences and other events, sharing her personal story and talking about solutions.
Ali founded a business called Baby Yams to fund grants to Black and Indigenous birth workers and students. Her team makes heritage baby quilts in vivid ankara and batik fabrics. Each quilt has a special name and represents protection and strength.
"They're this storytelling machine of the possibility, the hope," explained Ali.
Baby Yams donates part of the proceeds to the Birth Future Foundation, which provides grants to midwives, doulas and student birth workers.
"There are solutions. The solutions exist now," Ali said. "There are birth centers, there are midwives educating themselves, doulas going into practice."
A midwife in Alabama is one of many birth workers who has benefited from Ali's financial support. Nadia Gramby says she completed her licensing requirements to advance from a doula to a midwife thanks to a Birth Future Foundation scholarship funded by Ali.
Gramby, 41, says her work helping families across Alabama is especially important because nearly 40% of counties in the South are maternity care deserts, according to March of Dimes. Gramby says her practice is an important option, especially for Black families that may not otherwise have immediate access to care.
"It is an amazing joy to see families who feel safe and know that they're seen, and they made decisions to make sure that their children are born in safe environments, where they feel comfortable, and they feel cared for and they have been educated and they are empowered," she told NPR.
Black midwives and doulas have had a rich history in African American life and communities for centuries.
Midwives are medically trained to perform many of the same functions and procedures as doctors when women are having babies in low-risk situations. They deliver in hospitals alongside physicians, birth centers and in homes. They also frequently collaborate with doulas, who provide non-medical support. Research shows midwife births lead to lower rates of complications.
A report released this year by March of Dimes finds midwives are critical and part of the solution to expanding access to maternity care, especially in rural and under-resourced communities. The group is calling for policies to remove requirements for physician supervision and increase reimbursement rates from Medicaid and private insurance.
But some physicians and policymakers worry about the safety of giving birth outside of hospitals, especially when there's an emergency. Midwives can't perform surgery for example, so that can mean delays to getting emergency treatment. Some states have laws making it harder for midwives to practice.
When Ali became pregnant with her second child, she and her husband searched carefully for the right midwife and found one. She says that time around, her birth plan and desires were acknowledged.
"We deserve to be cared for. We deserve to have choices. We deserve to have control over our own bodies," she said. "We are beautiful. We are deserving of loving hands."

The United States is in the throes of the largest tax revolt in a generation, and the revolutionaries are winning.
Since 2020, nationwide home values have climbed roughly 50 percent, leading property-tax bills to increase 19 percent and contributing to a 71 percent increase in the cost of homeowner’s insurance. At the same time, the price of gas, utilities, food, and everything else has risen, stamping out entrepreneurship, dimming the fertility rate, and making even six-figure earners feel financially strained.
Homeowners have had enough, and grassroots groups have mobilized to turn private kvetching into public policy. Over the past four years, nearly two dozen states have slashed property taxes: Alabama by capping annual assessment increases, Colorado by lowering marginal rates, Indiana by creating credits, Nebraska by setting a limit on local collections, New York by sending checks to homeowners, Wyoming by carving out loopholes for seniors. My back-of-the-envelope accounting suggests that the measures have reduced property-tax revenue in those states by 7 percent, saving homeowners as much as $45 billion a year.
This November, voters will consider a spate of similar proposals, the most radical one coming from legislators in Tallahassee, Florida. Amendment 3, popularly known as “Save Our Homes,” would raise the “homestead” exemption on owner-occupied properties in the state from $50,000 to $250,000, meaning a couple with a condo with an assessed value of $400,000 would pay their county’s property-tax rate on $150,000 of their home’s value, rather than on $350,000. The amendment would eliminate levies on more than half of dwellings. In time, Florida legislators want to phase out property taxes on owner-occupied homes entirely.
Amendment 3 would give property owners a giant tax cut: $12 billion a year by one estimate. It would ease the local cost-of-living crisis too, its proponents argue. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians,” Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman and the front-runner in the governor’s race, said on the stump last month. “It doesn’t matter what your politics are. It doesn’t matter what the color of your skin is. Because when taxes and insurance are more than principal and interest, you got a problem.”
Yet what is being framed as a populist fight for affordability is in reality a form of class and generational warfare. Property-tax relief gives to the rich and takes from the poor. It aids seniors and harms children. It puts homeownership even further out of reach for many Americans, and it makes daily life even more expensive for low-income Americans.
To be fair to the amendment’s supporters, these arguments are not exactly intuitive. The annual cost of owning a home has climbed precipitously. Millions of working-class and middle-income families own their home. If you cut property taxes, you reduce their costs. This much is true.
Yet homeowners’ insurance and property taxes don’t function on a family’s balance sheet in the same way that rent, groceries, gas, cars, child care, and airfare do. Their cost goes up when familial wealth goes up. In Florida, real-estate appraisals have increased 83 percent since 2019, according to the state’s revenue department, suggesting that homeowners’ net worth has increased by trillions of dollars. Does public policy really need to solve the problem of rising taxes due to rising valuations? Is it even a problem at all?
If retirees on fixed incomes can’t afford their insurance payments and families can’t figure out how to cover their tax bill, maybe. Yet the number of Florida homes and buildings that are delinquent on their property taxes has fallen slightly since 2020. The number of foreclosures has increased a bit, but remains low. The state’s housing market is fraying and distressed sales are increasing, but that’s because of climate change and mortgage rates, not tax assessments. Floridians may not like paying a higher tax bill, and carrying costs might be spurring some of them to downsize. But in general, property taxes are levied on people who can afford them. The typical homeowner earns twice as much as the typical renter, and has 43 times the net worth.
Tenants are “the loser in all this,” Ken Johnson, a professor of finance at the University of Mississippi, told me. Many cities and counties offset lower taxes on owner-occupied properties with higher taxes on commercial residential properties. Landlords pass those costs on to their renters. The policy will also benefit longtime homeowners at the expense of prospective homebuyers. Low property taxes increase home prices, making it harder for people without a lot of money in the bank—such as new parents and just-married couples—to get approved for a mortgage. Then they remain tenants, subject to never-ending rent increases.
In addition to distorting the housing market, Amendment 3 will devastate public finances. Property taxes provide 43 percent of revenue to Florida’s municipal general funds, the bank accounts that cities and counties use to finance day-to-day services. Amendment 3 will cut collections by as much as 30 percent, and will hit hardest in areas with a lot of homes and not a lot of commerce. To cover the $12 billion budget hole, cities and towns will likely raise or impose sales taxes and sin taxes; increase fees at the DMV, permit offices, registrars, and courts; charge more for waste removal and water; and put additional taxes on tourists. The state will trade out a solidly progressive, uniformly applied tax for an obscure, regressive mishmash of charges.
But municipalities aren’t expected to make up all of the lost revenue. They’re expected to cut. Amendment 3 explicitly protects tax financing streams for schools, meaning that cities and counties are contemplating draconian budget reductions for public-safety offices, libraries, after-school programs, summer camp, day care, flood prevention, public transit, roads, parks, senior services, homeless shelters, legal-aid clinics, domestic-violence shelters, and many other things. Austerity will be regressive too, harming the poor more than the wealthy. Rich Floridians aren’t relying on the bus to get to work. They’re not picking up free meals, taking adult-literacy classes at the library, or seeing a dentist at a pop-up clinic in a middle-school gymnasium either.
In the worst-case scenario, State Senator Tina Polsky told me, cities and counties “wouldn’t have enough money to keep going, even to pay their elected officials.” They would need to merge, or “come begging in Tallahassee, and those with the best lobbyists and the best connections are going to get the money.”
Add the possibility of a recession to that worst case. In a downturn, Florida would have no revenue from individual income taxes. (Florida voters banned them in a 1924 constitutional amendment.) It would have less income from property taxes than it did before. Yields from sales, corporate, and tourist taxes would fall. The state’s revenue base would collapse, meaning cuts to public services and layoffs and a secondary decline in consumer spending, leading the revenue base to shrink even more.
Despite these risks, Amendment 3 is expected to pass, as are many similar measures on the ballot in November. Voters have approved 78 percent of statewide property-tax measures in recent years. No wonder: Americans hate inflation and love homeownership. They believe in higher taxes, but also think other people should be the ones paying them. They may not perceive the connection between slashing property taxes and cuts to services, rising sales taxes, and increasing fees. They don’t understand that slashing property taxes means gutting the most effective wealth tax the country has, or taking from the poor to give to the rich. “It is an intellectual challenge to figure out ways to talk about these things, if you even have the guts to talk about them at all,” Texas State Senator Nathan Johnson, the solitary holdout on a property-tax relief measure that passed last year, told me.
Maybe California could convince them. Back in 1978, state residents revolted against a brutal cost-of-living crisis, a miserable housing market, and ever-increasing tax bills. By a two-to-one margin, they passed Proposition 13, which capped most property-tax rates at 1 percent, reset assessments to their 1976 level, and barred assessments from increasing more than 2 percent a year, unless a property changes hands or a new structure is built.
Prop 13 broke California. It nudged homeowners to remain in their properties for as long as possible, freezing neighborhoods in amber and trapping would-be buyers in rentals. (One recent study found that raising California’s average property-tax rate from 0.8 percent to 2 percent would increase the state’s homeownership rate by 4.6 percent.) It starved towns and cities of revenue, prompting them to rely on less progressive, less reliable, less equitable, and more distortionary taxes. It helped Boomers and it hurt younger generations. (I would say, “It helped Boomers and hurt their grandchildren,” but that would not be literally true. In California, Pappy and Gamma can bequeath their home to Junior without triggering a property-tax reassessment, meaning the state directly subsidizes dynastic fortunes.) Perhaps most salient: Prop 13 made California less affordable, radically so. It stymied real-estate development and created a trillion-dollar incentive for property owners to fight against reform.
What California did two generations ago might be the best argument against what Florida and other states are doing today. With these property-tax measures, well-off families are helping themselves now and hurting everyone else tomorrow.

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

Trump doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
- Published
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.
He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.
On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin in Dublin.
Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".
He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.
He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".
"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," he said
"It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together.
"That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree."
The president sidestepped a question about Scottish independence.
"I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.

  - Published18 hours ago
- What's next after Donald Trump's united Ireland comments? 
  - Published7 hours ago
The taoiseach said the president's remarks did not come as a "surprise" to him.
Speaking on Sunday at The Open, Martin referred to Trump asking about a "merger" of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland at an event in Washington during the Saint Patrick's Day celebrations, which some believed to be a comment on unity.
"He would make the point this is his view. He believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised," Martin said.
A major security operation is continuing for Trump's visit to Ireland.
He will leave from Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.
Protests continue against Trump visit
More than 10,000 people marched through Dublin on Saturday to show their opposition to the US president.
Others protesting against the visit have been arriving in buses to Doonbeg on Sunday, with about 100 protesters present.
A small crowd were moved from the president's hotel by Gardai (Irish police), Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting.
On Saturday evening, three women were arrested for trespassing on the golf links at Doonbeg and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court.
Rev Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, attended the anti-Trump protest in Doonbeg.
"I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus," he told BBC News NI.
Foster added: "As a church leader, it's important for me to be visible, and the church needs to be visible in this regard."
Foster said the "type of welcome he has been given sends out a terrible message".
Golf course is a 'massive employer'
However, others have praised Trump for the benefits and jobs his golf course brings to the local area.
Martin Kelly is a local businessman from Doonbeg and said the village is "very fortunate" to have the Trump International Golf Course.
"It's a massive employer here to be honest with you," he told BBC News NI.
"There's nothing else about here at that scale; they're very decent people to work for, they're very fair."
He said local people are "very proud" that the golf tournament is taking place there.
"We're not into politics here, we're into business. And it's a massive business to us. Doonbeg is one of the best links course in the world. Donald Trump isn't perfect but look he's not doing a bad job either.
"Hopefully Shane Lowry can win now with the help of God, and hopefully he can come to Doonbeg afterwards for a beer, I'll buy him one if he does."
Seoirse Comerford owns the Comerford bar in Doonbeg. He described the tournament as "unbelievable".
"If you look at the red double decker buses going up and down the street full of people, we never thought we would have seen the like of that."
He said the golf course is a big employer and is keeping Doonbeg "alive".
"Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back.
"Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course , it's a big boost to the local economy. You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here.
"I probably wouldn't have taken over the bar business other than the golf course being up there.
"We would have had 1,000 plus through the pub on Saturday night and the same Friday night, so there's a lot of people around the village, which is great to see."

Mumbai, Sep 13: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Sunday said BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce Uniform Civil Code (UCC) before 2029.
Shah was speaking to reporters here while highlighting the achievements of the Centre over the last 12 years and the BJP's 25-year journey under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership.
"Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029," Shah said. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.
He said the government had strengthened the country's criminal justice system through the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and claimed that several states had recorded a 30 per cent increase in the conviction rate in a single year.
He also said a system was being established to ensure justice could be delivered within three years.
On national security, Shah said the abrogation of Articles 370 and 35A had been achieved without a single drop of blood being shed or a bullet being fired, and asserted that Kashmir was now fully integrated with India.
He said the government had ended five decades of Naxalism and signed more than 14 peace agreements in the country's North-East region.
"More than 9,000 people have surrendered and today we have taken the North-East on the path of development," Shah said.
He said surgical strikes, air strikes and Operation Sindoor have established a policy of zero tolerance towards terrorism.
On being asked whether the 1951 baseline would be used for implementing National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Manipur, Shah said the Centre was holding discussions with its allies and political parties on the issue.
"We are discussing these issues with our allies and also with the political parties of Manipur. Whatever decision is taken, we will inform you," he said.
Asked about illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators and their detection in cities such as Mumbai, Shah said the government would not disclose the tools used to identify them.
"You are asking the Home Minister to make the tools public and tell you how it will be done. Then how will we catch them? They will also come to know," he quipped.
Shah reiterated the government's resolve to identify and deport illegal infiltrators from the country.
"I repeat our resolve that we will take out each and every illegal infiltrator from this country, identifying them one by one and sending them out," he said.
On the government's anti-drugs campaign, Shah said he had recently launched the 'Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan' and would visit every state as part of the campaign.
He said he had spoken to a chief minister the previous day and a full-day meeting would be held to ensure the campaign reaches the grassroots.
"It will definitely reach the grassroots and India will achieve victory over drugs," Shah said.

With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.
The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.
Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade
Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.
Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.
If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.
Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?
We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.
All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.
While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.
The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.
All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.
To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Apple has taken its time with its first foldable, enabling it to learn from the best folding phones already on the market. Eschewing the more prevalent book- and flip-style foldables, Apple has gone with a passport-sized form factor for the iPhone Duo, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current favorite). The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.
The iPhone Duo has a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating for solid dust and water resistance. But at 254 grams and 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded, the Duo is not the slimmest or lightest foldable around (the Fold8 is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded).
Foldables don’t have as much space for cameras, so the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). But it has room for the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.
Where Apple will likely add a lot of value to the foldable phone category is with its software design. Controls have been pushed to the side and stacked vertically to free up more screen real estate. Apps offer plenty of split-screen support, and transitions between displays look slick. Apple has also included features that take advantage of the fact that you can prop the Duo open on a table or nightstand, so there’s StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you.
Who it’s for: You want something different. You’re curious about folding phones or already convinced they’re great and can’t wait to experience Apple’s take.
The iPhone 18 Pro is similar to last year’s 17 Pro, with a 6.3-inch display, though the Dynamic Island has been slightly slimmed and can now show three Live Activities notifications at once. It keeps the same aluminum unibody, with Ceramic Shield on the back glass, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and an IP68 rating. Black is back, and there’s also a new Burgundy color, alongside Glacier and Silver. Those colors look more uniform than the 17 Pro’s two-tone finish.
Two standout upgrades stand out: the new A20 Pro chipset is faster and more power-efficient, and the main camera now has a variable aperture. The A20 Pro also enables better on-device AI and is aided by a redesigned vapor chamber to keep it cool while it works. Apple reckons you can expect 34 hours of video playback; that’s three hours more than the 17 Pro.
The camera introduces a physical lens aperture. Like the pupil of your eye, the aperture is the lens opening that lets light in. A bigger aperture can let in more light for better photos when it’s darker, and a smaller aperture can help you avoid overly bright photos when the sun is shining. But the aperture also impacts depth of field, so a bigger aperture can help you achieve that bokeh blurred background effect for a portrait photo, while a smaller aperture can help retain detail across a wider landscape shot. The camera app has new features and controls to help you take advantage of it.
Who it’s for: You don't want a big phone, but you want full-strength Apple silicon, a top camera, and all the latest features.
If foldables aren’t for you, the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the biggest screen you can get at 6.9 inches, and it is a battery-life beast. Apple says you can get up to 43 hours of video playback out of a full charge; that’s a six-hour increase on last year’s already impressive 17 Pro Max. It has the same design and colors as the regular Pro, just bigger.
You also get the new chip and variable aperture camera. Both Pro models now boast a versatile triple 48-megapixel camera system with pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. The class-leading video capture goes up to 4K at 120 fps. The iPhone 18 Pro phones are the right pick for photographers and videographers.
Who it’s for: You want the best Apple has to offer, including a big screen and long battery life, in a familiar form factor.
How to Get the iPhone 18 Unlocked
It makes sense to buy your iPhone unlocked, since it's much easier to switch carriers or use an international eSIM when you travel. The iPhones sold through Apple's storefront are unlocked, so Apple.com is the best place to buy them. During a preorder period, you can only purchase a newly announced iPhone from Apple.
Don't forget to take advantage of Apple's promotions: You get three free months of Apple One, which includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, Apple Arcade, News+, Apple Fitness+, and extra iCloud storage. Just watch out, because it will auto-bill you after the trial. Set a reminder to cancel if you don't want to continue subscribing to these services.
- The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256 GB
- The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256 GB
- The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256 GB
Apple has some financing options. If you have an Apple Card, you can pay for your iPhone over 24 months at 0-percent APR, and most carriers offer financing deals, too. Apple also offers Apple Upgrade, enabling you to lease your new iPhone from $35 a month for 24 months for the entry-model iPhone 18 Pro (12 months starts at $50 a month). We don’t think it’s a good deal, but if you’re tempted, remember you must return it in good condition (AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss costs an extra $15 a month).
