ఆల్ఫాజియో తన క్లైమేట్ రిస్క్ & రెసిలెన్స్ ఇండెక్స్ (CRRI)ను ఉపయోగించి ప్రపంచంలోని 72 అతిపెద్ద నగరాలను విశ్లేషించింది. ఈ సూచిక వరదలు, అధిక ఉష్ణోగ్రత, కరువు, కార్చిచ్చులు, తుఫాను గాలులతో సహా ఆరు భౌతిక వాతావరణ ప్రమాదాలను అంచనా వేస్తుంది. ఈ అధ్యయనం ప్రకారం, పాకిస్తాన్లోని హైదరాబాద్ 41 రెసిలెన్స్-అడ్జస్టెడ్ రిస్క్ (RAR) స్కోరును పొందింది, ఇది విశ్లేషించిన ప్రధాన నగరాల్లో ఆరు అత్యంత తక్కువ ప్రకృతి విపత్తును తట్టుకోగల నగరాల్లో ఒకటిగా నిలిచింది. అయితే, ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో భారతదేశంలోని హైదరాబాద్ ప్రపంచంలో రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా ఈ అధ్యయనం పేర్కొనలేదు.
అత్యధిక ప్రమాదం ఉన్న నగరాల జాబితాలో RAR స్కోరు 41తో అహ్మదాబాద్ (భారతదేశం) మొదటి స్థానంలో, 41తో హైదరాబాద్ (పాకిస్తాన్) రెండో స్థానంలో, 38తో ముల్తాన్ (పాకిస్తాన్) మూడో స్థానంలో, 36తో ఢాకా (బంగ్లాదేశ్) నాలుగో స్థానంలో, 35తో కోల్కతా (భారతదేశం) ఐదో స్థానంలో, 35తో లాహోర్ (పాకిస్తాన్) ఆరో స్థానంలో నిలిచాయి. మరోవైపు, RAR స్కోరు 8తో చికాగో అత్యంత తట్టుకునే సామర్థ్యం ఉన్న ప్రధాన నగరంగా మొదటి స్థానంలో నిలిచింది.
చివరిగా, ఆల్ఫాజియో అధ్యయనంలో ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా నిలిచింది  పాకిస్తాన్లోని హైదరాబాద్, తెలంగాణ రాజధాని హైదరాబాద్ కాదు.

Australia's largest proposed data centre could draw a quarter of Queensland's energy use
In short:
A proposed data centre at a feedlot in Queensland would have a total peak capacity of 2.16 gigawatts, equivalent to 1.5 million average Australian households.
The Western Downs Regional Council is considering the development application for the project, currently the largest proposed data centre in Australia.
What's next?
Experts say new energy generation assets need to be introduced as soon as possible to power the artificial intelligence boom.
This paddock is usually home to cattle, but it could host a hyper-scale data centre with the potential to increase Queensland's daily electricity use by 25 per cent.
The $31.9 billion data centre is proposed for the feedlot on the Western Downs, 250 kilometres west of Brisbane, in the heart of the state's coal seam gas country.
Singapore-based developer Zerra DC's proposed Western Downs Digital Park would have a peak capacity equivalent to 2.16 gigawatts (GW), a power draw comparable to 1.5 million average Australian households.
At the end of its four-phase rollout, it could draw about 47 gigawatt-hours (GWh) a day, significantly adding to Queensland's average daily energy consumption of 170GWh.
Put simply, it is an "enormous amount of energy" according to electro-mechanical engineer Andreas Helwig.
Zerra DC's application was submitted to the Western Downs Regional Council last month during a national debate about how to manage the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technology.
Dr Helwig said the project could be a test case of how to power the computing facilities.
"Getting this wrong will impact grid stability and cost to consumers," the associate professor at the University of Southern Queensland said.
Climate Finance Energy director Tim Buckley said the increase in power demand would need to be matched by investments into new energy generation, which could transform the regional and rural areas.
"The beauty of the land grab in the data centre gold rush that's underway right now is that capital is pouring in," Mr Buckley said.
Power play
It is early days for the Western Downs Digital Park.
The development application lodged with the local council could take years to be approved, and the data centre could take four to six years to build.
A Zerra DC spokesperson said the project would be well positioned among existing energy infrastructure, including three gas-fired power stations.
Solar and wind farms are nearby along with a major substation that acts as a "critical electrical junction" sending power to south-east Queensland and New South Wales.
The spokesperson said the digital park would connect directly to the substation rather than relying on Ergon Energy's local distribution to the small surrounding towns.
It comes as the federal government outlined plans for developers to use renewables as the national standard to power data centres, while Queensland and the Northern Territory governments pushed to use gas or coal.
Premier David Crisafulli has lobbied for an "energy-agnostic" approach to powering data centres, arguing that increased generation alongside the projects could decrease prices.
"By virtue of doing that, it can in fact help us drive down power prices," Mr Crisafulli said during a recent trip to the US, where he met with AI companies.
Mr Buckley said gas could play an "important small and declining" role in powering data centres, predominantly to back up renewable generation.
He said the climate science was "absolutely crystal clear" that relying on fossil fuels would backfire because of the cost and the impact on climate change.
"We need to embrace these industries of the future, but we've got to make sure they're not powered by industries of last century,"
Farmer cautious, mayor happy
An hour's drive south from the proposed site, cotton and grain grower Liza Balmain said she had witnessed the impacts of energy generation projects in the past.
Ms Balmain, a spokesperson for the anti-gas group Save Our Darling Downs, said many of her neighbours had lost farming viability because of the impact of coal seam gas drilling on their land and groundwater.
While she was not opposed to data centres, she said she wanted guidelines in place around what natural resources they would require.
"As we've seen with coal seam gas, it can fracture communities," she said.
She said leaders should learn from previous industrial booms.
"You have to question what is the long-term legacy benefits for the communities that are being expected to absorb those impacts,"
Western Downs Regional Council mayor Andrew Smith said the project was the dawn of a new era for the region.
While the Western Downs Digital Park will be subject to regulatory and environmental hurdles, his council will have a say on whether the project is approved locally.
He said the area was the "energy capital of Queensland" and well positioned for the project.
"We need to be looking ahead at what's going to sustain this region," he said.
"We've got a perfect mix of coexistence of ag [agriculture] and energy."
Cr Smith said conversations about community benefit agreements with the developer were already underway.

Jadavpur University (JU) saw night-long rampage and vandalism on August 20, when a mob, armed with sticks and rods, allegedly stormed the campus.
The violence followed a heated altercation late on August 19 between activists from the Akhil Bharaitya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) from the university’s engineering department and members of the Left-wing student outfit, Democratic Students’ Federation (DSF), and other student organizations. The ABVP alleged that its members were assaulted and that several workers required hospitalisation. Students from the engineering faculty disputed the claim and offered a counter-account of the incident.
By midnight, an armed mob allegedly entered the campus, apparently seeking to avenge the earlier altercation. The attackers tore down and set fire to placards, festoons and flags belonging to various student organisations active on the campus. The mob also surrounded Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building, trapping students inside.
The violence was captured by CCTV cameras installed across the university campus. Students and journalists also recorded several videos of the incident. Alt News accessed multiple such recordings and analysed them to establish the identities of those involved in the ruckus.
What happened at JU: A Blow-by-Blow Account
Around 9:30–10:30 pm on August 19, the DSF-run Faculty of Engineering & Technology Students’ Union (FETSU) held a general body meeting on the campus. The meeting had been announced through the union’s social media account.
ABVP and the allied Right-wing student outfit, Nationalist Students’ Front (NSF), opposed the meeting, citing a Calcutta high court ruling that no activities could be undertaken from student union offices until fresh student union elections were held. According to students present, ABVP and NSF members were outnumbered and were forced to leave the spot. A few DSF members were also injured in the ensuing scuffle.
Ayantik Pal, a third-year B Tech student who attended the meeting, said the GB meeting had been convened to elect signatories for the union’s email ID, Facebook account and bank account. Since the last FETSU election was held in 2020, he said, the meeting was intended to allow the union to continue its functioning.
According to Pal, ABVP activists at the meeting repeatedly objected that it was illegal. He said they nevertheless participated when names for the signatories were being proposed, before becoming agitated as the meeting progressed. They allegedly abused some students, calling them “Naxals” and “Maoists”, following which a scuffle broke out.
Accounts diverge over what happened immediately afterwards.
According to students, Nikhil Das, an ABVP research scholar and president of the organisation’s JU unit, attempted to enter the undergraduate and postgraduate students’ GB meeting and allegedly tried to provoke a confrontation. Students said they intervened to stop him, escalating the situation. They alleged that three DSF workers were injured in the assault by ABVP activists and that one was taken away towards the Sulekha Crossing. ABVP denied these allegations.
ABVP, meanwhile, claimed that Das was assaulted during the GB meeting and subsequently had to be hospitalised at KPC Medical College and Hospital. BJP MLA from Jadavpur Sarbari Mukherjee visited him at the hospital. Students alleged that during the visit, she threatened that ABVP and BJP workers would retaliate if those accused in the assault did not surrender. She later repeated this on camera.
Around midnight, a crowd of approximately 50–60 people gathered outside Gate 4 of the university, which is the only entrance that remains open at night. By around 12:30 am, the group entered the campus.
Pramita Basu, an undergraduate Philosophy student, said that after 7 pm, everyone entering the campus is required to show an ID card, including hostel residents. However, according to her, the crowd entered without being stopped by the guards stationed at the gate.
The group moved from Gate 4 towards the Science-Arts crossing, where some wall graffiti was allegedly damaged, before turning towards Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building. Videos from the night accessed by Alt News show some members of the group carrying saffron flags.
Meanwhile, students who had remained on campus after the earlier confrontation gathered inside Aurobindo Bhavan. According to them, they had decided to stay back until morning because they had heard that ABVP activists were looking for them outside the university.
Pal said an all-faculty GB meeting was also convened that night, with students from the arts, science and engineering faculties discussing what to do next. Around 12:30 am, he said, a university staff member alerted them that a mob had entered the campus and advised them to protect themselves.
“Within minutes, we saw a stream of mobile flashlights coming towards Aurobindo Bhavan from the side of the green zone. A few students present at the green zone were thrashed by this mob,” Pal said.
The students then woke the guards at Aurobindo Bhavan, obtained the keys and locked themselves inside, according to Pal.
The crowd that reached the building tried to break through its collapsible gates but failed. It then tore down red flags, festoons and posters belonging to student organisations and set them on fire outside the administrative building. Students trapped inside alleged that members of the crowd abused them verbally, threw stones and eggs at the building, and attempted to throw burning flags inside. Footage of the episode was broadcast live on television and recorded by students and journalists.
The violence continued until around 2 am. Around the same time, another group gathered outside Jadavpur police station and allegedly attempted to breach the entrance to the university’s main hostel, located next to the police station.
At the protest, ABVP West Bengal leaders were reportedly heard telling the media that the organisation was “putting the last nail in the coffin” of the “Dimagi Naxals” and would carry out “surgical strikes” at Jadavpur University to suppress them.
By around 2:30 am, the crowd had dispersed. The students who had taken shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan began leaving the campus at around 5 am.
Alt News procured a third CCTV footage from University sources, where several persons of interest can be spotted as present on the campus on the night of August 20.
The confrontation did not end with the dispersal of the mob.
Around noon the following day, the Student Federation of India (SFI) and other Left student organisations held a protest near the Lenin statue at Jadavpur 8B bus stand. Kolkata Police barricaded the area and stopped the protesters from proceeding towards the university. Around 2 pm, an ABVP rally that began from Golpark reached Gate 4 of the university. Students inside the campus also gathered in response. As Gate 4 was kept locked to prevent outsiders from entering, a face-off between the two groups on either side of the gate ensued.
During the confrontation, members of the ABVP crowd were seen standing on the historic university emblem designed by artist Nandalal Bose as they attempted to cross the closed gate and enter the campus.
Visuals of Rajyeshwar Sinha, a professor of Bengali at JU, holding the partially damaged University emblem went viral.

ABVP Denial
Directly denying any role of ABVP, the outfit’s central working committee (CWC) member Subhabrata Adhikary said on a talk show on ABP Ananda, that ABVP had no connection with the rampage at Jadavpur University on August 20. When pointed out by the anchor that people in the mob were holding ABVP flags, Adhikary said, “It doesn’t prove anything. SFI workers have done the vandalism while holding ABVP flags”. When asked if ABVP was condemning the night-long violence, he again said, “It is clear that ABVP has no connection with the incident.”
Talking to The Times of India, south Bengal ABVP secretary Neelkantha Bhattacharya, too, denied his presence during the campus violence. However, he then said, some of ABVP boys entered the campus “out of over-enthusiasm. The gate was open. We just pushed inside. I went at most 10 steps inside the university to get them out”.
Adhikary, on the other hand, contradicted his own statement on ABP Ananda, and told TOI, “I was standing right by the gate. I have no connection with the mob. After hearing about the situation, I went there to ensure that no untoward incident happened. ABVP has no involvement in any vandalism.”
CCTV and Video Footage Disprove ABVP Claims
Alt News examined CCTV footage from the intervening night of August 19-20 and identified several prominent ABVP faces and BJP-linked political figures on the campus.
1. Subhabarta Adhikary
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 (Captured by a camera fixed on the external wall of PG Arts building)
As the gate opens at 12.38.17 am, Adhikary is one of the first persons to enter the campus, followed by a crowd. When the group nears a large white SFI banner, he is seen saying something in an animated manner. Within seconds, others in the crowd tear down the banner. It is not clear whether he instructs them to do it or tries to dissuade them.
2. Neelkantha Bhattacharya
Visible in JU CCTV footage-2 (Captured by a camera installed on a pole at the science-arts crossing).
Around 12:40 am, Neelkantha Bhattacharya is seen carrying a rod or a stick while instructing a group. In the same footage, at the 12:39:22 am mark, Subhabrata Adhikary is seen next to him. They are in front of the PG science building. At 12:40:28, the two once again can be seen together. This time Bhattacharya is carrying sticks in both hands.
It is worth noting that Bhattacharyya first told TOI that he was not present on the campus. Then, he claimed, he had barely taken 10 steps inside the gate. The distance from Gate 4 to PG Science building, according to Google Maps, is over 360 feet, i.e., about 110 meters.
3. Somsurya Banerjee
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Banerjee, an NSF activist, is spotted on the campus around 1.14 am on August 20. Banerjee had earlier courted controversy by claiming that cows were slaughtered within the University during Iftar.
4. Aditya Mondal
Visible in footage captured by Mrittika TV, a local media outlet.
The portal captured the exact moment when the crowd entered the campus, in a livestream. Although the video was later deleted from the page, Alt News accessed the footage. In that video, (embedded in the story above) Aditya Mondal, the ABVP candidate for the recently held election to internal complaint committee (ICC) of the Arts Faculty, was spotted near the PG science building. The wall had an SFI graffiti, where a person was seen urinating on the Nazi Hakenkreuz. The writing next to it said, ‘Break Fascism with Red’. Mondal was seen with a group that tried to rub the symbol off. Mondal can be heard saying, “The left-naxals had insulted the symbol of India, Swastik. We are correcting it.”
5. Partha Chakraborty
Visible in the footage captured by students stuck inside Aurobindo Bhavan, during the rampage.
Partha Chakraborty, a Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM) worker from the Dhakuria area, was also present at the scene. In videos captured by the students stranded inside Aurobindo Bhavan, he was seen burning flags of SFI and other Left organizations in front of the collapsible gate of the building, and throwing the burning flags inside. Three days later, on August 23, he was seen with BJP’s losing candidate from Kasba assembly Sandeep Banerjee and South Kolkata Yuva Morcha leader Shatadru Ghoshal.
6. Abhijeet Roy (Raja)
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Another prominent face identified in the footage from that night is Abhijeet Roy alias Raja, the election agent of Jadavpur MLA Sarbari Mukherjee. In a video posted on social media, Roy was seen standing with a group outside Gate-4, with one member holding an ABVP flag. ABVP leader Neelkantha Bhattacharya is part of the group. Roy’s entry into the campus was also captured on CCTV footage. He is seen interacting with a group of men with former VC Buddhadeb Sau standing at an arm’s length.
7. Buddhadeb Sau
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3.
The most talked about entry on that eventful night was perhaps that of Buddhadeb Sau, professor of mathematics and ex-VC of the university. Sau’s presence raised eyebrows not only for the fact that it is unusual for an academic of his stature to be on the campus past midnight, but also because of his Sangh connections. He is associated with the RSS-backed Akhil Bhartiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), and represented the organisation at a joint press meet held by Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh JU unit, ABVP JU unit and ABRSM JU unit, held after the campus violence.
Sau can be spotted in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3. In the JU CCTV footage-1 feed, he is seen entering the campus through a side gate at 12:39:44 am, and exiting through the same gate at 12:44:35 am. For the entire duration, he stood in front of the security guards’ room, occasionally speaking to others. From 12:44:09 till his exit 26 seconds later, he is seen watching others tearing down what appears to be political flags put up on Gate-4.
Sau is seen once again in JU CCTV footage-3. This time he was captured by the camera installed on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4, at 1:06:33 am. This time also, he is seen standing in front of guards’ room.
Asked about his presence during the rampage, Sau told TOI, “I went to the spot as soon as I received news of the disturbance. No one from the authorities was present there. I was concerned. I told the police to get additional cops to manage any potential flare-up. Once the group retreated and the situation was brought under I returned to my quarters. I went and tried to protect the students; is that my crime?”

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv for the first time amid skepticism that Washington’s renewed peace outreach would end Russia’s four-and-half year old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
President Donald Trump’s hand-picked negotiators were greeted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the historic St. Sophia’s Cathedral in central Kyiv after arriving in the capital by train.
“There will be an opportunity for extensive discussion,” Zelenskyy said. “I thank Trump for allowing them to come.” Sunday’s talks will also include officials from the U.K., Germany and France, according to the Ukrainian leader, Zelenskyy said.

Speaking to India Today, former Indian Ambassador to China Ashok Kantha analyzed the state of bilateral relations following official discussions and statements. He dismissed notions of a breakthrough, stating, "I will not characterize it as a new dawn in India-China relations or a reset of relations." Kantha highlighted key differences in the diplomatic readouts from New Delhi and Beijing, noting that India treats peace and tranquility at the border as an essential prerequisite for normalization, whereas China seeks to advance relations on parallel tracks. He pointed out unresolved operational realities on the ground, such as reports of Chinese transgressions in Arunachal Pradesh and an absence of de-escalation. Furthermore, Kantha cited structural hurdles, including widening trade imbalances, Chinese decrees restricting technology transfers, China-Pakistan battlefield coordination during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, and unilateral hydropower dam construction in seismically active Tibet.
Chief Ministers from non-BJP and opposition-ruled states, including Karnataka, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu, did not attend the gala dinner hosted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi for BRICS leaders despite receiving invitations. Although there were indications until around 6:00 PM that some leaders might attend the 7:30 PM event, none showed up. While Chief Ministers from BJP-ruled states attended, the absence of opposition leaders emerges as a political flashpoint alongside a controversy over the all-vegetarian menu.
The Ministry of External Affairs has condemned an attack on the commercial vessel MT Al Gaya off the coast of Oman. Out of 14 Indian crew members on board, 13 have been rescued, while search and rescue operations continue for one missing Indian national. The Indian Embassy in Oman remains in contact with local authorities. The MEA reiterated its call for immediate de-escalation of tensions, dialogue, diplomacy, and the restoration of safe commercial navigation. The development comes as Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the urgent need to secure seafarers' networks during his address at the BRICS Summit and in interactions with global leaders.
In an interview on India First, former External Affairs Minister and senior Congress leader Salman Khurshid shared his assessment of India-China bilateral relations and border engagements. Responding to recent high-level dialogues, Khurshid underscored the necessity for domestic political consensus, stating, "If you can't take a conversation with the opposition further, how will you take a conversation with China any further?" He observed that overall relations have worsened over time and that diplomatic generalities are insufficient without candid communication. Regarding the massive trade imbalance between the two countries, Khurshid highlighted that the solution does not rest entirely with Beijing, urging India to take internal steps to address the deficit. While acknowledging positive developments such as resuming visas and flights to sustain people-to-people contacts, he emphasized that building sustainable ties requires sharing information, mutual trust, and actionable measures on both sides.
In an interview, former External Affairs Minister Salman Khurshid analyzed the outcomes of the BRICS Summit and the unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration. He noted that while progress has been made, India might have to look further, stating, "We may have to go beyond the declaration. We may have to go beyond BRICS to the larger diplomatic, diplomatic outreach that we have to continue." Khurshid addressed concerns over Pakistan not being named in the terror condemnation, explaining that multilateral declarations often work through consensus and diplomacy. Regarding foreign policy and global power dynamics, he questioned the concept of multi-alignment and emphasized that non-alignment provides nations the strategic freedom to engage as needed. He also stressed the importance of strengthening multilateral institutions by ensuring the voice of the Global South is represented in global platforms like the United Nations, IMF, and World Bank.

Man loses case to claw back $369,000 he spent on lavish gifts for ex-girlfriend
- Published
A Singaporean man has lost a court case to claw back hundreds of thousands of dollars that he had lavished on his ex-girlfriend while they were together.
The S$468,000 ($369,200; £273,260) that Chander Agarwal attempted to recover from Felicia Lee was money he had "willingly" spent on her, the Singapore High Court ruled.
Agarwal "displayed a consistent pattern of showering [Lee] with lavish gifts" even before they got together and would reassure her that he did not expect repayment, Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin said.
Agarwal, the CEO of a logistics company, met Felicia Lee, a former flight attendant, during a flight in 2019. They were in a romantic relationship from September 2022 to December 2023, the court heard.
Their relationship fell apart after Agarwal suspected Lee of having an affair.
Agarwal, who launched the suit in March 2024, argued that Lee had "requested various interest-free loans" from him over the course of their relationship.
He claimed that these included S$206,000 in credit card charges, S$129,000 for overseas trips, S$17,000 to engage a fengshui master for her apartment, and S$20,000 to pay for her life insurance premiums.
Lee argued that these were "gifts made out of love and affection" and not loans.
In agreeing with Lee, the judge noted that Agarwal's case lacked documentary evidence - for instance, he could not produce any proof that Lee had acknowledged receipt of the loans that she had allegedly requested.
"The evidence before me clearly shows that the claimant, smitten by the defendant, had showered her with expensive gifts during their relationship," the judge said.
"Unfortunately, when their relationship ended on a sour note, [Agarwal] became embittered and was determined to extract a price from her."
The judge also noted that Agarwal was "clearly a man of ample means who has expensive tastes", in contrast to Lee "who was not in that league".
In many text messages Lee had "expressed her awe when [Agarwal] suggested expensive gifts, and on occasion, her spontaneous reluctance to accept them", the judge noted.
In concluding his written judgement, the judge cited English playwright William Congreve, who wrote in his tragedy satire The Mourning Bride: "Heav'n has no rage, like love to hatred turn'd, nor hell a fury, like a woman scorn'd."
"This case shows that such emotion is not the sole province of one gender," he said.
In early 2023, another Singaporean man had filed two lawsuits – in claims amounting to over S$3m - against a woman who rejected his romantic advances.
K Kawshigan claimed that Nora Tan's rejection brought him emotional trauma and caused damage to his reputation.
The Singapore courts struck out his suits. Tan later counter-sued Kawshigan to claim back expenses she said she had incurred while defending herself from his alleged harassment.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" in recent months that AI needs to slow down. And rogue OpenAI agents are part of the reason.
Amodei cited the July Hugging Face breach, in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing environment to hack into the AI platform and then hide their tracks, as one of the catalysts for his heightened alarm.
"Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," he wrote in a blog post published Saturday.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Saturday that he agreed with Amodei. "We need to pace the frontier," he said on X. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."
Elon Musk, whose SpaceXAI competes with Anthropic and OpenAI, also backed Amodei's proposition on Saturday, writing in an X post, "Dario is right."
Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google's AI program, DeepMind, said on X that "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward." He reminded everyone that two months ago, he outlined his own vision for how AI should be developed and governed.
Amodei also cited the rapid advancement of AI in recent months and its increased capacity for "recursive self-improvement," which is essentially an AI model's ability to learn on its own.
Amodei proposed a three-step plan to slow down AI development to ensure the tech's safety "while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas."
Central to Amodei's plan is embedding independent safety evaluators inside frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, giving them "employee-like access" to the companies' systems and work.
"This is the key step for verifiability of any pacing commitments," Amodei wrote. "Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now."
In his X post, Altman said OpenAI would also implement third-party evaluators into its company. "We'll have more to share soon," he said.
The AI community has been in a furor this week after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon quit, issuing a public warning that AI agents could "kill us all by the end of the decade."
Coxon's warnings were shared widely and signal-boosted by other Anthropic employees, one of whom, the company's alignment science lead, said on X, "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!"
On Saturday, Coxon reposted Musk's "Dario is right" post. Earlier in the week, Musk accused Coxon of orchestrating a "setup."
OpenAI's chief scientist, meanwhile, also said in a blog post last week that leading AI labs need to coordinate a slowdown. "No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Jakub Pachocki said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reposted Pachocki's comments on X, calling it an "important post." Bloomberg reported this week that, during an employee meeting, Altman said OpenAI was willing to slow AI development in conjunction with rival labs.
In his Saturday essay, Amodei reiterated previous calls for the US government to intervene and establish guidelines for American labs. The Trump administration, so far, has resisted regulating the American AI industry to maintain its narrowing lead over Chinese AI labs.
Democratic lawmakers, for their part, proposed stringent legislation this week that would severely hamper AI development. Sen. Bernie Sanders, in a recent interview with MSNOW, said AI companies "need to stop right now."
Amodei and other leading AI researchers and engineers have not argued for a full stop to development. In his essay, Amodei said American AI labs should continue developing, just with more robust safeguards.
He said there remains a need to compete with China, and said the Trump administration could ensure this by not selling the rival the advanced chips needed to power AI models.
"The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Amodei said.

The presence of E. coli and coliform bacteria in bottled drinking water in Kochi, Keralam, has prompted authorities to take measures to address contamination risks and ensure water traceability. The Kochi Corporation is planning to make it mandatory for hotels to use only Kerala Water Authority (KWA) water, which would help ensure the use of safe water and enable traceability.
Chairperson of the Health Standing Committee Seena Teacher said the decision was taken after inspections found contamination in water used at some hotels.
“The idea is to make them use only KWA’s water, thereby ensuring the veracity of the source of the drinking water. We have plans to create a QR code for this, through which they can get water from the KWA using the My Kochi mobile application. We will also hold a meeting with the stakeholders to trace the source of the water and take necessary action,” said Ms. Seena.
The contamination was observed in the samples collected from eateries as part of the surprise checks carried out jointly by the Health Department, Kochi Corporation, Food Safety Department and police.
Food Safety Assistant Commissioner Jose Lawrence said that while inspections are periodically carried out at the water bottling units in the city, the presence of E. coli was not observed. “We carry out checks in packaged drinking water (water bottles) from random locations. In this light, we will focus more on the cans as well. We recently received a complaint from the Kalamassery area about fungal growth in a can from a supplier. Test results are awaited,” said Mr. Lawrence.
The most probable number (MPN) of coliform bacteria detected in the samples ranged from 17 per 100 ml to 1,600 per 100 ml. According to experts, the MPN should be zero in drinking water and the high MPN values indicate faecal contamination and render the water unfit for human consumption.
More checks sought
According to Kerala Hotels and Restaurants Association (KHRA) representatives, more inspections need to be carried out to find the source of contamination.
KHRA State president G. Jayapal said that only packaged water with Indian Standards Institute (ISI) marking is used in hotels. “We will be directing all hoteliers to procure water from reputed agencies,” said Mr. Jayapal.
Not dismissing the chances of such contaminated drinking water cans entering into households, Consortium of Flat and Villa Owners Association, Kerala State chairperson Saju Abraham said awareness among the end user was crucial.
“While KWA’s water is used in apartment complexes, a significant percentage of the residents rely on canned water. Tracing the source of the water used by these agencies as well as tankers is important,” said Mr. Abraham.

NEET to move to computer-based test ‘very soon’, says NTA DG: ‘It’s the future'
NTA director general Abhishek Singh said the Nandan Nilekani-led high-powered task force was “working on it.”
National Testing Agency director general Abhishek Singh said the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) will be moving to a computer-based mode “very soon”, adding that it is “the future.”
“All our examinations are CBT (Computer-Based Test) except the NEET examination. On NEET also, we will be moving to CBT very soon,” Singh told news agency ANI. He added that the Nandan Nilekani-led high-powered task force was also “working on it.”
Speaking on CBT, Singh said it requires augmenting the testing infrastructure and “building the safeguards.” “So that is the future,” the NTA director general added.
“Currently, the JEE examination, the UGC-NET examination, the CUET examinations, the NIFT examinations are all done in CBT. So CBT is the future. All our examinations will be CBT in the days to come,” he stated.
The high-powered task force (HPTF), led by Infosys co-founder Nilekani, was constituted in the aftermath of the 36-day student agitation in Delhi's Jantar Mantar and other parts of the country against alleged irregularities in NEET. The protests led to the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, with the Centre also announcing steps to reform the examination system.
‘Cross-border examinations are the next step’: NTA DG
NTA director general Singh projected cross-border examinations as “the next step”.
“Our endeavor right now is to improve our systems so that we are able to conduct Indian examinations in a fair and transparent manner without any malpractice or without any error or without the need of having any review of our own systems,” Singh told ANI.
He added that once the domestic systems are strengthened, the NTA would look towards “conducting examinations for other global bodies.”

When asked about how BRICS countries can collaborate on securing question paper technology, Singh said, “There are multiple ways. Every country faces this challenge. It's not that examinations are conducted only in India; examinations are conducted globally.”
He highlighted China's pen-and-paper examination Gaokao, saying “a lot was heard” about it. “A lot has been heard about how they shut down whole cities and conduct the examination. So, every examination will require generation of question papers,” the NTA official stated. He added that there were areas of discussion and collaboration between the BRICS countries in terms of examinations.
Singh said that the NTA was also looking at the use of artificial intelligence not just for testing but also to prevent fraud. “Not with the BRICS partners, but we are currently looking at use of AI for conducting not only testing but also fraud prevention, trying to look at logs, trying to look at data, trying to look at analytics in order to ensure that the examinations are conducted without any error or without any problems,” he told ANI.

Iliman Ndiaye says "you don't say no" when Manchester City come calling, and playing in the Champions League is where he belongs.

Despite Everton finishing in the bottom half of the table in his two seasons at the club, Ndiaye became a fans' favourite for his skills on the flanks and scoring 17 goals.
"When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her that if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League," he said.
"It was difficult to leave Everton. I created a great connection with the fans and the players there, but we have to move on sometimes and it's how football is."

The Spectacle of 1980s Hollywood
Jackie Collins wrote flashy Hollywood thrillers, but isn’t often thought of as a canonical Los Angeles writer.
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
Jackie Collins, who wrote flashy, sex-filled Hollywood thrillers, isn’t often thought of as a canonical Los Angeles novelist. I didn’t regard her as one, at least—until I read Sophie Gilbert’s essay about Collins, the latest entry in The Atlantic’s series “The Writer’s Way.” Collins wrote shiny 1980s “bonkbusters,” as one critic called them; in her novels, including her breakthrough, Hollywood Wives, she turned gossip about scheming producers and backbiting socialites into gripping, soapy dramas long before reality shows made such stories commonplace. Until I learned more about these works, they felt to me like a surface treatment of the complex city best captured by Raymond Chandler, Joan Didion, Octavia Butler, and Eve Babitz. It didn’t help that they were set in Beverly Hills, which, in my nearly five years living in L.A., I knew mostly as a nexus of unaffordable baubles and posh podiatrists’ offices. But Gilbert’s exploration of the writer and the enclave made me realize that her novels fit right into the city’s long literary tradition.
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
In addition to creating steely characters who advanced the idea of middle age as a woman’s powerful prime, Collins was a “devoted” fan of Mickey Spillane, the hardest of hard-boiled-detective novelists, and the influence of noir comes through in her treatment of Beverly Hills: “Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky,” Gilbert writes, “but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation.” Beneath the shimmering surfaces, dark shadows always lurked.
“Sunshine or Noir?” Mike Davis asked in his nonfiction masterpiece about Los Angeles, City of Quartz. The binary of light and dark is ingrained in the L.A. canon; it animates not only Chandler’s literary potboilers, but also Babitz’s sad-girl stories, Butler’s numinous dystopias, and Didion’s alienated meditations. Collins was, like these writers, an insider with an outsider’s soul. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told an interviewer (while sitting poolside at her stark-white mansion, mind you). “I move in it. I’m an observer.”
Gilbert does some observing of her own as she roams Jackie’s neighborhood—she refers to her by first name, like a friend—and she discovers that the city has changed a great deal since Collins’s time. The author captured a different Hollywood, before it was supplanted by “brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails,” before celebrity became “its own art form.” L.A. in the 2020s requires a new kind of best seller, and the city still produces them. This summer in The Atlantic, Carolyn Kellogg wrote about the work of Angeleno Jordan Harper, whose latest novel, A Violent Masterpiece, concerns a TMZ-style celebrity videographer and a plotline ripped from the Epstein files. Steph Cha, Gary Phillips, and Ivy Pochoda “are also bringing today’s Los Angeles, in all its awful, beautiful chaos, to life on the page,” Kellogg notes. Their books don’t repudiate the existence or value of Collins’s 1980s spectacle: They’re proof that L.A. is constantly evolving, and also that it is perennially, insistently itself.
Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
By Sophie Gilbert
The novelist imagined women enjoying equality in the bedroom and the boardroom. Are we any closer to living in that world?
What to Read
Guilty Pleasures, by Arielle Zibrak
The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity. She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret, along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down. So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads. — Sophia Stewart

A Great Novel Becomes a Bad Show
By Jeremy Gordon
For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom. The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero, an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles. It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book. Nevertheless, Ellis’s renown skyrockets. By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers (American Psycho, The Rules of Attraction) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

This week, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), prodded by the Supreme Court, proposed a simple but overdue idea. Packaged foods high in fat, salt, or sugar should carry a bold red warning on the front of the pack, not buried in fine print on the back. Someone picking up instant noodles, a breakfast cereal, or a “health drink” will finally be told, at a glance, that it is not as wholesome as its advertising claims. This is a welcome step. It is also, on its own, nowhere near enough.
The number of children presenting with morbid obesity and diabetes has climbed sharply within just a few years. The World Obesity Atlas 2026 bears this out — 41 million Indian children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 are now overweight or obese. This is not just because children are eating more; it is about what they are being sold. Breakfast cereals, sweetened yoghurts, and “health drinks” are marketed to parents as filling gaps in a child’s diet, emphasising “energy” and vitamins while saying little about the sugar content inside. In 2024, a leading multinational was found adding sugar to infant food sold in India and other lower income countries; sugar was left out of the same product in Europe. When a health drink, popular in Indian homes, turned out to be nothing more than flavoured sugar syrup, it took a social media storm, and not a regulator, to force the company to prescribe a 15% cut in its added sugar.
The problem is worse around schools and colleges, where studies show that the cheapest, most easily available snacks are also the least healthy. A popular “energy drink” among teenagers, priced at just ₹20, packs close to 17 grams of sugar, caffeine, and artificial colour into a single bottle. Its label says it is not meant for children, yet nothing stops a child from buying it. This is the market pricing unhealthy calories to fit within the range of a child’s pocket money.
Need for enforcement
None of this is a secret. What has been missing is enforcement. The FSSAI and the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) have long recommended what schools should not sell, but optional rules get treated as optional, and canteens stock whatever sells cheapest. A red warning label only works if it is actually enforced.
Moreover, the new rule stops at the edge of organised retail. Most of India’s sugar, salt, and trans fat is eaten unbranded, from street stalls, dhabas, and sweet shops that make up the unorganised sector, none of which is required to declare anything. A red label on a biscuit packet does nothing about the jalebi sold loose beside it. Regulation that reaches only packaged food leaves the unregulated half of the plate untouched.
Then there is the conversation India keeps avoiding — a tax on sugar. When the U.K. introduced its soft drinks industry levy, sugar consumption among both children and adults fell. Manufacturers reformulated their drinks to slip below the tax threshold rather than raise prices. A well-designed sugar tax does not just discourage people from buying a product, it pushes the industry to make the product itself less harmful.
India already taxes sugary drinks heavily; just not usefully. Since September 2025, aerated and sweetened beverages, sugar free versions included, were folded into one 40% GST slab — so a ‘normal’ cola and its zero-sugar counterpart pay the same tax, leaving manufacturers with no reason to cut sugar. The U.K.’s levy worked differently, taxing drinks in tiers by sugar content, so that companies could lower their bill by reformulating the product. India could tax products in the same way so that manufacturers have a reason to cut sugar.
The standard objection — that such a tax would hit the poor the hardest — is not wrong, but it is only half the argument. Unregulated, cheap sugar already extracts a heavy price from the poor, who bear the brunt of the diabetes, hypertension and childhood obesity epidemic that sugar heavy diets drive, with the least means to treat it. Doing nothing is not neutral; it is a slower, costlier tax, paid in ill health rather than rupees at the till. The answer is to design the tax calibrated to sugar content so that it nudges reformulation, with part of the revenue set aside to make healthy food cheaper.
The FSSAI’s proposed red label is a genuine, if belated, first step. What India needs now is the resolve to finish what it has started — mandatory food standards; limits on how unhealthy food is marketed to children; rules that reach the unorganised sector; and an honest debate on taxing sugar in a way that protects families with the least room to absorb either cost, the tax, or the disease.
Dr. Praveen George Paul is Assistant Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology and Metabolism, Department of Pediatrics, Christian Medical College, Vellore. Dr. Vandana Jain is Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology Division, Department of Pediatrics, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)

The Best Robot Lawn Mowers
Featured in this article
Lawn care is a monotonous, thankless task. Who wants to mow the lawn when you could be lollygagging in a hammock with a cold drink, watching a robot do it for you? That’s right: no one. Robot lawn mowers were once the preserve of the wealthy, and yes, they can still be on the pricey side. But they’re getting cheaper and better all the time.
I’ve tested a handful of the best robot lawn mowers over the past three years, and after comparing a fresh crop this mowing season, I'm delighted to tell you that robot mowers are actually good now. I've got some recommendations, honorable mentions, and a list of robot mowers you should avoid. Read on for everything you need to know about lawn-tending bots.
Updated September 2026: I added mowers from Roborock, Segway, Eufy, and Sunseeker, added information about night mowing to the FAQ, and updated prices.
Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked
Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.
After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.
Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick, and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day, and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.
It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).
Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and twenty minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.
It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell
Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.
Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.
Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.
Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.
Avoid These Mowers
Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.
EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.
Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.
How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work?
Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall).
They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum.
What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower?
There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard.
Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines.
There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance.
- Satellite: Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.
- Light Detection and Ranging (lidar): This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.
- Cameras: Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
- Wire boundary: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.
- Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically.
Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket.
To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close.
How Noisy Are Robot Mowers?
Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command.
Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather?
Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models.
How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut?
Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough.
It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible.
Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself?
Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut.
Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night?
Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk.
How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers
I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.
