In September 2026, a rumor circulated online about a black bear that apparently took a wounded raccoon, and later a wounded fox, to a wildlife center where the bear itself had been treated.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) said:
The first time, nobody believed it. Security cameras at a wildlife center captured a black bear approaching a rear entrance carrying a wounded raccoon in its mouth. It placed the animal gently beside the door. Then disappeared into the woods.
[…]
Several weeks later, cameras recorded a bear approaching a side entrance with an injured fox. Same careful approach. Same gentle placement near the door. Same quiet exit into the trees.
Both animals were found alive and received treatment.
Workers compared the two recordings. Both bears had the same unusual white mark on their chest. Same bear. Two deliveries. Two injured animals brought to the one place that could help them.
Staff searched old photographs and records of bears previously treated at the facility. That's when everything clicked.
Years earlier, the same bear had been rescued, treated at that very wildlife center, and released back into the wild. He had been a patient there. And now he was bringing patients back.
Officials believe the bear remembered where it had once been helped and returned because it somehow understood that injured animals would be safe there.
Other Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same text. The black bear story also appeared in a YouTube short (archived).
Snopes readers sent emails and searched the website wondering whether the story was true.
There's no evidence supporting the rumor that a black bear took a wounded raccoon and a fox to a wildlife center it had previously received treatment at. It was posted online by a page with a history of posting heartwarming — though fictitious — animal stories generated with artificial intelligence tools.
As such, we've rated this claim false.
We searched Google for "bear brought raccoon to wildlife center" and "bear brought fox to wildlife center," and also searched DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo using the same phrases. None of the searches yielded credible evidence supporting the story's veracity.
Snopes also used Google Lens to conduct a reverse image search on multiple different images posted alongside the story purportedly taken at the unidentified wildlife center.
That search revealed the story appeared to originate from the Facebook page StoryTime, which posted (archived) prior to the other social media posts linked in this fact check.
StoryTime's history
Snopes has been fact-checking StoryTime's animal rumors for more than a year. The page frequently posts fictitious, AI-generated animal stories supported by AI-generated images that are usually purposefully grainy and/or blurry, all meant to generate clicks because of their surprising or heartwarming nature.
At one time, the intro section on StoryTime's Facebook page read, "story (noun) - an account of imaginary or real people and events told for entertainment." At present, the page's intro section reads, "Animal rescue storytelling from around the world 🌎🐾 Real moments, inspired stories, and emotional second chances ❤️."
Facebook users can subscribe to the page using real money, which gives the page incentive to continue pumping out the animal stories it's known for, regardless of their reality.
AI-generated text
StoryTime's version of the claim begins with the headline "Wildlife Center Releases Statement After Bear Saves Two Injured Animals." StoryTime, much like the other Facebook pages telling the story, doesn't name the wildlife center or the worker quoted, or describe any geographic details about where these events took place. (Even without those identifiers, the wildlife center's statement, which isn't directly quoted in the post, should have showed up in search engine results, if real.)
When we input the text of StoryTime's version of the claim and that of another version of it into Pangram, which is widely considered the most reliable AI-text detection tool available as of this writing, it concluded that 100% of both versions were written or assisted by AI.
It's important to note that even the best AI detection tools can be fallible. Snopes cautions against using them to find definitive answers on the authenticity of texts or images without additional corroborating evidence.
AI-generated images
Each of the four Facebook posts linked in this story uses a different pair of images of the black bear carrying the raccoon and fox to the wildlife center, which is already a major red flag for the tale's authenticity.
In one version, the size of the object at the bottom left of the building's wall is sized differently in the pair of images presented.
In another version, the building is different in each of the two images presented. The bottom of the pair appears to depict a door opening inward from the right even though the door's handle is on its left side.
In a third version, the building and its door are once again inconsistent from one image to the other.
In StoryTime's version, neither the building, the stone patio nor the gravel-covered grounds around the building are the same between the pair of images.
The general lack of consistency between images is a telltale sign of AI generation, as artificial intelligence tools usually generate each image from scrap and therefore sometimes struggle in keeping details consistent when trying to emulate multiple images of the same place.
StoryTime does not keep its DMs open, leaving Snopes unable to contact the page for comment. StoryTime has not replied to past attempts by Snopes to contact the page's administrators, either.

Opener may not have to be specialist - Trescothick
- Published
England's Test opener does not necessarily have to be a specialist at the top of the order, according to Marcus Trescothick.
England have a decision to make over how to accommodate Jacob Bethell when he returns from a knee injury for the tour of South Africa in December.
Emilio Gay, in his first summer as a Test cricketer, has opened alongside Ben Duckett. Gay has made three half-centuries, though he ends the season with an average below 25.
Duckett, one of England's senior players, made the team's only century of the summer, against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June. However, the 31-year did not reach 20 in the three-match series against Pakistan and averages less than 24 since the beginning of the Ashes.
Jordan Cox has impressed as Bethell's replacement at number three. After finally making his debut this summer, Cox has averaged more than 42 and opened in first-class cricket early in his career.
Bethell has been touted as a potential opener and has moved up to open in England's one-day team.
The other new member of England's top six for the Pakistan series, Dan Lawrence, may be exempt from conversations over who is squeezed out because of the off-spin he offers, though Bethell's return would also bring some left-arm spin.
Trescothick has been England's interim coach for the Pakistan series and will now hand the reins to New Zealander Stephen Fleming, who is due to travel to the UK in the coming days to begin planning for the trip to South Africa.
"You generally want your best top seven, however that looks," said Trescothick. "Who that's going to be, I don't know. That's for someone else to work out."
Trescothick is one of England's most successful Test openers and was part of the team that famously won the 2005 Ashes. The former Somerset man believes the game is different to when he ended his 76-Test career in 2006.
"I reckon times have changed a little bit," said the 50-year-old. "I think you look at your best batting line-up, however that fits up.
"If that's with a specialist opener, great. If not, I think you can plan around it in this day and age. Players adapt pretty quickly because they're chopping and changing formats."

Fleming was appointed England's new Test coach in July, yet he missed the 3-0 series win against Pakistan.
The former New Zealand captain will now arrive for meetings with the England hierarchy.
He is expected to watch some of England's white-ball series against Sri Lanka, with the ODI and T20 teams still led by Fleming's fellow Kiwi and good friend Brendon McCullum. Fleming could also visit some of the counties.
When McCullum was in charge of both the Test and white-ball teams, he kept the same backroom team across formats, including Trescothick as an assistant.
However, it now looks likely that the staff will be reorganised. Former Australia batter Mike Hussey said he was approached by Fleming, though it has been reported down under that Hussey has declined.
Trescothick said he has not got clarity on his future role. He confirmed he has a preference but declined to reveal it.
"It's probably best I don't mention it at the moment because it may not be the case of what happens," he said. "I love doing both formats. It's brilliant and I've been privileged to be in the position of assistant coach."
Trescothick will be joined on England's staff by former team-mate Kevin Pietersen, who has been appointed as a consultant for the white-ball team.
Pietersen, one of the most flamboyant and innovative batters to play for England, returns to the national team 12 years after he was effectively sacked following the 5-0 Ashes defeat in 2013-14.
The 46-year-old's first day back in the England set-up is on Sunday, joining preparations for the first T20 against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday.
"We've spoken already, to plan a little bit," said Trescothick. "I gave him a couple of things that I wanted him to look at, to get his advice on.
"He is buzzing. Putting back on the shirt or the tracksuit, he is buzzing for that opportunity.
"Having his presence around and the knowledge he has about batting – he sees batting in a different light to many different people. If we can tap into that, it's only going to benefit the team."

Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s $20m Brisbane mansion after fundraising events held for One Nation, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On one occasion, Joyce conducted a live television interview with Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from a room that appears to be a bedroom in Rinehart’s home.
The interview took place on Monday 13 April, the morning after a fundraising event at the mining magnate’s house on the banks of the Brisbane River in Hawthorne.
The new details underscoring the depth of the relationship between Australia’s richest person and One Nation have been revealed in the first episode of the Guardian’s new podcast about the party, The Populist, released on Monday.
Parliamentary expenditure records show that Hanson and Joyce declared flights on 13 April courtesy of Hancock Prospecting, with flight-tracking data showing that the pair flew on Rinehart’s luxury Gulfstream jet from Brisbane to Sydney that afternoon.
The accommodation at Rinehart’s home has not been declared to the parliament, which has rules in place mandating that gifts or hospitality valued at more than $300 – or any interest “where a conflict of interest with a [parliamentarian]’s public duties could foreseeably arise or be seen to arise” – should be declared.
The guidelines state that “hospitality” refers to “free or concessional accommodation” provided to the MP, the MP’s spouse or partner or dependent children “wholly or partly by any person, organisation, business or interest group or foreign government or its representative”.
The provision of meals or accommodation excludes “hospitality provided in a purely social way by friends or colleagues”, but the guidelines are designed to place on the public record interests that may conflict, or be seen to conflict, with an MP’s public duty.
Joyce told Guardian Australia that Rinehart “was a long-term friend over decades not a motel”.
“When I stay with family or friends they don’t charge me, nor do I see it as work,” he said.
“I will never be ashamed of doing the research to do a better job.”
Guardian Australia can also reveal that Hanson has been using one of Rinehart’s bodyguards for her personal security.
The man, who has been seen escorting Hanson in Perth and Canberra, has been one of Rinehart’s closest bodyguards for more than a decade.
The New South Wales supreme court heard in 2013 that Rinehart had asked the bodyguard to offer one of her daughters, Bianca Rinehart, a $25m loan to pull out of a court battle contesting the family trust. The offer was rejected.
According to his LinkedIn, the man works as a security manager with an undeclared company but a post from 2023 shows him listed as an employee of Hancock Energy. It is unclear if he remains employed by Hancock Prospecting.
Guardian Australia has previously reported multiple breaches of Senate rules, with One Nation failing to declare flights gifted by Hancock Prospecting to Hanson going back to August last year.
The fresh details of the company’s financial support for One Nation come despite Hanson telling reporters in February she was not being funded by Rinehart, and after the party’s national director, James Ashby, said in December last year: “We have not seen any money from her.”
The Labor senator Murray Watt criticised Hanson for failing to disclose the links between her party and Rinehart, including the undeclared flights.
“I think that the lengths that she and her colleagues have gone repeatedly to conceal donations, staffing matters, all sorts of other things about their operations, it does make you think that there’s something to hide,” Watt told the Guardian.
“In a democratic system like Australia, there is a responsibility of politicians to be transparent about decision making, about their operations, and again Pauline Hanson seems to want to get all the benefits of power without any of the responsibilities of power.
“The level of concealment that goes on suggests a guilty conscience.
“I think that one of the reasons that One Nation goes to such efforts to conceal their financial gain from Gina Rinehart and her companies is because there is such a close alignment between what Gina Rinehart and Hancock want to see happen and One Nation’s policies.”
One Nation did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia.
A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting said: “Donations will be disclosed in accordance with applicable laws and reporting requirements.”

Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof studied how muscles use chemical energy to contract and recover. Hill measured the heat produced by working muscles, while Meyerhof traced the relationship between oxygen consumption and lactic acid metabolism. Their work earned them the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The prize was divided equally. Hill was recognised “for his discovery relating to the production of heat in the muscle”, while Meyerhof was recognised “for his discovery of the fixed relationship between the consumption of oxygen and the metabolism of lactic acid in the muscle”. The prize was awarded for 1922 but presented in 1923 because the Nobel Committee had initially decided that no 1922 nomination met the required criteria.
Measuring muscle heat
Hill approached muscle physiology as a problem in physics as well as biology. Working largely with frog muscles, he developed precise methods for measuring the very small amounts of heat generated during contraction.
The changes were tiny. In one experiment described in his Nobel lecture, a single contraction of a frog’s sartorius muscle at 20°C raised its temperature by no more than about 0.003°C. Hill used sensitive instruments and carefully controlled contractions to separate heat produced during activity from heat generated during recovery.
His measurements showed that heat production did not end when the muscle stopped contracting. A second phase, which Hill called recovery heat, continued after contraction and depended on oxygen. When oxygen was removed, this recovery heat was abolished.
This was important because it showed that the energy changes associated with muscle contraction and recovery occurred in distinct phases rather than as one continuous process.
Meyerhof traces the chemistry
Meyerhof investigated the chemical side of the same problem. In experiments on frog muscle, he measured heat production and oxygen consumption and followed the conversion of carbohydrates into lactic acid.
He showed that during muscle activity, lactic acid was formed from carbohydrate. During recovery, some of the lactic acid was oxidised while the remainder was converted back into carbohydrate. These observations helped establish the relationship between oxygen use and lactic acid metabolism for which he received the Nobel Prize.
Meyerhof’s work went further. Between 1918 and 1922, he provided evidence that glycogen was converted into lactic acid when oxygen was absent. He also found that only a fraction of the lactic acid produced during anaerobic muscle activity was subsequently oxidised in the presence of oxygen, with much of the remainder being reconverted to glycogen.
Two sides of muscle metabolism
Hill and Meyerhof were investigating different aspects of the same physiological problem. Hill measured the physical consequences of muscle activity -- heat, work and energy expenditure. Meyerhof examined the associated chemical reactions.
Their findings connected the physical and chemical sides of muscle metabolism. Hill’s measurements of recovery heat could be explained by Meyerhof’s observations on lactic acid and oxygen consumption. Hill himself acknowledged that Meyerhof’s biochemical work helped complete the picture that physical measurements alone could not provide.
A link to modern metabolism
Meyerhof’s research contributed to the emerging understanding of glycolysis, the pathway through which cells break down glucose and other sugars to obtain energy.
His observations also led to what became known as the Pasteur-Meyerhof effect: respiration can suppress the breakdown of carbohydrates through glycolysis. His work provided early evidence that energy transformations in living cells could involve cyclical processes, an idea that became important in the development of modern intermediary metabolism.
The terminology and biochemical models have since changed substantially. Muscle metabolism is now understood to involve multiple pathways and energy carriers, including ATP, rather than being explained simply through lactic acid.
An interesting part of Meyerhof’s scientific career is that he did not remain committed to every interpretation that emerged from his early work.
The discovery of creatine phosphate in 1926 led him to question the idea that lactic acid itself was directly responsible for supplying the energy required for muscle contraction. He subsequently revised aspects of the model that had become associated with his work.
The Nobel recognition
Hill and Meyerhof delivered their Nobel lectures on December 12, 1923. Hill’s lecture was titled The Mechanism of Muscular Contraction, while Meyerhof’s was titled Energy Conversions in Muscle.
Their work established quantitative approaches to studying muscle metabolism, bringing together measurements of heat, mechanical work, oxygen consumption and chemical changes.
More than a century later, the details of muscle energy metabolism are understood in far greater molecular detail. But Hill’s measurements of heat and energy and Meyerhof’s work on oxygen, glycogen and lactic acid were important steps in establishing muscle as a system whose mechanical activity could be linked to measurable chemical and thermodynamic processes.

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
“What on earth are they building all of these data centers for?” an exasperated friend asked me recently.
They’re not the only one asking: We got several similar questions on our recent data center livestream. It’s a really reasonable thing to wonder about. After all, if AI is already making all these breakthroughs, why are tech companies taking on billions of dollars of debt and constructing some of the biggest power plants in the world to build even more data centers?
The answer isn’t to help the average user search for recipes or look up places to visit on a vacation; simple chatbot queries are an increasingly outdated way of thinking about how AI works. Now, AI is all about agents—there’s no official definition, but roughly speaking, agents are large language model-based systems designed to make autonomous decisions to execute a task—and the shift towards them is part of what’s driving Silicon Valley’s power buildout.
“Rather than asking an AI chatbot a simple question and answer, these agents can give themselves hundreds of small prompts based on a user’s original question,” says my colleague Maxwell Zeff, who writes the weekly Model Behavior newsletter. “For example, if someone asked an AI agent to build them a website, it might run for hours to build out features, re-prompting itself dozens of times in the process to build different web pages, menus, and datasets that power the thing.”
Agents are now at the heart of the frontier labs’ work on AI. They’re doing some astounding—and terrifying—things. Recently, OpenAI announced that a swarm of more than 10,000 agents sending 2.7 million messages had solved a longstanding math problem. (Mathematicians pushed back on the company’s claims.) While this is an outlier—AI labs are highly committed to solving supposedly unsolvable problems, and willing to throw unusual amounts of resources into doing so—all those messages burned through a lot of processing power. That equates to a lot of energy: probably tens of millions of dollars’ worth, Max tells me, though how much exactly is tough to say.
Private AI companies have historically been choosy about what to disclose when it comes to environmental metrics around their products. Many CEOs often point to single queries made by individuals as a measure of resource use. In a recent podcast interview, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman claimed that the water use needed to harvest a single almond amounted to 38,000 ChatGPT queries. (The calculation has been disputed.)
“The people that are scarfing down 12 almonds at a time don't feel like they're doing something horrible from a water perspective for the most part,” he said.
Introducing AI agents, which are much more energy-intensive than simple queries, into the picture makes these calculations a lot more complex. There’s a major dearth of information around the energy use of agents, whose tasks can range from simple jobs to a full day of autonomous coding involving a team of parallel “helper” agents. There’s a massive gulf in power use between these applications—and a potentially limitless expansion as tasks get more complex.
“In other technological growth areas, we're constrained by how many people are driving a car or streaming Netflix,” says Boris Gamazaychikov, the co-founder and CEO of Sustainable AI, a research and advisory group. “Now, this stuff is kind of decoupled from users—and if you listen to AI leaders, I think that’s what they want. They’re talking about unicorns that have one employee.”
Well, one human employee. In that imagined world, there could be hundreds or even thousands of AI agents working in the background. I don’t want to debate the odds of that happening, but suffice to say that’s the future AI companies are working toward—and it helps to explain the rush to build data centers.
With little reliable data coming from the companies about their energy use, some AI enthusiasts are trying to do the math themselves. Last month, climate scientist Zeke Hausfather authored a blog post calculating how much energy his own AI use—which leans heavily on agents—consumes. He used a variety of different sources to work out that his average daily Claude session may consume more than the energy needed to power two refrigerators. (Gamazaychikov, whose group will release research later this month with more precise calculations around the environmental footprint of agents running on closed models, noted that Hausfather made a good effort, but that his math was based on somewhat outdated findings. That’s unsurprising, given how little academic work there has been done on this topic and how opaque tech companies are when it comes to disclosing emissions metrics.)
Hausfather concludes that in the grand scheme of his personal life, his AI use being on par with keeping a few spare fridges running isn’t a world-ending number. But this AI use “also represents a net new source of emissions, at a time when global temperatures are skyrocketing and our emissions reduction goals are increasingly off track,” he writes. And it’s a lot bigger than the fraction-of-an-almond-sized numbers Altman is throwing around as a metric.
Hausfather says he uses AI and agentic tools “more than most people,” but that could change soon. Last week, Meta rolled out a personal AI agent that, the company said in a press release, is “built to work for billions of people worldwide.” Dubbed Muse, Meta trumpeted that it will maintain a “dedicated computer in the cloud” for each user that would work even when the user is offline; the company plans to integrate Muse with its AI glasses later this year. It is very possible that in the near future, Meta users toying around with their glasses or fussing around on Facebook may be outsourcing tasks to agents without realizing what they’re doing.
Again, when compared to things like taking regular flights or eating beef every day, the carbon footprint for personal agentic use is still relatively small. But if Meta envisions a future where everyone’s using an agent, it explains the massive scale of some of the data centers they’re building—like the Hyperion project in Louisiana, which will be powered by 10 natural gas plants.
“The technology that’s going to be trained by the data centers that are being proposed and built right now is three to five years away,” Gamazaychikov says. “It’s going to be a very different flavor than just the chatbot window.”
What You’re Asking
A reader asks: Would small nuclear power plants work for data centers?
The short answer is that yes, small nuclear power plants could be a great choice for carbon-free power for data centers. A number of startups and data center developers envision a futuristic utopia where data centers are happily coupled with what are known as small modular reactions running off the electric grid.
The problem (as always with nuclear) is how long that might take: No small modular reactors are operating commercially in the US, and just one model has been licensed for sale, despite decades of development. The Trump administration is trying to help the industry mature more rapidly, including creating a pilot project in the Department of Energy for 11 startups to hit a key milestone this year. At least a handful have succeeded in reaching that milestone. Now, they begin the long journey to bring their products to market.
But many data center developers don’t want to wait years for these companies to prove themselves, so they’re installing gas turbines now. In other words, they’re not waiting for utopia to come around. We’ll see what happens in the next few years!
What We’re Reading
For Scientific American, Austyn Gaffney travels to Memphis to document the backlash against SpaceX’s data centers.
The Wall Street Journal reports on how some states that gave out tax breaks for data centers are now walking back on those deals.
Texas’s KERA News covers how data centers are making some Republican voters consider leaving the party.

Dawson shooting survivor turned SPVM officer reflects on friend's death 20 years on
Anastasia De Sousa was 18 when she was killed by gunman
Warning: The story below contains details about the moments leading up to the death of Anastasia De Sousa.
Two decades ago, James Santos saw his friend die in a shooting at a Montreal college. Now he is a Montreal police officer working for the force he says saved his life that day.
Sunday marks the 20th anniversary of the shooting.
On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson College and opened fire on students in the hall. He killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 19 others.
Santos, then a 17-year-old student, was having lunch with De Sousa that day. The cafeteria was packed and the two found a free table close to the entrance, he recalled in an interview with The Canadian Press.
“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.
When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.
“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.
Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.
“That's when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.
Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.
“I didn't want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.
He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.
“I just didn't want to take other students with me,” he said.
He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.
When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say.
At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.
“He didn't say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.
Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.
“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it," said Santos.
"The shooter didn't say anything, he just laughed.”
The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.
Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.
“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.
In 2008, then-Governor General of Canada Michaëlle Jean awarded Santos the Star of Courage for his actions that day.
Dawson College commemorated the shooting on Friday in a ceremony that brought De Sousa's family, survivors and students together in the school's Peace Garden. Loved ones remembered De Sousa's cheerful and resilient character.
During the ceremony, De Sousa's mother, Louise De Sousa, called on the federal government to tighten gun control laws.
Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.
Talking about the events of that day two decades later, Santos seems calm, his voice never wavering.
“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don't put myself into it. I'm looking at it as a third person,” he said.
That wasn’t always the case, he said.
“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There's really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.
Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.
Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.
“What if I had given her the [other] chair?" he asked.
"It just goes down that spiral that it's extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it'll never change what actually happened."
He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.
“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police [officers] gave me another chance at life.”
The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.
Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.
“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.
After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.
“As a police officer, you never know what calls you're getting. [If] I get a call, I'm not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

The status of host has been accorded to Afghanistan for these three T20Is. It is perhaps a trivial detail, for the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Sunday (September 13, 2026) swerved to India’s beats as the Men in Blue sauntered to a seven-wicket win in the opener. Barring a small section of Afghan fans, the 25,165-strong crowd roared as and when Abhishek Sharma (82, 32b, 7x4, 7x6) and Ishan Kishan sparkled on their way to a successful chase of 157 in 13.4 overs. The two southpaws forged a 121-run partnership for the second wicket.
Abhishek was in delightful touch from the get-go. From inside-out drives to power-packed pulls, many of his signature shots bore fruit. Kishan wasn’t as gung-ho, but still made a 33-ball 42 (5x4, 1x6).
They came together once Sanju Samson, back in the XI in place of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, mistimed a pull off Azmatullah Omarzai to Darwish Rasooli at deep square-leg. A contribution of 10 will do little to bolster Samson’s spirits, a minor blemish in an otherwise dominant display by Shreyas Iyer & Co.
India’s frontline bowlers also came good. While Arshdeep Singh took three wickets, Jasprit Bumrah, Axar Patel and Varun Chakaravarthy scalped one each.
The lone bright spot for the Afghans was an 83-run sixth-wicket stand between Omarzai and Mohammad Nabi. The former finished unbeaten on 64 (44b, 4x4, 4x6).
Having won the toss on a balmy evening, India set the tone through Bumrah. Returning from an injury layoff, the spearhead quickly made his mark. Though he started with a wide down the leg side that raced to the ropes, he struck off his second legitimate delivery. A back-of-a-length ball cramped Rahmanullah Gurbaz as the opener steered it to Abhishek at slip.
Afghanistan was reduced to 43 for five in seven overs, much of its misery self-inflicted. In the fourth over, Ibrahim Zadran flicked Axar towards midwicket and charged for a second run when Sediqullah Atal sent the skipper back halfway through. It was too late for Zadran to reach the safety of the crease, with Axar collecting a pinpoint throw from Kishan to dislodge the bails.
Afghanistan’s situation portended a capitulation, but Omarzai and Nabi didn’t give in. Omarzai’s cover drive off Bumrah for a four stood out for its majesty.
Naib was a suitable ally, ensuring that the partnership swelled steadily. A forehand slap off Arshdeep, which soared over long-on for a maximum, was the pick of Nabi’s strokes. It was a source of mere solace at the close.

My husband and I were both college athletes. When we had two boys, I think people naturally assumed we'd push the sports route hard. After all, I was a four-year starter on my college soccer team, while my husband played football for an Ivy League college.
But we've actually taken the opposite approach, and in addition to the expected soccer, baseball, and flag football dalliances, many of my kids' activities are non-sports-related. Think piano, musical theater, and Cub Scouts. Our kids are 6 and 8, and we're not pushing sports on them right now. Here's why.
We want them to be well-rounded
Kids around us are engaging in competitive sports earlier and earlier. Hospital for Special Surgery, citing the National Council of Youth Sports, reports that about 27% of the 60 million children and teens who participate in organized sports each year play only one sport. These kids are often practicing year-round, competing on travel teams, and in some cases, playing on multiple teams for the same sport.
While parents' intentions are good — their kid loves a sport, they're good at it, why not encourage it? — research has shown that there's not always a clear benefit to early sports specialization, or ESS. Instead, I've read that it could be detrimental to kids' sports success, as it can lead to overuse injuries and burnout, and may actually impede overall motor development.
Free play is a priority for us
One of the rules we have in our home is that each kid can play one sport per season. With two kids, we have practice at most twice a week and games on Saturdays. That leaves lots of time for free play. Studies have shown that unstructured play is immensely important to kids' developing brains, but it is being summarily replaced by youth sports and its demands.
I consider it a win that with two kids, I'm able to reserve three afternoons a week solely for free play. Will that change if they choose to embrace travel sports? Sure. But for now, they make up elaborate games with their neighborhood friends, ride their bikes and scooters, and honestly, make the biggest messes, both inside and out.
We want to avoid injuries and burnout
My laundry list of soccer-related injuries is long. I've had countless sprained ankles, a broken nose, a badly hyperextended elbow, chipped teeth, and torn ligaments in both my knees, one of which resulted in surgery. My husband suffered two concussions, which ended his collegiate career.
Early sports specialization (ESS) is a surefire way to increase the risk of overuse injuries. At this stage, I'll do just about anything to avoid the ER, including putting off competitive sports. With two boys, we're already frequent fliers. We also don't want them to burn out. As seasoned athletes, we know what it's like to burn out, and we don't want the same for our kids.
After sitting in school for 7 hours a day, we want them to choose extracurriculars that truly light them up, speak to their passions, and are, well, fun. That means that sometimes it's flag football, and sometimes it's ukulele lessons. Both are equally valuable.
We're taking a thoughtful approach
Both my kids play baseball, but with a few caveats. Both are playing on an official Little League team, which means fields are uniform, playing time is mandated, and there are limits on things like the number of pitches allowed per day. We don't require them to practice on their own time, unless they want to.
We do require them to finish the season if they sign up to play on a team, but we don't require them to sign up for any sport again if they truly don't like or enjoy it.
More on youth sports
It sounds random, but it seems I've modeled my philosophy after the Norwegian approach to youth sports. This was brought to my attention after the recent Winter Olympics. In short, Norwegians prioritize joy over winning, don't keep score until kids are older, and don't allow ESS. The result is a country that boasts a record of 447 Winter Olympic medals (including 166 gold), an impressive soccer team (hello, Erling Haaland, who we all enjoyed during the World Cup), and many other elite athletes — all without pressuring children to excel in sports early.
But don't get me wrong. I'm not anti-sports.
Playing soccer for most of my life gave me so much — a work ethic, lifelong friends, a sense of belonging, and a sense of responsibility to the greater good. But sports aren't the only way to learn those skills, and I won't freak out if my children choose not to pursue the college sports route. At the end of the day, all I want is for them to be happy, well-rounded kids. And if that means playing sports, great. If not, that's OK, too.

What is the difference between a dead pixel and a stuck pixel?
Look closely and you can tell them apart.
Many electronics users have felt the wave of panic that comes with trying to wipe away a mark on their screen, only to realize it's actually an issue with the screen itself. Sometimes, this can be caused by factors like source or cable issues, and isn't cause for alarm. Other times, however, it's a pixel problem, which can be much more dread-inducing due to varying levels of repairability.
Even the best monitors aren't safe from a potential pixel issue, of which there are two main types: stuck pixels and dead pixels. Both are dots — or, even worse, clusters of dots — that no screen user wants to see. However, though both screen annoyances look a lot alike shape-wise, there are some distinct differences between them, namely in their exact appearance and if they can be fixed.
Spotting the difference
One of the biggest differences between a stuck and dead pixel is the presence of light. A stuck pixel is permanently on, displaying a constant blue, red, green or bright point, while a dead pixel is, as the name suggests, no longer functioning and is always black. This visual difference can help you determine which particular problem you're facing.
The other main defining factor between the two is how fixable they are. A stuck pixel has a myriad of troubleshooting routes that can be taken, and can often be returned to normal. A dead pixel, on the other hand, cannot be salvaged. If you've got a dead pixel, you'll unfortunately either have to get a replacement or learn to tolerate it. On the bright side, it's a generally less obtrusive visual issue than something like screen burn-in.
How to test for dead and stuck pixels
Stuck and dead pixels are so small it can sometimes be tricky to identify if they're even the issue at hand, and, if they are, which instance in particular you're dealing with. First, it's best to rule out all other display issues that could be going on. Clean your display thoroughly, see if the problem persists across different applications and, if you can, try both a new cable and input device.
Once you've ruled out other problems, conduct a final test designed to concretely pinpoint the issue. There are several sites and apps that can be used to sniff out pixel problems, like Dead Pixel Buddy, and even some that purport the potential to solve the issue as well, like JScreenFix or Dead Pixels Test and Fix. It should be noted that stuck pixels can sometimes be harder to diagnose, as those with power or heat problems as the underlying cause may only appear intermittently. If that's the case, try to pull up one of these tests as soon as you notice the issue's returned.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): 'Bhopal Ke Raja', like Independent India, has turned 80 this year. The Shri Dol Gyaras Samiti has been installing an idol of Lord Ganesha - popularly known as 'Bhopal Ke Raja' - at Peepal Chowk in the Old City since 1947.
Brijbhushan Goyal, Uddhavdas Mehta and Mohanlal Simhal were among the founder-members of the Samiti, which started the tradition of celebrating Ganesh Utsav in Bhopal.
“Now the third and fourth generations of the founders are managing the things. But the tradition remains unbroken,” Deepak Goyal, the patron of the Samiti, told Free Press.
He said that public celebration of festivals was not permitted when the city was under the rule of the Nawab and hence in 1947 and 1948, the idol was installed in a shop. Since 1949, the Samiti has been celebrating the Ganeshotsava publicly.
Besides Ganesha, the idols of goddesses Riddhi-Siddhi and Ganesha's sons Shubh-Labh are also installed at Peepal Chowk. The idol is decorated with different fresh flowers every day and 'Chappan Bhog' is offered as 'prasad' to the Lord.
Goyal said that they will spend around Rs 15 lakh on the event this year. “We have been following the same traditions and rituals for the past 80 years. We haven’t changed anything. The height of the Ganesha idol will be six feet like always,” he said.
Hundreds of pandals will open their doors to the devotees in the city on Monday - the first day of the 10-day Ganesha Utsav.
In New Market, a replica of Pune's Shrimant Dagdusheth Halwai Ganpati Temple will be the central attraction of the Ganesha Utsav celebrations.
A 13-foot idol of Lord Gan Gajanand will be installed in a 3,000-sq-foot pandal. Ranjeet Manjhi, coordinator of New Market Ganesh Utsav Samiti, said that the total expenditure of this year is Rs 10 lakh.
A 17-foot idol of Ganesha will be installed at Mata Mandir, while in Chandbad, the devotees will be able to see the Lord of Wisdom holding a 'Chakra' in his hands.
In Somwara, a 12-foot idol of Ganesha riding a Nandi will be installed. The pandal in Sindhi Colony will be themed on the Simhastha and will showcase Mahakal and the Kshipra river.

Actor Triptii Dimri has joined D2C eye-focused beauty brand Peep Beauty as an investor and co-creator as the startup looks to build a beauty category around coloured contact lenses and eye makeup. As part of the association, Dimri has been involved in the startup’s creative direction, product discussions, and brand storytelling from its early stages, the startup said in a statement. Dimri’s investment is part of the startup’s pre-seed funding round of ₹12 Cr ($1.2 Mn) led by Sadev Ventures, with participation from iSeed, ISV and TDV. The round also saw participation from a clutch of angel investors, including Arjun Vaidya (V3 Ventures cofounder), Puneet Gupta (Astrotalk founder), Roman Saini (Unacademy cofounder), Gaurav Khatri (Noise cofounder), Dhruv Bhasin (Arata cofounder), among others. Founded earlier this year by ex-Keventers cofounder Aman Arora, Peep Beauty operates in the coloured contact lens and eye makeup segments. The startup claims to be India’s first dedicated eye beauty brand. Betting On Coloured Lenses Peep Beauty launched with coloured contact lenses as its flagship product and is positioning them as everyday beauty and fashion accessories. The startup said its products have been designed specifically for Indian eye tones. The startup currently offers lenses in five shades currently, priced at ₹399 per pair. It has also launched six liquid eyeshadows. While its matte range is priced at ₹799, metallic eyeshadows cost ₹849. Arora told Inc42 earlier this year that the eyeshadow range was introduced to allow customers to build complete looks around the coloured lenses. The startup plans to add products such as mascara and eyeliner to its portfolio, allowing customers to create different eye-focused looks instead of using its lenses as standalone products. Peep Beauty also plans to expand its contact lens portfolio to around 15-20 shades over the next few years. Besides conventional colours such as brown and grey, it intends to introduce more experimental shades for occasions such as Halloween. As a digital-first brand, Peep Beauty plans to sell through its D2C platform while expanding its presence on ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms. It also intends to collaborate with creators, makeup artists, dancers, and other artists to promote the brand. The development comes as D2C brands increasingly bring celebrities on board as investors and strategic collaborators to boost visibility and strengthen their consumer connect. Earlier this year, D2C jewellery brand GIVA onboarded actor Kriti Sanon as an investor. In June, D2C kids’ lifestyle brand Rosada brought actor Shilpa Shetty Kundra on board as a strategic investor as it looks to expand its footprint across India. Sportswear startup Agilitas Sports also onboarded actor Anushka Sharma as an investor and strategic collaborator. Meanwhile, footwear brand Chupps roped in Indian cricketer Ajinkya Rahane as an investor and strategic advisor.

For a child bursting with energy, few things are more fun than hurtling through a bouncy castle, launching into the air, and ping-ponging between every surface. But that childhood buoyancy will quickly deflate when it turns out those surfaces are smeared with a hypervirulent, multidrug-resistant pathogen.
That was the horrifying reality for a community in Ireland in fall 2025. Neighbors had gathered for an afternoon of merriment, complete with a barbecue, a sweets station, and three bouncy castles. Officials estimate that about 120 people joined the festivities, and around half of them were children and teens. Within a day, some children began developing signs of an infection. In all, 48 children in the community developed aggressive skin and soft-tissue infections.
Of the 48 cases, 33 were treated by their regular doctor, and 15 sought emergency care. Four children ended up being hospitalized. Luckily, all of the children recovered. The results of the outbreak investigation were reported this week in the journal Eurosurveillance.
Party crashers
Local health officials became alerted to the outbreak nine days after the event, when a 12-year-old boy was hospitalized for a skin infection. His doctors had determined he was infected with MRSA—aka methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. By then, there were around 25 other, less severe cases identified.
Genomic sequencing revealed the outbreak was caused by a rare strain of MRSA capable of producing a cytotoxin called Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL). This toxin can destroy immune cells and spark inflammation. It’s often linked to necrotic lesions.
The bacterium’s hostilities were clear in the outbreak; most of the infected children developed symptoms within four days of the event, much faster than the usual incubation period of 4–10 days. Some saw their infections develop within hours. The infected children reported a range of skin and soft tissue symptoms, including spots, pustules, blisters, and abscesses. Most of the skin infections erupted on the children’s legs, particularly their thighs, fitting with an exposure in the bouncy castles. Twelve cases also reported systemic symptoms, such as fever, nausea, or vomiting.

About 500 evacuated as wildfire rages on Croatian island of Brac
ZAGREB: About 500 people have been evacuated on the Croatian Adriatic island of Brac as a wildfire raged on the popular tourist spot famous for its white sand beach.
Authorities sounded the alarm shortly before midnight on Saturday (Sep 13) as flames threatened to get close to homes in the small town of Milna in the west of the island.
Fanned by strong winds, the fire has consumed about 3,500ha (8,600 acres), an area roughly two-thirds the size of Manhattan, authorities said.
Two people have been wounded, including one seriously, firefighters told the official Hina news agency.
"The wind is still blowing but I think we have a good chance of controlling the fire by the end of the day," firefighting chief Nikola Martinic Dragan was quoted as saying by Hina.
Four Canadair water-bombing aircraft have been at work since the morning, while more than 220 firefighters backed by 69 vehicles have worked through the night to douse the blaze, the firefighters' statement said.
Several boats from the harbourmaster's office and the maritime police worked alongside private vessels to get people out of the areas near Milna threatened by the flames.
In total, about 3,500ha of pine forest and scrubland were devastated by the blaze, Hina reported, citing a senior firefighter.
As with elsewhere in Europe, Croatia has seen an extremely hot and dry summer, which has created tinderbox-like conditions for wildfires to rage.
Scientists have long warned that climate change driven by humanity's burning of fossil fuels is making periods of extreme heat and drought more frequent, intense and longer-lasting.

- Blizzard has announced its next Diablo game, Diablo 5, slated for release in Spring 2029.
- The company also revealed a new cinematic focused on the Lord of Terror's return to Sanctuary.
- According to designer Joe Shely, Diablo 5 is set in a world where "Sanctuary has fallen, and Diablo has won."
Blizzard shows no signs of slowing down at BlizzCon 2026, keeping its announcement streak alive by announcing the next entry in the Diablo series, Diablo 5, set for Spring 2029. The company also unveiled a new cinematic teaser for the highly anticipated release, centered around a post-apocalyptic “fallen Sanctuary”.
According to Blizzard designer Joe Shely, Diablo 5 is set in a world where “The heroes are gone, Sanctuary has fallen, and Diablo has won.” He further continued, “For the first time, you won’t be fighting to stop Diablo from taking Sanctuary; you’ll enter a world where he already has, with no towns and safe places waiting to protect you.”

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.

Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis
Heading west at 40 transformed his writing—and American literature.
To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape. The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook. By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin. McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing. His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change. As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian.
Few life swerves are so productive. The book represented a fresh direction. Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western. It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people. From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work.
His next five novels, including the best sellers All the Pretty Horses (1992) and No Country for Old Men (2005), used desert plains and bleak landscapes to unspool a grim pessimism, shocking readers with stark visions of depravity while preserving the slenderest candlelight of hope: a few good souls carrying the fire. It was as though Appalachia’s dense woods and city fringes had prevented him from seeing the page clearly. Out west, there is nothing but sky.
In Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited, the first major biography of McCarthy, who died in 2023, Tracy Daugherty depicts his western reorientation as a turning point in his life and work but also looks for continuity. “The desert can be anywhere,” he writes; “the soul’s site of testing”—McCarthy’s lifelong fixation—is not limited to any one place. Although his departure was hurried, the transition took time. McCarthy made laps back to Tennessee during the 1970s and finished his Knoxville novel, Suttree, from his new base. The book was finally published in 1979 and unfairly panned by one critic as a “limited use of an enormous talent.” As for Blood Meridian, although it promised wonders to come, McCarthy’s first Western started off as a cult classic and only later, in the 1990s, began to find success.
Yet once cemented, the relocation was the fulcrum of McCarthy’s life. After the ’70s, he never again lived in Tennessee or made Appalachian culture his subject. He eventually came to be so closely associated with the dusty boots and bleached bones of the West that new readers may be surprised to learn that the first half of his life was spent elsewhere. So why did he leave Knoxville? Daugherty presents a combination of personal failures and artistic imperatives that chased and lured him, respectively. Daugherty’s fascinating biography, which reflects impressive research in the Cormac McCarthy Papers at Texas State University, is very well told and filled with astute judgments about McCarthy’s 12 novels. Although Daugherty declines to elevate one part of his oeuvre over the other, the lesson of the biography—and the work—is clear. The cultural South may have been McCarthy’s home, but the West was his muse.
McCarthy’s father and namesake, Charles McCarthy Sr., represented urban order; he was set on taming the young Cormac’s backwoods waywardness. McCarthy later claimed that his father had beat him savagely during his childhood, afterward calmly sitting back down to finish his supper. Cormac’s artistically inclined mother helplessly watched the abuse. McCarthy Sr. worked as general counsel for the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency that displaced tens of thousands of Appalachian families to make way for hydroelectric power. He did so with brisk pragmatism and a clean conscience, infuriating his son. Each man was baffled and hurt as the other rejected his outlook. The tension drives the early pages of Suttree : “The world is run by those willing to take the responsibility for the running of it,” the father in the novel tells his meandering boy.
Siding with the evicted, McCarthy slept on the porch, explored the forests, and caroused with Knoxville’s degenerate class. “Like Shakespeare’s Prince Hal, he liked to go slumming—remaining, just slightly, apart,” Daugherty writes. McCarthy listened and gathered material for his novels as often as he participated in the outlaw revelry. Yet he was no angel: A night with John Sheddan, a local misfit and frequent confederate, could as easily find the two sleeping in a barn or confined to a jail cell for public intoxication as discussing Thomas Hobbes. McCarthy studied physics and engineering at the University of Tennessee but never earned his degree, and began to read Dostoyevsky, Melville, and Faulkner during an uneventful stretch of Air Force service in the 1950s. His first marriage, to Lee Holleman, ended in divorce.
Family and friends offered few durable tethers to home, terrain that lacked lasting fictional appeal too. McCarthy’s early novels, beginning with The Orchard Keeper in 1965, chronicled the types of Appalachian outsiders and scofflaws he liked to run with. They proved off-putting company for readers. The books stood out as much for their desperate circumstances and ghastly subject matter (incest in Outer Dark, from 1968; necrophilia in Child of God five years later) as for their baroque prose and gothic settings. Suttree, the best of these novels and an excellent book, was nevertheless digressive and full of obscure, almost impenetrable writing (“rhomboid and volute shapes of limestone jutted all brindled with mud like great bones washed out”). Critics recognized a rare talent but also a voice struggling to break free of Faulkner’s influence.
As his books misfired, McCarthy lived in an eccentric poverty that has become the stuff of legend. He cut his own hair and cooked canned food on hot plates. Working odd jobs (warehouse attendant in Chicago, garbageman in New Orleans), he recalled scraping by in “cellars on unemployment and welfare.” Without gainsaying these sacrifices, Daugherty calls out some exaggeration and myth building. Both DeLisle and Holleman contributed income; McCarthy’s Random House editor Albert Erskine helped him land fellowships and grants; and his parents, despite his strained relationship with his father, were a ready safety net. Still, between McCarthy’s failed marriages, family tensions, dead-end buddies, and dry artistic well, he had little to keep him in Tennessee as his 30s drew to a close.
A western reinvention allowed McCarthy to continue exploring timeless, elemental themes in a setting that befitted their gravity. In the American imagination, a cowboy’s journey is fraught, and his last breaths are tragic; a hillbilly’s exploits are hapless, and his final moments are merely uncomfortable. We cry for our heroes but wince for our outcasts. McCarthy sensed the difference. For a flailing author, the West also held commercial promise. “I ended up in the Southwest because I knew that nobody had ever written about it,” McCarthy later said. “Besides Coca-Cola, the other thing that is universally known is cowboys and Indians.”
Daugherty bristles at McCarthy’s dismissal of “decades of Southwestern literature”—by Leslie Marmon Silko, Katherine Anne Porter, N. Scott Momaday, and Larry McMurtry, to name just a few—yet the remark reveals a certain canniness: McCarthy cared more about selling books than his austere reputation suggests. It is not the only time Daugherty upends his subject’s ascetic image. In person, McCarthy was courtly and gregarious, a warm conversationalist who liked to sing. One striking scene has him dressed in a new cream suit, dancing into the night on an ocean liner as he twirls and spins his partners.
Blood Meridian proved to be McCarthy’s best novel and a modern masterpiece. Its protagonist is notably a young man who flees Tennessee for the West. The book follows the Glanton gang of scalp hunters in the mid-19th century along the U.S.-Mexico border. In ominous, hyper-violent language, McCarthy displays a nihilism that situates humankind on the raw continuum of predator and prey, river and rock: “The men as they rode turned black in the sun from the blood on their clothes and their faces and then paled slowly in the rising dust until they assumed once more the color of the land through which they passed.” Like an ancient mystic, McCarthy foresaw the endless reenactment of a horrifying cycle of brutality without meaning or purpose, a cursed birthright. “It makes no difference what men think of war,” says his most fearsome character, Judge Holden. “War endures. As well ask men what they think of stone.” To Daugherty, Blood Meridian’s clear-eyed view of American history was as amoral as realpolitik: “Politics as force.”
The Border Trilogy followed—the best-selling All the Pretty Horses leading on to The Crossing (1994) and Cities of the Plain (1998)—adding accessible characters and love stories to at last attract sales and awards. McCarthy’s writing began to shed some of its most ornate flourishes, taking on a stripped-down veneer. (Many of his later books were conceived as screenplays.) Critiques of the works as lightweight fare from the oracular McCarthy overlooked their hidden depths. This arresting insight, for example, comes to the young cowboy John Grady Cole in All the Pretty Horses: “He thought the world’s heart beat at some terrible cost and that the world’s pain and its beauty moved in a relationship of diverging equity and that in this headlong deficit the blood of multitudes might ultimately be exacted for the vision of a single flower.” Daugherty views McCarthy’s evolution in the Westerns as the pairing of a mature style with a genre framework. A similar combination has produced some of the best American movies of the past generation, by filmmakers such as Kathryn Bigelow and the Coen brothers, who directed an Oscar-winning adaptation of No Country for Old Men.
Although he started over, McCarthy could not escape the past. His celebrated 2006 novel, The Road—a sort of postapocalyptic Western—is built on a tender father-son relationship that both reflects McCarthy’s experience as a late-in-life parent and implicitly rejects his own father’s heavy hand. Daugherty quotes wrenching correspondence in which McCarthy and his father tried to reconcile as grown men. “There was and is a strong artistic streak in me that I inherited from my mother’s family and it has caused me a great deal of anguish in my life but an even greater joy,” McCarthy wrote. “I think this was always suspect to you.” Another relationship that echoed in his fiction was one that endured longer than his three marriages combined. McCarthy met Augusta Britt several years after moving out west; they became lovers when she was 17 and he was 43. They remained close for 47 years, but she protested the way he kept using her in his books, including in plotlines that seemed to mirror her life. “Well, baby, that’s what I do,” McCarthy replied. “I’m a writer.”
McCarthy attempted a second reinvention, a turn toward science. By the late 2000s, he was spending much of his time at the Santa Fe Institute, a multidisciplinary research center, where he hobnobbed with physicists, favoring philosophical conversations over writing books. The year before he died, he published a final pair of related novels, The Passenger and Stella Maris, which had been in progress for years; one of the main characters is a mathematics prodigy with a mental illness. In startling new reporting, Daugherty contends that McCarthy’s literary agent assembled the hodgepodge of pages and made the decision to break the mess into two books; McCarthy’s friends told Daugherty they suspected that the ailing writer had not even read the finished product. The result was unconvincing characters, mashups of McCarthy’s many interests, strange psychiatric sessions, and a lack of cohesion.
Maybe we all have only one good pivot in us. Or perhaps it was just too late for McCarthy to change course again. Whatever the case, his turn west in the 1970s reveals not just a man escaping personal failures but a restless writer who sensed that a wide new horizon might require him to expand his vision if he was to find his voice and his audience. The small-town hustles and degradations of Tennessee were ultimately too provincial for such an epoch-spanning talent, which demanded plains, mountains, and an endless expanse of sky to bring out its full potential. After all, deep in the Appalachian woods, you can’t see the buzzards circling.

India's Modi and China's Xi seek to reset ties on BRICS sidelines
It's the latest effort to repair ties strained by a border clash six years ago.
NEW DELHI -- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping met Saturday on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the latest effort by the rival neighbors to repair ties strained by a deadly border clash six years ago.
Xi said China has approached relations with India from a “strategic and long-term perspective” and called for the two countries to draw on each other’s strengths, support one another and pursue common development.
He also urged “high-quality cooperation” between the two countries, saying China and India, as major members of the Global South, should promote a more multipolar world and contribute to global peace and stability.
Modi thanked Xi for China’s cooperation in hosting the summit. China will host the summit next year.
The two leaders held talks in China last year during Modi's visit to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a regional political, economic and security group founded by China.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and yet another effort toward a cautious thaw between the rival neighbors, six years after a deadly border clash badly damaged ties.
A military clash in 2020 killed at least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese along a grueling frontier in the cold desert region of Ladakh. It turned into a long-running standoff in the rugged mountainous area, where each side has stationed tens of thousands of military personnel backed by artillery, tanks and fighter jets.
India and China have since taken steps to ease tensions, but deep mistrust remains.
The two nuclear-armed powers still dispute some parts of their border, while India’s large trade deficit with China, restrictions on Chinese investment and technology and their competing strategic interests in Asia continue to weigh on relations. India has also significantly expanded military infrastructure along its disputed frontier with China, while Beijing has built roads and defensive positions on its side of the contested border.
Xi’s visit is expected to test whether the recent thaw can translate into a broader stabilization of ties.
Since their 1962 war, the economies of both countries have grown substantially, but China has far outpaced India and runs a large trade surplus with its neighbor. Their growing economic rivalry has added to longstanding territorial and strategic differences.
India has sought to capitalize on China’s rising labor costs and strained ties with the United States and Europe to position itself as an alternative base for foreign manufacturers. New Delhi has also viewed China’s multibillion-dollar Belt and Road Initiative with concern and has strongly opposed it.
At the same time, India’s growing strategic partnership with the U.S. has raised concerns in Beijing, which views the relationship as part of efforts to counter China’s rise.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is considering appointing former Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Hideki Murai as parliamentary affairs chief of her ruling Liberal Democratic Party in a party leadership reshuffle, informed sources said Sunday.
It is customary for the post of LDP parliamentary affairs chief to be held by a former Cabinet minister, so appointing someone who has never served in the Cabinet would be an unusual move.
The prime minister apparently aims to signal a fresh start for the LDP leadership team by naming Murai, who is active in parliamentary reform, to the post, party sources said.
Murai, 46, has been elected to the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of the Diet, Japan’s parliament, six times.
The former Finance Ministry bureaucrat served as a special adviser to the prime minister in the administration of former Prime Minister Fumio Kishida and as deputy chief Cabinet secretary, a role that serves as a coordinator between the LDP’s Diet affairs committee and the Prime Minister’s Office.
Since then, he has been involved in negotiations between the ruling and opposition parties in the Diet, serving in roles such as the ruling bloc’s chief director of the Lower House steering committee.
In the extraordinary Diet session scheduled to be convened in early October at the earliest, the focus will be on bills related to a consumption tax cut on food products and a bill to reduce the number of Lower House seats.
Meanwhile, Takaichi held talks with Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara at the prime minister’s official residence Sunday. She plans to conduct the reshuffle of the LDP’s leadership as early as Wednesday, followed by a Cabinet reshuffle and appointments of state ministers and parliamentary vice ministers.

This is the existential question confronting the AI industry, a debate that only intensified after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit last week with a stark warning. He said AI giants are "gambling with our lives" and that the people building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
The swift reaction to Coxon's warning boiled over on Saturday when the leaders of the biggest AI companies publicly agreed on what should happen next.
In a Saturday essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says he's "become convinced" the breakneck pace of advancement must change and proposed a three-step solution to ensure the tech's safety.
Shortly afterward, Elon Musk and Sam Altman publicly aligned with Amodei's plan in a rare sign of support. "Dario is right," Musk tweeted. Altman agreed, too, saying the pace of development has been a "primary topic" of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks.
Altman also said OpenAI might not move forward with an IPO this year. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said in a Fortune interview.
As fears over AI safety intensify, employees at Anthropic and OpenAI have also been speaking out.
My colleague Sarah Needleman reported on a big question facing many concerned AI employees: Should they quit or stay amid fears of an AI apocalypse?
Some AI workers believe they can do more good by staying on the inside. That means raising concerns, pushing for safeguards, and trying to influence decisions before they are made. Others worry that staying at these companies only helps legitimize a race that some believe is getting dangerously out of control.
BI's Alistair Bar explored some of these theories in this week's edition of AI Insider — you can subscribe here to his weekly newsletter.
Are employees at the big AI lab companies better off leaving or staying if they feel like their work is contributing to a possible AI apocalypse? Send me a note at srussolillo@businessinsider.com and let me know what you think.

Top elected official in Pakistan's Balochistan rules out talks with insurgents
The top official in Pakistan's Balochistan province has ruled out negotiations with insurgents
ISLAMABAD -- The top elected official in Pakistan’s southwestern province of Balochistan on Saturday ruled out negotiations with insurgents, indicating that the government will continue operations in which hundreds of militants have been killed in recent months.
Balochistan has long faced a separatist insurgency by ethnic Baloch groups who regularly target security forces and civilians working on development projects. While Pakistan’s government says it has quelled the insurgency, violence has persisted.
Sarfraz Bugti, the chief minister of Balochistan, said in a statement that the “fight against terrorism would continue until the last terrorist is eliminated” in Balochistan. “There will be no negotiations with terrorists, those who have taken up arms against Pakistan and those raising slogans for the country’s disintegration.”
His remarks came as attacks by the Baloch Liberation Army, which has been designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S., have increased. Bugti said the time had come for “major surgery” to eliminate terrorism.
“We are in a state of war,” he said, adding that authorities had never claimed everything in Balochistan was normal. “The security forces are performing their duties under extremely difficult conditions in the province, and all state institutions are working in complete coordination against terrorism.”
Though Pakistan’s largest province, Balochistan is its least populated. Some Balochis have complained about discrimination by the government. There are also deep grievances about enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and the exploitation of the abundant natural resources.
Several regional political parties and activists have called in recent years for dialogue with insurgent groups, but BLA and other Baloch groups have not sought talks. No spokesman for the group was immediately available for comment.
Pakistan’s federal government and officials in Balochistan have rejected such calls for dialogue, saying leniency could be considered only for militants who surrender. Some BLA leaders and their associates have surrendered at ceremonies, where they laid down their weapons and were welcomed by local officials.
In 2025, BLA killed 18 paramilitary security forces in one of the deadly coordinated attacks in Balochistan.
