Afghan woman deported from US in first use of 'alien terrorist' court
- Published
An Afghan woman living in Texas with legal US permanent residency has been deported from the country in the first-ever use of a secretive court.
Nazira Haji Zada, 47, chose to leave the US rather than continue to argue her case before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and her lawyers.
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996, but had never heard a case before the proceedings in July. It is meant for non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges when the evidence is confidential and related to national security.
Lawyers for Haji Zada argued that the case violated her right to due process under the US Constitution.
Afghanistan citizen Haji Zada was never charged with a crime, but prosecutors had tried and convicted her son and son-in-law for terror offenses.
Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed, were both found guilty of a plot to carry out a mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, inspired by the group calling itself Islamic State.
Haji Zada, who has been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of the group, who had worked "to radicalize the family".
In a statement on Friday, the justice department said she "conceded that she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous [immigration] status".
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
"Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."
Court-appointed lawyers for Haji Zada said they were denied access to the evidence in her case.
"Our client's choice to consent to removal should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy," public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras said in a statement to The Washington Post.
"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," they said.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Expressing grave concern over the high prevalence of child marriages resulting in underage pregnancies and deliveries in the State, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (September 7, 2026) said that the State had recorded nearly 60,000 underage institutional deliveries in the first six months of 2026.
Details of underage institutional deliveries from January 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 had been obtained from the State Health Department, and the numbers were alarming, Mr. Adhikari said.
“As a result of the previous government, we are now number one in two criteria across the country — marriage of girls below 18 years of age, and deliveries before 18 years of age. These numbers are so high that there aren’t enough jails in which to put these people,” the Chief Minister said, addressing media persons at the State Secretariat.
Mr. Adhikari read out the provisions of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, adding that the law prohibited marriage with a child below 18 years of age. In such cases, “Police action will be initiated and arrests will be made,” he said.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the practice of child marriage could not be allowed to prevail, and the State Health Department would issue a show-cause notice to the offenders, especially the husband, who would have to provide documentary evidence within a month that both he and his ‘wife’ were adults in accordance with the law.
“If he fails to do so, the DGP (Director General of Police), who is sitting right next to me, will take action as per the law,” Mr. Adhikari said. The State government would stop delivering benefits under all Central and State government welfare schemes to these families, he said. Action would be taken against the priest and qazi who solemnised the marriage, and against other family members, he added.
Sharing district-wise details of cases of underage pregnancies, the Chief Minister said 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls were recorded in Murshidabad district alone, followed by South 24 Parganas at 4,178.
West Bengal has recorded the highest number of child marriages over the past few years, despite schemes rolled out to keep girls in schools. According to the Sample Registration Survey report published in September 2025, West Bengal recorded 6.3% of females getting married before the age of 18 years, whereas at the national level, 2.1% of females got married before the age of 18 years. Murshidabad remains a hotspot for child marriages. About 55.4% women in the district aged 20 to 24 years said they were married before the age of 18 years, according to the National Family Health Survey-5.
Experts working on the ground, however, say that child marriage is a complex issue involving not only parental or social pressure but also cases of elopement, and minor grooms. They warn that the arrest of husbands may result in placing a strain on already marginalised families, and impact marital relations adversely.

- An Intricate Key mould can be found by exploring the Winding Tunnels and destroying rubble piles or defeating certain enemies.
- The Intricate Key Cast can be crafted at level 4 Black Forge, using 5 Bloodgold Ingots.
- Use the cast at a Frost Foundry with Liquid Frost to create the Intricate Key.
The Deep North in Valheim 1.0 is packed with dangerous enemies, freezing conditions, and mysterious dungeons that clearly want you to grind in the game. Among the biggest roadblocks are the massive locked gates of Morkhalla that demand a special item: the Intricate Key. Unfortunately, you cannot simply loot it from any chest; rather, it has a dedicated crafting process. So, check this guide to learn everything about how to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim.
Items Required to Craft an Intricate Key in Valheim
Crafting an Intricate Key in Valheim will require you to have the Cast: Intricate Key alongside the Frost Foundry to use the Cast. Now, this cast is made using two key ingredients: the Intricate Key Mould and Bloodgold. So, here’s how you can get both items:
How to Get Intricate Key Mould in Valheim
The first thing you need to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim is its mould. You won’t be able to craft the key directly without having this item. Here’s what you need to do:
- Head to the Winding Tunnels, an area found beneath the settlements in the Deep North biome.
- Since these areas are full of enemies, make sure you’re equipped with the best weapons and armor in Valheim 1.0.
- Defeating the enemies in Winding Tunnels will give you a chance to obtain the Intricate Key mould.
How to Get Bloodgold in Valheim
Obtaining Bloodgold will be a tough task because you’ll have to defeat one of the most powerful creatures in Valheim. If you’ve explored the Deep North biome, you must have spotted the massive Gammeltroll.
Defeating the Gammeltroll will turn it into a petrified state, and then you can throw Ember Charges on its body to obtain the Petrified Tissue. Put this Petrified Tissue into a Blase Furnace to obtain Bloodgold in Valheim. If you need further help, our linked guide will help you out.
How to Make the Intricate Key
Once you have collected 5 Bloodgold Ingots and the Intricate Key Mould, you’re ready to learn how to craft the Intricate Key in Valheim. Follow the steps below to get the item:
- Combine the ingredients on a Level 4 Black Forge to create the Cast: Intricate Key.
- Take the cast to a Frost Foundry and use Liquid Frost to complete the crafting process.
- Note that Liquid Frost can be obtained by putting ice inside a Frigid Kiln.
- Once the crafting process is complete, the Intricate Key will rise from the Foundry, and you can collect it by pressing ‘E‘ or the interaction key.
How to Use the Intricate Key in Valheim
The Intricate Key isn’t just a collectible item. Its main purpose is to open the locked gates of Morkhalla, located in the Deep North.
While exploring the Deep North, you will come across some settlements that have the passage to the Winding Tunnels. Near them, you can find a tall tower with no gates on the ground. The only way to enter this tower is by using a Grappling Hook in Valheim.
Inside the tower, you will find stairs leading to a basement, where the locked gates to Morkhalla are located. Here, you can use the Intricate Key to open the gates and enter one of the major Deep North dungeons.
And that is all about how to craft an Intricate Key in Valheim. So, have you checked out the best Valheim seeds to have the dream start in the 1.0 update? Tell us in the comments below.

Electric two-wheeler (E2W) maker Ultraviolette Automotive is set to raise an additional ₹373.04 Cr as part of its ongoing Series E funding round from investors Yali Capital, TDK Ventures, among others. As per an MCA filings accessed by Inc42, Ultraviolette’s shareholders consented to allot on preferential basis through private placement 8.15 Lakh Series E3 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) worth ₹2,435 each, aggregating to ₹197.5 Cr. The startup also allotted 7.24 Lakh Series E4 CCPS, netting ₹175.5 Cr. “The investments are part of a currently ongoing fundraise; we have nothing further to add at the moment,” the startup said in response to Inc42’s questions pertaining to the round. Of this, Ultraviolette has raised ₹249.2 Cr from Yali Capital’s Yali Deeptech Fund I as well as TDK Ventures. TDK Ventures first backed the startup in August 2025 when it led its $21 Mn funding round while Yali Capital will be new to Ultraviolette’s cap table. There are a host of angel investors participating in this round including, Adi Hirji Jehangir, Anshumi Desai, Janak Desai, Mahak Khabia, Zafar Ahmadullah, among others. The investment comes almost a year after the startup raised $45 Mn as part of the Series E round from Zoho and Lingotto. Overall, the startup has raised more than $135 Mn till date from other investors like TVS Motors, Qualcomm Ventures, Breathe Capital and Mudhal Partners. The new investment comes as the E2W manufacturer is building its manufacturing facility, the BIGGA factory. Ultraviolette To Invest ₹1,000 Cr In Manufacturing The E2W maker is investing more than ₹1,000 Cr over the next five years to expand its manufacturing footprint, with its upcoming BIGGA Factory set to take its annual production capacity to as much as 2.5 Lakh vehicles in the initial phase. The startup intends to invest approximately ₹800 Cr in the new facility, while another ₹200 Cr is being deployed to expand its existing Bengaluru plant. The new facility will initially have an annual capacity of 2.5 Lakh vehicles, which can eventually be scaled to 5 Lakh vehicles, cofounders Narayan Subramaniam and Niraj Rajmohan told Inc42. The capacity expansion comes as Ultraviolette looks to move beyond its initial premium, performance-led positioning and target larger segments of the E2W market with new products such as the Shockwave and Tesseract. However, the startup said the strategy itself has not changed. “Ultraviolette was conceived from the outset as an electric-vehicle platform company,” the founders said, highlighting that the F77 was the first expression of this approach, followed by the X-47 crossover. The upcoming products, they said, will allow the company to address “significantly larger customer segments” while retaining its focus on technology, safety, performance and range. The cofounders claim that demand across its existing portfolio already exceeds 10,000 units a month, while it has received tens of thousands of bookings for upcoming products. It plans to commission capacity progressively in line with demand. Ultraviolette currently has an installed capacity of around 30,000 vehicles annually at its Bengaluru facility, which is being expanded to 50,000-60,000 units. The plant will continue to serve as a manufacturing, engineering and technology hub after the BIGGA Factory comes online. It is also targeting international markets, with exports expected to account for around 25% of revenue over the next five years. “BIGGA Factory converts that technology foundation into industrial scale,” the founders said, positioning the facility as a key step towards building a global electric-mobility business. To note, the startup launched its F77 motorcycles in the United Kingdom, in November last year, and claimed to be present in 12 countries across Europe, as of its last fundraise. For the month of August, overall E2W registrations fell by 16.2% to 1.72 Lakh units from 2.05 Lakh units in July, based on Vahan data. Ultraviolette sold 583 E2Ws, down 17% from 702 vehicles in July. It holds 0.3% market share in the domestic market.

TOI correspondent from Washington: It’s a club MAGA boss 
Donald Trump
 loves to hate -- one that New Delhi not only refuses to leave but wants to lead. As India hugged Brics without breaking up with America, presiding over a geopolitical game of musical chairs where nobody gets eliminated, reviews in Washington of the just-concluded summit sounded more wary than alarmed despite the group's growing strength and a reprimand of Uncle Sam without calling him by name.
While the New Delhi Declaration took aim at unilateral tariffs, trade barriers, and sanctions, warning that such measures distort global commerce and violate the spirit of the WTO -- while dancing around the issue of wars involving the US, Russia, and several members -- the reaction in Washington to the summit has been more hmmm than horror. The broad consensus in the American commentariat is that Brics is acquiring political heft, but remains far too divided to become a coherent anti-American alliance.
Time went so far as to headline its assessment “Why a Divided Brics Poses No Challenge to America,” while emphasizing that India, the summit host, still wants Brics to accomplish things without antagonizing Washington. “Brics leaders gather in New Delhi as wars and rivalries strain the expanded bloc,” noted the Washington Post, while the NYT observed that while “China wants Brics to challenge American power, India wants it broad enough that countries don't have to choose.
”

Brics diplomacy: Iran president says Tehran, UAE want to 'turn the page' on war
That may well be the central paradox of the New Delhi summit: Brics is becoming bigger, louder, and more confident about challenging Western dominance, while one of its key, pivotal members is simultaneously deepening ties with Washington. The Modi-Xi encounter was therefore watched especially closely, even more than the Modi-Putin engagement with one wag -- referring to the Galwan flare-up -- characterizing it as a diplomatic equivalent of reopening a restaurant that had been closed after a rather serious kitchen fire.
Several analysts noted that Beijing's longstanding concern has been India's growing alignment with the U.S. “China wants to shape India’s strategic choice. It wants an India that does not see China as a threat. It also wants India to not side with the US by default because of China,” Stimson Center’s Yun Sun told FT, whose headline, "World’s biggest relationship? Xi and Modi look to rebuild ties for 2.8bn people" emphasized the size of the two nations.
Jeffrey Sachs, the Columbia University economist and prominent critic of U.S. foreign policy, made the argument much more emphatically. In an interview ahead of the summit, he said: “India and China together can really make a multilateral world,” describing their cooperation as central to the emergence of a genuinely multipolar order, while noting that Brics represents roughly half the world's population and economic output. Sachs, in fact, has gone further in pushing for an Asian partnership, arguing that “India should leave the Quad, period.”

'I don't care': Trump on Gulf-Iran talks at Brics Summit
However, New Delhi, which seems quite happy to collect diplomatic memberships the way some people collect airline miles, is staying on as a member of a rather moribund Quad while using its Brics chairmanship to portray itself as a leading voice of the Global South. PM Modi is expected to attend the G20 leaders' summit to be hosted by President Trump in Miami December 14-15.
Then there was Modi-Putin tango that has long irked traditionalist foreign policy boffins in the U.S. The Russian president's appearance alongside Modi provided another visual rebuttal to the US idea that Moscow has been diplomatically quarantined, with the optics of Putin, Xi, Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in the same frame demonstrating that Russia's international relationships is more durable that U.S would like to believe. If anything, some analysts noted that Trumpian Washington was the one getting isolated – or isolating itself. “Trump gets wrecked at Brics,” read the headline for in MeidasTouch, a trenchantly anti-Trump vlog.
Still, American analysts are hardly proclaiming the arrival of a Brics era or empire. While the expanded grouping now accounts for about half the world's population, roughly 40% of global GDP and more than a quarter of global trade, one analyst smirked that Brics also looks like a family reunion where several relatives have hired lawyers. India and China remain strategic competitors; Iran and the UAE have sharply different interests; and Saudi Arabia and Iran have their own complicated history.
So Washington takes comfort in the fact that Brics has not displaced the dollar, created a common currency or produced anything resembling Nato in reverse – things that President Trump growled against. Which is probably why, with its eminence grise out causing ripples in Ireland, there was no substantive public White House or State Department statement about the summit.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Saudi authorities said Friday drones launched from Iraq led to the temporary closure of a crucial oil export route used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.
Riyadh has increased its use of the East-West pipeline, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, since the start of the Middle East war to bypass strait of Hormuz closed by Iran.
The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”.
“The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries,” an energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier.
Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
The news comes as Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes.
The office of Iraqi prime minister Ali al-Zaidi confirmed the attack originated from Iraqi territory and said on X that the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed.
The Iraqi government said it condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [that] originated from a location within the governorate”.
Riyadh said that, at the Iraqi prime minister’s request, it had chosen “not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government …to prevent attacks launched from Iraq against the Kingdom and neighbouring countries”.
Riyadh previously accused Iranian-backed Iraqi militias of targeting its oil infrastructure. But it stressed that the kingdom “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities,” and its people.
Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar also condemned the attack on the Saudi pipeline, while the Gulf Cooperation Council denounced “a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom”.
Oil prices have climbed past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday – a potential headache for president Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade in July against Saudi Arabia – which supports the Yemeni government – attacking its oil tankers in the Red Sea.
By taking control of the Yemeni Red Sea coast and the islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday, the Houthis consolidated their grip on the strategic passage linking Europe and Asia.
Navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia after the latest advances, the Houthis said.

Boris Johnson hits out at Putin after Russian drone struck train just minutes behind his
A Russian drone hit the train behind the one the former prime minister was travelling on
Boris Johnson has hit back at Vladimir Putin after a Russian drone targeted the railway line he was travelling on.
The former prime minister was alerted at 5am on Sunday as he returned from a security conference in Kyiv and told to prepare for an evacuation after another passenger train behind his was attacked in Volyn, near the Polish border.
In a post on X, Mr Johnson wrote: “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning.”
It is understood that Mr Johnson was not evacuated or delayed by the incident but an ordinary passenger train was vacated. Ukrainian Railways service Ukrzaliznytsia said no one was injured in the attack on the locomotive.
He continued: “What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways. So far Putin has been responsible for the deaths of 1,700 staff of Ukrzaliznytsia – Ukrainian Railways. They and their daily passengers are absolutely heroic.
“When are we going to give them the air defences they need? Why won’t we unfreeze Putin’s cash and give it to Ukraine? There is more than €140 billion in a Belgian bank account – and about £10 billion in London. Britain could show a lead.
“The Ukrainians are going to win – that much was clear from the last three days in their wonderful country. But we will get this dreadful war over much faster if we all get serious and give them what they need and deserve.”
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, back with Mr Johnson was in power, he has remained a close ally to the Ukrainian people. As prime minister, he was one of the first world leaders to offer humanitarian and military support to Ukraine.
Since leaving office, he has remained outspoken in his support for Ukraine in the fight against Vladimir Putin.
The attack on the passenger train was one of a number of strikes along the border, with a Polish border guard spokeswoman claiming a Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn overnight, less than a mile from the Polish border.
Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Moscow’s “barbaric strikes” on the Ukrainian Polish border on Sunday.
"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Sybiha said on X.
"This is Putin's terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he added.

A rumor circulated online in September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media post threatening to turn off the water to Niagara Falls, a natural landmark famously shared by the U.S. and Canada, unless Canada agreed to pay a "100% tariff."
People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a Truth Social post that appeared to show Trump complaining about trade relations with Canada. The text read (emphasis ours):
NO MORE FREE NIAGARA FALLS FOR CANADA! For far too long, Canada has been enjoying our water, our views, our tourists, and our great American waterfall — NIAGARA FALLS! They get the Canadian side, they take the mist, the water, and billions of dollars from tourism, all while treating the United States unfairly on trade, lumber, energy, and so many other things. It's a total disgrace! Effective immediately, unless Canada agrees to pay a 100% TARIFF on Niagara Falls, we will be turning off the tap to the falls. That's right — NO WATER FOR CANADA! We have the control. We have the valves. We can reduce the flow, or shut it down completely, and we will if necessary. Canada has been taking advantage of the United States for decades, getting a world-famous natural resource basically for free while insulting our country and making it harder for American businesses. That ends now! If they want the water, the mist, the tourism, and the beauty of Niagara Falls, they must pay 100% or they don't get it. No more free rides, no more unfair treatment, and no more taking advantage of the United States. AMERICA FIRST! KEEP OUR WATER IN AMERICA! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
President DONALD J. TRUMP
The alleged post circulated online as Trump escalated an ongoing trade war with Canada, leading many Snopes readers to ask us whether it was real.
(@CoffinItUp on X)
The post was fake. Searches of the president's Truth Social and X accounts, as well as an online archive of Trump's Truth Social posts, revealed no such post.
Addtionally, searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo returned no relevant results from reputable news outlets. If the president had really said he planned on "turning off the tap to the falls," journalists with reputable news outlets such as The Associated Press or Reuters would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case.
A reverse image search of the screenshot in question found only other social media accounts posting the same fake image.
The fake screenshot included a watermark for Real America's Voice, a conservative media outlet that highlights community contributions. However, a search of ARV's social media accounts and website revealed no mention of a Trump post discussing Niagara Falls.
The fake post circulated amid the United States' trade war with Canada, which has led to tit-for-tat tariffs on goods from both countries.
It appeared the fake post was created to poke fun at these events, including a real social media post from Trump about renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
Snopes could not determine the origin of the fake post or whether it was intended as satire, but its tone and relevance to current events matched the style of other fake Trump posts with satirical origins.
Trump alone couldn't simply "turn off the tap" for Niagara Falls, as its water is managed by the 1950 Niagara Treaty, which established a committee that "oversees the water flow over the Niagara Falls for display purposes" and "determines the amount of water available for generating power."
The committee reports to both the U.S. and Canadian governments "and is comprised of government and private sector interests, such as Ontario Power Generation," according to the Government of Canada's website.
For further reading, we fact-checked a claim that Trump posted an animated video of himself repeatedly hitting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney with a hockey stick.

The Best 3-in-1 Apple Wireless Chargers
Featured in this article
If you have an iPhone, AirPods, and an Apple Watch, congrats! You have the holy trinity of Apple products. But keeping all these gadgets powered up can be annoying, since they all have individual cables and proprietary charging solutions. Why deal with all that hassle when the best 3-in-1 Apple charging stations can accommodate everything? Our Best Wireless Chargers guide has a few recommendations, but many more great docking systems exist for Apple devices. After years of testing 3-in-1 Apple charging stations, these are my favorites. If you want one you can take on a trip, check out my new Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.
Be sure to read our other Apple guides, including the Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best iPhone 17 Cases, and Best iPad Accessories.
Updated September 2026: I added chargers from Nimble, Mophie, Journey, and OtterBox, removed some older devices, and updated prices.
Best 2-in-1 Chargers
With a weighty base, an adjustable Qi2/MagSafe charging pad, and a fold-out Apple Watch charger around the back, this Zens 2-in-1 is ideal for folks with an iPhone and Apple Watch. The Apple Watch pad folds out of the back, tucking your watch out of sight and allowing room for the strap to droop. The pad works great with StandBy mode. You can also fold the pad flat and charge AirPods or other phones if you need to, just not at the same time as your iPhone. Sadly, this has a barrel port for the provided cable and charger (USB-C would be better), the Apple Watch charger can be a little stiff and tricky to fold out, and it’s pricey, but I love the quality, look, and feel.
Belkin's UltraCharge 2-in-1 unseats our previous favorite, the BoostCharge Pro 2-in-1, which is still a great option. However, the latest model features Qi2 25W charging support to charge compatible devices even faster. It also has a folding design, allowing you to take it with you on the go, but it also works great as a permanent charger for your desk or nightstand. Over on the back, there's a spot to place AirPods or any wireless earbuds with wireless charging. What's also great is the spare USB-C port—you can pop in a cable to charge your Apple Watch at 5 watts (or another device); it just won't charge very fast. (Belkin also has a 3-in-1 version of this model if you want a dedicated spot for the Apple Watch.) Best of all, Belkin includes a very compact 45-watt power adapter and a USB-C to USB-C cable, which is better than many other wireless chargers that cost more. It's a nifty little thing, and looks great in blue. —Julian Chokkattu
iOttie Velox Duo for $60: This was our 2-in-1 pick for a while. The black-and-gold combo looks great, the magnet is strong, and there’s a weighted base. On the downside, it only charges iPhones at up to 7.5 watts. The permanently attached USB-C cable is a good length, but you do have to provide a wall adapter.
Belkin BoostCharge Pro 2-in-1 Wireless Charging Dock with MagSafe for $120: This was our old 2-in-1 pick for iPhone and Apple Watch. I like the soft-touch finish, the pad on top can move through 70 degrees, and the shelf for your Apple Watch works with any strap. The braided USB-C cable is permanently attached, but you get a 30-watt wall charger in the box. I don’t remember having issues when I first tested, but using it again, I found the weight of the camera end of my iPhone 14 Pro caused it to slowly droop when in StandBy mode. It’s also kinda pricey.
Belkin BoostCharge Pro 2-in-1 MagSafe-Compatible Wireless Charging Pad for $80: Qi2 support provides magnetic alignment for your iPhone and delivers 15 watts of charging, and there’s a spot for AirPods on this compact dual pad. A USB-C port allows you to charge something else, such as an Apple Watch, and you get a 5-foot USB-C cable and 30W power supply in the box. There is also a 3-in-1 pad ($110) that adds an Apple Watch charger on the right side.
More 3-in-1 Chargers to Consider
We have tested several other 3-in-1 Apple charging stations. Here are a few we liked:
With a refreshingly different look, the Nova from Journey is one of the most stylish 3-in-1 chargers I’ve tested. I love the black and walnut finish. Your Qi2 phone can charge at up to 15 watts; there’s a fast-charging Apple Watch pad that pops up around the back, and the space in the middle can charge AirPods at 5 watts. There’s also a handy night light with a touch-sensitive button that’s just enough to see what you’re doing. It’s compact and comes with a USB-C cable, but no power adapter, and I found the magnetic front a little weak.
OtterBox 3-in-1 Charging Stand for $140: This solid, fairly compact aluminum 3-in-1 charging station can charge all your Apple gadgets (25W for iPhone, 5W for Apple Watch, 5W for AirPods) and comes with a 6.6-foot cable and a 45-watt wall charger. While this new version of OtterBox’s 3-in-1 stand supports Qi2 25W, the design is unchanged, so you still can’t alter the angle of the pads. The integrated Apple Watch charger allows for Nightstand mode, but it is the weak link here, and I sometimes find my watch twists slightly.
Noco X Grid XDS3 for $130: Well made, with an eye-catching design, this 3-in-1 charger has a wide base that’s great for stability. It’s easy to remove your iPhone one-handed too, though it does have a relatively large footprint. It’s a bit bulky to travel with. You can stick your Qi2 phone to the pad in portrait or landscape, and the large bottom 5W pad is suitable for AirPods or even a second phone. You also get an adapter, generous 6.5-foot braided USB-C cable, and plug adapters for different countries in the box. It supports Apple Watch fast charging, but I didn’t like the way my Apple Watch tended to tilt to one side, and the charging pad positions are fixed (you can’t change the angle).
Twelve South HiRise 3 Deluxe for $100: Twelve South's 3-in-1 is an elegant wireless charger for the nightstand and gives the iPhone plenty of breathing room to rotate it to landscape mode and take advantage of StandBy. I like that the iPhone charger can swivel up and down. On the base is a fast charger for the Apple Watch that you can flip up, and the back has a spot for the AirPods or another wireless earbuds case. It's nice and weighty and doesn't slide around easily. It comes with a proprietary, removable charging cable, along with a charging brick, and international plug adapters for the US, UK, EU, and AU.
Anker Prime 3-in-1 Charging Station for $230: Sporting a tree design similar to our top pick from Belkin, the very latest Qi2 25W charging, fast Apple Watch charging, active cooling, and an interactive display, this is perhaps the most feature-packed 3-in-1 charger on the market. You can connect via Bluetooth and configure in the app to set wallpapers for the clock, schedule night mode to dim the display and turn off the cooling, and track your charging stats in a table. I’m just not sure it’s worth the premium. The finicky touch display is flat, so you have to sit up to see it, and it looks a bit cheap to me. It also feels superfluous when your iPhone already offers Standby mode.
Anker MagGo Wireless Charging Station Stand for $111: This good-looking 3-in-1 charging tree is more affordable than our top pick, boasts Qi2 certification for 15-watt charging, and comes with a charger and cable. It just misses out on a place above because of the offset pad for the Apple Watch. It is slippery, so your Apple Watch may tilt, though I never had an issue with it not charging. Anker included stickers to combat this, but they are a fiddly and inelegant solution. It’s also a shame that the main pad for your iPhone is fixed, so you can’t adjust the angle. But these are minor gripes.
Anker 3-in-1 Cube with MagSafe for $130: This dinky, dense, 2.5-inch cube from Anker was our previous compact pick. It has a MagSafe pad on top (15 watts), and the top section hinges to a 60-degree angle, revealing a charging surface for your AirPods. The small pop-out shelf on the side has a built-in Apple Watch fast charger. You get a 5-foot cable and a 30-watt charger in the box.
Zens Office Charger Pro 3 for $85: I’m a fan of some of the interesting, out-of-the-box designs that Zens turns out, but this 3-in-1, while well-made and perfectly functional, doesn’t really stand out. It’s Qi2 certified (15W for iPhone, 5W for Apple Watch, 5W for AirPods), looks nice, and comes with the cable and charger, though it has a barrel port.
Lululook 3-in-1 Charging Station for $60: This is a perfectly competent 3-in-1 with Qi2 certification (15W for iPhone, 5W for Apple Watch, 5W for AirPods). It’s compact, you can angle the iPhone pad, and I like the gold finish of my review unit, but I prefer the Twelve South above, or the ESR if you don’t want to spend as much.
QDOS SnapStand 3-in-1 for £80: This clever design feels sturdy and comes flat, and you can fold out and angle a magnetic pad for charging your iPhone (StandBy mode works fine). There’s a pop-out Apple Watch charger around the back, and the base has a pad for your AirPods. You get a black USB-C cable, but you’ll need a charger (at least 25W). I like that it’s partly made from recycled materials, and it folds away very neatly, but the charging speeds are relatively slow (7.5 watts for the iPhone and 2.5 watts for the Apple Watch).
Satechi 3-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Charging Stand for $130: This compact, attractive 3-in-1 is a little smaller than the Belkin, so it doesn't take up too much room, and it folds down compactly for travel. The aluminum build is attractive and sturdy (the iPhone mount is made of stainless steel). This is on former reviews editor Adrienne So's bedside table, and it recharges her Apple Watch Ultra 2 from 70 percent to full in around 30 minutes.
Case-Mate Fuel 3-in-1 Foldable for $58: Finished in a classy gray material, this 3-in-1 charges an iPhone in a case or any Qi smartphone, and it's easy to fold flat and pack in a bag. It also has a built-in Apple Watch charger and a spot for AirPods. A cable and a 45-watt charger are included. I also tested the solid Case-Mate Fuel 4-in-1 ($150), which is quite good, but the unnecessary LEDs and Fuel logo put me off.
Best 4-in-1 Chargers
The whole point of a 3-in-1 is to reduce clutter and cables while still getting all your devices charged. And if you have an extra device, a 4-in-1 is one step better. This stand has a lovely compact design with a tilting Qi2 25W pad for your phone, an Apple Watch charger around the back, and an indented pad on the base for your AirPods. That's all familiar. Zens 4-in-1 Modular Wireless Charger with iPad Charging Stand for $130: If you also own an iPad, why not a 4-in-1 charging station? The main drawback with this is the large size, and you have to connect a cable to the USB-C port on the side to charge your iPad.
Scosche Baselynx 2.0 Modular Charging Station for $100: What if three spots are not enough? Scosche has you covered with this modular charging station. The basic stand is a 2-in-1 for your iPhone and AirPods, but you can add an Apple Watch charger, a toast rack-style vertical station with USB-C ports, or even an AC outlet with USB-C port, for a big combined charger ($230). The trouble is, it gets quite big and expensive as you add modules, and I don’t love the way it looks, but it’s a neat idea.
Avoid These Chargers
Not every charger will be a winner. Here are the ones we didn't like.
Infinacore T3 Pro: The T3 Pro is a 3-in-1 stand that looks and feels very cheap, and it got warm when charging my iPhone. Its saving grace is that it is cheap. It also has Qi2 certification and works with StandBy mode. I also tried the fold-out triple pad Infinacore T3 Wireless Charging Station. Aside from the ugly plastic design, the weak magnets meant it did not work well when folded into the triangular configuration (this also blocks a pad).
Groov-e Asteria Wireless Charging Station with Alarm Clock: There’s a small clock on the front of this charging station, which can accommodate an iPhone, AirPods on a pad around back, and an Apple Watch up top. It feels and looks very cheap, slides around a little too easily, the magnet is weak, and the clock seems redundant when you can set your iPhone in StandBy mode. I also tried the Triton 3-in-1 folding pad, and it was okay. They are very affordable, but you must provide your own power adapter.
Zike 3-in-1 Z557C Stand: This 3-in-1 charger works perfectly well, but there are several better options above. The iPhone pad allows for StandBy mode but is not adjustable. The Apple Watch pad flips up or can be laid flat, and there’s a spot for AirPods on the gray felt pad. It has a barrel port, so you must use the supplied power adapter. What I really dislike about this charger is the ridiculously bright, utterly pointless white LED on the front that stays on the entire time.
Alogic Matrix Ultimate: This 3-in-1 charger has a folding design, supports fast charging, includes a detachable 5,000-mAh power bank, and comes with a nice pouch, but it is kinda bulky, and the white finish picks up dust and smudges very easily. I have also had issues with other Alogic batteries failing and not supplying the stated capacity.
STM Goods ChargeTree Go: This charging tree station folds flat and can charge a trio of Apple gadgets. But there’s no quick-charge support, my Apple Watch kept sliding out of place during the night, and there’s no adapter included. It’s not cheap either.
A Quick Primer on MagSafe
Most of the wireless chargers in this guide are MagSafe wireless chargers or Qi2 certified. That means they take advantage of the magnets embedded in the back of the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 range. I cannot stress this enough: If you buy a case, ensure it is a MagSafe case. We have several third-party options in the linked case guides above. A normal iPhone case will weaken the pull of the magnets in the device and will not stick to MagSafe accessories well.
What's the point of MagSafe? You don't have to worry about misalignment with the wireless charger, meaning you won't wake up to a dead iPhone. Technically, this perfect alignment enables chargers to deliver faster 15-watt charging. MagSafe is also available in the AirPods charging case (depending on your model). Apple's AirPods and AirPods Pro with the wireless charging case will work with nearly all of the standard Qi wireless charging pads on these chargers (as will many third-party wireless earbuds), but if you have AirPods with MagSafe, then you can hook them up to the magnetic mounts as well. If you don't have a MagSafe iPhone, then your device won't be able to attach to these chargers, though we do have some recommendations for older iPhones (and the iPhone 16e).
What About Qi2?
Qi2 is the latest wireless charging standard, and Apple worked with the Wireless Power Consortium to develop it. Compared to the original Qi standard, it brings MagSafe-style magnetic charging, faster charging rates, and improved efficiency—but where MagSafe is an Apple technology designed for Apple products, any device can support Qi2. Apple updated the iPhone 12 and newer to support Qi2, so Qi2 should be a term you look for when shopping for a magnetic wireless charger. Qi2 Android phones are still thin on the ground right now—it's officially available in Google's Pixel 10 series—though Qi2 Ready phones add magnets using a compatible case. Expect more Qi2 Android phones soon. A Qi2 charger can charge your iPhone and any other Qi2 phones.
While Qi2 charging generally goes up to 15 watts, the Qi2.2 update, branded as Qi2 25W, can go up to 25 watts. But support for Qi2 25W is currently very limited, and includes the iPhone 17 range and the Pixel 10 Pro XL.
What Are StandBy Mode and Nightstand Mode?
You'll see us bring up two specific modes throughout this guide: StandBy mode and Nightstand mode. What are they?
StandBy mode was introduced in iOS 17. When you place your iPhone on a charger in landscape orientation, it will turn the screen into a dock of sorts, showing the clock (with different designs you can choose from), photos from your library, or widgets. If you have an iPhone that supports an always-on screen, you can choose to have the display automatically turn off after some time when the iPhone isn't in use or if the room is dark. Head to Settings > Standby to customize it.
Nightstand mode has long been around on the Apple Watch. Basically, when the watch is sitting upright and charging, the clockface will stay on so you can always tell the time. You can customize this on your Apple Watch by heading to Settings > General > Nightstand mode.

How to set up HDMI-CEC on your Samsung TV
HDMI-CEC makes all the devices connected to your Samsung TV work together more efficiently, with a few quirks to know.
Disable just one setting on your Samsung TV, and it can suddenly feel a lot less smart. Turning on your game console will no longer wake the display, your soundbar won't respond to the TV remote, and changing inputs becomes a game of finding the last remote you left between the couch cushions. Much of this behavior is tied to Anynet+, which is Samsung's name for a feature call HDMI-CEC.
HDMI-CEC (Consumer Electronics Control) lets compatible devices send control signals over HDMI. This means your Samsung remote can control another device (like your soundbar), while turning on a streaming box will automatically turn on the TV and switch it to the appropriate input. HDMI still carries audio and video; CEC is just one feature that operates over it.
Most Samsung smart TVs made after 2008 support this functionality. Anynet+ is usually activated by default on newer Samsung TVs, so you might not have noticed it. It's also easy to turn off by mistake while exploring the Settings menu.
How to make sure HDMI-CEC is enabled on a Samsung TV
For newer Samsung TVs, press the Home button on your remote, then go to Settings > All Settings > Connection > External Device Manager. Make sure Anynet+ (HDMI-CEC) is turned on. If your TV doesn't have a Connection menu, look under Settings > General > External Device Manager. Samsung has moved this setting across models over the years, so it might be in another location. In case you still can't find it, check the TV's manual or support page.
That's the entire TV-side setup, but what's on the other end of the HDMI cable must cooperate as well. The connected device needs to support HDMI-CEC and, if it has its own CEC setting, that must be on. Unsurprisingly, manufacturers couldn't agree on what to call this "standardized" feature, so you'll see different names. LG uses SIMPLINK, Sony uses BRAVIA Sync or Control for HDMI and consoles or streaming boxes may give it yet another name. For instance, on PS5, the option is under Settings > System > HDMI > Enable HDMI Device Link.
For CEC to work properly, the connected device must be on or in standby mode. Samsung says it can take up to two minutes to establish the initial "handshake." Once this is done, you should be able to control the connected device with your TV remote and take advantage of automatic input switching. Turning a compatible device off (or putting it into sleep mode) will do the same for your TV.
Should you leave HDMI-CEC turned on?
Usually, yes. HDMI-CEC makes a collection of devices act more like a single entertainment system, reducing the number of remotes and manual input switching you need. A console can turn on the TV, a compatible soundbar can power on or off with it, and your Samsung remote can control supported playback or volume functions.
That convenience can sometimes be the issue, though. Samsung says by default, its TVs switch to an HDMI source when the connected device reports that it has turned on. Because of this, a faulty or unexpected CEC command can cause unwanted input changes. HDMI-CEC is worth checking if your TV turns on by itself, keeps switching to another HDMI device or suddenly stops controlling another unit. First, ensure CEC is enabled on both devices. Then reseat or replace the HDMI cable, restart the hardware and install available firmware updates.
You might also want to disable the feature for any devices where unwanted shutdowns pose a problem, like accidentally putting your game console to sleep while in a ranked match. Compatibility isn't 100 percent consistent between manufacturers, so two products that support HDMI-CEC may not support every command in the same way. There are also device limitations, though you'll likely need an HDMI switch before you hit these. Anynet+ can control up to 12 compatible devices, including up to three of the same type, but only one home theater system.
There's one important caveat if you're using a soundbar or receiver. HDMI eARC can only work if Anynet+ is enabled, so disabling CEC to fix an annoying input-switching issue may leave you soon troubleshooting a completely different audio problem.

Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
- Published
This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".
Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.
India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.
The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.
But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.
A counterweight to Western influence
For members such as China, Russia and Iran, Brics offers a vehicle to dilute the influence of the US and western Europe.
But India has been reluctant to cast Brics as an anti-Western bloc. Modi himself said at the summit that the group is "not against anyone".
That distinction matters for Delhi, which wants to preserve its relationships with nations at odds with each other.
"There are countries in the grouping which would like it to become anti-western, but it is not that," says Anil Trigunayat, a veteran Indian diplomat and former ambassador. What India has achieved, in his view, is a push for "strategic autonomy in an era of war" and initiatives to "enhance greater collaboration amongst themselves".
Inside the joint declaration
The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring.
Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions.
The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say.
On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame.
It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions.
It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations.
There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire.
Several Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American".
"Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
"I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added.
Beyond the summit
In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies.
What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago.
Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began.
This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure.
As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia.
As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour.
There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night.
But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade.
Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen.
"I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says.
What comes next?
The summit showed that Brics can create space for rivals to talk and manoeuvre outside Western-dominated institutions.
The harder question is what happens next. It's clear that members agree they need a new global order more than ever, but what exactly should replace it and how to get there is far more challenging to answer.

Legendary Canadian boxer George Chuvalo dies aged 89
- Published
Canadian boxer George Chuvalo, a five-time national heavyweight champion, has died at the age of 89.
Out of 93 total professional fights in his career - 73 victories, 18 losses, and two draws - Chuvalo was never once knocked down to the canvas.
"His photos have hung on our walls for decades. His stories have been passed down from one generation of fighters to the next," said Sully's Boxing, the Toronto gym where he trained, in a statement.
He battled Muhammad Ali in 1966 and 1972, and though Chuvalo lost both fights, Ali called him the toughest guy he ever fought.
Chuvalo was born in 1937 to Croatian immigrant parents, grew up in Toronto and got into boxing at a young age.
Widely considered "Canada's greatest warrior", Chuvalo was known for his iron chin, relentless durability, and fights against world famous fighters like George Foreman, Joe Frazier, and Ali.
"George Chuvalo was a heavyweight boxing legend, a family friend and a Canadian icon," Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media.
"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing."
After retiring from professional boxing in 1978, Chuvalo travelled the country as a public speaker advocating for anti-drug education and mental health awareness.
Chuvalo lost three sons and his wife to drug overdoses and suicide, he has said.
"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family," he once said, according to a CBC Radio report in 1998.
In retirement, Chuvalo also dipped his toes in acting, appearing in the 1998 comedy film Dirty Work and alongside Jeff Goldblum in the 1986 horror film The Fly.
He also served as a guest commentator for major boxing matches and co-hosted a TV boxing program called Greatest Knockouts with his friend and fellow fighter Charles "Spider" Jones.
Chuvalo is survived by his eldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, grandchildren, and second wife Joanne.
He died on Saturday, his birthday, said Sully's Boxing Gym.
