The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?
In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”
The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?
While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.
While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds
Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.
Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?
NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.
Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.
Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?
Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.
NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim visited All India Jamiyyathul Ulama general secretary Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliyar at the Markaz Central Campus here on Sunday (September 13, 2026) as part of his five-day visit to India.
Mr. Anwar, who arrived in Kozhikode after attending the BRICS summit in New Delhi, held discussions with Kanthapuram on issues including global peace, education and social development. The two leaders exchanged views on socio-cultural exchanges and discussed the prospects for peace talks among countries involved in conflicts.
Mr. Anwar was also presented with the first Excellence Award instituted by the Sheikh Abubacker Foundation. Mr. Kanthapuram presented the award to the Malaysian Prime Minister at a reception organised in his honour at the convention centre.
Later, Mr. Anwar attended a special prayer gathering. A discussion involving prominent figures from the religious, political and social spheres was also held.
Along with the senior Sunni leaders led by Mr. Kanthapuram, the Malaysian Prime Minister later visited the Madavoor C.M. Valiyullah Makham, a prominent spiritual centre in south India.
This was Mr. Anwar’s second visit to Keralam to meet the veteran Sunni leader. He was in Markaz campus in September 2022, about a month before becoming Prime Minister, and had visited the Madavoor Makham with Kanthapuram on that occasion too.
The Malaysian government conferred the Hijra Award, its highest honour for Islamic scholars, on Kanthapuram in 2023. At the initiative of the Malaysian government, international Hadith recitation gatherings led by Kanthapuram were held in Kuala Lumpur in 2023, 2024, and 2025 in recognition of his six decades of teaching Hadith.
Kanthapuram had earlier intervened in matters concerning the welfare and employment issues of Indian expatriates in Malaysia and had also taken up the demand for direct flights from Keralam, particularly Kozhikode, to Malaysia.
The meeting also came against the backdrop of differences between the two leaders on some social and religious issues. A day before his Kozhikode visit, Mr. Anwar, speaking to the media on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, had said he did not necessarily agree with all of Kanthapuram’s views. He was responding to a question about the cleric’s recent remarks that “women should remain confined within their homes”.
Mr. Anwar had described Kanthapuram as a traditional religious scholar who had contributed to the understanding of the Quran, religious tradition and the Prophet, and praised him as a great teacher. At the same time, he said the two did not necessarily share all their views and indicated that he would tell Kanthapuram directly that Malaysia guarantees women equal rights.
Sunni leaders said Mr. Anwar’s India visit, including his Keralam visit, was expected to provide fresh momentum to bilateral cooperation in trade, tourism, investment, economic cooperation, education, and connectivity. The Prime Minister’s visit was held amid tight security arrangements in Kozhikode. Traffic was regulated along key routes to facilitate the movement of the VVIP convoy.

SC lets manager off the hook, puts focus on Indian Bank in 35-year-old loan case
The Supreme Court acquitted ex-bank manager V Balakrishnan, revealing Indian Bank's failure to return ₹2.7 crore in excess auction proceeds to borrowers' heirs.
For more than three decades, a bank manager was made to answer for an alleged loss caused to Indian Bank by loans sanctioned in 1991-92. But when the Supreme Court finally acquitted him, it was the bank that found itself in the dock — over why it had kept more than ₹2.7 crore in excess auction proceeds with itself for years instead of handing the money over to the borrowers’ legal heirs.
In a striking turn in the 35-year-old case, the Supreme Court has not only overturned the conviction of V Balakrishnan, then branch manager of Indian Bank’s Anna Nagar branch, but also summoned the bank to explain what it did with the surplus money left after auctioning mortgaged properties to recover the loans.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran noted that the bank received ₹1.175 crore from the auction of one borrower’s property against loan dues of only ₹16.42 lakh, while another auction fetched ₹2.42 crore against dues of just ₹5.35 lakh. A further property fetched ₹34.5 lakh, which was also appropriated towards the loan account.
The court said the loans had been fully satisfied, yet the excess money from the auctions was still lying with the bank. “More intriguing is the fact…that the amounts received in auction, in excess of the appropriation to the loan accounts are still remaining with the bank,” said the bench, expressing surprise that “no attempt was made to find out the legal heirs and pass on the money”.
The court has now impleaded the branch manager of Indian Bank’s Anna Nagar branch and ordered him to submit a report on the two loan accounts, their satisfaction, the auction proceeds and how the excess money was utilised. The bank has also been directed to produce the title deeds of the mortgaged properties.
The case will return before the Supreme Court on October 5, specifically to ascertain the status of the excess auction money and ensure its due disbursal.
Balakrishnan had been working as branch manager in 1991 when CBI alleged that he conspired with P Kumaradevan, a retired Indian Overseas Bank officer, to sanction loans to two borrowers who were allegedly Kumaradevan’s domestic helps. The prosecution case was that inflated property valuations were used to secure the loans and that Kumaradevan ultimately appropriated the money.
A CBI court convicted Balakrishnan in 2016 and sentenced him to one year’s rigorous imprisonment, more than two decades after the alleged irregularities. The high court upheld the conviction, bringing the matter to the Supreme Court.
But the apex court found the prosecution evidence fundamentally deficient. It noted that the loans had in fact been sanctioned by the Indian Bank’s Regional Office, with official witnesses acknowledging the approvals. The bank subsequently recovered the loan amounts in full by auctioning the mortgaged properties.
The court also found that the prosecution had failed to establish that Kumaradevan had actually signed the cheques through which the loan amounts were allegedly received by him. It further rejected the inference that the properties must have been overvalued in 1991-92 simply because they fetched substantially higher prices when auctioned in 2010 — nearly two decades later.
The Supreme Court held that the prosecution’s case was “fabricated” and had “no legs to stand”, holding that CBI had failed not only to prove its case but also to properly frame it. The court granted Balakrishnan a clean acquittal, setting aside both the trial court and high court judgments.
But the final twist came after the acquittal. Having spent years prosecuting a bank manager for allegedly causing a loss to the bank, the record before the Supreme Court showed that the bank had ultimately recovered the loans, and was still holding a substantial surplus from the auctions.
The court has now turned its scrutiny on that money, making the 35-year-old prosecution end with an altogether different question: what happened to the money that remained after Indian Bank had recovered every rupee it was owed?

Uniform Civil Code will be implemented by 2029 in the 21 States where the Bharatiya Janata Party and the NDA are in power, Union Home Minister Amit Shah said in Mumbai on Sunday (September 13, 2026). He said the government was committed to deporting every illegal immigrant from the country.
Mr. Shah, who spoke to the press, refused to give a timeline for the implementation of the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Manipur. However, he said the government was discussing with allies and political parties the use of the 1951 baseline for the exercise.
Speaking about the Gen Z protests in July, he said everyone must express opinions in a democracy. “We want to communicate with everyone. We don’t want to run the country in an Emergency-like situation. Congress culture was different. Our culture is different,” he said.
Mr. Shah, who is on a two-day visit to Maharashtra, was speaking on the occasion of the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyaan’, a month-long national drive from September 17 to October 17 to celebrate Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and the completion of his 25 years of service as a Chief Minister and as the Prime Minister.
The Congress slammed the Home Minister for evading questions on the allegations of corruption surrounding the Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank Limited ‘scam’ involving alleged financial irregularities of ₹25,000 crore through improper loan disbursals and distress sale of cooperative sugar factories.
Mr. Shah is also the Union Minister of Co-operation, and when asked whether his Ministry planned to present a white paper in the case, owing to the differences in the probe findings by the Central and the State agencies, he said, “Why should we? The agencies are doing their work. They will file a charge sheet in the court. I now request you all to limit yourselves to the topic of the 25 years of service.”
Maharashtra Congress president Harshawardhan Sapkal said the Union Minister “ran away” from the press conference as he did not have the “courage” to answer questions on the multi-crore ‘scam’.
Mr. Shah’s visit to the State comes amid differences over making functional Marathi compulsory for cab and auto drivers. He will attend the Hindi Divas celebration in Mumbai on Monday (September 14, 2026). Asked about the conflicts over language and regional identity arising from migration, he said, “It is our government’s policy to prioritise the mother tongue, and the Constitution has issued specific directives to the States in this regard. I do not believe this will become a major issue. While isolated incidents may occur if certain individuals attempt to stoke tensions, the States have experienced leadership and will certainly find a way to resolve such issues.”
The BJP enjoys the electoral support of the migrant population, particularly in financial centres like Mumbai and Pune.
Mr. Shah, who presented the 52nd India Gem and Jewellery Awards at another event, urged the diamond industry to take a lead in controlling the lab-grown diamond ecosystem.
“In terms of volume, the market for lab-grown diamonds is poised to expand to nearly 50 times the size of the current diamond market. This represents a huge opportunity. It is my appeal to you that the lab-grown diamond ecosystem should be in the control of people of Bharat.”

I Tried 10 of the Most Popular Indoor Gardening Systems
Featured in this article
Are you missing being able to eat lettuce due to the recent cyclosporiasis outbreak? I'm not. Not because I'm throwing caution to the wind and buying it anyway, but because I'm growing multiple types of organic lettuce myself, in my own house, in less than a few square feet. And you can too.
For the past year, I've been testing various indoor smart garden systems in my home, which have given me year-round access to fresh tomatoes, peppers, strawberries, and even zucchini. Most of them are easy for anyone to set up and use, with minimal space and maintenance requirements—there's an indoor gardening setup for just about any household.
The Gardyn Home 4.0 ($899), for example, offers total success with no green thumb required if you pay for a subscription, while the Auk Mini 2 ($239) is the perfect attractive yet low-maintenance solution for those who just want fresh herbs. Are these gardens worth it? How much can you really grow? How can you be sure which option is best for your specific lifestyle? See which gardens stood out in testing and why, and which might be ideal for your home and needs.
Check out our other sustainable home-tech buying guides, including the Best Smart Bird Feeders, Best Kitchen Composters, and Best Water Leak Detectors.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the new Auk Mini 2 and more long-term testing notes on the Gardyn and EVE, moved a couple of previous picks to honorable mentions, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Honorable Mentions
Click and Grow Smart Garden for $125: Click & Grow Smart Garden's seed pods come in a Nespresso-evoking plastic three-pack with a tear-off cover. (A three-pack of pods starts at around $15.) Put a nutrient-packed “smart soil” seed pod in one of the Click & Grow’s cups with the wicking bottom, fill the reservoir, and that’s it. It was one of the simplest watering systems I tried: a wick at the bottom of the cup brings water up to the pods, and the roots stay in the cups. A little bobber on one end tells you when the water level is low and needs a top-off simply by floating lower than the growing surface. It's also small, so you can plop it on a shelf or countertop. (Note that the 9, pictured above, is currently out of stock, but you can sign up to be notified when it's available.) At the same time, this was also one of the slowest-growing gardens I tested—it took weeks to get even one lettuce leaf. One of my lettuce pods didn’t even sprout at all. Still, this isn't a terrible option for busy people who are interested in growing something like flowers, where yields aren't a concern.
Modern Sprout Garden Jars for $20: These cute Mason jars are as simple as it gets: Rinse the included gravel, then add seeds and water. They're guaranteed to sprout in five to ten days and make a fun hostess gift with a tea towel and/or a bottle of olive oil. However, they are definitely more for looks than harvests—I have had the basil, cilantro, and rosemary versions on my windowsill for a little over a year, and I’ve only seen a few usable leaves.
Lettuce Grow Counterstand Set for $149: New from the makers of the flashy Lettuce Grow Farmstand (8/10 WIRED Recommends), this simple, no-pump setup consists of three amber beakers that look straight out of a high school chemistry lab, plus an 18-inch LED lamp that runs on a 16- or 18-hour timer. It relies on the Kratky method of hydroponics, invented by horticulturist Dr. Bernard Kratky, where the plant sits in a cup above a nutrient-enriched water source. In the Counterstand's case, a wick draws water up to the seedling until its roots can grow into the water. Included with your order are three credits for live seedlings of your choice—I picked parsley, basil, and butter lettuce. This setup is stylish, but the yields are tiny for the counter space it takes up—maybe a small handful of leaves a week.
Vego EZ Microgreens Planter (2-pack) for $60: This system for growing nutrient-packed microgreens for salads, smoothies, and sandwiches isn't smart, but it is nifty enough to warrant a mention. Just fill each half-gallon reservoir (made of food-safe plastic) with water, and then cover it with the optional humidity dome. From there, bamboo-fiber capillary grow mats on top will absorb water to germinate your microgreen seeds (not included). Set it near a sunny window, use a grow light, or add Vego's 10 x 20 dome with a built-in grow light ($80), which fits over both planters. I placed my planters on a Ferry-Morse pop-up plant stand with a grow light from LetPot and had consistent success across multiple grows.
Not Recommended
Plantaform Smart Indoor Garden for $900: Plantaform is “the world's first smart indoor garden that uses fog to grow plants,” according to the company's press release, and it has definitely garnered attention, winning an Innovation Award at CES 2025. The “fogponics" technology, ostensibly building on NASA-developed aeroponics, delivers water and nutrients to plants' roots via an ultrafine mist. We were certainly captivated by the futuristic look of the egg-shaped planter. But when WIRED contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro tested it to grow lettuce, she found that you can't combine different types of plants (i.e., you can only grow lettuce at one time, or tomatoes, or herbs), and the machine also degraded her indoor air quality, as tested with an air quality monitor. Users are to add an included fertilizer mix to the water, with the resulting concoction being what's aerosolized in the container, which, as Wood Shapiro found, was not airtight. She suggests limiting the Plantaform's use to a basement or another space where air quality isn't as much of a concern. But it's probably best to hold off on this one until Plantaform can work out some more kinks.
LetPot Smart Seed Starter for $84: There are many grow-light–enabled seed starters on the market, but LetPot's Smart Seed Starter has more features than most, including a sensor for soil temperature and EC and a 24-watt heating pad underneath. A plastic lid with adjustable vents on either end sits on top. I love the concept, but sadly, quality control is lacking. On my test unit, the power adapter makes a high-pitched sound when the lights are on, the EC sensor only works intermittently, and auto-mode erases whenever it's unplugged. After about six months of regular use, the light stopped staying on, and to get the unit to cooperate, I had to unplug and replug it repeatedly.
FAQs
What Is Hydroponics?
In the simplest terms, hydroponic gardening means growing plants without roots in soil. Sometimes plants are suspended in water, like in the Rise or Gardyn; sometimes they're in pods attached to a wick, like in the Click & Grow; and sometimes water is sprayed or misted onto their roots, like in the Lettuce Grow. Usually, this process works alongside an artificial light source, either indoors or in an outdoor enclosure.
What Are the Benefits of Hydroponics?
In addition to the obvious plus of cleaner produce without mud, dirt, or synthetic pesticides, hydroponic systems use much less water than conventional growing methods, since all the water used is either recirculated or taken up by the plants. Some farmers also say they get higher yields from hydroponic systems, as the variables of weather, light, and nutrients are far easier to control. And, because of these variables, farmers are also able to grow varieties of plants in just about any season or region. And there are no weeds!
What Kinds of Things Can I Grow in a Hydroponic Garden?
Just about anything you can think of! I asked FX Rouxel, creator of Gardyn, if there was anything you couldn't grow in these systems, other than ground-dwelling plants like peanuts or potatoes. “All the things that have big roots,” he said—like carrots, parsnips, and so on. “Otherwise, mostly things that are too big, like apples or lemons.” So, there you have it: No long roots, no trees. But anything else is fair game to try.
What Are the Downsides of Hydroponic Systems?
First of all, it's no secret hydroponic systems cost more than just planting some seeds outside in the dirt. Then you've got to worry about power outages, pump maintenance, algae, and just general maintenance. And if you're not careful, water can harbor some nasty stuff, even if that's just fertilizer, as WIRED contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro found when she reviewed the Plantaform. Some also claim that hydroponically grown herbs, greens, and vegetables have less flavor than their soil-grown counterparts, but I personally have not noticed a difference. I've grown perfectly flavorful snap peas, cauliflower, shell beans, salad greens, and even strawberries in just nutrient-infused water. In fact, one of the best cucumbers I've ever had in my life came from my Gardyn Studio, of all places.
Will I Save Money by Growing My Own Vegetables?
In short, no. The ready-made systems simply remove a great deal of hassle and guesswork from the process, and usually look pretty cool in the process. It's also nice to have warranty and tech support in the event something goes wrong, and as is often the case with anything filled with water, when something does go wrong, it goes really wrong. (Speaking of, be sure to check out our guide to the Best Water Leak Detectors.)
How Much Can I Really Grow in These Things?
It largely depends on what you're growing and how many individual plants can fit in your system. My yields have ranged from a handful of lettuce leaves in the Click & Grow to huge bagfuls of salad greens per day in the Rise—more than my family could possibly eat. As a rule, lettuces and other greens tend to grow faster, while fruiting plants like tomatoes and peppers grow slower and sometimes need pollination to produce. (For instance, with strawberries I have to use a small paintbrush to brush the flowers each morning.)
Where Can I Put Them in My House?
Most of these systems take up only a square foot or two, so space isn't as much of a consideration as lights and pump noise. Lights for these gardens typically need to be on around 16 hours a day, and they are bright, so if this schedule would be disruptive, you may want to place them away from a bedroom or any other room where darkness is needed. On a related note, many of these gardens, like the Lettuce Grow and Gardyn, have loud pump cycles, while Rise's pump runs continuously. I wouldn't recommend placing a garden with a noisy pump cycle near a TV or office, where the noise could be disruptive during certain times of the day. If any noise is a concern, for instance, when living on the top floor of an apartment, you may want to consider a totally silent garden like the Auk or Click & Grow.
How Much Do They Cost to Keep Going?
Gardens with subscriptions and/or proprietary pods, like Gardyn and Click & Grow, are obviously going to be more expensive over the long run than a truly DIY system like the LetPot. On the one hand, with proprietary pods, you won't have to source seeds or sponges; you can be assured the seeds are appropriate for that system and hydroponics in general, and if something doesn't germinate, you will be able to get a replacement or refund. But on the other hand, this is a recurring cost that will reduce any savings you gain from growing your own food or flowers. As for power, systems with a continuously running pump, like Rise, are going to cost more than ones with no pump, like the Auk. However, I haven't noticed a significant bump in my electricity bill while testing these gardens, except for one period where I had seven (yes, seven) going at one time.
How I Tested
I unboxed, assembled, and set up each garden exactly as described in the provided instructions, using the seeds, pods, or seedlings that came with the garden. I paid attention to ease of setup, ease of use, maintenance needs, how much space each system required, and how well (or not well) the plants did and why. I noted what was or was not included with each system, and allowed all of the plants to grow to the harvest stage, paying attention to bolting, yields, and general health. I'm a full-time working parent, so I also paid attention to maintenance needs, light schedules, and any general hassles that came up and annoyed me.
How I Chose Which Gardens to Test
I am genuinely passionate about indoor gardening and have an eye on what’s going on in the landscape: what’s new, what’s hot, what’s working for people, what’s not working. I’m always on the lookout for interesting new devices that I personally think are cool and that I believe WIRED readers would appreciate. Affiliate status does not factor into my decision about what to test and write about. If you have a unique, tech-forward indoor garden you like that I haven’t featured, please let me know in the comments.
How Do I Acquire Gardens to Review?
Most of the gardens I receive to test are samples provided by the companies, with no guarantee of coverage or expectation of what that coverage will look like. Some of the gardens are kept by WIRED in order to perform extended testing, while others are donated locally.

On all fours or off to a wilderness retreat? How Hongkongers are reclaiming their calm
From animal flow to film therapy and journaling, residents are embracing movement, mindfulness and micro‑pauses to rebuild resilience in a fast-paced city
For Hong Kong film practitioner Ngai Tsz-wai, peace of mind begins on all fours.
The 40-year-old practises animal flow, a quadrupedal, ground-based movement system that blends elements of yoga, dance, gymnastics and martial arts.
“Moving on all fours helps me train strength, flexibility and coordination while rebuilding the connection between body and mind,” Ngai told the South China Morning Post.
“Just as water needs to flow, our body and mind need movement to create new possibilities … which is helpful for my creative work.”
Ngai’s journey into wellness began a decade ago while producing a video for a local yoga studio, where an instructor encouraged him to try a class.

There aren’t many differences between what you’d need for a good office chair versus a good gaming chair, but for some reason, they’re often marketed differently. And that’s usually what separates them: marketing. When Branch released variations of the WIRED-favorite Ergonomic Chair Pro in collaboration with Sega, I was stoked to try it from a gamer perspective for our buying guide rather than from an office warrior POV. It checks every box: It has the comfortable ergonomics you'd expect from an adjustable office chair, with the subtle, pleasing designs inspired by one of gaming's most revered companies.
Looks Good
This Sega collaboration comes in three aesthetically pleasing designs that pay homage to the company's icons. The Sonic version has a mesh back, while the Genesis and Dreamcast versions have vegan leather instead. I tested the Dreamcast version, and I love the way it looks. It has iconic wheel designs inspired by the controller, plus a slick orange stripe on the armrests that harkens back to the console's swirly logo.
Assembling furniture continues to be one of the most frustrating parts of reviewing gear, but I aim to do it the same exact way a WIRED reader might: by myself with copious amounts of swearing. In this case, the experience actually wasn’t that bad. The box it ships in should be lifted by two people, unless you're like me, who goes to the gym and lives alone with a cat. I managed all 50-ish pounds up the stairs and assembled it in about an hour. I especially liked the labeled bolt packaging, and the included Allen key, which was sturdy and much better than you’d typically find in a furniture package. Instructions weren’t too difficult, nor were any of the pieces particularly cumbersome.
I am slightly concerned that my Dreamcast version is a white gaming chair, while the other two designs are darker. I wear a lot of dark clothing and eat a slightly above-average amount of spicy chips, so staining and ease of cleaning will be two things I look for during long-term testing. In the meantime, I will just cross my fingers that my cat doesn’t take too much of a liking to it and that I don't absentmindedly drop too many Cheetos crumbs.
Feels Better
There’s a bit of a learning curve when adjusting the ergonomics. With 14 adjustment points, from lumbar support to seat tilt and depth to multiple armrest planes, it can be painstaking to dial everything in just right. But once you figure out the knobs and levers, it’s beyond easy to lock in a position to game (or work) for hours at a time. The included headrest wasn’t perfect for me—though it is adjustable, it doesn’t lower or move forward enough for my 5’ 1” frame. Otherwise, I stayed very comfortable in this chair. The Ergonomic Pro is compatible with Branch’s tall cylinder, which you may want if you’re 5’ 11” or taller.

AI Is Running Laps Around Our Political System
The technology is moving faster than elected officials can handle—and Anthropic’s CEO says the industry should slow down.
Politicians have no shortage of ideas about how to rein in AI: a 100 percent federal tax rate on data-center incentives, a pause on all development of advanced AI, new standards to block AI agents from going rogue, a halt to the construction of data centers altogether.
The flurry of proposals has been impossible to miss, with both Democrats and Republicans proclaiming that something must be done to avert a disaster foretold by AI insiders. Current and former Anthropic researchers have in recent days gone public with warnings that AI could wipe out humanity before the decade ends; the company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, wrote in an essay today that the industry must “slow the pace” at which the technology is being developed. Meanwhile, OpenAI agents escaped a test environment and conspired with one another to breach the servers of the AI giant Hugging Face, an incident that caused alarm both in Silicon Valley and on Capitol Hill. Politicians are also dealing with mounting public opposition to data centers and the fear that robots will soon replace humans across large swaths of the workforce. If this were an alien-invasion movie, now would be the moment when people of all persuasions put aside their differences and band together to save the human race. But that kind of bonhomie feels far out of reach.
Instead, technological advances and grassroots sentiment have been moving faster than politicians have been willing to act. Now some seem to be waking up. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Republican, said last Wednesday that he will soon unveil legislation, alongside Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, intended to head off AI-induced biological or nuclear catastrophes. Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a Democrat, and Representative Mike Lawler of New York, a Republican, teamed up earlier this month to introduce legislation that would direct the federal government to create standards for securely deploying AI agents and preventing them from going rogue. Several lawmakers have called for Congress to reconvene specifically for the purpose of addressing the threats posed by AI. Yesterday, Representative Ro Khanna, who represents part of Silicon Valley, called for the creation of an AI safety agency.
Others are shifting their position in real time. Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, released a lengthy plan in June for AI development to continue with greater regulation and restrictions. He said Wednesday that he now favors “an all-out pause” on AI development. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who once approvingly called the state “the epicenter of AI development,” ordered an audit of all data-center projects before any could move forward.
But whether politicians can act quickly enough to mitigate possible damage is doubtful, experts told me. “The developments are coming so fast and furious that it is very difficult to keep up with what the harms are and how to address them,” Nate Persily, a co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, told me. He said that although there’s a growing consensus that it would be “foolish” to allow AI to continue advancing without robust federal guardrails, the complexities and rapidly changing threat landscape would challenge any country’s leadership. “There are genuinely hard questions of statutory design here,” he said.
The next few weeks—and the upcoming elections—could determine whether or not politicians are able to deliver any meaningful results or whether they will instead default to the partisan gridlock that most Americans now expect. “The good news is that people across the political spectrum are understanding that we have a technology which is the most dangerous and transformational in human history,” Senator Bernie Sanders told me. The Vermont democratic socialist was among the first lawmakers to call for a moratorium on the data centers that facilitate AI advancement and for a broader pause on the industry’s growth. We spoke shortly after Sanders sent out an invitation to members of Congress for a closed-door briefing this week with top AI-safety experts. The briefing, which will take place on Wednesday, is designed to give lawmakers a clearer understanding of the threats posed by AI and ideas for legislative action.
The invitation was made especially timely by a Tuesday social-media post from the AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who wrote that he had resigned from Anthropic over concerns about the risks of the fast-advancing technology. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Coxon, a former employee of both OpenAI and Anthropic. His posts, which argue that the AI industry is “gambling with our lives,” were publicly boosted by several other AI researchers. The messages seemed to break through in a way that few other warnings have. Sanders told me that Coxon’s X post, which received more than 120 million views within 24 hours, landed among his colleagues in Congress as “an extraordinary wake-up call.”
President Trump’s signature will be needed to enact any significant change to federal AI policy, but so far, he’s not among those who seem particularly worried. As concerns about AI and data centers have proliferated, Trump has said “let Data Reign” and rejected calls to restrict AI development in the United States. His former AI czar took a similar laissez-faire approach, espousing a philosophy that he summarized as “let the private sector cook.”
Some other Republicans are also wary of saddling American AI companies with too much government oversight. Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said earlier this year that her proposed TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, which aims to codify the president’s pro-industry executive order on artificial intelligence, would “ensure America triumphs over foreign adversaries in the global race for AI dominance.”
Even for those Republicans who do believe in more muscular federal guardrails for tech companies, Trump’s position presents a significant political hurdle. The president has made clear that he does not want regulation to impede America’s ability to win the global AI race. As is his custom, he has shown no hesitation about attacking members of his own coalition who disagree with him. Even as a growing number of Republican lawmakers are embracing some limits on AI and data centers, few have been willing to openly cross Trump or sign on to more sweeping legislation to pause or restrict AI advancement. In recent years, America’s polarized political system has generated bitter stalemates on how to prevent school shootings, what to do about climate change, and where to draw the line in responding to a once-in-a-generation pandemic. The question of how to handle the race toward superintelligence might not be any different.
In July, about 1,400 AI-company employees signed an open letter calling on the government to help regulate their industry. In a nearly 6,000-word essay published last month, the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates wrote that powerful AI models “could begin to act against our interests and we could lose control.” In a report published Thursday, Anthropic said that it had intervened to stop several attempts by scientists to use its models in a way that could potentially help develop biological weapons. Amodei wrote that he worries that within the next 6 to 12 months, a swarm of models similar to the one that breached the Hugging Face servers “could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”
AI, of course, has already delivered advances in health care and science, and there’s no consensus on the scale of the threat it poses. Nuance is required to figure out how to manage it. But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle acknowledge that our current political landscape does not lend itself to sober, cross-party problem-solving. “It is possible to move bipartisan legislation,” Cruz said on ABC’s The View Wednesday after discussing the prospects of his proposed bill. He added, “But it ain’t easy. This is a very divided time.” So far, none of the recent AI-related legislation appears close to becoming law. A bill proposed by Sanders and Representative Greg Casar of Texas, which would ban superintelligence and pause advanced-AI development, faces long odds because no Republicans have signed on.
Democratic and Republican political strategists I spoke with said that the likelihood of bipartisan cooperation to properly govern AI is slim at best. “People are deeply cynical and deeply skeptical, and then you add into that this moment of severe economic disruption,” Joel Payne, a Democratic strategist, told me. “The politicization and the polarization is lighter fluid on top of that.”
That these warnings about AI are emerging in the heat of election season only heightens the likelihood of inaction. With Congress largely out of session for the rest of the year, politicians have settled into campaign mode, attempting to reposition themselves politically and outflank their opponents. In Wisconsin, the race for governor has been dominated by political posturing over data centers. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor, has run ads branding his Democratic opponent, David Crowley, as “Data Center David Crowley.” The Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has run television ads blasting the incumbent, Jon Husted, as “the face of data centers in Ohio.” A memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that data centers are “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck” that could ultimately cause him to lose in a state that Trump won handily in 2024. Crowley and Husted have responded with attacks of their own, attempting to link their opponents to data-center development. Political-ad spending nationwide on spots highlighting data centers has spiked in recent months; both Democrats and Republicans have spent millions to attack opponents on the issue, according to data from the firm AdImpact. Tech companies have also poured millions of dollars into political-action committees with the aim of boosting candidates who are friendlier to their cause.
Virginia has become central to this effort. Loudoun County, not far from Washington, D.C., has the largest concentration of data centers in the world, and advocates have tried to tout the benefits for the economy and tax revenue even as residents have raised quality-of-life concerns. The Data Center Coalition, whose membership includes Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, has recently stepped up lobbying efforts in D.C. and in Northern Virginia to oppose moratoriums on data centers and stricter regulations at the federal, state, and local levels. “Sweeping restrictions do not solve complex infrastructure challenges; instead, they risk stalling economic opportunity, defunding essential local public services, and undermining America’s technological edge,” Nicole Riley, the director of Virginia government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, told me.
The White House has shown little interest in halting the march of advanced AI. Trump attacked data-center detractors late last month, posting on social media that communities should oppose the projects only “if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” In May, Trump intervened to postpone an executive order aimed at regulating AI development, telling reporters that “we’re leading China. We’re leading everybody, and I don’t want to do anything that’s going to get in the way of that lead.” The president later signed a narrower order that allows developers to engage governmental review of advanced AI models before their release.
“President Trump’s bold leadership is turning data centers into engines of growth and opportunity for communities across the country that want them, all while cementing America’s dominance over China in the global AI race,” the White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told me, adding that the president’s push to require tech companies to pay for their own power and water resources has protected residents.
Some Republicans have bristled at the president’s rhetorical approach, even if they agree with him on the substance. “I actually think Trump is right, but, as usual, his language gets in the way of what he wants to accomplish,” Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and the former communications director of the Republican National Committee, told me. Heye acknowledged that voter “wariness” about AI is ubiquitous but said that politicians who are now trying to recant their earlier support for data centers are projecting a sense of fear rather than leadership. “Voters can smell that,” he said.
A Pew Research Center poll released last month found that just over half of Americans feel more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life, up from 37 percent in 2021. Voters have expressed concerns that the fast-advancing technology could replace human jobs, drive up energy costs, and pollute the environment. The AI industry has sullied its own image with “the worst sales pitch in the history of sales pitches,” said Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, who recently proposed a 100 percent federal tax on any state or local incentives provided to data centers. Speaking at the Ohio Energy Affordability Summit earlier this month, Moreno said that voters are angry and worried that “these data centers are going to come into our community and take our water and pollute our environment. They’re going to raise our electricity prices. They’re going to eventually put us out of work—and our taxpayer dollars are going to support the construction of these things.”
The latest warnings about superintelligence and human extinction have spurred even the largest AI companies to call on Congress to step in quickly to regulate their industry before it is no longer possible (or, perhaps, before smaller competitors can get a foothold). Amodei said that the government has a role to play in helping slow down AI development, including by implementing regulations “focused on keeping capabilities in balance with safety.” The government can also mediate or facilitate discussions between companies to help them set safety standards and embed third-party evaluators. Amodei wrote that he agrees with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and that the U.S. should take measures that include not selling powerful AI chips to China. “Companies and the US government should cooperate to make these steps as effective as possible,” Amodei wrote.
In a post Wednesday, OpenAI’s chief global-affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that the U.S. is facing a brief opportunity to create guardrails around AI development “before AI capabilities outpace the institutions responsible for governing them.” He said that OpenAI now supports several state regulations on the technology that the company had opposed just months ago.
“The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments. The United States needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation that can evolve as the technology does,” Lehane wrote.
Sanders told me that he is hopeful that at least some politicians will be willing to work across the aisle out of a sense of self-preservation. He said that his goal over the coming days is to get lawmakers to put pressure on Trump ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month, with the hope of encouraging Trump to focus on negotiating a kind of arms treaty with China to rein in AI advancement globally.
But getting Trump’s attention in this political environment may be a challenge in and of itself. On Wednesday, the president spent nearly two hours speaking about his agenda and a wide range of issues at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas. Trump promised to pay every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 if Republicans hold both houses of Congress, and he told a fictional story about a Democratic Senate candidate vomiting after eating barbecue. He also suggested that the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait.” He did not mention AI.

Brighton sign winger Azeez from Millwall
- Published
Brighton have signed Nigeria winger Femi Azeez from Millwall in a deal worth £12.5m - potentially rising past £15m with add-ons.
Azeez arrives at the Amex Stadium on a four-year contract and becomes Brighton's 11th signing of the summer window, including their club record £45m move for Tottenham centre-back Luka Vuskovic.
Azeez, 25, scored 11 goals and provided eight assists in 37 games last season, earning a place in the PFA Championship team of the year.
Azeez has been pushing for a move to the Premier League, with Millwall rejecting at least three bids from Brighton in recent weeks.
His departure is a club record sale for Millwall.
Brighton said the clubs submitted a deal sheet before Tuesday's 23:00 BST transfer deadline and concluded the deal before the extended deadline at 01:00 on Wednesday.
Azeez joined Millwall from Reading for about £1m in 2024 and has left the Den with two years left on his contract.
Brighton also signed defensive midfielder Chema Andres from Stuttgart in a deal worth £15.5m on deadline day.
Andres, 21, put pen to paper on a five-year contract at the club after the Seagulls agreed a fee with the Bundesliga outfit on deadline day.
The Spain Under-21 international made 41 appearances for Stuttgart last season after joining from Real Madrid in 2025.
Andres came through Real Madrid's youth set-up before making his La Liga debut in January 2025.
He helped Stuttgart qualify for the Champions League in his one season at the club.
Brighton raised significant funds through player sales, including Carlos Baleba's £70m move to Manchester United.

Claim: Video showing volcanic eruptions from Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano.

Mumbai: The use of the word “rent” in an agreement does not by itself make an occupant a tenant, the Bombay High Court has held while ordering the eviction of a woman from a commercial shop in Navi Mumbai after a 32-year-long legal battle.
Justice Sandeep Marne dismissed petitions filed by Navina Dinesh Shetty challenging a lower appellate court order and directed her to hand over possession of Gala No. 9 at APMC Market, Sector 19, Vashi, to its owner Shaikh Ayub Rehman by September 30, 2026.
Caretaker Agreements At Centre Of Dispute
The dispute arose from two 11-month “Caretaker Agreements” executed in 1994 and 1995. The agreements allowed Shetty to use the shop for payments of Rs 1,800 and Rs 2,000 per month. While the trial court treated her as a tenant, the District Court later held that she was only a licensee and had no tenancy rights.
Upholding the appellate court’s decision, Justice Marne said the entire agreement has to be considered while deciding the nature of the arrangement. “Mere use of the word ‘rent’ in the Caretaker Agreement does not elevate the status of the Petitioner from a mere licensee to that of a tenant,” the court held.
Temporary Licence Cannot Become Permanent Tenancy
The court said treating temporary licences as permanent tenancies would affect the very purpose of such arrangements and could discourage property owners from allowing others to temporarily use their premises.
The High Court also noted the owner’s prolonged legal battle, observing that he “would have never imagined in his wildest dreams” that an arrangement for just 22 months would lead to litigation lasting more than three decades.
The court noted that the occupant had earlier been directed to pay Rs 2,000 per month as compensation from August 14, 1996. However, she stopped paying even this amount after September 2012 and continued to occupy the shop without payment for around 14 years.
The High Court has now directed the trial court to conduct an inquiry into the market-rate compensation, known as mesne profits, payable by Shetty for the unauthorised occupation.
The compensation will be calculated from August 14, 1996, until she finally hands over possession of the shop.

How virtual safety car cost Norris win - and should F1 change rules?
- Published
Lando Norris says he was "insanely unlucky" to lose what seemed like a certain win in the Spanish Grand Prix because of the timing of a virtual safety car.
McLaren's Norris was leading comfortably when the VSC was called, seconds after he had passed the pit lane entry.
That allowed Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen to pit under the VSC, saving time, while the caution period ended before Norris could make it around to the pits again.
Of the VSC, Norris said: "It is a rule that should not define a whole race."
"I was the only one on the whole grid that didn't get the chance to do the pit stop," he said. "That's just unfortunate.
"There's been plenty of times where I've gained from it in the past and times where I've lost from it, and it's racing, but never when fighting for a win.
"So, it's probably one of the first times a win has been lost simply because of it."
After taking pole position with a lap his team principal Andrea Stella described as "a masterpiece", Norris was leading Antonelli by more than six seconds after 13 laps in Madrid.
He had just passed the pit entry at the end of lap 14 when a VSC was called because Lance Stroll's Aston Martin had stopped in the run-off area at Turn 20, while Antonelli and Verstappen were far enough behind to pit.
The VSC, which controls all cars to a specified maximum speed, then ended shortly before Norris completed the next lap, at the end of which he pitted.
Because a stop under the VSC costs 11 seconds less race time than one under green-flag conditions, Norris lost sufficient time that Antonelli and Verstappen were able to pass him.
Norris lost a further five seconds because of problems with his two right-hand side tyres at the stop and emerged from the pits more than 15 seconds behind Antonelli and more than nine adrift of Verstappen.
He caught the Red Bull before the end of the race but as overtaking was virtually impossible on the new Madring street circuit, he was stuck in third place.
Race-winner Antonelli, who extended his championship lead to 81 points, acknowledged Norris' bad fortune. "If I have to be realistic and honest, today we didn't deserve to win," he said. "Lando deserved to win, and so I think our result was probably P2 or even P3."

What is the VSC?
The VSC is a system by which the cars are forced to drive to a specified lap-time delta while a hazard on track is cleared.
It is used in certain circumstances in favour of deploying the actual safety car, usually when the hazard can be cleared relatively quickly, because it interferes less with the race and minimises the time lost under caution.
A physical safety car involves a modified high-performance road car entering the track and having the field line up behind it.
The various protocols around its operation mean a safety-car period usually goes on for several laps, while in this case the VSC was in operation for less than a single lap.
Why was it a problem for Norris?
The short duration of the VSC in this case was exactly why Norris was railing against the situation.
Every other driver in the field had the opportunity to decide whether to pit or not - the only driver not given that option was Norris.
The pit lane entry is before the final corner at the Madring, and Norris was in the last corner when it was called.
The VSC ended when Norris was in Turn 21, the corner before the pit entry, on lap 15. Antonelli, having stopped, was behind him in Turn 19.
On most circuits, Norris would have had a chance to pass Verstappen and perhaps even do the same to Antonelli before the end, given his pace advantage on the day, but as Antonelli put it: "In the race, you're just stuck behind."
Norris was withering in his criticism of the track layout, saying: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, 'Mint.'" But he did say there was "a lot of opportunity" to improve it for next year.
Could McLaren have done anything differently?
After the race, one question asked of McLaren was whether pitting on the following lap was the best idea, or should Norris have stayed out?
Norris said: "I had to come in at the end of the lap because it was the only chance.
"It was still effectively some pit loss, (but) the fact that everyone's kind of on colder tyres and you're still minimising the pit loss.
"The medium tyre (on which Norris had started the race) was destroyed and the hard tyre (to which Antonelli and Verstappen switched) was amazing.
"But the pace was very, very strong and on the hard tyre... I know they were stuck (behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who stayed out under the VSC), we caught up 13, 14 seconds or more, almost. So, plenty of positives. A day full of positives, just one thing let it all down."
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "We considered staying out, but you have to accept the fact that now you are on relatively used medium tyres. And the people behind you will be on new hard. So you're never going to open a gap on people on new hard."
The other question was whether McLaren would have been wise to anticipate that the race director would call the VSC and pit Norris before it was deployed.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "In hindsight, that would have been a good idea."
But he pointed out that, in the moment, it would have come with risks. The long pit lane at the Madring - the longest on the calendar - meant a pit stop cost a lot of time.
Stella said: "I would have to review with my engineers, see whether it was kind of obvious that it would end up in a virtual safety car. Therefore, you try to anticipate or not.
"Here, the problem is that you need to be extremely careful, because it's 27 seconds if you don't pit under a virtual safety car.
"So if you get it wrong, it would be extremely penalising. From the lead, you pit unnecessarily, and now you have lost the victory.
"So a good rule is to respond to what is a fact, to what is the real condition of the circuit.
"But we will definitely take a look as to whether in these conditions it was just simply, you know, obvious that he would end up in a virtual safety car. I cannot answer at the moment."
Has this happened before?
VSCs and safety cars are commonplace in F1 and they always afford drivers and teams the chance to gain or lose depending on the decisions they make when they occur.
Norris took his maiden victory in Miami in 2024 with the help of a safety car - he had delayed his stop and was able to make it under caution when race leader Verstappen had already stopped, and jumped into the lead.
And in Barcelona this year, Lewis Hamilton's maiden Ferrari victory was helped by a VSC that gave him a cheap pit stop on a different tyre strategy from rivals Mercedes.
However, this is the only example many could remember of a race leader losing a race in this fashion by being the only driver not to be able to choose whether to pit under a VSC or safety car.
Should F1 change the rules?
After the race, Norris and Verstappen said this kind of scenario had been discussed by drivers many times with governing body the FIA.
"I think there's always probably some cons to doing it, but it's tough," Norris said.
"I've won from it in the past, I've lost from it in the past. Over the course of a season, it's hard to know if it's a good thing or a bad thing.
"It probably equals out over time. Of course, it just hurts more, the fact that I lose a win. You know, there's literally nothing I could do as a driver today to do a better job."
Verstappen said: "We'll probably talk about it in the next briefing and see if there is anything that can be done."
Stella added: "Perhaps there's a wider reflection that the Formula 1 community should apply as to whether you keep things like they are or you introduce ways of maintaining more fairness.
"Offering the personal opinion. I'm puzzled myself as to what's right.
"Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions? So, for instance, the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap? Or you just keep it in the hands of the gods, and sometimes you are lucky, sometimes you are not. I'm not sure myself.
"But in general, there's the right place to have this sort of conversation, which is the Strategy Advisory Committee (SAC). And this is a topic that may be added to the agenda and discussed over there.
"But if there is to be a change, it will have to be a change that goes through the SAC, then the F1 Commission, and then we'll have to go at some stage to the sporting regulations.
"But I would envisage that this is a relatively lengthy process, unless there's a big push from F1, from the institutions, FIA or F1, to say, like, 'we need to make this different'."

The Rwandan eyeing Champions League history against Man Utd
- Published
Joy-Lance Mickels has been a Manchester United fan since childhood, and on Thursday the Rwanda international will fulfil a lifelong dream.
The 32-year-old is expected to start up front when Azerbaijani side Sabah travel to the home of the Red Devils in the opening round of the league phase of this year's Champions League (20:00 BST).
"I watch every [Man Utd] game when I can," he told the BBC World Service.
"It was the best draw we [Sabah] got in my opinion. It makes it even better because we're going to play in Old Trafford.
"Manchester United are one of the biggest clubs in the world so it will be a proud moment to step out on to the pitch."
Mickels is in his second stint with the side based in the town of Masazir, which lies about 16km (10 miles) north-west of the capital Baku.
He has played an important role in helping the Azerbaijan Premier League champions progress this far on their debut in the competition.
The forward scored four times in qualifying as the club, founded just nine years ago, navigated four two-legged ties to reach the Champions League proper.
One of those goals was the strike which ultimately sealed a 6-4 aggregate win over Israeli side Hapoel Be'er Sheva after a 94th-minute goal had forced the play-off tie into extra time.
"Reaching the Champions League is an historic achievement for Sabah and starting the league phase at Old Trafford makes it even more exciting," Mickels said.
"At the same time, we're not going there only to enjoy the atmosphere. We want to compete to represent not only our club but Azerbaijan in the best possible way and show we deserve to be there."
Making history for Rwanda
Mickels spent the first half of his career in the lower leagues in Germany, where he was born and raised, but has also had stints in the Netherlands and Saudi Arabia.
His first spell with Sabah came between 2021 and 2023, and he returned to the Bank Respublika Arena two years ago.
"My career has not always followed a straight or easy path," he explained.
"I have played at different levels and in several countries. But every experience has helped me grow both as a footballer and as a person."
He qualifies to represent Rwanda through his parents and made his international debut for the Wasps in March.
Mickels is now set to be the first footballer from the East African nation to play in the Champions League proper.
"I'm very proud of my Rwandan roots," he said.
"Representing Rwanda whilst playing the Champions League is very, very special.
"I hope my journey can help inspire young Rwandan players and show them that with belief, hard work and patience, it is possible to reach the pinnacle of football."

After beginning their Champions League campaign at Old Trafford, Sabah's fixture list is littered with glamourous ties including home games against former champions Borussia Dortmund and Barcelona.

LONDON — AstraZeneca said Friday that a breast cancer pill failed in a pivotal trial testing it as a first-line therapy in advanced tumors, a result that could limit the use of the medicine.
The drug, camizestrant, in combination with another medicine did not outperform standard treatment on a measure of how long patients went before their cancer progressed. The SERENA-4 trial enrolled patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced cancer who hadn’t had another systemic therapy for advanced disease.
Camizestrant earlier this month won accelerated approval in the U.S. as Etcamah as a treatment for patients who develop a mutation in their tumors that’s a sign of emerging drug resistance. The SERENA-4 trial, had it been successful, could have opened up a much larger market for the drug.

Yemen's Houthis capture a Red Sea island in threat to shipping
Yemen 's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured the island of Mayun at the entrance of the Red Sea, a key alternative for shipping Saudi oil and other exports since Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
The island's seizure was confirmed by a senior military official with Yemen's internationally recognized government and a Houthi official. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to journalists.
About 12% of the world's goods are typically shipped through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. It's especially important to Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally.
The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said in a statement Friday that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels." But markets are nervous, and experts have described the Houthis as highly unpredictable.
A United Nations spokesperson, Farhan Haq, said Houthi rebels in Mokha seized a compound that had housed U.N. staff, who all fled safely before the city's capture. Haq said that "no U.N. personnel remain in Mokha right now."
Saudi Arabia shuts down oil pipeline, citing attacks
Saudi Arabia said Friday it had shut down a major, cross-country oil pipeline as a "precautionary measure" following attacks the day before. The Saudi Energy Ministry did not say who carried out the attacks.
The East-West pipeline has been vital to Saudi Arabia continuing oil exports in the months since the Iran war has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement early Saturday, the Iraqi government said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the operations command in Maysan province and dismissed its commander after authorities determined that attacks targeting Saudi Arabia were launched from a site in the province.
According to the International Energy Agency, Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea port at the pipeline's end have more than doubled since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Anthropic blocks users in Houthi-held Yemen over weapons development
The AI company Anthropic said it blocked users in northern Yemen who were using its AI models to run weapons development programs, some using commercially available smartphones.
Anthropic said its models were being used to pursue sophisticated precision, long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The company said it identified the users during an internal investigation and banned their accounts.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels who control northern Yemen have been smuggling advanced weapons for years despite a blockade and U.N. arms embargo. Iran denies arming the rebels.
Anthropic said the accounts used Claude Code to develop software that "steers and stabilizes a flying vehicle" and were working to develop weapons including a guided rocket that allows mobile phone users to autonomously track targets.
There is no evidence the users in Yemen succeeded in fielding a weapon, the company said.
Iran to meet with Gulf Arab neighbors over Strait of Hormuz
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Friday that a regional meeting is planned between Iran and other Persian Gulf countries, including Oman and Iraq.
Baghaei told reporters the meeting will take place on Monday in Oman and will include discussion on prior talks between Iran and Oman regarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Located on either side of the strait, Iran and Oman have held talks over managing ship traffic through the critical waterway, which has been heavily disrupted by the Iran war.
Israel says it has destroyed Hezbollah tunnels in Lebanon
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Friday that his country's military has completed the destruction of tunnels in the strategic Ali Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, which he said were built by the militant group Hezbollah with Iranian funding.
The ridge has been the site of clashes between Israeli forces and Hezbollah in recent weeks. Nearby residents heard loud explosions and felt the ground shaking Thursday. There was no immediate comment from Hezbollah.
Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued to demolish houses in villages under their control in southern Lebanon.
Residents displaced from the coastal village of Mansouri watched from a distance on Friday as Israeli drones carried boxes of explosives to be dropped on their homes. The Israeli army did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A man is killed by an Israeli strike in Gaza
An Israeli strike on Friday killed a man walking in a street in southern Gaza and wounded several people, including children, according to Nasser Hospital, which received the body and the wounded.
The Israeli military said the strike in Khan Younis had targeted a Hamas member.
Meanwhile, mourners held funeral prayers for two of three men who were killed Thursday in Khan Younis. The Israeli military said one of the men, Mohammad Yazouri, was a Hamas commander.
Meeting between Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors set for next week
The Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors will meet at the U.S. State Department next week to discuss developments and the implementation of a trilateral framework, the State Department said Friday. "It remains the only viable mechanism to restore Lebanon's sovereignty and Israel's security," it said.
The next round of formal discussions will take place in Rome in October.
Formal talks in Rome were supposed to start next week, but planning for the U.N. General Assembly, the Jewish holidays and King Abdullah's Lebanese Armed Forces conference in Paris made that impossible, according to the statement.
