When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

Russian strike on Ukraine-Poland border stirs fears war is on Europe's 'doorstep'
In short:
A truck near Ukraine's border with Poland has been hit during Russian drone strikes on the region.

What's next?
At the BRICS meeting in New Delhi, President Vladamir Putin didn't rule out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US in October.
Fresh Russian strikes in close proximity to NATO sites have stoked fears among some European leaders that the war between Ukraine and Russia is spilling across borders.
A Russian attack on a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland was confirmed by Polish and Ukranian officials on Sunday.
The attack marks the latest strike to hit areas near NATO nations as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.
A Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, which is only 2km from Poland.
"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Mr Sybiha said on X.
"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,"
Polish border guards said that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 metres from Poland, but that the crossing had since resumed operations.
Fears the Russia-Ukraine war is expanding
Lithuania also briefly closed Vilnius airport on Sunday, local time, in response to a possible sighting of a drone, prompting NATO to summon at least one fighter jet, the National Crisis Management Centre said.
Lithuania later said the sighting turned out to be a flock of birds.
The air alert was lifted and the airport reopened within 38 minutes, after the NATO jet made a visual identification, Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre said.
"On initial radar readings, marks left by birds and drones can be similar," it added in a statement.
Military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO's northern borders with Russia.
Transport sites near Ukraine-Poland border targeted
In a separate statement, Ukrainian Railways said that in Volyn — another region bordering Poland, — a drone attacked the locomotive of a passenger train just 2km from the Polish border.
The company said no-one was injured.
Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine.
Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, as part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.
Putin told the war in Ukraine must end
In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.

Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Mr Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.
Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialised eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.
Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.
TASS cited Mr Peskov as saying that Mr Putin had informed Mr Modi of the situation "on the ground" in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.
Ukraine strike nuclear power plant in Russian-held territories

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant has been controlled by Russia since March 2022, and remains close to the front line.
A Ukrainian military spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In Russia itself, the mayor of the city of Nizhnekamsk, in the Volga River region of Tatarstan, said that "civilian and industrial" targets in the city had been struck by Ukrainian drones, causing at least two deaths and several more injuries.

Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on the strike on Nizhekamsk, but did say they had struck another refinery in the southern Krasnodar region.

In August 2024, Inc42 asked whether Swish could pull off what Zomato couldn't. Two years on, the question has turned on its head. Zomato has quit. So have Swiggy, Rebel Foods and Zing. Swish is still here. And it just raised $24 Mn this past week, less than six months after it had raised $38 Mn. As we said above, several startups and listed companies that entered the segment over the past two years have either scaled back or shut their offerings. Zepto Cafe has reduced its footprint, Eternal’s Zomato shut Quick and Everyday, Swiggy closed Snacc earlier this year, Zing shut operations, and Rebel Foods has halted QuickiES. Less than two years into its operations, at a time when quick food delivery was on everyone’s minds, Swish is now the lone ranger in the space. The latest round comes at an interesting point for India's 10 minute food delivery market. The Bengaluru-based startup now serves more than 1 Mn orders a month, with monthly orders tripling since March 2026. It operates in 50 pincodes across Bengaluru and Delhi NCR. The question now is whether Swish has found a model that can work where several better funded companies have struggled. Swish Is Scaling Up, But There’s A Long Way To Go Founded in late 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja and Saran S, Swish has a different model from the traditional food delivery model, which was popularised by Swiggy and Zomato, and which even Rapido has carried forward. Unlike the other platforms which are aggregators, Swish owns the kitchens, prepares the food, operates the technology and manages delivery. Its kitchens are placed close to customers, generally within a 1 Km radius, allowing the startup to control the time between ordering and delivery. That has allowed Swish to build a relatively small but dense network. The startup said in its latest funding announcement that it has crossed 1 Mn monthly orders at its peak, and that more than 80% of orders are delivered within 15 minutes. Its kitchens have an average preparation time of under four minutes. The menu has also moved well beyond the snack heavy proposition with which the category started. Swish began with around 75 SKUs and has since expanded it by 3X, spanning meals, snacks and beverages. Lunch and dinner now account for more orders than snacks and late night consumption. That matters because the larger opportunity for Swish is likely to be everyday meals rather than occasional impulse purchases. When Swish launched in Delhi, cofounder Shah revealed that more than four in 10 of its customers have ordered again, offering an indication of customer repeat behavior in Delhi. There is also a gap between where Swish is today and where it once planned to be. In late 2024, Shah had mentioned plans to have 150 kitchens across Bengaluru by March 2025. It currently has around 55 kitchens, even after entering Delhi NCR. The latest fundraise gives Swish more room to build more momentum in that regard. Swish wants to expand its kitchen network in Bengaluru and Delhi NCR and has an ambitious target of having more than 1,000 kitchens over the next five years. For context, Rebel Foods, one of the largest cloud kitchen companies from India, claims to run 450 cloud kitchens for 4,000 restaurants cumulatively across 75 cities in three countries. And it raised more than $785 Mn to get there over the course of 15 years. Scaling up physical kitchens requires several hundreds of millions of dollars, and if Swish has to get to that ambitious target, it has to continue raising large rounds, particularly because quick food needs higher cloud kitchen density than what Rebel Foods had in mind. Quick Food Players Exit Stage Swish's biggest advantage today may be that it is still in the game. The list of companies that have exited quick food delivery is almost as long as the list of players that entered this space. Zepto Cafe, which pioneered this concept, has been scaling down. As Inc42 reported, more than 50 Zepto Cafe kitchens were shut in 2025, with order volume falling from a peak of around 1 Lakh orders a day to nearly half that level. The problems were not limited to demand. Zepto also faced supply-chain constraints and a shortage of trained kitchen staff, leading it to pause operations across several cities. Eternal took a different route. It shut Zomato Quick along with Everyday in May 2025 just months after entering the space. Back then, Zomato cited weak demand and profitability concerns. Swiggy pulled the plug on Snacc in February 2026, with the company saying that product-market fit was not the problem, but unit economics was. Gurugram-based Zing, which shut shop last year after starting out around the same time as Swish, told Inc42 that the startup had overestimated demand, with customers preferring food from their favourite restaurants even if it took longer to arrive. More recently, Rebel Foods also halted its QuickiES vertical earlier this year, which had offered 15-minute delivery. Blinkit-owned Bistro remains one of the few dedicated players still operating in the category. Its model, like Swish, involves company controlled kitchens and fast delivery. It must be noted that Bistro is separate from Zomato’s past efforts Then there are Swiggy Bolt and Toing, which need to be examined differently from Swish. Neither requires Swiggy to build and operate its own kitchens. Instead, Swiggy works with restaurants that can prepare or pack selected items quickly, with deliveries generally limited to a 2 Km radius. By May 2025, Bolt was live across more than 500 cities and accounted for more than one in 10 Swiggy food orders. Swish and Bistro own the complete stack, so also carry more of the cost and risk. But while Bistro has Blinkit’s core business to rely on for less costly customer acquisition and can lean on the brand, Swish has no such fallback. So how does Swish fare with regard to unit economics? What Quick Food Unit Economics Look Like This is primarily where the startup's latest funding round becomes more interesting. As per a report in The Arc, Swish's food gross margin is around 60%-70% on an average order value of ₹250. This would translate to roughly ₹160 of gross profit per order before kitchen, delivery and corporate costs. At that level, the company needs every kitchen to generate enough orders to cover food preparation, rent, staff, delivery and corporate costs. The report added that close to 10% of Swish users order twice a day with customers placing just over three orders per month on average. However, compared to a conventional food marketplace, Swish’s model has the ability to retain a higher share of the order value. For instance, Zomato or Swiggy face pushback from restaurants when they raise commissions and have to maintain a fine balance. Swish instead has to look at managing costs to improve its net margin per order rather than focus on commissions. For this to work, the kitchen has to stay busy. Swish is currently doing around 30,000 orders a day across 55 kitchens and a few of its mature kitchens can have around 800 orders a day. On average, each kitchen caters to 800 orders per day. Growing this density will be key to Swish’s growth. It is also the part of the model that investors are betting on. This scale has to eventually translate into profits, but Swish has a longer rope than listed companies when it comes to profitability. At the moment the focus is on growing order volume, gross order value and growing the user base, and the aim is that this along with the cloud kitchen density will be able to deliver profits in a few quarters. The company plans to add advertising within the app as a revenue layer in the near future. A kitchen doing 800 orders a day is more profitable than one doing 100. Delivery riders can be stationed closer to the kitchen, staff costs can be spread across more orders and food waste can be monitored more closely. The problem is whether these numbers hold as Swish moves beyond its strongest Bengaluru neighbourhoods. Which means, the startup has to spend extra money on brand awareness when it enters new markets accompanied by heavy discounting. Swish has already raised $78 Mn across four rounds. For a startup that has been operational for less than two years, investor backing is lifeblood, but soon that reliance will need to be curbed. The next phase will be less about raising money and more about proving that when its cloud kitchen network grows, Swish doesn’t have a unit economics mess on its hands. Now, the startup has something most of its quick food rivals did not get: more time at the table. The harder question is whether that time will be enough to prove that quick food delivery can become a large food business, rather than another quick commerce experiment that works only in a handful of dense neighbourhoods. Trump dismisses AI safety fears to keep America ahead of China
US president claimed ‘very negative forces’ have been raising concerns about the rapidly developing technology
President Donald Trump has downplayed the necessity for his administration to restrict artificial intelligence development, arguing that maintaining the United States’ lead over China in global competition is paramount and that securing victory will help mitigate the hazards of the evolving technology.
Although he conceded that a degree of oversight is required, Trump offered no specific proposals for future rules. Instead, he dismissed warnings concerning the rapid pace of development and lack of supervision, attributing them to unidentified "negative forces", despite similar apprehensions being raised by tech sector pioneers.
"We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that ... shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen," Trump told reporters during a trip to Ireland over the weekend. "But whoever wins with AI wins."
The Republican president's remarks followed comments from Dario Amodei, chief executive of AI firm Anthropic, who urged the sector to slow its rapid progression to allow safety protocols time to catch up. Prominent industry figures, such as Elon Musk and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, have publicly backed Amodei's position.
When asked by a reporter whether the industry should be subject to regulation or decelerate its pace, Trump—speaking after watching play at the Irish Open at his Doonbeg resort—emphasised that America remains ahead of China in AI advancements, stating, "frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins."
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to visit the US later in September to meet with Trump, with artificial intelligence expected to feature on their agenda.
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a central issue during this US election year. Major technology firms are constructing extensive networks of data warehouses across smaller towns, prompting widespread concern from voters across political lines regarding the loss of agricultural land, strained water resources, and escalating electricity bills. Despite local opposition and hesitation from both major parties, Trump has maintained his backing for these data centres.
Former president Barack Obama suggested that his party ought to focus on AI as a key campaign issue.
"I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what it means if there’s going to be job displacement. Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?" Obama stated during a joint event last week with New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the US House, according to a transcript provided by his office.
Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, indicated that administration officials overseeing cyber, science, and technology policy are anticipated to convene this week to discuss subsequent measures. Trump may also confer with congressional lawmakers, a number of whom have voiced deep concerns regarding the rapid speed of AI advancements.
"I think the president wants to hear from them as well," Hassett noted.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said that "some guardrails, some safety measures" are necessary to prevent AI from running away. Nevertheless, mirroring Trump’s stance, he stressed the importance of ensuring America does not "lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat."
The Louisiana Republican suggested that tech leaders should be brought together for "one big meeting and work this out together in the same room." Having raised the matter with Trump, Johnson expressed that convening such a gathering promptly ought to be the "next step."
"So we’re going to pull everybody together and make sure we do this in the right way," Johnson remarked, describing the issue as a "top priority for me and for the Congress."
"But we don’t need everybody to panic right now," Johnson added.
Meanwhile, Jeffries took aim at House Republican leadership for permitting representatives to return to their home districts for the final part of September.
"We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, … the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," Jeffries said. He confirmed that addressing AI will be a "high priority" during a meeting of House Democrats on Tuesday.
Neither Johnson nor Jeffries outlined specific legislative steps. While there is broad consensus among lawmakers that regulatory boundaries are required, previous limited attempts to establish rules have repeatedly collapsed, underscoring Congress's persistent hesitation to regulate the tech sector.
Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee who resigned due to safety concerns and subsequently voiced his anxieties publicly, called for global regulatory frameworks alongside voluntary industry constraints.
Coxon warned of his growing fear that artificial intelligence models could soon develop advanced capabilities beyond human control.
"You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind, without understanding what it wants, or thinks, or the way it thinks," Coxon said.
Amid intense international rivalry for supremacy in the field, Coxon urged Washington and Beijing—the two dominant players—to collaborate on slowing development to address potential hazards.
"I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual — of mutual slowing," Coxon said.
Failing to do so, he cautioned, means "we risk running the same race with China, which could be equally dangerous."
Technology entrepreneur and investor David Sacks responded to calls for state intervention with a social media post challenging tech executives. Sacks, who serves as co-chairman of a White House advisory council on science and technology, contended that Amodei and his peers are themselves driving the speed of advancement.
He asserted that these industry leaders possess the authority to unilaterally curb development.
"The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it," Sacks wrote.

South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu.
Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though a more recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000. Most of the population are found in South Australia, with the remainder in Western Australia.
On Sunday, the state’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the sea lion was found dead at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, the third-largest single colony.
“We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest seal found in our Australian waters,” Bourke said.
“85% of the population is found here in South Australia. It’s an endangered species.”
She said the sea lion had been recovering from a shark attack, but that bird flu had caused its death.
“We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu … we might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering.”
The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at Seal Bay, but it was monitoring the population closely.
Bourke said there was “no real” mammal vaccine that “you could get off the shelf at the moment”.
“It was used in cattle in the US and they did an experimental trial in Hawaii on their monk seals, which they have seen that has been successful,” Bourke said.
“We have been working very closely with the federal government to highlight that we are willing and able to participate in a trial here in South Australia.”
Seal Bay has an estimated 800 Australian sea lions.
Bourke said the population was already diminishing by 2% every year, even before the arrival of bird flu, which will have a “devastating impact” on population levels if no vaccine can be administered.
“We’ve seen Heard Island [that there has been] a reduction in the population there for our seal pups by 75%. They were impacted by bird flu,” she said.
“And we’ve seen other experiences around the world where they were impacted by 95%. We know that this is going to be not the first and only case of [the virus] going into our sea lions.”
Last month, John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, told Guardian Australia that he feared the virus would quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.
“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.
“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.
“It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.”
H5 bird flu has already affected pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups.
  SA had confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August, after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.

Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law.
Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors.
Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.
The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK.
The two donors who gave Reform £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand. Reform said both donations were within the rules.
Senior government sources indicated the government was prepared to look again at the issue of domestic donations once it receives advice from a newly commissioned taskforce and from the Electoral Commission.
One No 10 source said they did not want to delay the elections bill – which gives votes to 16-year-olds and puts new curbs on foreign donors – but said the bill was “not the right vehicle but this is not the end of the story”.
Several Labour MPs said they had been assured by ministers that further legislation could still come before the general election. Trade unions are also understood to be wavering on the issue and a possible donations cap is expected to be part of discussions at the TUC congress next week, where Rayner and Burnham will speak.
Unions have been central to the decision not to impose a domestic donations cap after several, especially GMB, argued it would be a slippery slope towards future rightwing governments curbing union donations.
On Sunday the Unite trade union said it was in favour of a cap – and the largest trade union, Unison, said it would fight attempts by billionaires to influence politics.
“For individual donors there must be a cap,” said Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary. “I think at some point it gets beyond what people think as normal.”
Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary, said: “As his support dwindles in this country, Farage is turning to crypto billionaires in an attempt to undermine our democracy. The trade union movement will oppose him every step of the way.”
Stella Creasy, the Labour MP whose amendment on donations caps attracted support in the Commons, is liaising with peers about how they can raise the issue when the bill returns to the House of Lords this week.
The Labour peer Michael Wills said: “The government has already committed to urgently reviewing the questions of caps on donations. Now the bill is in the Lords, it offers an unmissable opportunity to say when that review will complete its work, and what its remit will be.”
Creasy said the Reform donations had “concentrated people’s minds about what is now happening in our politics and what it will do to the voices of working people if it’s not stopped – we have the chance with the Lords to amend this bill with a cap”.
Her amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. It was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.
The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell said it was time for the government to move faster and for unions to get onboard. “It’s clear now to the trade unions meeting in congress this week that action is needed to protect our democracy and there’s a growing expectation the government will respond with urgency,” he said.
Two influential big party donors also called for a cap on Sunday. The billionaire businessman and Phones 4U founder, John Caudwell, who previously donated to the Conservative party in 2019, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House: “There should be a definite change in law. We should not have very wealthy people making undue influence.”
Dale Vince, the Ecotricity founder who has given donations to the Labour party, said it was “urgent” the government dealt with donations rules. “Ridiculous sums of money don’t level the playing field – they distort it.
“Our current system of funding is anti-democratic – those with big money have more say than the simple vote we all have. A cap on donations would be a step in the right direction – the end game should be publicly funded politics.”
The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, suggested he was sympathetic to further action. Speaking before the opening of the TUC congress, he said: “No one wants the UK to become a country for hire in the way Reform is clearly a party for hire. Without a doubt, we are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics. But we’ll have to do that in a way that doesn’t cut across workers having their voice heard politically.”
Reform has said it is confident that its two donors will not be caught in a retrospective cap on donations from Britons living abroad. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill.
As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.
Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.
Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

Spiciness isn’t a flavor that usually comes to mind when you think of the average Japanese dish, but even so, peppers have a long history in the country.
Capsicum peppers were introduced to Japan in the 16th century, and by the Edo Period (1603-1867), two distinctly Japanese varieties had become established. The first is the small, fiery-hot takanotsume chili pepper. About 2 to 5 centimeters long, the name of this spicy hot pepper means “hawk’s talons” because the sharp, curved fruit is said to resemble the claw of a bird of prey.
The second locally cultivated heirloom pepper is the shishitō (literally, “lion’s head“) — so named because the fruit’s bumpy exterior mirrors the noggin of a shishi (a mythical lionlike guardian beast). Although most shishitō are quite mild, you may occasionally run across one that is quite spicy. This random trait was never bred out of the variety — on the contrary, fans of the peppers rather look forward to being taken unawares by a particularly piquant shishitō.

A train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways.
Ukraine’s foreign ministerAndrii Sybiha described the attack as “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”.
Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.
Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.
The strikes prompted air-raid warnings in Poland, which shares a border with western Ukraine.
Ukrainian and Polish authorities said a lorry less than a kilometre from the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between the two countries was also hit.
Katerina Sergatskova, the director of Daily Humanity, an organisation that provides training to people working in high-risk environments, was travelling on a Warsaw-bound train and witnessed the attack.
She said passengers were told to evacuate at about 9am as the train approached the Polish border having already been told to disembark for two hours in the middle of the night. “At this point, the mood was different, we were asked to move very fast,” she said. “Then I heard the first drone.
“Seeing and hearing Shahed [drones] just a few hundred metres from the border is a very unpleasant experience.”
No casualties were reported on the train.
A British economist who preferred not to be named, travelling on a night train from Kyiv towards Chelm in Poland, also witnessed the attack. “We spent 10 hours at the border and were evacuated three times. On the third evacuation a missile came over and totalled a locomotive in front of our train.”
Railway officials instructed the “grimly focused” passengers to hide in bushes by a lake, said the economist, calling the Ukrainian response “timely and disciplined”. They “gave us good warning of the evacuation and had a plan, which everyone followed”.
“The conductor said when we boarded that there was a high risk that we would be evacuated during the journey. The lady and her eight-year-old son who were in my compartment said they had been travelling back and forth every month to Kyiv from Warsaw since 2022 and they had never been evacuated, or the train attacked, while travelling the route. This is clearly an escalation by Putin and the Russians.”
Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries, as well as Johnson, the former British prime minister, and the former CIA chief Petraeus, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.
“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” the rail company said.
Johnson wrote on X: “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways.”
Three people were killed in the eastern Donetsk region, and a 71-year-old woman was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region.
Sybiha said the Russian strikes were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders”.
“This is Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he wrote on X.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.
He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.
Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who visited Kyiv this week, said on X after Sunday morning’s attack: “Putin is escalating.”
The Polish interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said: “We treat these events with the utmost seriousness. The situation is being monitored continuously. Russia is the enemy of the free world.”
Russia claimed it struck “railway infrastructure” in western Ukraine used to “transport military cargo” from Europe.
“Strikes have continued on railway infrastructure in the western regions of Ukraine, which are used to transport military cargo from European countries,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement.
Ukraine and Russia have increased attacks on critical infrastructure in each other’s countries as long-range drones and missiles take the war away from the frontlines.
The US president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday that Zelenskyy should “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing shortages.
“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said, adding that shortages were caused by the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the US war in the Middle East.

you’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?
To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including Netvue’s original Birdfy Lite Feeder and Birdbuddy’s Pro, for almost two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent squirrels. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.
Updated June 2026: I’ve added new feeders from ChirpCam and Wansview as well as preorder information for the new Birdbuddy 2, updated long-term testing notes on the Birdfy Nest Duo and Birdfy Bath Pro, moved a previous pick to Others Tested upon further use, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder
The world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience, and they may not be what you think. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.
Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features, in order to support the company's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it says so in the marketing materials or not, so you will need to do your due diligence before buying.
Mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, so this is another important detail to confirm before buying.
Wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range, or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.
App: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.
How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?
I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.
I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.
The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the company. Some are kept for longer-term testing, others are put in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and others are donated locally via the Buy Nothing Project.
What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?
- Keep feeders super clean. The last thing you want to do to your feathered guests is make them ill from eating moldy seeds or spread avian diseases. Every two weeks, scrub feeders with warm, soapy water, and then either soak them in one part bleach to nine parts water or one part white vinegar to one part water—both methods are recommended by Audubon. Rinse and dry thoroughly before adding more seed (you don't want bleach residue either). Keep an eye on bird flu outbreaks and pay attention to what the birds look like at your own feeders. If you suspect something is off, you'll want to remove the feeder until things look better.
- Only get a hummingbird feeder if you're dedicated to keeping it spotless. You need to be even more diligent about cleanliness here, committing to cleaning a hummingbird feeder every two to three days. Nectar sitting in the sun harbors bacterial growth quickly, which can cause hummingbird tongues to swell and almost always end in their death. Red attracts these birds, but don't use red nectar. There are no studies conclusively proving that dye harms birds, but at best it's unnecessary and at worst might make them sick. Instead, go for feeders with red pieces to get their attention or stick to planting hummingbird-friendly flowers and skip the feeder altogether.
- Add a water source too. Birds need clean water for drinking and bathing, so you can make your backyard more of an oasis by providing it. Birdfy makes a smart birdbath, reviewed above, or you can make your own fountain out of anything—even a favorite pot, or a bucket—using a solar pump kit. I'm currently testing this one and will report back. The same cleaning technique outlined above goes for baths. You can also consider adding regular bird houses—analog or smart versions, like Birdfy's Polygon, above—for birds to nest.
- Give birds time. You likely won't see birds at your feeder on day one. Give them time to find it and trust it. If after a few weeks you still don't have visitors, it might be time to reevaluate what kind of bird seeds you're using or where you've placed the feeder.
Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?
This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.
First off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.
It follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate through walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more important than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.
However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. So, really, a smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.
What About Squirrels?
As is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.
The yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.
Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one offered by Birdfy. Another option is using seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. Birds don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do, so they’re not affected by the taste. That said, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

Carney pushes idea of making Canada an ‘associate member’ of the EU: reports
The PM has spoken to leaders including France’s Macron about letting Canadians work visa-free in the EU, The Wall Street Journal reported
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney wants a closer relationship with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an “associate member” of the bloc, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet-to-be-created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.
Canada’s embassy in Brussels and spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.
Canada’s escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.
Relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year due to disagreements over trade and other issues. The trade dispute has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
Canada and the EU are discussing ways of allowing Canada’s goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defence and critical minerals to move freely, thus effectively shifting the EU border, the Wall Street Journal said.
Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks as well as infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.

A flurry of artificial intelligence algorithms have promised to help identify heart conditions early. By analyzing an electrocardiogram, a common 10-second test of the heart’s activity, AI has been cleared to screen for common arrhythmias and structural heart conditions, and algorithms in development aim to pinpoint patients at highest risk of sudden cardiac arrest.
While many of those models are focused on early diagnosis and prevention, AI also might help a patient when they’re having a heart attack. Last week, the Food and Drug Administration issued a rare de novo classification to a model from Powerful Medical that aims to help triage patients to the right care when they’re having chest pain. The vast majority of AI devices go to market through the FDA’s 510(k) clearance pathway; fewer than 10 each year receive de novo classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence.
The most severe kind of heart attack occurs when a coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart, is completely blocked off. Those patients need to get to a cardiac catheterization lab as soon as possible to open up the blockage and restore oxygen to the heart. On an EKG, doctors can identify these kinds of myocardial infarctions from their characteristic “ST-segment elevations.”

NSW public schools set for new screen time limits under government guidelines
In short:
Public school students in NSW will be allowed as little as 15 minutes of screen time a day under new state government guidelines.
The limits will increase as students progress through primary, but will be more relaxed for high-schoolers.
What's next?
The guidelines will take effect next year and will become mandatory from 2028.
Students in NSW public schools will be limited to as little as 15 minutes of screen time per day, under guidelines announced by the state government.
The 15-minute limit will apply to students from kindergarten to year 2.
Students in years 3 and 4 will have up to 30 minutes of daily classroom screen time, increasing to 45 minutes for years 5 and 6.
The guidelines will be introduced next year, but will not become mandatory until 2028.
Education Minister Prue Car said children needed to get back to basics, including using pens and paper.
"There's just too much screen time for our young people in our school system,"
"We want to make sure that at school it's not the default, that the default is pen and paper."
Screen time limits will be more relaxed for high-schoolers, with digital learning allowed to make up 25 per cent of a subject's coursework for years 7 to 10.
Students in years 11 and 12 will be able to spend half their class time on digital devices like laptops and tablets.
Raising standards
The state government said the screen time limits were designed to arrest a "worrying trend" of falling academic results.
Ms Car said according to the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), Australian students were nearly twice as likely to spend more than two hours a day learning using digital devices than the OECD average.
Last week, PISA data also showed reading and mathematics scores for15 year olds in NSW were going backwards.
"There's no doubt the two are linked, and they're linked around the world," Ms Car said.
Education secretary Murat Dizdar said while technology would continue to play an important role in classrooms, imposing screen time limits would help students concentrate.
"It's about backing in the research and evidence that our own students and our teachers are telling us around avoiding distractions in the learning process."
Digital detox a 'relief' for students
While mobile phones have been banned in all NSW classrooms for several years, some schools have recently been trialling their own limits on other forms of screen time.
Chatswood High School principal, Robin Chand, said since paring back the use of digital devices, staff had noticed an improvement in students' handwriting and engagement.
"I know that this will be welcomed by students because students directly tell me that they feel relieved at times when they are working directly with pen and paper and their course books," Mr Chand said.
"When screens go down, relationships go up.
"And the relationships that are the most important in our classroom are relationships between the students and their teachers," he said.
Seventeen-year-old student, Archie Newman, said learning with hard copy books, pens and paper had allowed him to slow down and think more deeply, without the temptations of a laptop or tablet.
"I was someone who could get distracted so easily with digital technology," he said.
"And [now] the emphasis on handwriting is allowing me and my learning experience to be maximised."

Twenty-five dead after fire on cargo ship in eastern China
- Published
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.
The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.
Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.
Qingdao is a major trading hub and ranks among the world's busiest ports.
It is unclear what caused the fire. An eyewitness told the AFP news agency there was thick smoke rising from the ship, but he heard no explosion.
The country's leader Xi Jinping earlier called for "all-out" search and rescue efforts while Premier Li Qiang stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters".
The fire comes nearly a month after a shipyard explosion in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian killed a rescue worker and injured 12 others.

In Algeria, new focus on English in schools rekindles debate over French colonial legacy
English is taking up an increasingly prominent place in Algeria’s education system at the expense of French – a shift that has stirred controversy across the North African country.
This school year, three years after its introduction in primary school, English is becoming the first foreign language taught to pupils, starting from the third grade.
“We have decided to teach English in the third year of primary school, and French (alongside English) starting in the fourth year. In third year, only English will be taught,” announced the Algerian education minister in July.
Until 2023, French was the only foreign language taught in primary school, starting in third grade. This had been the case since Algeria’s independence in 1962. But following a decision by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, English – previously introduced only at secondary school level – was added, starting in the third year of primary school, alongside French.
Tebboune argued that English is the language of science and it is therefore important to teach it in school.

The place of English will also be strengthened in secondary school through an increase in teaching hours and a higher coefficient in the end‑of‑cycle exam.
In high school, French teaching has not yet been modified. But English will be further developed, the education minister said.
Although the government’s announcements are significant, teachers’ associations have not commented. The main teachers’ union, Cnapeste, was dissolved last July by the authorities for violating regulations on the right to strike. The union rejects the accusations, viewing the procedure as an attempt to neutralise an organisation known for its mobilisations.
In the past, Cnapeste had called the promotion of English teaching a hasty decision, arguing that teachers are not sufficiently trained to handle the subject.
On the contrary, the National Federation of Parents of Students Associations – which is generally aligned with the ministry’s position – expressed satisfaction with the reform, considering English “the language that gives access to science and technology, and therefore, ultimately, to better study and job prospects for pupils”.
‘How will the state manage to provide every school with qualified English teachers in sufficient numbers?’
– Rachida Mahi, Algerian parent
Not all parents, however, agree. Rachida Mahi, a 36‑year‑old engineer living in Algiers, regrets a rushed decision that risks having a disastrous impact on children’s schooling.
She worries about the future of her son, who is starting third grade and will begin learning English this school year.
“How will the state manage to provide every school with qualified English teachers in sufficient numbers? Where does it plan to find them?” she told Middle East Eye.
Like many Algerians of her generation, Mahi speaks very little English.
“It was a secondary language in our schooling, unlike French. I did my engineering studies in French,” she said, adding that she is panicked at the idea of not being able to help her son with his English homework.
‘Improvised measures’
At the end of French colonisation in 1962, Arabic was established as Algeria’s national and official language. To definitively erase the colonial linguistic legacy, education was gradually Arabised. This policy reached its peak in 1991 with the adoption of a law generalising Arabic in all areas of public life and education.
But Arabisation was not entirely successful.
At university, only law and social sciences were Arabised. Scientific fields such as medicine or engineering continued to be taught in French, due to the lack of suitable teaching resources and the shortage of teachers trained in Arabic. Further, leading scholarly journals are still largely accessible only in foreign languages – primarily French and English.
President Tebboune chose in 2025 to progressively replace French with English in medical studies, calling it a “wise” decision that would align Algerian higher education with international standards and global scientific research, where English dominates.
Salah Derradji, a specialist in language didactics and former university rector, is sceptical about the new measure. He told MEE that he has long supported the generalisation of English at university and its gradual introduction at other levels of education. But, he warned, “This project must be carried out thoughtfully. And that is not the case today.”
He argues that the Algerian president made “a political decision” and believes that it is impossible to apply such a measure overnight “with a magic wand”.
“You cannot train teachers in a few weeks and send them into classrooms. You first need qualified trainers,” he said, regretting the absence of broad consultation involving specialists.
Sharing his view, Rabeh Sebaa, former professor of sociology and anthropology at the University of Oran, tells MEE that “Algeria does not have the means to teach English – or teach in English – whether in schools or universities.”
In 2022, as it prepared to introduce English in primary school, the Algerian education ministry announced a major recruitment campaign for 60,000 teachers, targeting university graduates in English language and literature, as well as interpretation.
‘This project must be carried out thoughtfully. And that is not the case today’
– Salah Derradji, language didactics specialist
The operation, however, drew criticism from education unions, who denounced the recruitment of people without pedagogical experience and who were trained hastily.
“My daughter, who is entering secondary school this year, still does not express herself well in English,” Hamid Hani, a 42‑year‑old parent from Bejaia, told MEE. “She had the same English teacher for two years – a young woman, inexperienced and unable to manage a classroom.
“This teacher admitted to me during a meeting that she had to manage on her own to find teaching materials and organise her lessons.”
Furious, Hani accuses the authorities of playing with children’s futures by multiplying “improvised measures”.
Ahmed Tessa, an education specialist and author of a book on the status of French in Algerian schools, agrees.
“Honestly, how can one expect proper language teaching when you recruit university graduates and send them into classrooms without at least two years of initial training – the minimum needed to teach well,” he told MEE.
Tessa argues that the new measure is “an ideological rather than pedagogical decision”.
Rejection of French heritage
The government’s announcement has triggered a broader debate over the legacy of French colonialism and Algeria’s relationship with France.
El Hachemi Djaaboub is a former minister from the Movement of Society for Peace (MSP), an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood, and known for his critical stance towards French influence. He argued that postponing French teaching is an act of sovereignty and accused Tessa of serving foreign interests.
The downgrading of the language of Molière in Algerian schools comes amid persistent diplomatic tensions between Algeria and France, fuelled in 2024 by President Emmanuel Macron’s support for Morocco’s claim of sovereignty over Western Sahara. The former Spanish colony, largely controlled by Morocco, is also claimed by the Sahrawi independence‑seeking Polisario Front, which is backed by Algiers.
‘We must put an end to France’s colonial legacy. Even President Macron speaks more English than French abroad’
– Abderrazak Makri, former president of the MSP
In France, some right‑wing and far‑right media have criticised Algiers’s decision to promote English, seeing it as an attempt to reduce the French cultural and political influence in the country.
In Algeria, social‑media conversations suggest that part of the population now regards French as a colonial leftover to be cast aside. Some even call for the complete suppression of French teaching.
For Abderrazak Makri, former president of the MSP, the change must be radical.
“We must put an end to France’s colonial legacy. Even President Macron speaks more English than French abroad. Today, English is the universal language; it is time for Algerians to adopt it and align themselves with great nations,” he said in 2022.
A few political parties, such as the Rally for Culture and Democracy and the Workers’ Party, are, by contrast, opposed to downgrading French, arguing that language teaching should be complementary and kept away from ideological quarrels.
Analysing positions hostile to the presence of French in education, Sebaa speaks of “visceral, ideologically driven postures”.
“Some of their promoters studied in English-speaking universities and consider English an international language, whereas French symbolises colonial domination,” he told MEE.
Author of a book analysing Algerians’ relationship with French, the sociologist rejects the notion that colonial schooling significantly contributed to the “francisation” of Algerians, whether culturally or linguistically. At the time, he noted, only a small share of Algerian children were in school – less than 20 percent at the time of independence.
Sebaa added that Algerians who lived under colonial rule saw French rather as a means of social advancement and cultural promotion. He pointed to the emergence, at the time, of Algerian literature written in French as evidence. One of its most emblematic figures, Kateb Yacine, famously described French as “a war booty”.
According to Tessa, this heritage is now threatened. He warns that downgrading French will have harmful consequences in many respects. He particularly fears a drying‑up of cultural production in French and an erasure of collective memory expressed in this language.
The educator also warns of Algeria’s distancing from its francophone geopolitical environment and a rupture with millions of children and grandchildren of the diaspora, living mostly in France and Quebec.
Currently, according to the International Organisation of La Francophonie, Algeria is the third‑largest francophone country in the world, behind France and the Democratic Republic of Congo. About 15.6 million Algerians reportedly speak French – about 33 percent of the population.
