Approximately one in eight girls/women, experienced rape or sexual assault before turning 18, according to UNICEF 2024 estimates. Global estimates have also documented substantial sexual abuse among boys. Child sexual abuse is predominantly seen as a social evil and crime against humanity, but it is equally a serious public health problem. Yet our response understandably revolves around the perpetrator. Was the crime reported? Has the accused been arrested? Will the prosecution succeed? What punishment will follow?
For the young person or child, however, punishment of the offender does not reverse what has happened. There may be physical injuries to treat, infections to prevent, pregnancy to consider and psychological wounds that may surface immediately or years later. Healthcare must begin even if justice is delayed.
The first contact with the healthcare system is crucial. Depending on the nature and timing of the assault, the child may require treatment for physical injuries, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and assessment of the risk of HIV. When indicated, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started as early as possible and within 72 hours. Emergency contraception can be offered to girls at risk of pregnancy who present within 120 hours. Hepatitis B and HPV vaccination, STI prophylaxis or treatment and pregnancy-related care may also be required. This is why medical examination after sexual assault cannot become merely an exercise in collecting evidence for a criminal case. Evidence matters, but the survivor is also simultaneously a patient sitting in front of the doctor.
Unseen injuries
The immediate psychological response to sexual abuse may include fear, confusion, shame, anger, numbness, disturbed sleep or silence. A child may not even have the vocabulary to explain what has happened. The first psychological intervention, therefore, is not necessarily psychotherapy, but safety. The child must be protected from further abuse, listened to without blame and helped to regain a sense of security and normalcy. Repeatedly asking the child to recount traumatic details can itself cause distress.
While some children recover with family support and appropriate care, others may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, nightmares, intrusive memories, hypervigilance or dissociation. Self-harm, suicidal thoughts, eating disorders, substance misuse and behavioural problems can also occur. Longer-term difficulties may involve self-worth, emotional regulation, trust, intimacy and relationships.
Experiencing trauma does not automatically mean developing a psychiatric disorder. Outcomes vary with age, developmental stage, duration of abuse, relationship with the perpetrator and support following disclosure. This is why every survivor should receive a baseline mental health assessment covering mood, sleep, behaviour, schooling, relationships, self-harm and suicidality. Its purpose is not to label the child as mentally ill, but to establish a clinical reference point from which recovery or emerging difficulties can be followed.
Trauma over time
Sexual abuse is also not invariably a single traumatic incident. For most children, particularly when the perpetrator has regular access or authority, abuse may recur for months or years. What clinicians encounter may therefore be the cumulative effect of repeated exposure.
Even after the abuse stops, recovery is not governed by a calendar. Memories, family responses, seeing the perpetrator, investigation and court proceedings can reactivate distress. Childhood is also the period during which emotional regulation, self-concept and ideas about safety and relationships are developing. Trauma occurring during these formative years can become entangled with these processes.
Healing consequently means more than making traumatic memories disappear. It means helping the child resume development. Returning to school, playing, sleeping normally, rebuilding relationships and recovering a sense of safety and control can themselves be important parts of recovery.
Paths to recovery
Treatment must be individualised. Supportive psychotherapy and counselling may be sufficient for some. Children with significant symptoms require assessment by trained mental health professionals. Cognitive behavioural therapy helps identify connections between thoughts, emotions and behaviour and develops healthier ways of responding to distress.
For children and adolescents with post-traumatic stress symptoms or PTSD, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, or TF-CBT, is an important evidence-based option. It can teach skills to manage anxiety, gradually and safely process traumatic memories, challenge beliefs such as self-blame and help restore normal functioning.
Other interventions, including interpersonal psychotherapy for appropriate emotional disorders and EMDR for PTSD, may have a role depending on clinical assessment. The principle is that every survivor deserves an assessment and access to care, but not every survivor needs the same treatment.
Families matter
Recovery also rarely happens in the consulting room alone. A supportive, non-offending parent or caregiver can be one of the child’s greatest protective resources. Families need guidance on how to respond to disclosure, avoid blaming or repeatedly questioning the child, recognise warning signs, and restore ordinary routines without pretending that nothing happened.
Where safe and appropriate, caregivers can participate in trauma-focused therapy. They, too, may require psychological support. A parent discovering that their child has been sexually abused may experience guilt, anger, helplessness and enormous distress. Helping the caregiver can indirectly strengthen the child’s recovery.
Building capacity
This requires more than appointing counsellors. The system needs to facilitate frontline doctors, paediatricians, gynaecologists, nurses and counsellors to provide immediate trauma-informed care. District services need access to clinical psychologists and psychiatrists, with clear referral pathways for children requiring specialised interventions. The healthcare providers themselves also need protection. Listening repeatedly to accounts of sexual violence can result in secondary or vicarious trauma. Supervision, manageable caseloads, debriefing, peer support, and periods away from continuous trauma work should be built into services rather than regarded as luxuries.
Eventually, the success of our response cannot be measured only by whether justice was set in motion: it is whether the infection was prevented, whether reproductive healthcare was provided, whether the child’s mental health was assessed, whether treatment was available when needed, whether the family knew how to support the child, whether the child returned to school and, ultimately, whether that child was able to move forward.
A humane health system must, at first, ask what needs to happen for the child, while law simultaneously addressing what needs to happen for justice.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

The Delhi Police swiftly acted against a woman accused of posing as a police officer and allegedly refusing to pay for services at a beauty salon in the Rup Nagar area.
The woman claimed to be associated with the force and allegedly misbehaved with the salon operator after availing services. She also reportedly intimidated the operator by invoking the name of the Delhi Police.
The salon operator said the woman had spent several hours at the establishment and, after getting the services, refused to make the payment. She allegedly continued to threaten and intimidate the operator while claiming to be from the Delhi Police.
Following the incident, the Rup Nagar Police Station team, under SHO Ramesh Kaushik, took swift action against the accused. The police intervened and ensured that the salon operator received the money that was withheld.

Telangana hotelier murdered after opposing wife's affair; woman, lover arrested
Police said a Nagarkurnool hotelier was allegedly killed in a conspiracy involving his wife and her alleged lover. Investigators linked the case to a relationship dispute and property transferred in the wife's name.
An alleged extramarital affair and a property dispute led to the murder of a hotel businessman in Telangana's Nagarkurnool, police said, arresting the victim's wife and her alleged lover for conspiring to kill him.
The accused have been identified as Salima Begum (36), wife of the deceased Mohammad Kareem (43), and Md. Gouse Pasha (29), who allegedly shared a relationship with her. Kareem, a hotelier and resident of Ramnagar Colony in Nagarkurnool town, was found murdered at his home on September 7.
Nagarkurnool DSP Burri Srinivas said the investigation revealed that the duo allegedly plotted Kareem's murder after he objected to their relationship.
According to police, Salima and Gouse Pasha, who runs a tyre puncture shop in Nagapur village of Revalli mandal and is related to the family, had allegedly been involved in a relationship for nearly two years. Kareem had reportedly discovered the affair, leading to frequent disputes between the couple.
Police said the matter had even been taken to community elders for settlement. During one such confrontation, Gouse allegedly threatened Kareem.
Investigators further alleged that Kareem had earlier transferred his property into Salima's name. Believing that the assets would remain with them if Kareem was eliminated, the two allegedly hatched a plan to murder him.
According to police, the conspiracy was executed on the night of September 7. Salima had travelled to a dargah in Nellore and allegedly made a WhatsApp call to Gouse, instructing him to carry out the murder.
Police said Gouse arrived at Kareem's residence around 2.30 am wearing gloves and carrying a knife. Kareem, awakened by a sound at the door, opened it and was allegedly attacked. Investigators said Gouse slit Kareem's throat, killing him on the spot.
After the murder, Gouse allegedly disposed of the knife, clothes and footwear used during the crime in bushes before fleeing the area.
The case came to light after Kareem's brother, Hussain, lodged a police complaint. During the investigation, police questioned Salima and uncovered details of the conspiracy and Gouse's role in the killing.
Both accused were arrested and produced before a court, which remanded them to judicial custody. Police said they have recovered the knife allegedly used in the murder, along with clothes and footwear believed to have been worn by Gouse during the attack.

The world’s most common childhood disability, cerebral palsy, has long been associated with birth complications like premature birth, infection, lack of oxygen, and perinatal stroke. But population studies suggest those factors account for only a fraction of cases. To fill this diagnostic void, modern medicine has routinely turned to gene sequencing to hunt for a root cause, and researchers have zeroed in on certain genetic variants in a substantial subset of children with cerebral palsy.
For families, gene sequencing offers a profound hope: of ending a gruelling diagnostic odyssey. Finding a definitive genetic root cause optimises patient management, reduces unnecessary testing, and finally gives parents concrete answers.
But a new study in The American Journal of Human Genetics suggests simply finding a pathogenic gene variant in a child is not proof that it caused their motor disability.
In resource-constrained healthcare systems like India’s, acting on a false alarm from a standard genetic panel can divert already limited medical resources away from treatments that actually work.
“The medical community previously has not comprehensively examined the statistical evidence in favor of a cerebral palsy association for genes flagged in large genomics cohort studies,” Peter N. Robinson, a computational biologist at the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine, U.S., and the study’s corresponding author, said. “Our study showed that there is convincing evidence for only a subset.”
Collapsing narrative
The researchers combed through 21 previously published genomic diagnostic studies involving 5,440 individuals diagnosed with cerebral palsy. Across these diverse cohorts, the original authors had pointed the finger at a staggering 515 different candidate genes, reporting them as the direct genetic cause of the patients’ symptoms.
But when Dr. Robinson’s team subjected this historical data to rigorous statistical analysis, the established narrative collapsed. Sufficient statistical evidence could only confirm a true association for 89 of those 515 proposed genes.
Sequencing the genomes of 460 patients across the Shriners Children’s hospital network in the U.S., the team also identified disease-causing mutations in 60 genes across 15.8% of children. Yet their stricter statistical paradigm whittled the list down to only 16 with significant evidence linked to cerebral palsy.
“What this paper is trying to suggest is some of the genetic variants may not be slam dunk,” said Kuntal Sen, a clinical geneticist and paediatric neurologist at Children’s National Hospital, U.S. “It might explain one problem, like intellectual disability, but it may not tie together everything. Which is a fair point to make, that some genetic test reports might be just a slight association rather than causal.”
False alarms
These false alarms can be traced back to a few traps. One is coincidence. Because roughly 5% of the general population harbours a rare genetic disease, sequencing a child with cerebral palsy frequently uncovers severe mutations entirely unrelated to the disability.
A previous large-scale study flagged the LIPH gene as a cause of cerebral palsy because an affected patient happened to carry it. However, mutations in LIPH actually cause a rare form of hair loss and possess no known neurological link.
Conversely, across both historical literature and the newly sequenced cohort, CTNNB1 mutations showed up far more often than random chance would allow, providing the proof necessary to confirm it is a real risk factor.
The confusion is also compounded by the fact that ‘cerebral palsy’ is a clinical catch-all rather than a single biological disease.
“For me, I think the term ‘cerebral palsy’ does not always make sense from a purely scientific perspective.,” Dr. Sen said. “The motor symptoms that the children have [severe muscle stiffness, and weakness affecting either one side of the body or all four limbs] are more scientifically informative.”
He noted the outdated label survives, rightfully, mainly because it guarantees patients access to specialised insurance and physical therapy in the western world.
But as an umbrella term for brain-derived muscle weakness, the diagnosis lumps a large variety of conditions together. While some stem from birth injuries, others are ‘mimics’: rare metabolic or genetic disorders masquerading as a muscle weakness.
Stakes of precision
This heterogeneous reality is why distinguishing a harmless genetic coincidence from a true biological driver carries large stakes.
If doctors accept an incidental mutation from a standard genetic panel as the final answer, they may halt their workup prematurely, leaving a true, treatable ‘mimic’ undiscovered. But accurately pinpointing the biological cause using strict statistical proof can fine-tune this personalised approach and open the door to highly targeted care.
“If the genetic test report gives you a slam dunk answer, you counsel them, you provide management guidelines, and you can also give a recurrence risk for other family members,” Dr. Sen said.
The researchers estimated that among 8.5% to 24% of individuals who receive a valid genetic diagnosis, the findings point to specific, available treatments. By catching mimics early, doctors can swap generic physical therapy for precise interventions, such as dietary changes for arginase deficiency or specific medications for vitamin-dependent epilepsies and hereditary dystonia.
For these families, getting the statistics right means much more than simply solving a mystery. It unlocks treatments that can alter the course of a child’s life.
For countries like India, where three in every 1,000 live births are affected by cerebral palsy and genetic testing is an emerging and rapidly growing field, studies like this offer an advantage. A severe mutation that breaks a specific protein and masquerades as cerebral palsy does so universally, regardless of ethnicity. And by identifying only the true genetic mimics, local clinics can skip the diagnostic trial-and-error phase of older, bloated sequencing panels, and pave the way to adopt highly accurate genetic testing, connecting families to precise treatments faster.
Cautious path
While the Robinson et al. study has set a rigorous new standard, the authors have also conceded their strict mathematical model might actually underestimate the true number of genes linked to the disorder.
“One must remember that the lack of statistical significance does not imply the absence of an association,” Dr. obinson said. “It is very likely that there are more genes with cerebral palsy association than the 89 we flagged.”
Realising the full promise of this approach will require the medical community to move beyond just sequencing DNA. Scientists need large, globally shared datasets of detailed patient profiles to finally calculate the exact degree of risk a specific genetic variant carries.
Ultimately, translating these statistical insights into daily practice will take time. “With appropriate caution, genomic testing can be a useful addition to CP diagnostics,” Dr. Robinson said. “Caring physicians will integrate many kinds of information when making the decision.”
Anirban Mukhopadhyay is a geneticist by training and science communicator from New Delhi.

Lyricist Sameer had a conversation with Komal Nahta where he criticized the current state of music in Bollywood. He began by saying, “Nowadays, there’s no meaning or thehrav in songs. This is because gaane ka matlab ab kahin bacha nahin hai. There’s no emotion or depth left in society. Cinema ultimately shows a reflection of society. Sameer recalls, “Karan Johar gave me a narration for 6 ½ hours for Kuch Kuch Hota Hai; he explained in such detail – what will be the colour of Kajol’s saree, Shah Rukh Khan’s suit…”
He added, “Moreover, the makers have sidelined music. It’s like a fill-in-the-blanks situation – yahaan kuch nahin hai toh gaana aise hi daal do. I remember when I was writing Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998), Karan Johar gave me a narration of 6 ½ hours. Celine Dion returns to the stage after battling rare illness
Celine Dion returned to the stage Saturday nearly four years after announcing she had been battling a rare, painful condition.
Dion, who is Canadian, opened up her 16-show residency in Paris at the Plenitude Arena with the French song "On Ne Change Pas," which means "we don't change" in English. After finishing the song, she was emotional with tears in her eyes.
"I had promised myself not to cry," Dion told the crowd, according to Variety. "Thank you so very much for coming. If it's your first time in Paris, I hope you fall in love with it just like I did. Finally, it's amazing we are all together. I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. So here I am, singing for you and singing for me, singing live!"
Videos posted online show Dion wearing a black dress and her hair in a bun singing hits "Because You Loved Me" and "Power of Love." Dion also sang "My Heart Will Go On," an iconic classic from "The Titanic" movie soundtrack.
A few hours before the show was slated to begin, Dion posted on her Instagram Story a photo of herself smiling and standing in front of fans with her hands in the air with the comment "En route!"
A native of Quebec, a French-speaking province of Canada, she is deeply loved in France. Her concerts are sold out and it's estimated they will bring in millions of dollars for the region.
The Grammy award-winning artist revealed in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition that causes stiff limbs and severe muscle spasms. She said then in a message on social media that the condition affected every part of her life, "sometimes causing difficulties when I walk and not allowing me to use my vocal cords to sing the way I'm used to."
Her last concert tour was disrupted in 2020 by the Covid-19 pandemic. She performed July 2024 at the Paris Olympics opening ceremony.

Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.
Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.
Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.
Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.
“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”
Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.
“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.
“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”
Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.
Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.
While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”
He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.
The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.
Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.
“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

The Excise Department of the Delhi government on Sunday announced that it arrested 730 people and registered 725 FIRs over the last five months, seizing 2.20 lakh bottles of illegal liquor and 197 vehicles in a major bid to crack down on the illegal liquor trade in the Capital.
Reacting to the development, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said that the Delhi government was following a zero-tolerance policy towards the illegal liquor trade and was working on an effective excise policy.
“The government is working on a new excise policy aimed at strengthening public safety, ensuring responsible regulation of the liquor trade, maintaining quality and increasing government revenue,” the CM said.
In the corresponding period from April to August in the financial year 2025-26, the department had arrested 312 people, registered 315 FIRs, recovered around one lakh bottles of illegal liquor, and seized 112 vehicles.
Ms. Gupta added that the government’s priority was to ensure adequate availability of legal liquor during festivals so that Delhi residents do not face any inconvenience, while also effectively curbing the sale and smuggling of illegal liquor.
According to the department, Delhi shares geographical boundaries with neighbouring states and has around 70 entry points, both large and small.
“Enforcement activities would be stepped up further in view of the upcoming festive season in Delhi. The department aims to take strict action against those involved in the illegal liquor trade while also ensuring the availability of liquor through legal channels in the city,” a statement from the CMO said.
The sale of liquor has been a highly contentious political issue in Delhi over the past few years, following the arrest of senior Aam Aadmi Party leaders over a new liquor policy introduced by the Kejriwal government. The new policy was ultimately scrapped and the old regime was brought back.
Checks on emissions
Meanwhile, in a video statement, Ms. Gupta announced all pollution testing centres in the city will be upgraded to effectively check emissions.
Noting a technology gap, she said private vehicles use petrol pump booths while commercial ones rely on outdated certification systems. To strengthen monitoring, every centre will be equipped with cameras. New automated stations in Tehkhand and Nand Nagri will each test 72,000 commercial vehicles annually.
Arpan centres
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Sunday said that over 41 tonnes of old clothes have been collected at Delhi Metro’s 10 Arpan centres and turned into useful products. These centres help residents who struggle to store or properly dispose of old garments.
As of August 31, 3,940 people deposited 41,181 kg of clothes. Self-help groups are using the material to make items like rugs, bags, and pouches, recording total sales of ₹27,036, according to a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office.
“Our effort is to make it easy and convenient for people to donate old clothes and ensure their maximum utilisation, thereby further strengthening efforts to make Delhi cleaner, more beautiful and greener,” Ms. Gupta said.
Five centres were launched on August 3, while the remaining centres became operational on August 12 and 17.
The government plans to expand the initiative by opening 10 more centres in January 2027 at major metro stations, including INA, Rajouri Garden, and Dwarka Sector 10.

Chinese scientists find ‘extremely high-value’ underwater gold mine in Pacific
Survey team says the ores, formed when super-hot water shoots from the seabed, are richer in gold and silver than those found on land
According to a report by state broadcaster CCTV on Friday, the discovery was made during a joint scientific expedition involving several Chinese academic institutions.
The ores within this seabed hydrothermal field – an area where hot, mineral-rich water shoots out from openings on the ocean floor – are exceptionally rich in precious metals. Silver, in particular, reaches more than 1kg (2.2lbs) per tonne of ore at its highest grade, while the average metal content exceeds that of typical terrestrial deposits.
“The [large seabed mining area] has extremely high exploitation value,” said Song Shiji, vice-dean of the Institute for Ocean Engineering at Tsinghua University and one of the lead scientists on the project.
These multi‑metal deposits form when super‑hot, metal‑rich water jets out of the seabed and hits near‑freezing seawater. The sudden cooling makes the metals bind with sulphur and drop out as solid sulphide minerals – mostly copper, zinc and lead, but often with some gold and silver as well.

GTA 6 is a little over two months away, releasing November 19, 2026, and it’s easily the biggest entertainment property of the decade. Most players have already pre-ordered GTA 6 to experience Jason and Lucia’s story on day one. However, some players are still hoping Rockstar’s next game arrives on Xbox Game Pass at launch. This begs the question: will GTA 6 release on the service at launch? Here’s everything we know so far.
Is GTA 6 Coming to Xbox Game Pass at Launch?
The answer is no, GTA 6 will not be available on Xbox Game Pass at launch on November 19, 2026. Rockstar has never released one of its major games on Xbox Game Pass at launch.
With reports claiming that GTA 6 pre-orders have surpassed 4 million copies, there’s no reason whatsoever for Rockstar to release their biggest game ever on a subscription service.

That’s not to say that GTA 6 won’t drop on Xbox Game Pass in the future. Rockstar has a history of releasing their games on the service several years after release, so the studio could follow the same path with GTA 6. However, just don’t expect it anytime soon.

Rockstar’s History with Xbox Game Pass
Previously, Rockstar’s two biggest titles, GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, had their fair share of stints on Xbox Game Pass, though none were particularly long. GTA 5 first appeared on Xbox Game Pass on January 3, 2020, more than six years after its debut on Xbox 360 and PS3 on September 17, 2013.

| Rockstar Game | First Run | Recent Run | 
|---|---|---|
| GTA 5 | January 3, 2020 – May 7, 2020 | April 15, 2025 – April 15, 2026 |

GTA 5 had its longest Xbox Game Pass run this year, while its previous stints lasted around four to six months each. On the other hand, RDR 2 has appeared only once, leaving Game Pass on September 7, 2020, and has not returned since.
Will GTA 6 Come to Xbox Game Pass in the Future?
Judging by Rockstar’s history with Xbox Game Pass, GTA 6 could eventually join the service, but not anytime soon. If anything, you might want to think beyond 2030. If that happens, the game will likely hit the service years after GTA 6’s PC release, which is rumored to arrive next year.
There’s no sugarcoating it, but players waiting to play GTA 6 on Xbox Game Pass will be sorely disappointed if they’re expecting Rockstar to follow the same path with Red Dead Redemption 2. GTA 6 is way bigger than Red Dead Redemption 2, both in sheer scale and in anticipation. It’s the biggest game of the decade, or likely, the century.
There’s a chance Hideo Kojima releases PHYSINT on Xbox before GTA 6 joins Game Pass, and the former likely won’t release on the service either. However, plans could change, and Rockstar may pivot to a quicker release for GTA 6 on the subscription platform.
One thing’s confirmed: GTA 6 is launching on November 19, 2026, on Xbox Series X|S, so you can put those delay concerns to rest. India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Train derails in France and injures 44 as authorities investigate possible sabotage
French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment in Normandy that injured 44 people
PARIS -- French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment that injured 44 people in Normandy, after a piece of rail was found on the track, police told The Associated Press on Saturday.
The regional train was carrying 186 passengers from Rouen to Caen when it derailed Friday evening at Cléon, in the Seine-Maritime department of northwestern France.
An 18-year-old woman was among the injured and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital, police said.
A spokeswoman for the French national police communications service, known as SICOP, said that the piece of rail found on the track was “probably” linked to the derailment. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn’t authorized to be publicly named in line with police policy.
Investigators were working to establish whether the circumstances were accidental or involved sabotage, the service said. The prosecutor’s office remained cautious about drawing conclusions, according to the police.
France’s previous rail disasters include the July 2013 derailment at Brétigny-sur-Orge, south of Paris, which killed seven people.
In November 2015, a high-speed TGV train carrying out tests derailed at Eckwersheim, near Strasbourg, killing 11.
More recently, a crash involving two high-speed trains at Adamuz in southern Spain killed 46 people and injured more than 100 in January, according to the Andalusian regional government.

World's tallest totem pole comes down in Alert Bay, B.C., after more than 50 years
Emotional day as the tallest totem pole in the world, representing unity between tribes, comes down
The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island.
For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness Book of World Records — represented much more than its height.
"This pole was so much more," said Ho’miskanis Don Svanvik, hereditary chief and elected chief councillor of the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation.
"It was a beacon for our people coming out of a pretty dark time in history," he said, referencing the potlatch ban — the federal law that outlawed potlatching on the coast for more than 60 years.
Svanvik said his great-grandparents were jailed in the 1920s for taking part in potlatch.
"The pole, in some ways, represents people being who they always have been and continue to be," he said.

"This is who we are. This is how we govern ourselves. This is how we celebrate and acknowledge things, through our ceremonies … this was a time when that was all coming back, coming into the forefront of things."
Crews began dismantling the 173-foot pole on Wednesday in a carefully staged, multi-hour process, after the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation confirmed the structure had become too unstable and hazardous to remain standing.
The nearby Gukwdzi (Big House) and its surrounding parking area were closed the evening before to establish a safety perimeter, and community members gathered nearby to witness.
Nothing lasts forever
The original pole was raised in 1973. It was one tree spliced into two connected sections, according to 'Na̱mǥis Hereditary Chief William Wasden Jr.
He said the pole was designed to carry the crests of 22 Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw tribes — a deliberate statement of unity.
Tribes have amalgamated since then, Wasden said, but it was a powerful symbol of solidarity, an essential theme of the times.
"Our Big House was finished around then too … it was the same theme … somewhere for everybody to come and utilize," Wasden Jr. said.
"Alert Bay was like Grand Central Station, it was almost like the center of Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw territories physically, but people were amalgamating there and so it almost became Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw central."
When the pole came down, Wasden said he felt proud.
"Nothing lasts forever, especially the cedar tree," he said, sharing a story of an ancestor who recognized in ancient times that neither a cedar tree nor a mountain would always stand.
For Wasden, the pole’s takedown is part of a much older pattern, one where each generation is left to answer for itself.
"It’s our ancestors challenging us now," he said. "Are you gonna ride on our coattails, or will you be as great as we were, by doing the things you need to do to uplift your people?"
The pole was carved by a number of carvers at the time, overseen by Jimmy Dick.
Wasden named Jimmy Dick’s son "Blackie," Ben Dick Senior, as the main carver. He named other carvers like Adam Dick, Andy "Beanie" Beans, Gus Matilpi and Dick Dawson.
Svanvik named Henry Hunt and Henry Speck, along with others who may have dropped in at the time.
Both acknowledged Dora Cook who learned to carve alongside the men, one of very few women to do so at the time.
"She was ahead of her time," said Wasden.
Both Wasden and Svanvik remember the pole being carved when they were kids.
Svanvik jokingly said he played a small role when he was called over by the carvers to "squirt oil on the saw" they were using. Wasden carries a photo of himself and his friends sitting on the pole before it was raised.
Both said they look forward to what’s next.
"This is not the end of anything," Svanvik said.

Welcome to Edition 9.10 of the Rocket Report! This week we’re celebrating a historic moment in Europe when a German rocket company successfully put its launch vehicle into orbit. Isar Aerospace became the first purely commercial European company to reach orbit, and impressively it did so on just its second launch attempt. How quickly can they scale up operations? How quickly will the second European launch firm reach this goal? Big questions, which for now we don’t have answers to.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Isar Aerospace takes a huge step forward. Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately developed rocket into low-Earth orbit on Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle. The two-stage rocket, Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit, Ars reports. With Saturday’s success, Isar becomes the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe’s stagnant launch market.
Private capital emerges … It took eight years for Isar to get to orbit, a timetable similar to other successful commercial rocket startups in the West. In that time, the company raised roughly $1 billion through several private financing rounds and now has a workforce of nearly 500 employees. European space officials hope a jolt of competition will light a fire under the continent’s rocket industry. European governments are accustomed to footing the bill and having a say in where rockets are built, a procurement model known as geographical return, or geo-return. The paradigm is different with companies like Isar, which established themselves on a privately funded basis, with ambitions to eventually attract commercial and government business.
Long-forgotten space plane is back? Ars Technica has written precisely one article about Ravn X, an autonomous aircraft and launch vehicle under development by Aevum. This was back in December 2020. We haven’t covered it since, I think it’s safe to say, there is a fair amount of skepticism about whether the project to build the space plane was all that realistic. And time has largely proved us right. The company’s initial target of an orbital mission in 2021 came and went. We largely forgot about the vehicle. Then something mysterious showed up at Long Beach Airport.
Don’t get too excited … TWZ reports that a handful of aviation photographers got a surprise eyeful of a very sleek and large aircraft silhouette last week at the airport and later learned that it was likely a mockup of Ravn X. Later on, in posts on X, Aevum founder Jay Skylus said the company “conducted Test 2 of Ravn X SN0 early this morning. Ravn X completed its first fully autonomous taxi. ~37 minutes of autonomy. We’re reviewing the telemetry and test data now and will share more as soon as I can.” We are not expecting any flights imminently. (submitted by Onychomys)
The Ars Technica Rocket Report
The easiest way to keep up with Eric Berger’s and Stephen Clark’s reporting on all things space is to sign up for our newsletter. We’ll collect their stories and deliver them straight to your inbox.
UK invests big time in northern spaceport. This week, the United Kingdom unveiled a new national space strategy that seeks to “drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies.” As part of efforts to reindustrialize the country, the government is investing 7.8 billion pounds ($10.5 billion) through 2030. About 40 percent of the funding will go toward strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defense communications programs, which “play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.”
German rockets to launch from there … The UK government also wants to help push forward a spaceport under development in Shetland, an archipelago north of the Scottish mainland. The government will provide 30 million pounds ($40.5 million) for the SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, with the aim of “helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.” No orbital rocket has ever successfully launched from the United Kingdom. The main tenant of SaxaVord is German launch company Rocket Factory Augsburg. (submitted by iCowboy)
Firefly to launch from Sweden. Firefly Aerospace announced on Wednesday a multi-launch agreement with SSC Space for two Alpha rocket launches from Sweden’s Esrange Space Center. Targeted to launch no earlier than 2028, the missions will serve Sweden’s national security customers as well as additional commercial rideshare customers.
More to come … Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace, said more Alpha launches will follow. “These first two missions are just the start of a long-term, multi-launch partnership with SSC Space that will provide assured access to space for years to come,” he said. SSC Space secured the full payload capacity and can allocate payload space to its government and commercial customers, providing flexible accommodations and launch opportunities for the European satellite market.
Avio seeks higher flight rate. Avio is looking to boost the pace of Vega-C rocket flights to six missions per year, roughly double the current level, and potentially go another 50 percent higher, Aviation Week reports. “We are working to increase, as a first step, the cadence of Vega to six per year, and potentially a second step to nine per year,” Giulio Ranzo said Wednesday during the International Space Summit in Paris.
Solid production is not so solid … The Vega-C rocket is used heavily by institutions for launch in Europe, where demand is rising. “We will follow what they need, what they ask us, and we will try to adapt to continue providing the service,” Ranzo said. One of the challenges in ramping up is that the Vega-C used the same solid rocket motors employed on Ariane 6, which is also looking to boost output. The combination is creating supply-chain bottlenecks that industry and government are trying to address.
Stoke Space eyes larger rocket. Stoke Space announced Tuesday that it has raised another significant round of funding, $1 billion, as it makes a final push toward its debut launch next year. The Washington-based launch company also revealed plans for a larger medium-lift vehicle, Ars reports. The quantity of new funding will enable the company to accelerate work on a larger “Block 2” version of the Nova rocket, capable of lifting 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in a fully reusable configuration.
Block 2 will rock you … “We have already started development on a larger vehicle, and we felt like now is the time to pour gas on that fire and really start full-force development of the larger vehicle, and so that’s the reason for the timing,” Stoke co-founder and Chief Executive Andy Lapsa said. The Nova Pathfinder vehicle has a diameter of about 12.5 feet, slightly larger than SpaceX’s Falcon 9 vehicle, although it is considerably shorter. The Block 2 version of Nova is intended to have a 15-foot diameter, Lapsa said. Stoke is targeting 2029 for the debut launch of Block 2.
Ariane 64 gets with Amazon for some more. Arianespace and Amazon Leo announced Wednesday an agreement at the International Space Summit in Paris for six additional Ariane 64 launches to continue deploying the Amazon Leo constellation into low-Earth orbit. The new order brings the total number of Amazon Leo launches with Arianespace to 24, up from 18, with missions scheduled through 2031 from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana.
Arianespace, the on-time provider? … To the surprise of some observers, including your humble correspondent, Arianespace has proven to be a more reliable launch partner to Amazon than the other two providers who inked deals with Amazon in 2022, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin. But Ariane 6 has gotten through its teething pains without major issues, unlike Vulcan and New Glenn. “We committed early because we believed in what Arianespace was building, and they’ve executed mission after mission,” said Chris Weber, vice president of Amazon Leo business and product. “Expanding from 18 to 24 launches reflects our confidence in Ariane 6 and our continued investment in European launch capability.”
Nyx will fly on Ariane 6. Arianespace and The Exploration Company announced this week that Nyx, the reusable space capsule developed by The Exploration Company, will launch into orbit on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana. The Exploration Company chief executive, Hélène Huby, has said she is targeting late 2028 for the launch of this spacecraft, which is due to fly a cargo mission to the International Space Station.
Commercial cargo redux … The launch deal follows the award of a service contract to The Exploration Company by the European Space Agency worth 760 million euros ($880 million) to support the development of Nyx, a demonstration mission, and two operational cargo missions. “We started the development of Nyx with private funding only, and we are now at a technical maturity level where ESA and Member States’ public funding can support us massively, as anchor clients, to help us finalize the vehicle,” Huby said.
Does Europe need a massive rocket? Speaking of Huby and The Exploration Company, the company also announced a $450 million Series C funding round this week, Ars reports. As part of this, the company will continue development of the Storm rocket engine, which is projected to have a thrust of about 400,000 pound-feet. This would be used to power a reusable rocket intended to launch 40 metric tons in reusable mode and 60 tons in expendable mode.
How to stay relevant … The expendable Ariane 6 rocket, by contrast, has a maximum lift capacity of about 20 tons. “If Europe wants to stay relevant—we will not be relevant without a massive rocket at a massive cadence,” Huby said during a teleconference with reporters on Tuesday. “And to do that we need a massive engine, and right now this is something we just do not have in Europe.” An aggressive timeline for the rocket’s development, she said, is 2033.
Terran R gets on-ramped by NASA. NASA said this week it has awarded a “Launch Services II” contract to Relativity Space that allows for on-ramping the Terran R rocket into the agency’s launch services program. Accordingly, the Terran R launch service will be available to NASA for future missions, including science, research, and human spaceflight.
Don’t expect Terran R to win awards right away … NASA still wants to see a new rocket like Terran R, which has yet to make its debut, demonstrate success in flight. However, by receiving this contract, Relativity can now follow a pathway for new launch service providers to compete for future missions. The current ordering period covers missions through December 2032.

Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
- Published
US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts.
"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.
One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.
On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".
The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.
The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.
On one hand, the sector is seen as huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.
But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.
In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.
The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.
And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.
The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

VAR in focus as Haaland goal gives Man City controversial derby win
MANCHESTER, Sept 13 : Erling Haaland's controversial goal proved to be the winner for Manchester City against Manchester United in their Premier League clash at Old Trafford on Sunday, but it is unlikely the big Norwegian will have the last word as debate rages whether the derby goal should have been allowed to stand.
Video reviews showed Haaland was onside when the ball was played, but an attempt by City midfielder Enzo Fernandez to head it into the net was seemingly ignored in the VAR deliberations, with the Argentinian appearing to be in an offside position when Josko Gvardiol played the initial ball in.
The Premier League Match Centre said on social media platform X that Fernandez didn't play the ball, and therefore the goal was allowed to stand, but needless to say the red side of Manchester did not agree with that assessment.
"I just don't get it, I really don't get it, I can't understand how we're trying to help referees, putting so many layers behind them, so many people, bodies and screens, and they can't make the right decision," United coach Michael Carrick fumed.
"It's worrying if that's how the game's seen by those who are officiating it ... I can't be too critical of the players, and I won't be because I think we've done a lot of good things. Today we didn't quite find what we needed.
The United boss, who has taken four points from his first four league games of the season, couldn't hide his disappointment.
"I'm feeling for the fans today. We haven't got as many points as we would've liked at this stage, there's no getting away from that. We've just got to move on and get winning again."
Defender Lisandro Martinez was equally frustrated.
"I think it was offside. What I can't understand is the rules. He was there. I went to him because he was there in front of me, that's why Haaland was free at the back," he explained.
"I want to be calm now, I want to control myself, it's so hard, because you lose, you lose a derby, you lose three points at home ... it's unacceptable. Because it's the best league in the world, you have the best teams in the world, the best players in the world, and now we have to go home with this injustice."

What to know as a Philippine region with a history of conflict holds its first parliamentary polls
Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots Monday in the region's first parliamentary elections
MANILA, Philippines -- Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots Monday in the region's first parliamentary elections, seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-determination and lasting peace after decades of insurgency and violence.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, or BARMM, covers five provinces, three cities and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters. It has nearly 2.4 million voters, with election officials aiming for an 80% turnout after polling was postponed for several years.
Here’s what to know about the Sept. 14 vote.
There are 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament, the region’s legislative body. These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
Unlike the direct voting under the presidential system of the national government, the region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, is not elected by voters. Members of parliament will choose the chief minister from among themselves by a majority vote during their first parliamentary session.
Voters will choose one regional party, one district representative and six sectoral representatives. The 40 regional party-representative seats will be distributed to nominees based on a party’s vote share.
Centuries of colonialism by Spain, the U.S. and Filipino Christian settlers turned Muslims into a minority group in resource-rich Mindanao, the southern third of the Philippine archipelago from which the BARMM was carved out. The region has seen decades of intermittent but bloody conflicts over land, resources and political power.
Since the 1970s, about 150,000 combatants and civilians have died in the southern Philippines, while development was stunted in the country’s poorest region. Western and Asian governments feared the tenacious insurgencies could help foster Islamic extremism in Southeast Asia.
The presence of private armies and long-running clan wars has added to the violent mix.
Under a 2014 peace deal brokered by Malaysia, the largest Muslim rebel group — the Moro Islamic Liberation Front — gave up its goal of a separate Muslim state in the south of the largely Catholic country in exchange for broader autonomy. The group’s 40,000 fighters would be “demobilized” and given livelihoods and other help to bring them back to normal life.
The Bangsamoro region was established under the peace deal to replace a poverty-wracked five-province autonomous region with a larger, better-funded and more powerful area, which has been governed by former guerrilla leaders under a transition period that ends with the first regular elections on Sept. 14.
The Moro Islamic Liberation Front last year suspended the disarming of its remaining 14,000 fighters after claiming that the government has not fully complied with socio-economic commitments it made under the 2014 peace deal. Then-presidential assistant David Diciano, who had been helping oversee the transformation of the Bangsamoro region, said in a statement at the time that the Muslim rebel front’s central committee had decided “to postpone the decommissioning of 14,000 of its combatants and 2,450 of their weapons.”
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance, a nonprofit policy and research center based in the region, has noted that the incomplete decommissioning of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s combatants as well as the organization’s split into two rival political parties vying in the elections pose a potential danger of violence that may affect voters’ confidence to go out and vote.
More than 20,000 military and police personnel are being deployed to secure the elections, officials said.
“We have just one goal: for them to be able to vote. All our preparations and efforts would be in vain if our fellow citizens couldn’t vote,” Commission on Elections Chairman Erwin Garcia said.
Michael Henry Yusingco, a senior research fellow of the Ateneo Policy Center, in an article published by the online portal Access Bangsamoro, said: “Without a party ethos that is rooted in collective responsibility, mutual respect, and orientation toward the common good, parliaments risk devolving into arenas of personal rivalries, factional disputes, or transactional politics."
He said it is the right time for regional parties to show they can embody such party ethos to sustain parliamentary democracy.
“Clearly, the BARMM’s history of clan politics, electoral violence, and patronage-based loyalties presents formidable challenges.”

Although the photograph recirculated in 2026, it dates back to at least December 2018.
"In 1973 Japan planted trees in concentric circles as part of an experiment in forestry spacing. This is what they look like today from above," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the photograph.
(Reddit u/Impressive_East_)
That image and other photographs showing the same formations have circulated online for years, appearing on platforms such as Instagram, 9GAG, Facebook, Pinterest and X.
In short, the photograph was real, and the claim about the forest was also accurate. It showed two experimental plots of Japanese cedar near Nichinan, a city in Miyazaki Prefecture on the island of Kyushu. According to the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, the experiment was established in fiscal year 1973 to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The photograph circulating in 2026 was not new — we traced it to at least December 2018.
The same forest has attracted attention before. We previously investigated similar photographs of the experimental plots in September 2024. One of the images circulating at the time was also available in The Associated Press' image archive.
Origin of the photograph
The photograph first gained attention when Japanese news outlet Sankei News published it in a story about the forest.
(www.sankei.com)
The outlet credited the image to Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, a regional office of Japan's Forestry Agency. Its caption (translated from Japanese via Google Translate) read, "A circular pattern visible in the mountains of Nichinan City, Miyazaki Prefecture."
The image later appeared in numerous social media posts and articles.
What the photograph shows
The photographs circulating online show Japanese cedar trees arranged in two groups of concentric circles in a national forest near Nichinan, in Miyazaki Prefecture. An AP caption describing the forest said the trees in the outer ring were approximately 20 meters (66 feet) tall, about 5 meters (16 feet) taller than those near the center.
The circular forest was also discoverable on Google Maps and Google Earth, as the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office gave its location as 31°43'50.0"N, 131°23'05.0"E.
According to the office, the experiment was linked to changes in the local timber industry. Obi cedar was planted sparsely in the area for shipbuilding timber, but demand later shifted toward wood for general construction.
Researchers created the experiment to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. It was established in fiscal 1973, with the cedar seedlings planted in March 1974. The trees were arranged in concentric circles at different distances from one another, creating planting densities of about 377 to 10,027 trees per hectare. Seen from above, this produced the circular pattern that earned the site the nickname "mystery circles."
Later surveys showed that planting density affected the trees' size and growth. A 2011 study concluded that around 2,000 to 2,800 trees per hectare was suitable for lower-cost forestry. The experiment's final report, completed in fiscal year 2023, concluded that planting densities of 1,500 trees per hectare or fewer could be effective in terms of financial returns and afforestation costs.
For further reading, in January 2015 we investigated whether a law in Japan makes it illegal for citizens to be fat.

OpenAI is open to slowing the development of AI systems in coordination with other leading AI companies amid growing concerns about the safety of frontier models. CEO Sam Altman told employees at a company-wide meeting this week that OpenAI could moderate the pace of development alongside other AI companies, Bloomberg reported, citing sources. However, Altman said that some companies might not agree to such an approach, according to the report. Inc42 has reached out to OpenAI for a comment on the development. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Competition among OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and other AI companies has raised concerns that commercial pressure could lead developers to advance or deploy powerful models before adequate safeguards are in place. OpenAI has previously acknowledged that the pace of frontier-model development may eventually need to be moderated. In July, the company said AI development could accelerate to a point at which the world would “need to pace the rate of AI advancement”. Yesterday, OpenAI also backed mandatory national AI safety requirements in the US, citing the possibility that advanced systems could help accelerate their own development. The latest development follows a series of incidents that have intensified scrutiny of the controls surrounding autonomous AI agents. In August, OpenAI said it paused reinforcement-learning training for some of its latest models for two weeks while strengthening its security measures. The measures followed an incident in which an OpenAI agent escaped a controlled environment, accessed the open internet, and compromised systems belonging to AI developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI subsequently introduced stronger sandboxing, tighter internet restrictions for high-risk workloads, and enhanced monitoring of potentially unsafe model behaviour. Pro Subscriptions Paused In a separate development, OpenAI has temporarily stopped accepting new subscriptions to its $200 per month Pro plan amid a surge in demand for Astra, its latest flagship AI model. Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, an OpenAI product leader responsible for products including ChatGPT and Codex, said in a post on X, “To make sure our current users have an incredible experience and continued access to Astra, we are going to pause subscriptions to our $200 Pro plan.” He added that Pro subscriptions put the greatest strain on OpenAI’s systems and that the company wanted to take the “smallest step” required to continue providing broad access to Astra. The pause will not affect existing Pro subscribers. OpenAI’s other subscription plans and its API remain available, while the company works to add more computing capacity. Launched on September 3, Astra has been rolled out across OpenAI’s Pro, Plus, Enterprise and Business plans. OpenAI described Astra as the beginning of its “AGI era” and a generational leap in AI capabilities. AI Misuse Risks Grow Meanwhile, warnings from researchers who have worked at leading AI companies have added to concerns over the pace of AI development. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, accused the companies of pursuing increasingly capable and potentially self-improving systems without adequately addressing the risks. Coxon said researchers at the companies “earnestly believe” that advanced AI could pose an existential threat, while accusing the developers of racing towards self-improving superintelligence. Separately, Anthropic’s latest threat-intelligence report, released yesterday, documented the use of its Claude models in activities ranging from cyberattacks and surveillance to fraud, biological misuse, and conventional weapons development. The report, titled ‘Detecting And Countering Misuse Of AI: September 2026’, covered malicious activities identified and disrupted by Anthropic between December 2025 and August 2026. It examined seven areas of harm – cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological misuse, conventional weapons development, and illicit model distillation. Anthropic said Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus were used in the cases covered by the report. None involved its Fable or Mythos-class models, except for one illicit distillation case. The company said it disrupted the identified activities, strengthened its safeguards using the findings, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate. According to Anthropic, AI is reducing the expertise and resources needed to carry out sophisticated cyberattacks. In several cases, attackers used AI agents to execute or coordinate tasks including reconnaissance, exploitation, malware modification, and data exfiltration. While human operators continued to select targets and review stolen information, Anthropic said AI’s role had moved beyond answering questions and increasingly involved the direct execution or orchestration of cyber operations. Together, the developments underscore the competing challenges facing AI companies: meeting surging demand for more capable models while strengthening safeguards against loss of control and malicious use.

Intensifying vaccination of dogs and ensuring that people bitten by dogs receive timely and complete rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) could save far more lives in Keralam than routine pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) vaccination of children, according to a new modelling study on the cost-effectiveness of rabies interventions.
What the study found
The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, estimates that routine childhood PrEP—vaccinating children against rabies before any animal exposure — would prevent only about 10 additional deaths over 10 years, while adding an estimated $10.5 million to $36.5 million to healthcare costs.
In contrast, comprehensive vaccination of dogs, combined with improved post-bite treatment and efforts to close gaps in PEP, could reduce rabies deaths by 83% compared to the current strategy, the study says. Scaling up vaccination of both owned and free-roaming dogs to 70% coverage could potentially bring human rabies deaths down to zero in Keralam within three years, according to the model.
The research was led by the University of Glasgow in collaboration with researchers from the Directorate of Medical Education, Kerala University of Health Sciences, the School of Public Health, the Directorates of Health and Animal Husbandry in Keralam, and the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Rabies in Keralam
Rabies prevention is already one of Keralam’s most intensive public health interventions, with more than 9,00,000 people receiving free treatment every year following animal bites. The State also has a PEP completion rate of over 90%. Yet human rabies deaths continue to occur, with 33 deaths reported in 2025, including among children.
The findings add a new dimension to the ongoing debate over whether Keralam should introduce routine PrEP for children as a rabies prevention strategy. Paediatricians and several public health experts have advocated childhood PrEP because children are particularly vulnerable to severe bites, including injuries to the face and hands, which could become fatal, despite post-exposure treatment.
The study does not rule out PrEP. Instead, it argues that PrEP may be more appropriate for specific high-risk populations who face difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities quickly after exposure, including some geographically dispersed tribal communities.
It argues that given Keralam’s relatively strong access to PEP, universal childhood PrEP may produce relatively little additional mortality reduction for the huge resources required, whereas improved dog vaccination and better wound management and timely PEP may produce greater population-level gains.
Cost effectiveness
“The study is a comparison of the cost effectiveness of PrEP against other interventions as a population-level strategy to reduce rabies. It points out that, as a public health strategy, investing in dog vaccination is more cost effective because it stops virus transmission in the community, and takes us closer to rabies elimination,” said Zinia T. Nujum of the School of Public Health, KUHS, who led the research in Kerala.
According to Martha Luka, researcher at the University of Glasgow’s School of Biodiversity, One Health & Veterinary Medicine and lead author, PrEP for children is unlikely to be the best use of public health resources in Keralam, where access to post-bite vaccination and completion of the regimen are already high.
Canines are the reservoir of the rabies virus and accounts for 70% of the rabies cases. Vaccinating the dog population interrupts transmission before people are exposed, whereas PrEP mainly protects vaccinated individuals while the wider risk remains.
The researchers modelled 12 different combinations of dog vaccination, post-bite treatment and PrEP over a 10-year period from 2026-2035. The study’s sensitivity analysis underlines the importance of improving access to PEP. Raising the proportion of bite victims who seek medical care from 70% to 95% could prevent more than 1,100 additional deaths—over 20 times the mortality reduction achievable even with maximum PrEP coverage in the model.
Vaccination of domestic dogs
The researchers also found that increasing vaccination coverage among domestic dogs alone could produce substantial health gains. “About 70-80% of dog-bite cases in the State are due to domestic dogs. Mandatory licensing and vaccination of domestic dogs, can help improve coverage. We could focus on completing domestic dog vaccination and then move on to vaccinating strays,” said Dr. Nujum.
However, she pointed out that the population of free-roaming dogs in Keralam could be at least five times the official estimate, highlighting the need for better data to plan vaccination programmes. The researchers argue that the State’s priority should therefore be a sustained One Health-based dog vaccination programme targeting at least 70% coverage, involving local bodies, Animal Husbandry and Health departments, veterinary teams, NGOs and communities.
