Madrid – Kylian Mbappe scored twice as Real Madrid enjoyed a 4-1 victory over Rayo Vallecano in LaLiga at the Santiago Bernabeu on Saturday.
Mbappe got his sixth goal of the season in the 14th minute, from a penalty, after Rayo defender Florian Lejeune fouled Alvaro Carreras in the box.
Three minutes later Carreras exchanged passes with Mbappe, after Lejeune had gifted the ball to Vinicius Junior and sent a shot into the net.
Wingers Vinicius and Yan Diomande, making his first start for Real since joining in August, found ample space to operate in and after 34 minutes the Brazilian raced down the left before picking out Jude Bellingham, just inside the box, who side-footed into the bottom corner with minimal fuss.
Mbappe hit the post late in the first half but the only danger to Real goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois’s clean sheet came from a long-range strike by Andrei Ratiu which the Belgian pushed away.
The lack of tension was evident early in the second period, with Rayo’s Pedro Diaz hitting the post. The visitors pulled a goal back after 51 minutes when, after a cheap giveaway, Sergio Camello sneaked the ball through Ibrahima Konate’s legs and into the corner of the net.
Rayo were now enjoying comfortable possession in the Real Madrid half and were keeping Courtois busy. On the Real Madrid bench, manager Jose Mourinho’s anger was mirrored by whistles from the crowd.
With 13 minutes to go, Real’s Denzel Dumfries drew a spectacular save from goalkeeper Emil Audero after connecting with substitute Arda Guler’s cross.
Real Madrid closed out the game with a second goal from Mbappe on the counter-attack in the 91st minute, moving him on to seven goals in six games in all competitions.
The result put Real Madrid on 12 points, level with leaders Barcelona who play Levante on Sunday.
Espanyol beat Osasuna 2-0 with an early brace from Roberto Fernandez, while Racing Santander came from behind to defeat in-form Alaves 2-1.
Elche went ahead at San Mames through a second-half penalty from Facundo Buonanotte, but Athletic Club captain Inaki Williams found an equalizer with 11 minutes remaining and the game finished 1-1.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Can you imagine a universe without a new 'Star Trek' on the horizon?
Ask actress Jeri Ryan about the endurance of Star Trek, and she answers with the earnestness of a truly converted fan.
"The way that Star Trek has always held a mirror up to society and always been political in a non-threatening way … it's fascinating to me. It was groundbreaking," said Ryan, who knew little about Trek when she joined Voyager in 1997 to play the character Seven of Nine.
Ryan marveled at how the original series, which debuted on NBC in 1966, featured a Russian character as the Cold War was raging in real life, alongside a Black female officer and a Japanese helmsman, sending a not-so-subtle message of what it might take to survive and thrive in the future.
"It was an optimistic view … of what we could achieve if we stop screwing it up," she added, ruefully. "If we learn to appreciate and celebrate our differences and stop being afraid of everyone who is different from us."
Star Trek officially notched its 60th birthday last week, joining a select few TV and film franchises that have survived six decades of pop culture upheaval. The original series, starring William Shatner as Capt. James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy as Mr. Spock, aired for three seasons on NBC. It gave rise to a franchise of TV shows, films, video games, novels, comic books, conventions and collectibles.
They're all centered on characters connected to Starfleet — an exploratory and peacekeeping armada co-founded in the distant future by humans, who scoot between planets in giant starships and are connected to other alien species in a United Federation of Planets.
In the streaming era, Trek has spawned seven series and a movie, including Discovery in 2017, the animated series Lower Decks in 2020 and the last two franchise TV series, both planning to wrap up their runs: Starfleet Academy and Strange New Worlds.
And that is where Star Trek's biggest challenge in many years may begin. Though an executive at Paramount+ told Deadline that the company wants to find a new iteration of Star Trek — and a new writing team is also supposedly working on a script for a new Trek movie for Paramount Pictures — there is no definitive film or TV show announced yet.
If no new Trek projects are revealed soon, next year may mark the first time in about a decade that there have been no new Star Trek TV series or movies in production.
Could it be possible that, one year after its 60th birthday, there could be an entertainment universe without new Star Trek, at least for a while?
Why Star Trek may need a break
Critics have a lot of ideas about why Trek might not be resonating with new fans, from dissatisfaction with the direction of recent series, to the limitations of Paramount+, where most new iterations of the franchise have been confined.
Akiva Goldsman, who co-created and serves as co-showrunner on Strange New Worlds, admits that some traditionalist fans may have objected to the big creative swings that the series has taken during its run, including a musical episode and an episode in which most of the crew of the Enterprise is transformed into Muppet-like puppets.
Still, he says Trek's appeal as a morality play that shifts with the times is key to its enduring appeal over decades. "[Its] about optimism, about exploration, about this notion that decency and kindness and empathy are the strengths of our culture," he said. "I think the world often isn't that. And I think we often yearn for that."
Goldsman saw firsthand how early Trek conventions in the mid-1970s pioneered the gigantic science fiction and fantasy-based fan conventions of the modern era. He keeps the program from his first convention in 1974 framed in his office, remembering how fans from across the country gathered to watch an episode screened in a theater with better color and more scenes than the TV version. "From that point on," he said, "all we wanted was more."
So why isn't there more Trek definitively on the horizon after next year? Goldsman blames the impact of streaming TV for reducing viewers' desire to see lots of seasons of one series. "Maybe people just want one or two great seasons of everything and then they move along," he said. "This relationship that we once had with entertainment, was also when there was far less entertainment."
Have changing attitudes about the future made Trek's success tougher?
But Ira Steven Behr, who was showrunner for Deep Space Nine over four seasons in the '90s, has a different point of view on Trek's challenges.
A notorious contrarian with a goatee dyed blue, Behr says Star Trek was born during a time when people believed — amid unrest over the Vietnam War, the Civil Rights Movement and assassination of President John F. Kennedy — that the world could get better through movements that brought massive change.
And, thanks to the success of the space race and moon landing, people also believed technology would be a big part of that success.
"The secret message of Trek is that technology is good and that in the [future] it will be even better and its impact on our lives will be both beneficial and benign," Behr said, rattling off gadgets from the Trek universe that fans love. "In spite of warp drive and replicators, transporters and holosuites, tricorders and tractor beams, our essential humanity will be unchanged."
These days, he added, in a world filled with divisive social media, disinformation spreading across the internet and a backlash against data centers powering artificial intelligence, few still believe the future will be better thanks to technology.
"Those two major thoughts that Star Trek kinda relies on don't make it anymore for people," Behr said. "That s*** doesn't fly."
Some professed Trek fans say the new shows are too focused on identity issues or classically liberal causes — saying it's grown too "woke." Behr noted some of those fans seemed focused on big space battles and high adventure episodes, with little patience for the smaller, emotional storylines.
"All these spaceships would explode and everyone dug it so much and no one's thinking about the hundreds of people getting killed," he added. "Now I realize there's a whole segment larger than anyone thought that would watch Trek for those explosions. They're not interested in any larger thing the show is saying."
Balancing fan expectations with the need to innovate
Relaxing in his Nashville home after completing filming of all Strange New Worlds' final episodes, star Anson Mount, who plays Capt. Christopher Pike, is feeling a bit like a favorite summer camp has ended.
Noting that Trek has been around for almost a quarter of America's lifetime, he says the show is "baked into the cake of our culture" because humans are by nature "fatalistically optimistic" in a way that the franchise highlights.
And while he also acknowledges some fans have criticized Strange New World's more ambitious episodes, Mount is convinced such experimentation was necessary to keep the franchise alive in the 21st century.
"I'd rather it be completely polarizing while doing something new and taking a risk," he said. "I think Star Trek would be dead if we delivered the midline of people's expectations … I'm not happy that people are offended; I am happy that people are having a response."
While trying hard to be diplomatic, Mount does have one criticism of the current Trek franchise: "Trek has one problem to figure out," he added. "And that is that its audience is aging and the current strategy is not bringing in a new audience. There needs to be a well-considered plan aimed at changing that."
On that score, Star Trek may suffer from timing, technology and circumstances. Fans often came to older Trek series by watching syndicated reruns on broadcast TV, catching shows like the original series or The Next Generation after school or on the weekends. They also eventually had movies, which could bring the franchise to even bigger audiences.
But the last Trek theatrical movie, Star Trek: Beyond, was released 10 years ago, which further limits access to younger fans.
The fanbase that remains has wildly different visions of what the franchise should be based on when they started watching it — even down to series structure. (For early fans, Trek was an adventure of the week — while Deep Space Nine and Discovery had more extended plotlines.)
But Jeri Ryan wonders if Trek also isn't stalled at Paramount because it might conflict with the politics of the company's latest owner, CEO David Ellison — who has faced criticism for taking action in other parts of the organization to curry favor with conservative President Donald Trump. (Ellison has denied bending news organizations under Paramount's control, including CBS News, to please Trump.)
"I have a hard time believing some of the disinterest is not political," Ryan added, noting Trek's historic devotion to diversity and inclusion. (Paramount notably eliminated its diversity, equity and inclusion programs in 2025.) "I don't think that they necessarily appreciate the message of Star Trek so much. And I don't know that [the franchise's message] fits into where they're trying to take things."
Behr remembered the last time Trek took a sizable break; when the series Enterprise was cancelled by UPN in 2005, there wasn't a new tv show or film until Abrams' Star Trek movie in 2009. He said Star Trek needed a break back then, and it might not be a bad thing for the franchise to get a break right now.
"[Back then], we were talking about sheer overkill," he added. "You know, give fans a chance to want Trek back again … Even freakin' chocolate gets old after a while if you eat too much of it."

Days after India pointed out “anomalies” in a world map that was used during the passing of the “Correct the Map” resolution at the UN General Assembly, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said, that the “UN has not published any map with borders”. In an exclusive interview with The Hindu, Mr. Guterres insisted that “it’s not for the UN to define” borders.
Earlier, The Hindu had reported that a map, created by the UN Geospatial and used during the consultation process for the ‘Correct the Map’ resolution, depicted Arunachal Pradesh and Aksai Chin without the specified Indian and Chinese “claim lines” that previous UN maps had used.
“There is no such thing as a ‘UN map with borders’. The resolution that was approved in the General Assembly is not a map. It is a resolution that says — quite correctly, I think — that there are distortions in the landmasses that correspond [to real sizes]. These come from power relations of the past. And those distortions should be corrected,” Mr. Guterres said in the interview.
ALSO WATCH Is the United Nations broken?Antonio Guterres on reforming the world body | The Hindu Exclusive
‘Contribution of NGO’
The map published by the UN Geospatial has been on the website of the UN even though the Ministry of External Affairs had said that the “anomalies” were being taken up with the United Nations. Referring to the issue, Mr. Guterres said the map on the website was “not an official UN map. It’s the contribution of an NGO”. He added: “The map is indicative, but there is no definition by the UN of what borders should be.”
India had voted in favour of the “Correct the Map” resolution passed by the UN General Assembly on September 3, which sought to replace the Mercator map, created by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator in the 1500s, with maps that follow the “equal area” principle.
Claim lines omitted
The map in question, titled the ‘Map of the World’, was published on July 1 and subsequently taken up for discussion at the UNGA. It showed the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir as a dotted line, with a separate note at the bottom of the map explaining that the “dotted line represents approximately the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir agreed upon by India and Pakistan. The final status of Jammu and Kashmir has not yet been agreed upon by the parties.” However, there is no note explaining why the map did not include any similar explanation for omitting Indian and Chinese claim lines in Arunachal Pradesh and Aksai Chin.
Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal explained on September 8 that India’s vote for the resolution was in support of the underlying principle of “equal area representation”.
“The United Nations does not endorse any map. The United Nations doesn’t issue any map. There may be maps for reasons of consultation, etc,” Mr. Jaiswal said. Regarding the absence of Indian and Chinese claim lines in the map, he said, “We have taken note of the anomaly and we are taking it up with the United Nations.”

September is typically the time when television gets serious again. The summer’s biggest TV shows have aired their finales, the fall schedule is kicking into high gear, and streamers are rolling out everything from high-concept sci-fi to prestige dramas. There’s plenty of familiar IP in the mix, but also some genuinely original shows worth putting on your “to watch” list.
While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Reacher), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.
From returning favorites to ambitious new series—and at least one show that might rekindle your love of traditional anime—these are the TV shows we think you should make time to stream this month.
The Paper
What happens when a newspaper attempts to not just survive, but thrive, in a world where digital media has become the norm? The Paper, a spinoff of The Office from Greg Daniels and Michael Koman, follows the staff of a struggling Midwestern paper as they attempt to revive it.
Ultimately, its idealistic new editor-in-chief Ned Sampson (Star Wars and Harry Potter alum Domhnall Gleeson) and his hungry young reporter Mare Pritti (Chelsea Frei) end up grappling with what journalism looks like in the digital age. Season 2, which arrived on September 9, finds their Toledo Truth Teller newly revitalized and searching for its next big scoop, making the show a surprisingly sharp comedy about the future of journalism—and who gets to shape it.
Lego Star Wars: The Mandalorian
Though this summer’s The Mandalorian and Grogu (which is streaming on Disney+ now) seriously underperformed at the box office, Lucasfilm is partnering with Lego to take another stab at the fan-favorite Star Wars series—which might be exactly what the franchise needs right now. Lucasfilm and Lego are going back to the beginning, reimagining all three seasons of the Pedro Pascal-starring live-action series as a 49-minute animated comedy.
For anyone who somehow managed to miss Mando and Grogu until now, the story follows Din Djarin (Pascal in the live-action series, Gavin Hammon in this iteration), a bounty hunter known as the Mandalorian, who takes a job transporting a mysterious Force-sensitive child. That child, of course, is Grogu, aka Baby Yoda. What starts as a simple assignment turns into a galaxy-spanning adventure as the pair become unlikely partners. Consider this version an entertaining way to play catch-up.
South Park
It’s hard to remember a time when the world didn’t have South Park. For nearly 30 years, audiences have watched as four potty-mouthed fourth-graders—Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny—navigate life in the bizarre mountain town of South Park, Colorado, in this very much adults-only animated comedy. Along the way, they’ve encountered alien life forms, celebrities, and Elon Musk (yes, the real one). They’ve also watched Kenny die on at least 100 occasions.
Last year, the seemingly never-ending comedy reinvented itself as a particularly pointed political satire by taking aim at figures including JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem, Donald Trump, and Donald Trump’s manhood. The White House, unsurprisingly, had thoughts. And so did the Emmys; the show just took home the 2026 award for Outstanding Animated Program. Clearly, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have no plans to take their foot off the gas; they just announced they’re taking a page out of Trump’s renaming book and rechristening the show South America for its 29th season, which premieres on September 16.
Slow Horses
What if television’s best spy show was also one of its funniest? If John le Carré and (the original) The Office had a baby, it would look and sound a lot like Slow Horses, which returns for a sixth season on September 16.
Based on Mick Herron’s Slough House book series, the series follows a dysfunctional team of MI5 misfits who are banished to the infamous Slough House unit, where they work under the notorious Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), a foul-mouthed, flatulent, chain-smoking wreck of a man who also happens to be the most brilliant operative in the room. It’s a prestige spy thriller that doesn’t take itself too seriously, bouncing effortlessly between shoot-outs and the kind of droll office banter you’d expect from the best workplace comedies. In a career full of memorable performances, and an Oscar to show for it, Slow Horses just might be the role Oldman is best remembered for. It’s also the project that has made Jack Lowden oddsmakers’ top pick for the next James Bond.
City of Blood
In City of Blood, an eight-episode miniseries from Germany, climate change has turned Berlin into a sweltering city teetering on the edge of collapse—and vampires are ready to take advantage of the chaos. While the privileged few live beneath a climate-controlled dome, the rest of the city’s denizens are left to battle the heat, crime, and corruption that have become part of everyday life. But when estranged sisters Bea (Lea Drinda) and Phoebe (Soma Pysall) reunite, they uncover a nefarious political plot and learn that, thanks to that aforementioned undead population, blood has become the city’s most coveted commodity. It’s a perfectly strange mix of climate dystopia, family drama, and vampire thriller. And it arrives on September 16.
MobLand
Season 2 of MobLand is almost here—whether Tom Hardy likes it or not. (Despite all the recent headlines surrounding the Oscar winner’s behind-the-scenes drama, he has already signed on for Season 3.) The highly underrated, or perhaps just underseen, crime drama returns with the Harrigan family’s criminal empire under threat from rival forces, forcing their street-smart fixer Harry Da Souza (yep, Hardy) to navigate increasingly bloody internal tensions.
As Harry works to keep the fractured family from tearing itself apart, he’s aided by his trusty sidekick Zosia (Jasmine Jobson), a tech specialist who brings a distinctly 21st-century skill set to their old-school criminal enterprise headed up by Conrad (Pierce Brosnan) and Maeve Harrington (Helen Mirren). Meanwhile, rival forces close in, loyalties shift, and violence spreads through every corner of the family’s world. Expect more bloodshed, shifting allegiances, poor decisions, and one of television’s most kickass theme songs (Fontaines D.C.’s “Starburster”) when Season 2 premieres on September 18.
Outlander: Blood of My Blood
Before there was Jamie and Claire, there were their parents. Like its predecessor, this Outlander prequel follows two separate timelines as it details the courtship of Jamie Fraser’s parents, Brian Fraser (Jamie Roy) and Ellen MacKenzie (Harriet Slater), in 18th-century Scotland, alongside the story of Claire Beauchamp’s parents, Henry Beauchamp (Jeremy Irvine) and Julia Moriston (Hermione Corfield), in World War I-era England. Their two love stories unfold across different time periods, weaving together romance, family drama, and the time-traveling forces that kept Outlander fans enthralled for eight seasons. The series’ second season arrives on September 18.
American Horror Story
Season 13 of Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk’s horror anthology is shaping up to be what has at various points called an Avengers-esque “endgame-level event” of “greatest hits.” While the details, as always, have been kept rather quiet, what we do know is that the new season of American Horror Story will pull bits and pieces from each season of the series, with a heavy emphasis on its witchcraft-laden “Coven” and “Apocalypse” storylines.
We also know it is reassembling an all-star cast of past stars, some of whom will play double—or even triple—character duty. Among them: Murphy mainstays Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Jessica Lange, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, and Angela Bassett. The new season arrives on September 26, which gives you plenty of time to brush up on your AHS lore.
Neon Genesis Evangelion
Before Netflix gave it a new English dub—and, depending on who you ask, stirred up a lot of feelings—there was the original Japanese-language version of Neon Genesis Evangelion. The landmark anime, released in 1995, follows a group of teenagers recruited to pilot giant biomechanical weapons called Evangelions, or Evas, as they defend a post-apocalyptic Tokyo (now known as Tokyo-3) from mysterious creatures, aka Angels. But what starts as a fairly straightforward battle-for-humanity story soon becomes something far stranger, delving into trauma, loneliness, identity, and human connection.
The Criterion Channel is bringing all 26 episodes of the classic (pre-Netflix) English dub to streaming for the first time, alongside the original Japanese-language version for all you purists. It’s a fitting return for one of anime’s most boundary-pushing series.

New Delhi, Sep 13: Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Sunday that increasing geopolitical tensions are adversely impacting ordinary lives globally, emphasising that BRICS must unite to address these challenges and drive inclusive growth, particularly across the Global South.
In an address at the BRICS summit, the prime minister also flagged serious concerns over the "weaponisation of technology and critical minerals", saying it could hinder shared progress and prosperity.
Modi made the remarks in presence of top leaders of the grouping, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
"Under India's presidency, we have focused our efforts on four pillars: resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability. I am pleased that, with your cooperation and support, we have been able to transform our shared vision into a win-win situation," the prime minister said.
Modi also touched upon rising geopolitical tensions and their impact on the lives of common people across the world. The world is witnessing increasing tensions and they having a significant negative impact on the lives of ordinary people. Pandemics, climate disasters, and supply chain disruptions have demonstrated that in today's interconnected world, no crisis remains confined to a single region," Modi said. "Therefore, we have placed special emphasis on enhancing resilience within the BRICS group. It is equally essential to identify challenges in a timely manner, remain prepared for them and take immediate action," he said.
"With this approach, a consensus has been reached on a BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for the prevention of and response to infectious diseases," he said. Modi said guidelines for an early warning data integration mechanism have also been formulated.
The BRICS logistic supply chain cooperation framework will help make our supply chains more reliable and resilient, he said.
Under the framework of innovation, the BRICS incubator network will connect our startups and incubators, he said.
The prime minister said the BRICS must work together to address challenges facing the Global South. The Global South's confidence in BRICS has increased, he said.

Trump Will Never Mail the $5,000 Checks
Deconstructing a policy proposal that makes no sense on any level
Donald Trump’s new promise to give a $5,000 check to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the midterm elections may be an effort to answer a variant of an age-old riddle: Can Trump devise a policy so ill-conceived that even Trump’s intelligence is insulted?
Candidates often make inducements part of their campaign pitch. One obvious peculiarity of this plan is that Trump’s party already controls both chambers of Congress. Why, then, should the bonus checks be contingent on voters giving Republicans another two-year majority?
Trump has told reporters that he could distribute the loot without congressional approval. This is untrue. (It’s a facially unconstitutional infringement of Congress’s spending authority.) If it were true, however, it would make his decision to hinge the checks on the election’s outcome even more mysterious. If the choice were his alone, the outcome would seem totally irrelevant.
Under certain economic circumstances, distributing checks to everybody can make sense. In a deeply depressed economy, in which consumer spending is too low to maintain high employment levels, juicing it with a cash infusion can help keep it alive.
However, current circumstances are quite different. Unemployment is low and growth is healthy. The problem is that inflation is running well above target levels. Injecting roughly $1.2 trillion (the one-year cost of the checks) into the economy would likely make inflation worse—more cash would be chasing the same number of goods and services, driving up their price. This, in turn, would probably force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to tamp down inflation, which would throw recovery into jeopardy.
J. D. Vance has suggested that the checks could be paid for with tariff revenue. In theory, that would offset the inflationary effect of the new spending. But the tariffs are already in place, meaning that he’s citing a current revenue source to fund a new cost—at a moment when revenue is nowhere near sufficient: The U.S. government is running a deficit of nearly $1.8 trillion.
Trump, for his part, explained to reporters that he intends the checks not as an economic policy but as a treat: “I’m doing it as a reward for people having to put up for five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden … It’s almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden’s policy.”
When Trump ran in 2024 against Joe Biden’s policies, the “reward” was supposed to be having Trump and his policies in place. Now he seems to be suggesting that Trump’s incredible economy is not enough. This explanation is also impossible to square with his claim that the bonus would be contingent on Republicans winning the midterms. Why do Americans deserve a retroactive bonus for living in Biden’s America only if Republicans win the midterm elections? By Trump’s logic, if we were forced to endure two years of Democrats sharing power, that would make us more, not less, deserving of compensation.
The pretense that these checks have any economic logic has proved too great to bear for at least some Republicans. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis dissented mildly, causing Trump’s advisers to heap them with ridicule. “Ron and Ted—the co-captains of your old high school Math-Lete Team—will nerd out on this while jockeying for 11th place in ’28,” a senior adviser to the White House told Politico Playbook.
In a normal administration, These guys understand high-school-level math is a credential, albeit a minimal one, to opine on economic policy. Only in the Trump era can it be presented as a disqualification.
The actual defense of the policy, obviously, is that it’s never going to happen. Last February, Elon Musk floated a DOGE dividend (which never arrived, in part because DOGE never produced meaningful savings). That year, Trump repeatedly promised tariff-rebate checks, which also never happened.
The Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked Trump why he doesn’t simply send the checks out now. He replied, “Because the Democrats can’t do it. Because for them, it’s negative growth. With us, it’s so positive.” What does this answer mean? Does it mean anything at all? Does Trump even believe it has any meaning, other than constituting a string of sentence fragments conveying the general sentiment Democrats bad; me good?
The actual divide within the party pits the Republicans who think that their voters are dumb enough to fall yet again for Trump’s free-money promise against those who suspect that the ruse has worn thin. Trump has spent his career betting against the intelligence of the American voter. The $5,000-check promise may be the moment he finally underestimated his audience.

Yoga and Ayurveda have moved beyond their traditional wellness identity and are increasingly becoming part of India’s global health and diplomatic strategy, with the Centre seeking to expand their footprint through medical tourism, international education, practitioner mobility and trade agreements.
The shift is particularly evident in India’s recent trade diplomacy. The India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), operationalised in June 2026, and the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) contain dedicated provisions on health-related services and traditional medicine. These include measures to ease licensing, develop standards and facilitate the mobility of AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors.
The India-European Union (EU) FTA, signed in January 2026, goes further, allowing AYUSH practitioners to use their Indian qualifications in EU countries where no regulatory framework exists and providing for AYUSH wellness centres and clinics.
Also Read | India partners with WHO to mainstream Ayush globally through agreement on traditional medicine interventions
The agreements represent an attempt to transform AYUSH from being a cultural export to a formalised health and services opportunity.
The India-Oman CEPA contains what the government describes as its first comprehensive commitment on traditional medicine across all modes of supply, while the India-New Zealand FTA has a dedicated ‘health and traditional medicine’ annex covering Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy.
The New Zealand agreement also provides structured mobility pathways, including a dedicated visa quota for AYUSH practitioners and Yoga instructors. The government said the agreement would institutionalise cooperation in education, training, standards development and wellness services.
Comment | The growing relevance of traditional medicine
Need to convert market access to demand
However, the diplomatic push also raises questions about how far formal recognition and market access will translate into actual international demand.
Experts point to the need for credible standards, evidence, regulation, practitioner quality and patient safety if AYUSH is to establish itself in increasingly regulated global healthcare markets.
Senior officials in the Ministry of Ayush said the Ayush visa, overseas training and exchange programmes were also helping expand the sector.
“Foreign medical arrivals rose from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.44 lakh in 2024, as per our data. Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Germany, Russia, Malaysia, Mauritius and Saudi Arabia are among the important markets for AYUSH and Ayurveda treatment. The government does not publish a current consolidated country-wise ranking of AYUSH patients,” an official from the AYUSH Ministry said.
However, the figure of 6.44 lakh refers to overall foreign medical arrivals and not specifically AYUSH patients. The absence of consolidated data makes it difficult to assess AYUSH’s actual share of India’s medical-value-travel market.
The Ayush visa, introduced in 2023, is another component of the strategy. Between January 2023 and December 2025, a total of 3,375 foreign nationals travelled to India on Ayush visas or e-Ayush visas, while another 579 travelled on Ayush attendant visas or e-Ayush attendant visas. Earlier, the Ministry had reported that 1,646 Ayush visas had been issued to nationals of 75 countries between January 2024 and February 2025.
Education is also emerging as another channel of influence. Under the Ayush Fellowship Scheme, 260 students from 32 countries were studying AYUSH in Indian institutions.
The Ministry’s international cooperation programmes also support training, seminars, conferences and knowledge exchange, including Yoga teaching and education overseas.

The rock guitarist whose killing shocked India's north-east
- Published
When Chongtham Vikram Singh finally came home to India's north-eastern state of Manipur, his old friend Dhiren Sadokpam went to the airport to receive him.
It was not the homecoming he had imagined. Vikram arrived in the cargo hold, inside a steel container.
Three days earlier, the 54-year-old musician had been beaten to death outside his home in south-east Delhi.
"Nobody seemed to have the strength to speak," Sadokpam told the BBC. "What could be said?"
Vikram had spent much of his life travelling with his guitars, carrying his music from small stages in Manipur's capital, Imphal, to jazz clubs, classrooms and concert halls in Delhi.
According to police and his family, he had gone downstairs late on Sunday night after a group of men were shouting and drinking outside his apartment building. When he objected to the disturbance, the men allegedly attacked him.
His wife, Joshna Chongtham, said Vikram returned upstairs but was pursued and assaulted outside the family's apartment.
Hours later, after complaining of breathlessness, he was taken to hospital by his 20-year-old son. He died there early in the morning.
Seven men and a juvenile have been arrested in connection with his killing. Police say they are investigating the circumstances of the attack.
The death has prompted an outpouring of grief and anger, and renewed concerns about the discrimination faced by people from India's north-east in Delhi, where members of the community have for years reported racial abuse, harassment and violence.
Police say they have so far found no evidence of a racial motive. But north-eastern groups have held protests and demanded an impartial investigation.
The case has also drawn attention to Vikram himself - a familiar figure in Manipur's music scene who, over four decades of playing and teaching, gathered around him a large circle of students, friends and admirers.
At a press conference two days after his death, his wife Joshna said: "We are not seeking revenge. We are seeking justice. He had a name, a family and a life that mattered."
For most of his 54 years, that life had revolved around music.
Vikram grew up around it. His mother, Chongtham Kamala, was a celebrated singer who lent her voice to Matamgi Manipur, the first feature film made in the Manipuri language.
As a boy, he accompanied her to All India Radio for recordings. Before long, he had auditioned there himself and become a child artist, playing the accordion.
There is an old black-and-white photograph of Vikram from those years. He is kneeling stiffly in front of a microphone with an accordion balanced across his lap. Beside him, another boy sits behind a pair of drums. Both wear the grave expressions of children who have been told that a photograph is being taken.
The boy with the accordion would soon discover guitars - first Hawaiian and Spanish, then electric - and, somewhere along the way, acquire thick black glasses and a splendid moustache.
By the mid-1980s, Imphal had become an unlikely outpost of rock music. The sound travelled there largely on cassette tapes, bringing with it the hard rock and heavy metal being played thousands of miles away.
Young men formed bands and crowded into local halls, working with whatever they could find - modest sound systems, locally made amplifiers, guitars turned up as loud as they would go. They listened, copied, experimented.
Vikram was studying at Don Bosco School then and still playing accordion and Hawaiian guitar. Years later, he remembered how he and his friends would ask the priests for permission to leave school to watch a local band perform.
"Those were sweet and innocent days that actually inspired me to go for rock," he recalled in a 2014 interview, external.
Soon, watching was no longer enough. Vikram took up the electric guitar and began playing in bands himself - first Ultra Vires, then Phoenix and Eastern Dark - becoming part of the generation that was giving Imphal's new rock scene a sound of its own.
It was around this time, in 1987, that Dhiren Sadokpam first met him.
They were setting off from Imphal to study in Shillong, and Sadokpam remembers them waiting at a temporary interstate bus terminal with backpacks, steel luggage boxes and bedding for the long journey.
Vikram was boyish and energetic, he recalls, but mostly kept to himself.
"He would spend long hours in his room, mastering each and every composition that came his way," Sadokpam said.
With each band, Vikram's playing evolved. Ultra Vires became a place to experiment. Phoenix, which would become one of the defining bands of Manipur's early rock scene, brought greater precision and a devoted following that endured long after its heyday.
By the time he joined Eastern Dark, Sadokpam remembers the quiet young man disappearing into the instrument, making its six strings "cry and sing".
In the early 1990s, he spent two years in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where he encountered musicians at the Calcutta School of Music, a century-old institution with a strong tradition of Western classical music, and was drawn more deeply into jazz and classical music. His own playing began to range across styles, from rock and blues to jazz and fusion.
By the 2000s, Vikram had moved to Delhi, where he built a life around performing and teaching music.
In 2010, he reconnected with an old musician friend and formed Fubar Ghetto. The band played jazz, blues, rock and fusion, with improvisation at the centre of it. Their first performance was a charity concert near the Yamuna river.
From there, they worked their way through Delhi's live-music circuit: universities, clubs and cultural festivals, the National School of Drama and, on one occasion, the Czech Embassy.
Vikram never became a major star. Instead, he built the quieter reputation of a working musician - among the people he played with, the students he taught and the musicians he helped along the way.
Since his killing, many of those people have remembered the man who was gentle, generous and largely uninterested in recognition.
Former student guitarist Sachidananda Angom remembered him as "always kind, helpful" and someone who "could really light up a room".
Mame Khan, the Rajasthani folk singer with whom Vikram performed for several years, told The Indian Express, external that Vikram was "a really kind and lovely person" who never picked arguments with anyone.
Sadokpam is careful not to make more of their friendship than it was.
They had met as young men in 1987, lost touch for two decades and found each other again in middle age. In between, Sadokpam followed Vikram's musical life from a distance, as a fan and a friend.
They last met in Delhi in 2019, when Vikram invited him home for dinner.
"Vikram picked up his guitar and played and spoke excitedly about his students," he recalled.
When it was time to leave, Vikram asked him to come again soon. Sadokpam said he promised he would.
"I never made it back."

One problem with Android Auto can be fixed with a simple update
Your phone isn't the only device that may need an update when Android Auto starts acting up.
There are many reasons why Android Auto may stop connecting, and the initial fixes typically focus on the phone and connection. You inspect the cable, restart the device, forget the car, reconnect it and make sure Android Auto is up to date. If all that fails, however, the software that requires attention might be in the dashboard.
Your car's infotainment system also has software, and if it's out of date, it can cause Android Auto connection problems. Google advises users to restart the infotainment system and, if the receiver is an aftermarket Pioneer or Kenwood unit, to visit the manufacturer's website and check for a firmware update.
Android Auto relies on the phone and car working correctly, and if you just focus on the phone, you may be missing half the equation. If none of the above has worked, including changing cables, reconnecting the phone or restarting the phone, then the car's software is another area to consider.
Your car might need an update as well
Automakers have been sending out infotainment updates that can improve Android Auto, and Hyundai's February 2026 infotainment update for ccNC-equipped cars in Europe included improved wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay connectivity, quicker reconnection if the phone goes unresponsive and automatic restoration after a restart. Chevrolet makes the point more directly: on applicable vehicles, it lists updating both the phone and vehicle software as the first troubleshooting step when Android Auto won't connect.
How you install an update depends on the car. Some systems can download software via Wi-Fi, while others use a USB drive or SD card, and some manufacturers also offer dealer assistance. For example, Uconnect allows supported systems to be connected to Wi-Fi via the vehicle's settings menu.
Therefore, there is no universal button for updating infotainment firmware. Start at your car manufacturer's website and follow the directions for that infotainment system. If the site asks for your VIN or model details, provide them. If the process is not clear (or the manufacturer states that it must be installed by a dealer), a dealer is the safer route than getting an update file from elsewhere.
A firmware update won't fix every Android Auto problem
If Android Auto stopped working right after a phone or Android Auto update, check Google's Android Auto Known Issues page before changing the car's software. Google recently addressed connection problems affecting Pixel 10 and Samsung S26 phones and was still investigating an S25 connection issue. That timing can help you decide which side of the connection deserves attention first.
If Android Auto has stopped working right after a phone or Android Auto update, begin there before making any changes in the car. Google advises users to verify that the car is compatible, check that Android Auto is turned on in the infotainment system and test the USB connection. For wired Android Auto, its current guidance is to use a quality cable that is under 3 feet long.
Updating the car is a troubleshooting measure and not a magic bullet. If Android Auto was working before, the standard phone-side troubleshooting has failed and newer infotainment software is available, an update is one more thing to check off before scheduling a service appointment.
Firmware is not without its restrictions. It's not always able to add Android Auto to hardware that didn't support it to begin with. Uconnect says its systems can't simply be upgraded to add Android Auto or CarPlay, while Uconnect 5 and select Uconnect 4 and 4C systems include both.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jordan Karp, 30, founder and CEO of Jordan Karp LLC, a real estate brokerage in South Florida. Karp started his own brokerage at 26 years old and has nearly reached $1 billion in transaction volume. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
I started my business at the beginning of 2023.
Before, I was working on investing for my family and creating a portfolio of acquiring diverse assets from 2020 to 2022.
I was cold-calling for properties to acquire, invest, assemble, buy, lease, and manage across all asset classes. I was doing it for industrial, commercial, retail, residential, single-family, development sites, creative, and opportunistic multidimensional strategic assets across Florida.
I was brokering deals for myself on the side where I saw value in the market, and did that until the end of 2022. Then I started my business full-time.
My transaction volume is about $500 million from January until now, and about $1 billion lifetime.
I love my job because no day is the same. Here's a glimpse at what my workdays look like.
I catch up with clients on restaurant rooftops, boats, and the padel court
I have all different types of clients. I have celebrity clients and I also have private equity clients. I have clients who've sold businesses, CEOs, people in private businesses, founders, chairmen of businesses, lawyers, managers.
One of my clients and close friends, Austin Rosen, manages Post Malone, and he has a private restaurant rooftop at the Electric Feel Studios in Miami, where I'll usually have client meetings, dinners, and spend a lot of time.
I work with a lot of music artists, managers, and people in the music industry, and we'll meet at Feel. I'm very dynamic, and I'm very adaptive to where I meet clients.
It's definitely important to meet people in person, whether it be at the office, on the padel court, in the street, or at a certain property.
I usually work with a boat or yacht company, and they service me whenever I have a client in town to look at different properties on the water.
If the client is not familiar with Miami or Florida as a whole, I'll take them by boat or a yacht.
We'll start at the southernmost point of Miami and go all the way to Bal Harbour, the northernmost part. I'll give them a full education and information about the market, what properties trade for, the price per foot, the trends of where things are going, and they can see the level of houses.
I'm available to my clients whenever they need me — even at 3 a.m.
There's no difference to me between 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. — my phone is going off all day.
I've taken calls at all hours of the night; I've done 2 a.m., I've done 3 a.m.
When I was selling the SLS Brickell Hotel for $55 million in 2023, I was selling that for the Royal Family of Qatar, and they were based in London.
I represented the seller, and I also represented the buyer, which was a private Albanian group, Kastrati Group. They were in Albania and traveling through Eastern Europe, and the main office for the Royal Family of Qatar was in London. So I was up all hours of the night.
They would call me at 4 a.m., 3 a.m., and 2 a.m. They would send me documents. I'd have to get on calls with them; they were in the same time zone as each other, or slightly different ones, but a closer time zone than where I was.
My work-life balance is work, work, work. My work and my life, and the balance of working within my life, are vertically integrated.
I live to work. I don't work to live.
For me, this is fun. It's not work.
Sometimes, my days run into a workout right after, and I'll take the adrenaline or the rush of work into it.
I'll go on a run from where I live on North Bay Road up through to Allison Island, to La Gorce Island. Sometimes I'll run from North Bay Road down through Sunset Island, to Venetian Islands, to downtown Miami, and I'll run the properties I usually sell.
I get a running perspective when I'm running by them and see, "Oh, that's an address I should keep in mind." Then I'll be taking calls for work while I'm doing that. So I'll be fielding different properties, but also fielding calls and working on the progression of that all at the same time while running those routes of the neighborhoods.
Sometimes the important call comes in the middle of that time or when you're outreaching to a client, and they're busy, and the worst time for you is the best time for them. You have to take that call in that moment and bring three different people who have three different time schedules together.
You're in the middle of your workout. But what you do doesn't really matter compared to what the greater goal is.
Then, from the workout, I'll shower, and it'll be 10 o'clock at night, and then I'll decompress from 11 p.m. to 12 a.m. and be on my phone and still be available for calls, and look at calls that I missed while I was in the shower.
I have no shame and still door-knock
Door-knocking goes exactly how you could imagine. It's uncomfortable, but I think where there's discomfort, there's growth.
If you come with value and you come with service and you come with persistence, I think there's a level of appreciation and acknowledgment that you went out of your way and are expensing the time to generate value and bring something to the table.
People have an appreciation and acknowledgment for that, especially people on the other side, who live or have built these types of homes and have this type of net worth. They were likely, at some point, at this stage in their life, so they can relate to you in a sense; there's a connection that sometimes gets built in that way.
I want to door-knock on as many homes as possible, so I'm not looking at the percentage of acceptance, but rather at the volume of business that I get from playing the numbers game.
If you call 200 people and you get 10 people to respond, you're busy. One hundred ninety people are rejecting you, but the 10 people will keep you busy. And if you call 500 people and you get 20 people, you're a little bit more successful.
I actually take rejection well, meaning I can handle rejection and I can continue to persist and work on that opportunity. I know there's the long term and there's a long game, and the opportunity can always be around the corner, and you just have to keep chipping away.
I'm relentless, I'm fearless, and I have no shame — that's my business model.
Life is very short, and at the end of the day, people want to see results.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler says Yankuba Minteh could still "fulfil his dream" move in the future after the club rejected Liverpool's offers in the transfer window.
The Reds had bids of £50m and £60m turned down for the winger, with Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola having wanted to bolster his attacking options.
It is understood Brighton were seeking closer to £70m for the 22‑year‑old Gambia international.
Minteh, who joined from Newcastle for £30m in 2024, plays primarily on the right and has scored 10 goals and supplied nine assists in 73 Seagulls appearances.

When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.
It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.
“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.
Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.
The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.
“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.
“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.
Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.
In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.
Despite these pushes, Udogaranya wanted to make natural hair creation easier and more user-friendly. “After doing some research, and looking at all of the hair tools that are available still to this day, Black hair has just been accommodated in tools that are primarily created for straight hair.”
Udogaranya came across the scholarly paper Curly-Cue: Geometric Methods for Highly Coiled Hair. Published in 2024, it presented new coding techniques to improve both the look and movement of Black hair in 3D animation. With this insight, Udogaranya coded a plug-in for Blender—the free, open-source 3D creation app she normally uses to make custom content.
The Loc & Kinky Strand Generator Tool allows fellow custom content creators to make textured styles that normally could take weeks in under an hour. In just a few clicks, a user can switch from a curl to a coil to a loc. Udogaranya trained her own local AI to assist with automating the processes she did by hand and to fine-tune the code, but no generative AI was used. To use the tool, creators still have to design by hand and can’t type in prompts to generate their styles.
“The whole point of [the Loc & Kinky Strand Generator] tool is that when you do go to draw a strand or apply the actual modifier to a strand, it immediately gives you that kink,” Udogaranya says.
Though the life-sim gaming industry has struggled with diversity, there have been efforts for improvement—in some cases, thanks to Udogaranya herself. In addition to making custom content, she has also served as a gaming consultant for The Sims 4, Life by You, and Love Island: The Game. For other IPs, such as Paralives, Udogaranya notes that there is a shift in interest for Black hair inclusion. Because of this, Udogaranya hopes to eventually make the Blender add-on an independent app and create a licensable version. She tells WIRED that there has been interest from creators for games like Paralives, Roblox, and Second Life, as well as from game developers like Triple-A studios.
The tool is still under development but has been undergoing beta testing. Udogaranya says the test feedback has been “overwhelmingly positive.” Elements of the tool are also patent-pending.
Udogaranya hopes her tool will help eliminate the time, effort, and monetary barriers both content creators and game developers have when it comes to Black hair representation in games. “There’s limitations on the exploration of your identity and self-love and self-worth when the tools that you need are genuinely just missing,” she says. “ I'm ready to get rid of all of that and provide the absolute basic identity identifiers when it comes to games and animation.”
