ESDS Software Solution extended its post-listing surge into a sixth consecutive trading session today, with its shares touching the upper circuit once again and climbing to more than four times their IPO price. The rally underscores strong investor appetite for the enterprise cloud and AI infrastructure play. Shares of the enterprise cloud and AI company jumped 10% to touch an intraday high of ₹1,740.40 on the NSE. However, the stock subsequently pared some of its gains and was trading 9.7% higher at ₹1,735 as of 14:00 IST. At its intraday high, ESDS was trading 305.7% above its IPO issue price of ₹429 per share. On the BSE, ESDS shares remained locked at the 10% upper circuit of ₹1,716.35. At this price, the stock was up 300.1% from the issue price, while the company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹20,117.5 Cr (about $xx Bn). ESDS made its stock market debut on September 4, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over its issue price. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹746.30, nearly 74% above the issue price. The stock subsequently hit its 20% upper circuit at ₹908.40 on the NSE and ₹895.55 on the BSE on the listing day. It has continued to hit its upper circuit in every trading session since then. After being locked at the 20% upper circuit for three consecutive sessions, the stock’s circuit filter was reduced to 10%. The rally has also drawn regulatory scrutiny. The BSE sought a clarification from ESDS earlier this week over the sharp movement in its share price. The company said it was unaware of any undisclosed information that could explain the surge. “The company is not aware of any specific reason for the significant movement in the price of its security,” ESDS said, adding that the movement in its share price and trading volumes was consistent with the activity typically observed in a newly listed security. ESDS’ ₹720 Cr IPO, comprising entirely a fresh issue of shares, was subscribed 135.88X during its three-day bidding period. Ahead of the IPO, ESDS raised ₹216 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 50.3 Lakh shares to 19 entities at ₹429 apiece. The anchor investors included Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Bandhan Mutual Fund, Quant Mutual Fund, ITI Mutual Fund, and JM Flexicap Fund, among others. Founded in 2005, Nashik-based ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. The company plans to deploy ₹576 Cr from the net IPO proceeds towards purchasing and installing cloud computing equipment and other infrastructure at its data centres in Airoli, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Nashik. A portion of the proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. On the financial front, ESDS’ consolidated net profit more than doubled to ₹120.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue increased 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

2 killed, 12 injured in multi-vehicle crash on Pune-Bengaluru highway
Two people were killed and 12 injured, three seriously, after an Ashok Leyland truck hit an Eicher truck on the Pune-Bengaluru highway.
Two people were killed and 12 others injured in a multi-vehicle accident on the Pune-Bengaluru highway near Jambhulwadi in Maharashtra’s Pune district early Sunday morning, police said.
The deceased were identified as Hridaynath Mohan Gaikwad (47), a resident of Jogeshwari East in Mumbai, and Anandibai Ramchandra Wadkar (50), a resident of Sector 10 in Nerul. Both died while undergoing treatment.
Senior police inspector at the Ambegaon police station Sharad Zine said the accident took place at 12.10am in front of Laxmi Lodge near Dari Pool. An Ashok Leyland truck travelling from Satara towards Pune allegedly rammed into the rear of an Eicher truck.
“The impact caused both vehicles to veer into the opposite lane, where they collided with a Maruti Suzuki Ertiga and a Tata Altroz travelling towards Satara. The Eicher truck, Ertiga and Altroz were severely damaged,” Zine said.
Police said several occupants sustained serious injuries and were shifted to Bharati Hospital, Morya Hospital, Silver Birch Hospital and Shreyas Hospital. Twelve people were injured in the accident, three of whom are reported to be in serious condition.
Police cleared the accident site and restored traffic movement. A case was registered at Ambegaon police station under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Motor Vehicles Act.
The truck owner, Sandeep Gorakh Suryawanshi (45) from Khatav, was taken into custody, police said. Teams have been formed to arrest the truck driver, Pramod Vitthal Wagh (40), a resident of Khatav taluka in Satara district.
Further investigation is being carried out by a team from the Ambegaon police station.

Trump Loses the Other Strait
The Houthi advance is bad news for the U.S., and even worse news for Saudi Arabia.
As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor. The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes. The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms.
Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise. His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day.
It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side. The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.”
The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported.) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided. The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised.
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia. For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border. Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces. A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle.
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making. The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere. In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties. The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates.
“There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me.
The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me.
The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.”
With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located. They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east. All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons.
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either. The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran.
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for. And the Houthis do not need to win every battle. As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

- The claim that attendees of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, caused an outage of popular gay dating app Grindr circulated online in September 2026.
- The rumor stems from incident reports shared on social media, taken from a third-party service called Downdetector during the time of the event. However, the incidents were not isolated to Dallas, and Grindr itself did not report any major outages connected to the event.

With high-stakes midterms looming in November 2026, the Republican National Convention took place in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026. Rumors spread that the convention's attendees were causing an outage of the popular gay dating app Grindr.
People on social media sites shared a purported screenshot that showed a map depicting hotspots of Grindr outages across the country, with the brightest spot focused on Dallas.
The popularity of the rumor led many Snopes readers to reach out via email and social media, asking if the claim was true.
We weren't able to independently verify claims of Grindr outages in Dallas, so we've left this claim unrated. The screenshots appeared to be taken from Downdetector, a third-party service that tracks outages of popular services, and did not show signs of fabrication or misleading editing.
According to Downdetector, users did report incidents at the time and location in question, but the incidents reported on Sept. 9 and 10 were not limited to Dallas or even Texas. There was also no way to confirm that the reports reflected real issues with the app, as Downdetector does not require users to submit any proof.
Grindr itself did not report any outages during that time.
A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes via email: "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page."
The company's status page showed no outages or incidents in August or September 2026.
Downdetector tracks data for the prior 24 hours and does not archive its history.
Snopes first checked Downdetector's page for Grindr on Sept. 10, 2026. It showed a spike of reported outages on Sept. 9 around 8:49 p.m., with the highest number of reports clocked at 460.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
When we checked Downdetector on Sept. 11, the past 24 hours showed a peak of only 73 reports around 3:18 p.m. on Sept. 10.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector)
The incident heat map provided by Downdetector, which we first checked on Sept. 10, showed the highest concentration of outages in Dallas and Austin, Texas, but also indicated reports were being submitted in other major cities like New York, Boston and Chicago.
Grindr outage map on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
A look at the same map one day later showed lower concentrations of reports of problems in the same cities.
(Grindr outage map on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector))
The page explains that Downdetector "calculates a baseline volume of typical problem reports for each service monitored" based on an average over six months, and "only reports an incident when the number of problem reports is significantly higher than the baseline."
Further, Downdetector allows users reporting the issues to comment on the page. During the period of Snopes' review for this claim, multiple comments on Grindr's Downdetector page referenced the RNC with comments like, "Convention in Dallas, as always." There was no indication those comments came from people genuinely experiencing connection issues in Dallas.
So while it appeared that some users may have had trouble with the service on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026, including in and around the area where the RNC was being held, there was not enough evidence to conclude without a doubt that the reported errors were entirely authentic or that they were indeed caused specifically by attendees at the RNC.
We reached out to Ookla, the parent company of Downdetector, for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we've investigated similar claims about Grindr, such as rumors of alleged Grindr outages near Charlie Kirk's memorial in September 2025.

Provinces are turning to U.S. health-care workers to help with shortages. And it’s working
Recruitment can help fill gaps, but experts say Canada needs to do more to retain its own health-care workers
Registered nurse Shane Tyson was done with the U.S.
He was working in Minnesota at the not-for-profit Mayo Clinic Health System and the Olmsted Medical Center. But in 2025, Tyson says he became increasingly concerned about the deterioration of health care, as well as tighter immigration enforcement.
Then ICE agents arrested a patient as they were leaving a primary care appointment where he worked, Tyson says.
“That was definitely a wake-up call," he said. "And I am married to a U.S. permanent resident that was born in Bolivia … and it scared the crap out of me for him and for the others in that situation,” Tyson told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of CBC’s White Coat, Black Art.
Tyson says he’d been noticing Facebook ads from provincial recruitment service HealthMatch BC. The more he researched, the more he contemplated a move north. So he registered, got interviews with two B.C. health authorities, and received two job offers within a week.
Tyson is one of many health-care professionals making the move from the U.S. With shortages of nurses, physicians and other health workers, some provinces are actively recruiting U.S. health-care professionals — and they’re getting results.
CBC reached out to health ministries in all 10 provinces for data on health-care professionals recruited from the U.S. since efforts ramped up in 2025.
The number of doctors recruited ranged from three in Saskatchewan to 33 in Nova Scotia and 570 in Ontario.
Ontario also recruited 2,300 nurses in 2025, while, all told, more than 580 health-care professionals accepted jobs in B.C. since March 2025.
For Tyson, the targeted recruitment worked. It took him just three months to get his B.C. nursing licence through a fast-track process, and eight days to receive a provincial nomination for permanent residence.
Since January, he’s been working in the emergency department of Nanaimo Regional General Hospital (NRGH) on Vancouver Island. Tyson says he’s pleased with the community, the weather, and what he sees as more inclusive health care.
“There’s not the insurance companies and corporate health-care companies taking billions of dollars. The patient is the focus here and whether you're the unhoused or the banker or lawyer, you have equal access to care in Canada,” he said.
The recruitment push
Health-care workers are bringing experience and ideas from some of the largest hospitals in the U.S., says Damian Lange, executive director of clinical services at NRGH.
“The American system has significant talent,” Lange said.
He said Island Health started recruiting from the U.S. in April 2025. Since then, it has hired 76 physicians and 102 nurses — 31 of them at NRGH. He said another 87 U.S. health-care providers will hopefully join by year’s end.
Lange said the new recruits make for a “better staff experience ... better patient experience, improved quality care, improved access to care. And so it's been a real benefit as we close the gap there with our vacancy rates.”
Even with the new hires, Lange said Island Health still has a 15 per cent vacancy rate for nurses.
And recruiting U.S. health-care workers is only part of the equation. A lot of questions go along with an international move.
Volunteers helping ease the move north
Tod Maffin and his wife, Jocelyn Maffin, are helping pave the way with an online community they started in early 2025. Tod is a digital strategist and former CBC journalist, and Jocelyn works with Spinal Cord Injury BC.
It started with Tod’s invitation to Americans to visit Nanaimo last year. So many health-care workers interested in moving to Canada came that Maffin made a Discord channel where people can chat and ask questions about everything from health-care licensing to real estate to services for autistic children.
Tod said it’s about connecting people.
“If you're an ER nurse in Dallas and you're ready … to move into Canada, you've figured out which area you're going to go to, but you have a trans kid and you just need to talk the parent of another trans kid in that community to make sure that your daughter is going to be OK,” you can find that support in the Discord group, he said.
It includes out-of-area health-care workers (mostly Americans), recruiters, immigration consultants and local citizens who just want to help out. Of around 1,200 current users, 84 have recently accepted job offers.
Tod created a template for other Healthcare Infusion communities and there are now 45 of them across Canada.
Jocelyn said she initially worried about poaching health-care workers from the U.S., but: “Canada has dealt with brain drain to the U.S. for years and that's always been a big issue,” she said.
“So maybe we're just borrowing them back.”
Call for better retention
In an email to CBC, the Canadian Medical Association said that with a shortage of more than 23,000 family doctors, Canada needs to remove barriers to immigration and licensing for internationally trained physicians. It also needs to make it easier for those currently practising in Canada to stay, the association said.
Canadian Nurses Association CEO Valerie Grdisa emphasized the need to retain the nurses Canada already has.
“We welcome U.S.-educated nurses into the nation, but we don't see it really as a long-term recruitment strategy,” she said. “We really have to get back [to] what matters to Canadian and domestically educated nurses.”
Grdisa said Health Canada's Nursing Retention Toolkit lays out strategies to retain nurses, like safe staffing levels, manageable workloads, mentorship and career support. But she said health-care systems haven’t implemented or evaluated them consistently enough to determine what actually works.
“If those things were to happen, would we be losing such a large cohort — up to 40 per cent of the workforce by the age of 35?”
Meanwhile, though, nurse Shane Tyson says he is here to stay. He recently got his certificate of Canadian citizenship. A kind stranger also left a moose sticker and a welcome note on his car.
“That really made me emotional, you know. I was concerned, driving around with Minnesota plates, how I'd be received, because at that time the tariffs were coming in, talk of the 51st state — and that just really meant a lot to me.”
Now Tyson is logging onto the Maffins’ Discord community to help other U.S. health-care workers come to Canada.
“Have to pay it forward.”

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”
The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.
Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.
Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.
“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.
Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

The US government launched at least three previously unreported investigations into trading on the prediction market Polymarket, according to documents obtained by WIRED through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Voting records from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates prediction markets, shed new light on how the government approaches these investigations. In early May, CFTC chairman Michael Selig approved an order allowing the agency’s enforcement division to launch a private investigation into potential insider trading on Polymarket event contracts related to pardons issued by former president Joseph Biden. The order granted permission to take testimony, obtain subpoenas, administer oaths, and require the production of documents in the course of the investigation.
The documents obtained by WIRED did not specify which trades were under suspicion, but the order came several weeks after an NPR report on a suspicious Polymarket trader who netted over $300,000 on pardon-related markets in the final days of the Biden administration. The trader correctly wagered that the former president would issue preemptive pardons to a number of prominent MAGA critics, including former US representatives Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, and US senator Adam Schiff.
At the end of May, Selig approved another investigation order. This time, the topic was “Iran event contracts” on Polymarket. As with the Biden pardon documents, the investigation order did not provide details, but it came two weeks after 60 Minutes aired a report on a network of suspicious Polymarket accounts that made $2.4 million on Iran-related trades, with a 98 percent win rate.
“If these investigations are being prompted solely by press reports of potential violations of the Commodities Exchange Act, that’s a significant sign of weakness in this regulatory scheme,” says Joseph Konizeski, a former chief trial attorney in the CFTC’s division of enforcement. The agency has come under fire in the second Trump era for its perceived friendliness to the prediction market industry.
In July, Selig greenlit a third investigation, this time focused on suspected insider trading on Google-themed Polymarket event contracts. In an email exchange included in the documents obtained by WIRED, Paul Hayeck, the acting director of the CFTC’s department of enforcement, noted that the investigation would focus on “additional individuals who may have engaged in insider trading related to Google’s 2025 Year in Search Ranking.” Hayeck wrote that the Southern District of New York is conducting a “parallel investigation.” He specified that the CFTC's investigation would be separate from the ongoing case against Michele Spagnuolo, a Google engineer accused of insider trading.
SDNY declined to comment. Google declined to comment. It pointed WIRED to a statement it released in June noting that Spagnuolo was no longer with the company. The CFTC did not respond to requests for comment and questions about the status of the investigations.
“While we do not comment on specific investigations, we regularly refer matters to law enforcement and support ongoing investigations as part of our commitment to protecting the integrity of our markets,” Olivia Chalos, deputy chief legal officer at Polymarket, told WIRED in an email.
The CFTC is also reportedly investigating Polymarket itself. The company, which had its flagship platform banned from the United States in 2022, was permitted to launch a US-regulated version with a narrower set of markets in late 2025. It recently underwent a fundraising round led by Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, which valued the company at $21 billion.
The CFTC has also launched investigations into potential insider trading on Kalshi, Polymarket’s archrival, in the past. According to The New York Times, Kalshi has referred at least 32 cases to the agency. The CFTC fined former US representative George Santos $35,000 for his behavior related to a Kalshi contract about whether he would attend Trump’s 2026 State of the Union address.
Kalshi issued its first-ever lifetime ban to Santos for violating its rules on market manipulation for the same behavior, and also fined him just over $71,000. Santos was not criminally charged.
So far, two arrests have been made stemming from Polymarket insider trading investigations. In April, federal authorities arrested a US special forces officer who prosecutors say used classified information to make more than $400,000 in profits on event contracts related to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. And in May, Spagnuolo, who allegedly made over $1.2 million on insider trades, was arrested while traveling to New York. In both cases, the CFTC filed civil charges, and the Department of Justice filed criminal fraud charges. Both men are fighting back by arguing that Polymarket trades are a form of betting and not subject to commodities law.
It’s unclear if the Department of Justice has launched parallel investigations into the Iran War or Biden pardon contracts. The DOJ did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A former CFTC staffer tells WIRED that parallel criminal investigations are likely, “given the significance of the matters.”
Additional reporting by Maddy Varner.

Iran-US war latest: Houthis claim drone attack on Saudi base as military advance in Yemen intensifies
The US military, which has previously struck Iranian vessels in the region, did not issue an immediate statement
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed on Sunday to have struck facilities at a military base in Saudi Arabia as the burgeoning conflict threatens to throw the region back into chaos.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said that the Iran-backed group had targeted “weapons depots and command and control centers” at the southern Sharurah base.
Saree claimed that a joint ballistic missile and drone attack hit its targets and warned of wider measures if the Saudi attacks on Yemen continue.
The escalation follows a lightning Houthi advance to the Red Sea coast this week, giving the group greater power to attack Saudi ships around the Bab-al Mandeb strait.
Oil hovered around $100 per barrel on Sunday amid growing fears the clashes could drag in the US to help its ally in Riyadh, prolonging the six-month conflict with Iran to the east.
Separately, a crew member was killed early on Sunday when an Iranian commercial ship was attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.
There has been no statement so far from the US military, which has previously struck Iranian vessels to enforce its blockade of the country's ports.
Trump says he’ll ‘probably be able to settle’ UK’s Falkland Islands row with Argentina
US President Donald Trump has said he expects to be called upon to “settle” any potential conflict in the ongoing row between the UK and Argentina on the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
Speaking to reporters during a visit to Dublin, Mr Trump said the UK would not “be willing to travel that far” if there was an invasion similar to the one in 1982, explaining that it would take the UK “weeks by boat” to get there.
His comments come after Mr Trump previously suggested he might not back Britain if Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, in apparent retaliation for the UK’s stance on the Iran war.
Trump says he’ll ‘probably be able to settle’ Falkland Islands row
At least two killed in Israeli strike in Gaza, witnesses say
An Israeli airstrike on Sunday killed at least two Palestinians in a vehicle and wounded 13 others in the Gaza Strip, medical staff said.
The strike in the Tel Al-Hawa neighbourhood in western Gaza City, left the vehicle mangled, according to footage circulated on social media.
Local medical staff told Reuters that they urged people to provide information that could help identify the two people who were killed and whose bodies were dismembered by the explosion.
The Israeli military said the strike targeted two Hamas militants, without giving further information.
Explained: The US has made progress in reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but the Iran war is far from over
In recent weeks, the United States has succeeded in loosening Iran's grip over the Strait of Hormuz while virtually shutting down Iran's own oil exports, accelerating its economic free fall.
But the war launched by the U.S. and Israel in February — intended to last a few weeks — is still far from over, and the stalemate is costly for both sides. An agreement reached in June quickly crumbled, with so sign of diplomatic progress since then. Low-level fighting persists, and the U.S. does not seem to have an exit strategy.
The mounting economic pressure on Iran has yet to stoke an uprising, and if its leaders are backed into a corner, they may opt for military escalation rather than capitulation. Their Houthi allies in Yemen have meanwhile stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, helping to push oil prices back up.
Here’s the state of play after nearly seven months:
The US has made progress in reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but the Iran war is far from over
Houthis claim strike on Saudi military base
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed on Sunday to have struck facilities at a military base in Saudi Arabia as the burgeoning conflict threatens to throw the region back into chaos.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said that the Iran-backed group had targeted “weapons depots and command and control centers” at the southern Sharurah base.
Saree claimed that a joint ballistic missile and drone attack hit its targets and warned of wider measures if the Saudi attacks on Yemen continue.
The escalation follows a lightning Houthi advance to the Red Sea coast this week, giving the group greater power to attack Saudi ships around the Bab-al Mandeb strait.
Oil hovered around $100 per barrel on Sunday amid growing fears the clashes could drag in the US to help its ally in Riyadh, prolonging the six-month conflict with Iran to the east.
Report: Hamas 'planned to carry out attacks in European capitals last year'
Hamas planned to carry out terror attacks in European capitals last year to mark the second anniversary of the October 7 attacks in Israel, according to an indictment filed by Germany’s federal prosecutor.
The Palestinian group reportedly intended to carry out attacks on Israeli and Jewish ‘interests’ in Berlin and Vienna around October 7 2025, according to the indictment, as seen by German broadsheet Die Welt.
It was said to have been backed by “an international weapons-procurement network” that moved pistols, a rifle and ammunition through Europe.
The plot is claimed to have come undone just days before the attacks were due to be carried out, as German authorities swooped on three suspects in Berlin during the handover of a cache of weapons that prosecutors say were intended for the operation.
Federal prosecutors in Germany last year said they had arrested men linked to Hamas who were suspected of planning attacks on Israeli and Jewish targets in Germany.
Trump says Iran probably behind attack on Saudi Arabia
Donald Trump said on Saturday that Iran was probably responsible for the aerial attack on Saudi Arabia that shut down its East-West pipeline, one of the kingdom's main routes for exporting crude while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
"I think they are, probably they are," Trump told reporters in Dublin when asked if Iran was responsible for the attack on the vital oil conduit.
The president also said that he had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he described as a "good friend."
Trump added that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis had called his administration and indicated they did not want the United States to become directly involved in the conflict.
“There's just one country that they're not too happy with, and we'll get that straightened out," Trump added.
Where are peace talks six months on?
There have been no talks between the United States and Iran to end the conflict since a June agreement that collapsed within weeks.
In a post on X on Saturday, Ebrahim Azizi, head of the Iranian parliament's national security committee, said: "As long as the American side does not accept all of Iran's conditions, dialogue and negotiation are of no use."
Iran's foreign ministry announced on Friday that Iran would be attending a meeting with Gulf Arab states in Oman on Monday, at which the future of the Strait of Hormuz would be discussed.
But a senior Iranian official, speaking to Reuters on Saturday, played down the chances of a breakthrough, saying the meeting, called at Oman's initiative, was intended to discuss issues including the strait but was not expected to yield a signed agreement.
Oman has not officially announced the meeting, and other Gulf countries have remained silent. Bahrain said on Saturday it would not attend meetings with Iran.
Recap: China accused of handing Iran intel for strike on Jordan air base
Chinese ‘entities’ may have supplied Iran with high-resolution satellite images of a US military base in Jordan ahead of a strike that killed three troops in July, according to a report.
Three soldiers were killed and four injured at the overnight strike at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base on 17 July.
US officials told the Wall Street Journal that the alleged handover of images represented the most clear evidence so far that Chinese support for Iran had had lethal consequences for US forces.
China has repeatedly dismissed Washington’s concerns, refusing to acknowledge that any Chinese companies are engaged in such activity, the officials said.
Emerging story: Iranian commercial ship is struck near Strait of Hormuz
Iranian state media reports that one person was killed after an Iranian commercial ship was struck near the Strait of Hormuz.
There was no immediate comment from the US military, which previously struck Iranian-flagged ships during its blockade of ports.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor separately reported a vessel was hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, with no details.
What’s happening with the Houthis and Saudi Arabia?
The Iran-aligned Houthis have been fighting Saudi Arabia for more than a decade as part of the Yemen civil war. But clashes have flared up in recent weeks around the US-Iran conflict.
The Houthis are reasserting control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which controls access to the Red Sea, at a time when Iran has all but closed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz to the east. That makes it difficult for countries like US ally Saudi Arabia to export oil, driving up global prices.
In Yemen, the Houthis embarked on a lightning offensive west this week, bringing them closer to the Red Sea and granting them greater control over traffic through the waterway.
Yemeni government sources said that the Houthis had seized the strategic island of Perim on Friday in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb strait — the "Gate of Tears" at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis also launched attacks in southern cities in Saudi Arabia, causing injuries and damage to energy infrastructure.
In a separate attack, Saudi Arabia’s crucial East-West oil pipeline was struck by a drone from Iraq this week, where Iranian-backed militia operate. Donald Trump said Iran was “probably” behind the attack, without providing evidence.
Washington now faces a dilemma over whether to help their allies fight the Houthis, potentially expanding the deeply unpopular war.

The price of diesel is skyrocketing. Here's why Canadians may soon feel it at the grocery store
Ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran is biggest threat to overall inflation by driving gas prices up
With diesel prices skyrocketing due to ongoing global conflicts, filling up the trucks that carry food and goods across Canada has never been more expensive, experts say — and Canadians could be feeling it soon.
"It's very bad," Tej Dulat, director of government and public affair with the Canadian Truck Operators Association, told CBC News.
A commercial truck goes through hundreds of litres every week, making fuel one of the biggest costs for trucking companies, Dulat said. And while the industry can usually absorb a brief spike in prices, he said, the margins have been tighter since prices jumped in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine.
Now, prices are even higher.
"End of the day, companies have to pass that cost to the consumers," Dulat said.
"You're going to see that impact coming on the grocery prices."
As of Saturday prices sat at $2.62 per litre across Canada for diesel, surpassing last week's high of $2.52 after a brief dip earlier this week. That's more than a dollar higher than it was this time last year, according to Natural Resources Canada, and higher than the top weekly average in 2022, which came in at $2.30.
It's worse in some regions — Vancouver sat at $2.92 per litre on Saturday. And in the U.S., the average price of diesel hit a record-high on Friday at more than $6 US per litre, sending shockwaves across the country.
Much attention over the past few weeks has been on the potential impact of tariffs on the price of Canadian goods, but this jump in oil prices suggests that geopolitical conflicts are having a bigger impact right now, experts say.
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said last week that while tariffs could hit some sectors hard, they don't expect them to strongly impact Canada's overall level of economic activity.
But the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran, which is the main driver keeping gas prices high, could mean a spillover in cost from gas to other goods shortly, he said.
"The longer oil prices and refinery prices stay high, the greater the risk that higher energy prices spill over and turn into persistent inflation."
- Who are the Houthis? How they could send oil prices surging even further
- Renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges send oil price back over $100 US for first time in several weeks
Not enough supply
The problem is that diesel is in extraordinarily short supply, experts say. Net exports of diesel/gasoil from the Persian Gulf region had dropped to just over a quarter of pre-war levels as of August, according to a report published Friday by the International Energy Association.
Meanwhile, other geopolitical stressors are also putting strain on the amount of diesel available. One of the world's biggest producers, Russia, recently extended a ban on diesel exports after Ukraine damaged a number of oil refineries.
Canada's largest refinery, the Irving Refinery in New Brunswick, is also shut down until November for maintenance, further limiting supplies.
The federal government announced last week that a temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax, including a four cent per litre tax on diesel, would be extended through January 2027, instead of expiring on Sept. 7.
But experts say that doesn't absorb enough of the costs.
"This is going to be somewhat of a secret killer of the North American economy, if this is not addressed in the next few months," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis firm Gas Buddy, told CBC News.
Although conflict has continued between U.S. and Iran since a brief agreement in June crumbled, Iranian officials said Friday that Iran will be meeting with Iraq and other countries around the Persian Gulf in Oman on Monday to discuss safe commercial shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
Should Canadians brace for an expensive winter?
Diesel prices historically rise even more in the winter, according to energy analyst Dan McTeague, meaning "we could be looking at a very, very expensive winter ahead, not just for truck, for transport industry, airlines, trains and whatnot, but also for consumers."
It's a concern for Canadians, as any time the price of diesel goes up, it impacts every part of the food supply chain: shipping, storing and producing, according to Evan Fraser at the University of Guelph's Arrell Food Institute.
Usually there's a long lag between a bump in diesel prices and the trickle down to grocery shelves, and some diffusion of impacts, but he suspects this time will be different.
That's due to how many factors are impacting it, he said, including heat waves affecting harvests.
"You've got a perfect storm of problems creating endless upward pressure on the price of food."
Fraser worries we could be heading for a "new normal" of elevated food prices for the next decade because assumptions we once relied on for global food production and trade — low and stable energy prices, a productive environment for food growth and "easy geopolitics for trade" — are no longer so reliable.
"In the short term, it's going to be really hard for low- income Canadians."
With files from Cameron MacIntosh

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning. Chelsea Cirruzzo here. Today we remember 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. While I was too young to have many recollections of the attack, I did grow up in New York and vividly remember the impact it had on the people around me. So, I always take the time each year to reflect.
Today, we’ve published a First Opinion essay by a thoracic surgeon in New York City who treats first responders still facing extraordinary health challenges after being exposed to the toxic aftermath of ground zero. I hope you spend time with it, too.
Trump’s $500 Obamacare promise
President Trump has promised to send $500 refund checks to nearly 1 million Americans on Affordable Care Act plans, who also happen to live mostly in swing states, with checks arriving ahead of the midterms.
The checks will only go out to people who don’t receive federal subsidies for their insurance plans — after Republicans declined to extend enhanced ACA premiums that expired at the end of last year.
The White House said the money will help “Americans most exposed to the higher costs imposed by the Biden administration’s gross mismanagement of Obamacare.”
People are eligible for the $500 if they live in one of the 30 states that use the federal government’s ACA marketplace, such as Ohio and Florida. It’s unclear whether only people with current coverage qualify, or whether people who had plans in the past may also get checks.
My colleagues Bob Herman and Tara Bannow have more on the unclear legality of the move.
Can AI catch a heart attack? The FDA thinks so
A number of artificial intelligence algorithms have promised to help identify and treat heart conditions early, but how about when a patient is actively having a heart attack? Last week, the Food and Drug Administration issued a rare de novo classification to an algorithm from Powerful Medical that aims to help triage patients to the right care when they’re having chest pain. The vast majority of AI devices go to market through the FDA’s 510(k) clearance pathway; fewer than 10 each year receive de novo classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence.
Here’s how the new algorithm, Queen of Hearts, works: It can detect patterns indicating a patient is experiencing the most severe kind of heart attack, when a coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart, is completely blocked off. In doing so, it can help doctors make sure a patient gets treatment as soon as possible to open up the blockage and restore oxygen to the heart.
My colleague Katie Palmer has more on what it means for patients and doctors if we can more quickly detect these ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction patterns with an EKG.
A valuable childhood cancer treatment with long-term implications
A platinum-based treatment for children with certain cancers can be a lifeline, but it can also cause healthy cells to mutate, potentially increasing the risk of new cancers later in life, my colleague Annalisa Merelli reports.
That’s according to a new study published Thursday in Science, seeking a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is most commonly diagnosed in childhood.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. Researchers sampled both healthy and cancerous liver tissue and blood from the patients and compared the results to samples from children given different treatments.
What they found were hundreds of mutations in the samples exposed to platinum, usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Read on for what this means for long-term monitoring and treatment.
Sorry to burst your (bouncy castle) bubble
What kid doesn’t love getting to carom around in a bouncy castle? But the inflated structures could be the source of skin infections, an investigation into a large outbreak of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — more commonly known as MRSA — in eastern Ireland reveals.
About four dozen children who attended a community party in August 2025 later developed skin and soft tissue lesions and abscesses caused by the bacterium, Irish public health officials reported Thursday in the online journal Eurosurveillance.
The event, attended by about 120 adults and children, featured three bouncy castles. Many of the kids reportedly spent considerable time — hours, even — playing in them. About a quarter of the cases had symptoms beyond skin lesions, such as fever, nausea, or vomiting. Four of the infected kids were admitted to the hospital, though all recovered. One of the infected children hadn’t attended the party but had close contact with a child who had.
The MRSA outbreak is the largest on record in Ireland. — Helen Branswell
Boycott launched against Diabetes Association includes journal
In the latest escalation of members protesting how the American Diabetes Association has handled the removal of members from its June meeting, four editors of the ADA’s flagship journal will no longer review manuscript submissions. Their move is part of a boycott announced Thursday against the professional organization.
Steven Kahn, the editor-in-chief of Diabetes Care, is one of the five members who were ousted from the conference center in New Orleans for handing out copies of an editorial published in the journal about federal cuts to research funding. The other editors are Cheryl Anderson of UC San Diego, John Buse of the University of North Carolina, and Elizabeth Selvin of Johns Hopkins. At issue are the expulsions, the immediate response by ADA leadership, and the summer-long review of what happened.
“We are aware of the efforts taking place,” an ADA spokesperson said. “We remain focused on serving the millions of people counting on us to deliver on our mission.”
Kahn told STAT their actions are effectively “a strike against a major corporation.”
“Except we’re seeing this now as a boycott by members of a nonprofit organization, where the leadership of the organization is operating like a corporate board, rather than leadership of a membership organization, and the membership has said, ‘We’ve had enough,’” he said. — Elizabeth Cooney

Uganda's King Oyo buried amid calls for unity over his successor
- Published
Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried on Saturday, days after a row broke out over who would succeed him.
Oyo, 34, who had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three, died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the US.
Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. They were abolished in 1967 but restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
Thousands of mourners lined the streets as the king's casket was transported to the royal tombs in Fort Portal where a private ceremony took place.
Oyo was just a toddler when he was named as Tooro's king and, according to Guinness World Records, was the world's youngest monarch while he reigned.
TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, who was named as the next monarch by clan elders, reportedly cast nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, a ritual signifying the end of one reign and the start of another.
But days earlier, Oyo's family rejected Kijanangoma, the late monarch's cousin, as Tooro's new king.
Oyo's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will, written in 2022, naming his young son as his successor.
The boy's identity has never been disclosed.
Meanwhile, his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, said royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed. This, she said, restricted the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing it as "house arrest".
On Saturday, the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kazimba Mugalu, urged unity.
"Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict. It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning," he told mourners.
Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni also called for the matter to be resolved "and to favour unity over division".
The clan overseeing the succession defended its choice of Kijanangoma.
Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, head of the Babiito royal clan, said: "We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity."

Bengaluru-based restaurant company Popo Global, which operates gourmet food brands including The Pizza Bakery, Paris Panini and Smash Guys, has raised ₹532 Cr (around $56 Mn) from Artal Asia. Popo Global did not disclose its valuation and the size of Artal Asia’s stake. Founded in 2017 by brothers Nikhil Gupta and Abhijit “AB” Gupta, Popo Global began with gourmet sourdough pizza brand The Pizza Bakery. It later expanded its portfolio with Paris Panini, which offers French-inspired paninis, sandwiches, wraps, and crepes, and smash burger brand Smash Guys. The company claims to operate 41 outlets across Bengaluru. With the latest investment, Popo Global plans to expand beyond Bengaluru and scale its portfolio of food brands across India. Popo Global said its operating model combines the convenience of quick-service restaurants, the customer experience associated with fine dining, and the scalability of delivery kitchens. The company said its model focuses on core products, dine-in and delivery channels, standardised processes, and restaurant real estate selection. It also claimed to have recorded strong same-store sales growth, repeat rates, and unit economics, but did not disclose the underlying figures. Popo Global added that it had largely bootstrapped its expansion in Bengaluru before the latest transaction. “Bringing Artal Asia into Popo lets us think considerably bigger while keeping the spirit that got us here - never cutting any corners on quality. They have partnered with some of the world's most successful food businesses, and they understand that the product has to stay at the centre of it,” said the cofounders. Artal Asia is an affiliate of global investment firm Artal Group. Its India portfolio includes Capital Foods (later acquired by Tata Consumer Products), Burger Singh, and Jumbotail. The investment comes amid continued investor interest in Indian restaurant and food brands looking to expand their offline presence and enter new markets. Foodtech startup Dil Foods recently raised ₹72 Cr to expand its footprint and launch more cuisine offerings. Similarly, Gen Z-focussed cafe chain Alienkind raised $3.2 Mn in June to enter new markets and support its next phase of growth. Meanwhile, Bengaluru-based bubble tea and QSR brand Boba Bhai raised ₹40 Cr to expand its offline presence earlier this year.

Rajouri, Sep 13: Two minor sisters died after being bitten by a snake at Manma Barmari village in the Kalakote subdivision of Rajouri district on Sunday, officials said.
An official told the news agency—Kashmir News Observer (KNO) that the sisters were sleeping in a room along with other family members when a snake appeared on the bed and bit both of them.
The sisters were immediately shifted to a hospital for treatment, however they succumbed to their injuries. The deceased were identified as Amiba (5) and Amiza (3), both residents of Rajouri.
Meanwhile investigation has been initiated.

EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti has pledged 34.51 Cr shares of the online travel aggregator, worth ₹211.9 Cr, to Motilal Oswal Financial Services for “personal use”. The pledge, created on August 24, covers 8.66% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital, according to an exchange filing. The shares were valued at ₹6.14 apiece at the time of the transaction. The filing pegged both the value of the pledged shares and the amount involved at ₹211.9 Cr, implying a security cover ratio of 1:1. The 34.51 Cr shares covered by the latest pledge represent about 76.1% of Pitti’s 45.37 Cr share holding in EaseMyTrip. Before the transaction, 10.36 Cr of Pitti’s shares were already encumbered. Following the creation of the pledge, his total encumbered holding stood at 44.87 Cr shares, representing 11.26% of EaseMyTrip’s total share capital. The pledged shares represent 98.89% of Pitti’s individual holding, leaving him with 50 Lakh unencumbered shares. The pledged shares account for 25.83% of the combined shareholding of EaseMyTrip’s promoter group, which includes Nishant Pitti, Rikant Pittie, and Prashant Pitti. Total Pledge Unchanged However, Pitti’s overall pledged holding remains unchanged from April, when he had pledged a total of 44.87 Cr EaseMyTrip shares. While the latest filing classifies the transaction as the creation of a pledge, the unchanged post-transaction holding suggests that existing encumbrances were restructured. The filing did not elaborate on the reason for the change. Pitti had pledged 6.86 Cr shares worth about ₹55 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services in March this year. This followed a string of pledge creations and releases over the preceding year. In June 2025, Pitti pledged 9 Cr shares worth ₹94.5 Cr to Motilal Oswal Financial Services, also for personal use. At the time, his total pledged holding stood at 17.01 Cr shares. Pitti’s pledges have come alongside a reduction in his stake in EaseMyTrip. He sold nearly 5 Cr shares worth ₹78.3 Cr in December 2024 after offloading 24.65 Cr shares for about ₹920 Cr in September that year. His stake in the company subsequently declined to 12.8% at the end of FY25 from 28.13% a year earlier. Pitti stepped down as EaseMyTrip’s CEO in January 2025 and was succeeded by his brother and cofounder Rikant Pittie. At the time, Nishant Pitti said the share sale was due to “personal reasons” and assured shareholders that he would not sell any more shares. Another cofounder, Prashant Pitti, resigned as the company’s MD in August 2025. EaseMyTrip Under Pressure The pledge disclosure comes at a time when EaseMyTrip’s earnings remain under pressure. The OTA slipped into the red in Q1 FY27, reporting a consolidated net loss of ₹11.7 Cr as against a net profit of ₹44 Lakh in Q1 FY26. This came despite operating revenue rising 18.4% YoY to ₹134.7 Cr. The weak quarter followed a challenging FY26. EaseMyTrip reported a ₹47.5 Cr loss in FY26 as against a profit of ₹108.6 Cr in FY25. Revenue from operations declined 8.8% YoY to ₹535.7 Cr. EaseMyTrip's board in May approved a proposal to raise up to ₹500 Cr through a rights issue. The company had earlier said the capital would be used to strengthen its technology and platform, expand into segments such as hotels and holidays, and pursue strategic acquisitions. Shares of EaseMyTrip were trading at ₹5.83 at 15:10, 0.5% higher from the opening price on BSE.

The New Mexico Supreme Court held a ChatGPT-using lawyer in direct contempt of court for submitting a brief with “false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” including fake police testimony and other mistakes. The state’s top court referred the lawyer to a disciplinary board for further proceedings and concluded that he “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client.”
Attorney Stephen Aarons “admitted to the Court that he did not verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief before signing it and filing it with the Court, and that he did not inform his client of this failure or that the brief in chief contained multiple factual and legal misrepresentations,” the state Supreme Court said in an order on Wednesday.
Aarons has been a criminal defense lawyer in New Mexico for over 40 years and was hired by a defendant’s family members to appeal a murder conviction. Aaron’s now-former client, Oscar Renee Sandoval, was sentenced to life in prison in February 2025 after being convicted of killing Shiereen Al-Jibury, who was his partner and the mother of his children.
A little over a year ago, in August 2025, Aarons submitted the brief containing fake testimony and other errors. Weeks later, the state of New Mexico filed a motion to strike portions of that brief.
“Respondent admitted to the Court that the brief in chief contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses—Officer Michelle Amarillo, Officer Sanchez, Manal Al-Jibury, and Teresa Marquez,” the court order on Wednesday said.
Lawyer fed trial transcript into ChatGPT
Aarons further admitted submitting “false testimony from Danny Stanton that he received threats,” “false testimony from Linda Stanton about the threats her husband received,” and “false testimony from Mariah Chavez and Teresa Marquez (fabricated witness) regarding the shooter’s clothing and appearance,” according to the order, which said Aarons also “misrepresented legal authority” in citations to previous cases.
Many lawyers have been caught citing fake cases in briefs or inaccurately describing real cases. While Aarons didn’t cite fake cases, he inaccurately described real ones and cited fake testimony.
Aarons told the state Supreme Court at a hearing on August 21 that he fed a computer-generated transcript of the murder trial and other documents related to the case into ChatGPT, which outputted the fake quotes.
“It’s of little comfort to know that my stupidity is what brings us together this afternoon,” Aarons told the court. Aarons admitted his brief quoted “several witnesses who were never called at trial,” another “witness who was called but the brief got the name wrong,” and that his brief inaccurately described precedents.
Aarons indicated that he used a version of ChatGPT powered by the OpenAI o3 model, which was released earlier in 2025. “I assumed that it generated a bulletproof summary of proceedings,” he said at the hearing, explaining that he thought it would be accurate because of how widespread AI use is in the legal and medical fields.
Aarons was barred from appearing before the New Mexico Supreme Court pending the outcome of any disciplinary board investigation and proceedings. He was fined $5,000, to be paid to the State Bar of New Mexico Client Protection Fund, but more penalties could come out of the disciplinary proceedings ordered by the court.
The state Supreme Court ordered the public defender office to appoint a new lawyer for the defendant, struck all previous briefs from the record, and said the case will proceed in the court’s 2026-27 term.
Justice: “You buried your head in the sand”
Justices lambasted Aarons during last month’s hearing. They expressed surprise that Aarons didn’t know AI tools could generate false information and pointed out that attorneys must verify the accuracy of information no matter where it comes from. Whether a lawyer gets help from an AI tool, a law student, or a fellow attorney, the lawyer signing the brief must attest to its accuracy, they said.
Justice C. Shannon Bacon was particularly withering in her criticism of Aarons. She told Aarons that there are “at least eight or nine provisions in the code of conduct that you violated.” Bacon said she was “really struggling with” Aarons’ claim to be unaware of AI hallucinations, noting that her 13-year-old nephew and 75-year-old stepmother are both aware of the problem.
“So counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world? Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day,” she said. “So either you buried your head in the sand—and that’s a choice to do that, an intentional choice to be uninformed—or you took a gamble, and neither of those are consistent with the code of conduct.”
Aarons responded that he submitted the brief a year ago and “a lot has come out in the last year.” However, the problem of lawyers using AI in briefs that cite made-up cases has been in the news regularly for well over three years.
Aarons added that the cases he cited in his brief were not fake, although his brief described them inaccurately. Bacon responded that there’s no “material distinction” between inaccurately describing a real case and citing a fake one, as the rules about candor to the court apply “with equal force” either way.
“I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts”
Aarons provided a statement when contacted by Ars today. He said:
In March 2025 I agreed to handle an appeal and used ChatGPT to summarize the trial proceedings. I wrote the brief but the table of contents and the summary contained numerous errors. At the time, I didn’t know that AI could hallucinate facts not only in my brief but in pleadings submitted by other attorneys. I am glad the court threw out my defective pleading and ordered the public defender to write a new brief on behalf of my former client. As for myself, I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake. It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.
Aarons told the court that he began by using Rev.com, a service that provides AI transcripts of audio files, and then put that transcript and other materials into ChatGPT.
“I believe I did confirm” that the trial transcript was accurate, he said when asked if he confirmed its accuracy before inputting it into ChatGPT. “The problem wasn’t in the transcript. It was when I loaded it and all the other information” into ChatGPT, he said. In addition to the transcript, Aarons said he put “the record proper, the statement of issues, and some of the discovery” into ChatGPT.
Aarons said he hoped the court would take steps to prevent other lawyers from making the same mistake he did, such as by issuing a standing order requiring that briefs contain a certificate of compliance regarding the use of AI. Justices treated Aaron’s suggestion as a distraction from the main problem, his failure to verify the accuracy of the brief.
“Assume with me that you had relied on the work of a first-year lawyer that was working for you and that they had just made stuff up… and you signed it. You’d be in the same exact soup you are right now,” Bacon said. “So the idea that, the suggestion in your briefing that because the court didn’t tell you at the time that you did this, ‘be careful,’ it somehow relieves you of obligation, falls on absolute deaf ears because the rules of professional conduct already tell you what your obligation is.”
“Your client is the one suffering”
“The other thing that’s completely missing from your response is anything about what this has done to your client,” Bacon went on to say. “That’s who I’m worried about. You have presented briefing to the court that we cannot rely on, and your client is the one suffering because of this far more than you will ever suffer.”
Chief Justice Julie Vargas similarly told Aarons, “I’m really interested with the approach you’re taking in this hearing. You seem to be telling us all the policy that we’ve been thinking about for years about what to do with AI, but you’re not talking about how to address the situation that’s in front of us, which has significant impacts on a criminal defendant who is in custody, who’s going to stay in custody until we resolve this matter. And I really don’t care about the policy concerns right now. I care about what we’re going to do with your client and what we should do in this circumstance based on the behavior that you showed us.”
Justice Michael Vigil said there’s nothing wrong with using AI to help write a legal argument as long as the lawyer verifies its accuracy. “It doesn’t matter what the tool is. It doesn’t matter how advanced the AI-generated program is or what improvements they make, whatever,” he said. “It doesn’t matter whether you use a C-student lawyer or a A-student lawyer [if] you didn’t check their work before you filed the brief. That’s the issue. And I wish, or I’m hoping you would focus on that, take responsibility for it.”
Aarons replied, “I hope I don’t present myself as not accepting responsibility. I mean, my only hope is that the mistakes that I made that somehow can prevent someone else down the line from repeating my mistake because the AI capacity is amazing.”
Lawyer didn’t tell client and family about ChatGPT use
Bacon criticized Aarons for not disclosing the problem to his client. “I have not. He’s a Spanish speaker and I wanted to see what happened today,” Aarons told Bacon when she asked if he told Sandoval about the problem.
Aarons said he was hired by Sandoval’s brother and cousin, and that he told them there was a problem with a brief. “They’re aware that there was a problem with the first brief that I filed and that the court’s looking at that. That’s pretty much it,” he said.
Bacon replied, “You didn’t say, ‘I relied on ChatGPT and it submitted lies to the court and the court is mad at me and now there’s a hearing.’ I’m guessing you didn’t tell your client’s family members that.”
“I didn’t talk about ChatGPT,” Aarons said. “I just said there was a problem with the brief that I filed.” Bacon told Aarons that his client needed to know the extent of the problem so he can make an informed decision “about whether you’re the right person to represent him.”
Bacon asked Aarons whether he was working on the case on a public defender contract or as private counsel. Aarons answered that he was hired as private counsel but hadn’t been paid yet.
“I’m not sure that’s going to happen,” Bacon replied.
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

Suspected drug dealers aged 89 and 73 arrested in house full of cocaine, marijuana and firearms
Both men are Cuban nationals and are being detained on immigration holds, according to jail records
A Miami drug bust at a house filled with cocaine, marijuana, and guns ended with two senior citizens facing charges for drug dealing.
The sting occurred on Wednesday and followed an August undercover operation targeting the men, according to arrest reports.
An undercover agent allegedly purchased a $60 bag of cocaine from Magdaleno Medina, 73, on August 19 at his trailer in Miami. At 3 pm on Wednesday, police — including a SWAT team — raided the home, according to an arrest report.
The officers reported finding a total of 141 grams of cocaine in multiple small plastic bags, 1,278 grams of marijuana, which was also stored in small bags, a Smith & Wesson .38 revolver and a Sig R365 .9mm handgun, as well as ammunition for both weapons, according to The Miami Herald.
Police said the revolver had been reported stolen from another county, and that the .9mm had been reported in Doral.
Magdaleno and Cesar Valdes, 89, were arrested at the house. Both were booked into the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center on charges that include armed cocaine trafficking and grand theft of a firearm.
Both of the men were born in Cuba and are being detained on an immigration hold, according to jail records.
The men are being represented by Miami-Dade County's Public Defender's Office, according to the paper.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

BRICS leaders on Saturday (September 12, 2026) called for stronger cooperation in disease surveillance and medical product regulation, welcoming the establishment of a dedicated sub-working group to advance an integrated early warning system for the prevention and response to mass infectious diseases.
In their New Delhi Declaration, the leaders stressed the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products to enhance preparedness for future health emergencies and ensure timely, affordable and equitable access to healthcare services, vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics.
They also called for strengthened collaboration among BRICS medical products regulatory authorities and welcomed efforts to develop a common GxP white paper consolidating regulatory best practices and technical approaches.
Public health emergencies transcend national borders
The leaders recognised that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require stronger international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated action.
"Acknowledging that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require strengthened international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated collective action, we underscore the importance of enhancing global health security through resilient surveillance systems, effective early warning mechanisms, and strengthened preparedness and response capacities," the declaration said.
The leaders recognising the central role of the World Health Organization and the amended International Health Regulations (2005), underscored the importance of resilient surveillance, early warning and rapid response systems and coordination.
"In this regard, we welcome the establishment of a dedicated Sub-Working Group to advance the BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for the prevention and response to Mass Infectious Diseases, and its Terms of Reference," they said.
Collective preparedness
The initiative is aimed at strengthening collective preparedness against infectious disease threats through closer coordination among member countries and faster sharing of information.
The declaration also called for greater regulatory cooperation to ensure that medical products remain available, accessible and meet standards of quality, safety and efficacy across BRICS countries.
"We encourage strengthened collaboration among BRICS Medical Products Regulatory Authorities by extending the scope of the existing Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in the field of medical products regulation to the Regulatory Authorities of all BRICS member countries," the declaration said.
Collaborative regulatory approaches
They reiterated the importance of strengthening collaborative regulatory approaches to ensure the continued availability and accessibility of quality, safe and efficacious medical products.
The leaders also welcomed the collective efforts of BRICS regulatory authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper.
"We welcome the collective efforts of BRICS Regulatory Authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper, consolidating best practices of regulatory experience and technical approaches," the declaration said.
The GxP refers broadly to good-practice standards followed in areas such as manufacturing, laboratory and clinical processes, with the common framework expected to facilitate greater sharing of regulatory experience and technical approaches among member countries.
Strengthen domestic health infrastructure
The leaders also linked health security with stronger domestic health infrastructure and local production of medical products, calling for greater preparedness for future health emergencies.
"We emphasize the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products, enhancing preparedness for future health emergencies through stronger surveillance systems, laboratory networks, leveraging digital health technology and Artificial Intelligence," the declaration said.
They also called for technical cooperation among public health institutes, development of robust regulatory frameworks, skilled health workforces and collaborative research and development.
The declaration stressed that these measures were needed to improve access to healthcare products and services and strengthen the capacity of BRICS countries to respond collectively to health emergencies.
People-centred digital healthcare systems
The leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to people-centred digital healthcare systems and welcomed the BRICS Compendium on Digital Health Architecture for Continuum of Care, including access to healthcare in remote areas.
The leaders also supported the activities of the BRICS Vaccine Research and Development Centre and recognised the importance of collaboration in nuclear medicine.
They welcomed the activities of the BRICS Nuclear Medicine Working Group and noted the importance of the BRICS Health Journal in disseminating research findings and promoting scientific cooperation within the BRICS framework.
The declaration also emphasised the importance of sharing experiences, innovations and best practices among BRICS countries to improve health outcomes and advance universal health coverage.
