HKIS paid substantial amount to US church co-founder to end ‘bad marriage’: source
Parties’ ‘fundamental’ differences would have led to more litigation if their partnership had continued, insider tells South China Morning Post
The US church group that co-founded Hong Kong International School (HKIS) accepted an out-of-court payment to end a “bad marriage”, a source has told the South China Morning Post, saying their differences would have led to more litigation if the partnership had continued.
He told the SCMP that the settlement might give the impression that the church had filed the lawsuit for pecuniary reasons but the LCMS regarded the payment as a necessary “penalty” the school needed to pay for a number of “breaches”.
“They paid a very, very substantial penalty because they were not aligned with the Lutheran mission,” the source said.
The church had accused the school of serving only the “rich and privileged few”, violating its mission and amassing a large amount of financial reserves. The school management countered that the LCMS’ legal action was financially motivated as the church had explored multiple options to develop part of the HKIS campus in Repulse Bay into a US$1 billion commercial project.
A High Court writ earlier indicated that the plaintiff threatened to evict the school from its Repulse Bay campus, while also seeking an indemnity of US$1.75 million. The LCMS remains the current registered owner of the campus.

For a week every month, I take a two-and-a-half-hour flight from Chicago to Winnipeg, Canada.
That might sound surprising: It's a lot of time to spend in the air, and Chicago has so much to offer. However, I've been in a long-distance relationship with my Canadian partner, Andrew, for over two years, and neither of us is ready to move just yet.
Andrew and I met at a conference for financial bloggers a decade ago, and we were great friends and colleagues for many years before we became a couple.
Today, we run an online business together, which allows us to work remotely and travel regularly between our countries. Because we both have children from previous marriages, neither of us plans to move countries anytime soon.
There are challenges, but I feel like I get the best of both worlds
As an American, I've gotten used to certain apps, tools, and conveniences that I can't access in Canada.
For example, Canada doesn't have Venmo or Cash App, so Andrew and I split costs or pay each other back using Wise. If we start a movie on Hulu, we can only watch it when we're in the States, since the streaming service isn't available in Canada.
As inconvenient as that can be, I often feel like I get the best of both worlds. Take food, for instance: Andrew looks forward to getting Chick-fil-A when he visits me, because there isn't a location in Winnipeg. (Although the chain does exist in some bigger Canadian cities, like Toronto.)
And, though we have A&W here in the US, it doesn't have poutine on the menu, which is the unofficial Canadian national dish. So, I always make sure to order that when I visit him.
I've found that the pace and culture feel very different in both places, too. As someone who's been self-employed for almost 15 years, I appreciate being able to surround myself with other motivated entrepreneurs whenever I'm here.
In Winnipeg and other Canadian cities I've visited, though, I've been able to slow down more. The pace feels more relaxed, and I often think of Canada as my safe haven.
In the future, we might choose both
There are also structural differences between the two places. Canadians fund their universal healthcare system through taxes, whereas a majority of Americans have private insurance.
What's nice about Canada's system is that residents don't have to stress about an unexpected bill or an expensive ER visit.
That said, there can be trade-offs, like longer wait times for emergency care and surgeries. In the US, I appreciate that I can usually make medical appointments quickly, even though they come at a cost.
There are parts of American culture that will always feel hard to leave, but spending so much time in Canada has also shown me that stepping away from hustle culture can be soothing for my soul.
There are parts of American life that Andrew appreciates, too — but I know that if we live elsewhere, he'll miss many aspects of his home, like his close-knit family and the beautiful, wide-open prairies in Winnipeg.
I'm not sure what the future holds once all our kids go to college, but we will likely spend half the year in Canada and then work remotely in a warmer area during the winter.
Whatever we choose, I know what will matter most is making sure we create a lifestyle that feels unique to us, a perfect blend of our cultures together.

Is the UK heading for a breakup? A fresh challenge is emerging as leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland prepare to join forces in a push for greater self-determination and the right to hold independence referendums.
According to The Telegraph, the leaders of the three devolved nations are set to meet in Wales' Cardiff for an unprecedented summit, where they are expected to sign a joint declaration asserting their right to hold independence referendums and determine their own constitutional futures.
The gathering comes at a politically sensitive moment for Westminster.
UK PM Andy Burnham recently told MPs that he would authorise another Scottish independence referendum if there were a “clear consensus” in favour of one.
The issue has gained further momentum after US President Donald Trump weighed in on Irish reunification. During a visit to Dublin on Saturday, Trump said he would “love” to see a united Ireland, describing Northern Ireland joining the Republic as “a great thing” and asking: “How can it be bad?”
The comments have added to pressure on the Burnham-led UK government as nationalist parties push for a greater say over their nations’ futures. 
PM Burnham has made the devolution of power in England a central part of his political agenda.
John Swinney, the SNP leader and Scottish first minister, has seized on the changing political landscape, claiming Burnham was “facing up to the idea that he will go down in history as the final prime minister of the United Kingdom”.
Pro-independence parties gain ground
The balance of power across the devolved nations has shifted significantly following Labour’s poor performance in Wales at May’s elections. For the first time, pro-independence parties are now in government across Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Plaid Cymru emerged as the largest party in the Cardiff Senedd, paving the way for its leader Rhun ap Iowerth to become Wales’ First Minister.
In Scotland, the SNP remained the dominant political force despite losing six Holyrood seats, with Reform and the Greens making gains.
Northern Ireland has also been under Sinn Fein leadership since Michelle O’Neill became First Minister in 2024. Sinn Fein had emerged as the largest party in the 2022 Stormont elections, although a DUP walkout delayed the formation of the executive. The party is widely expected to retain power when Northern Ireland votes again next year.
The Cardiff summit will bring together the three first ministers along with Mary Lou McDonald, Sinn Fein’s president and leader of the opposition in Ireland.
The leaders are expected to explore closer cooperation and discuss a renewed campaign for greater constitutional autonomy at the five-star St David’s Hotel overlooking Cardiff Bay.
‘Status quo is not sustainable’
Swinney said on Sunday: “For the first time ever, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are led by pro-independence first ministers. There could be no clearer sign that the status quo is not sustainable, and that Westminster must prepare for a post-UK future.
“The momentum behind serious constitutional change is undeniable. Andy Burnham must now be facing up to the idea that he will go down in history as the final prime minister of the United Kingdom.
“Tomorrow in Cardiff, I am looking forward to discussing a better future with partners from across these islands, and that only comes with the fresh start of independence.”
The joint declaration is expected to underline the three nations’ claim to self-determination while putting further political pressure on Westminster.
Burnham’s recent remarks have already opened the door to renewed debate over Scottish independence. During Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday, he said another referendum could be held if public opinion backed one.
He told the House of Commons that the trigger for a separation vote was “exactly the same situation in Scotland” as Northern Ireland.
The Good Friday Agreement provides a potential constitutional route for Northern Ireland to hold a referendum on reunification with Ireland. Under its terms, such a vote should be held if it “appears likely” that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would choose to leave the UK.

Leaders in the United Kingdom nations of Wales, Scotland, Ireland, and Northern Ireland are planning to start a campaign to break up the Union, as per a report by The Telegraph.
The publication reports that a summit is being organised in Cardiff on Monday in which the the first ministers of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland will converge to sign a joint declaration that will demand their right to hold referendums of independence from the United Kingdom. Also present will be Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald.
This move brings together governments and political leaders who wish to sever their constitutional ties with Westminster.
This meeting comes in the wake of UK PM Andy Burnham suggesting to MPs that if there was 'clear consensus' favouring a referndum in Scotland, he would authorise the same.
What is happening in Cardiff?
John Swinney, the First Minister of Scotland, Rhun ap Iorwerth, the First Minister of Wales, and Michelle O’Neill, the first minister of Northern Ireland are expected to meet on Monday to talk on constitutional changes. The gathering is set to take place at the five-star St David's Hotel, The Telegraph reported.
They are expected to put forward a joint memorandum that would assert the rights of their citizens to hold independence referendums.
The meeting gains significance because this is the first time the three governments will pursue constitutional ambitions in unison, thus making their challenge to London's supremacy a more coordinated effort.
Swinney said regarding the development, ""The momentum behind serious constitutional change is undeniable. Andy Burnham must now be facing up to the idea that he will go down in history as the final prime minister of the United Kingdom," as per the publication.
Why is this happening now?
Leaders from Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland are coming together at this time because of the sharply changed political climate in the UK.
After the May elections in Wales, Plaid Cymru emerged as the largest party in the country's Senedd, which made Rhun ap Iorwerth its First Minister.
On the other hand, in Scotland, the centre-left Scottish National Party (SNP) continues to remain the dominant pro-independence force while the government of Northern Ireland is led by Sinn Féin through Michelle O’Neill.
This means that all the three devolved administrations are led by pro-independence politicians who have been advocating for major constitutional change.
Donald Trump adds fuel to fire
The Irish question has received attention from US President Donald Trump, who, during his visit to Dublin, said that he would like to see a united Ireland.
Describing the prospect as positive, Trump told reporters, "You have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together," as per a report by Reuters.
However, he said that he won't be talking about Scotland yet: "You asked about Scotland. That one I won't talk about yet. I'll save that for another day."

Tamil Nadu Minister for Health and Family Welfare K.G. Arunraj on Tuesday (September 8, 2026) announced in the Legislative Assembly that the State government would implement a Statewide mission to reduce the amount of salt in the daily diet of the public.
Dr. Arunraj said non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and kidney disorders were among the most important public health challenges in Tamil Nadu. Nearly 50% of medically certified deaths in Tamil Nadu are caused by cardiovascular diseases. Approximately 1.8 crore people in Tamil Nadu are living with hypertension.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that a person should consume less than five grams of salt a day. However, scientific studies indicate that the people of Tamil Nadu consume an average of 7 to 8 grams of salt per day. Studies have also found that approximately 88% of the salt consumed as part of the South Indian diet comes from salt added during cooking at home. Global scientific studies have established that even a reduction of just one gram of salt per day can significantly lower blood pressure, he said.
Further, an international study involving approximately 21,000 people who used a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of the sodium was replaced with potassium, demonstrated a 14% reduction in strokes and a 12% reduction in overall mortality. Based on this scientific evidence, the State government has decided to formulate and implement an integrated strategy to reduce high salt consumption in Tamil Nadu, Dr. Arunraj said.
Statewide survey
Announcing the key initiatives under the mission, Dr. Arunraj said for the first time, a Statewide survey based on urine samples would be undertaken to scientifically determine the current level of salt consumption among the people of Tamil Nadu.
Standards would be implemented to gradually reduce the amount of salt used in kitchens under the direct control of the government, including those serving the Nutritious Meal Programme, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, government hospitals and hostels, he said.
The feasibility of making available to the public a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of sodium is replaced with potassium and which does not produce a noticeable difference in taste, would be studied as a pilot project in selected areas, he said.
Through the ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ initiative and Health and Wellness Centres, people with hypertension would receive systematic counselling on reducing salt intake. A Statewide awareness campaign will be undertaken to educate people about salt content in food and simple ways to gradually reduce the excessive use of salt in everyday home cooking, he added.

In the last decade, the cost of youth sports has skyrocketed. Cheaper, more local rec leagues have lost out premium travel leagues funded by private equity. The Covid-19 pandemic made things worse. As a result, some families are now paying thousands of dollars to keep their kid in a sport that they love.
The cost of youth sports is out of control
Private equity is having a field day — but kids are not.
Caitlin Moscatello wrote about the phenomenon last month for New York magazine. She says the shift started during the pandemic when park and rec budgets were slashed and the premium leagues became the only game in town. Private money saw the opportunity and seized it. Now, participating in youth sports means you’re caught in a pay-to-play model.
In return, elementary-aged children are being railroaded into a professionalized environment before they’re ready. More children are suffering from overuse injuries and are getting locked into a sport before they even have time to decide if they love it.
Moscatello joined Today, Explained co-host Noel King to break down what happened to youth sports, the impact on children, and whether it’s possible to reverse this trend.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Private money in youth sports doesn’t seem to make a ton of sense. Who’s going to make money off of an 8-year-old playing soccer? And yet what you found is there’s a lot going on here. Give me a broad sense of what’s been happening.
It was a little over a decade ago that you really started to see this influx of big money coming into the youth sports sector. And what you see right before and then certainly after Covid is investors using what’s called a roll-up strategy — where they own, or have a financial stake in, different touch points that families would have in the sport that their child’s playing.
For instance, they might have a stake in the league itself, but also the apparel company where families are required to buy the uniforms, and the software or the app that families need to go on to look at the team’s schedule, and in some cases look at updated stats and standings. There can be a hotel partner, so even though there’s a less expensive hotel down the street, they’re required to stay at this specific hotel.
There’s also money to be made on what’s being called the media side of all this. Parents described to me not being able to record video at their child’s game, but then being sold a package of photos and videos, which, again, is just another financial touchpoint.
How much are parents spending on sports?
But ultimately, in their quest to do something good for their kids, the way that the sports ecosystem has changed and is continuing to change can potentially set them up for long-term harm.
The average spend is a little over $1,000 a year, but many of the families that I spoke with, especially in this travel private club sector, can spend anywhere from $3,000 a season. It can be $5,000 or $10,000 a season depending on the sport, where you are, the level of play. I spoke with numerous families who were spending $25,000 a year.
There was one mother that I spoke with. She’s a single mom. She was pet-sitting on the side in addition to her full-time job to help offset the cost of her son’s $25,000-a-year hockey program. I also came across a lot of GoFundMes for families who are trying to get their 6-year-old or their 7-year-old or their 8-year-old who made the travel fill-in-the-blank soccer, baseball team. And they’re fundraising to try to make that happen.
And for your $25,000 or more a year, what are you getting?
It’s a loaded question. Part of what’s drawing families to this in some areas is that they really feel like they have no other choice. Rec programs are sparse. They also don’t extend as long as they used to.
I’m an elder millennial, I guess I would say, and back in the ’90s, it was still very much that you could play a rec sport through eighth grade and then if you chose to, go on and play in high school. What’s happening is that rec programs now are ending much earlier. In some places it can be difficult to find a rec program after maybe third or fourth grade. And these programs are also getting diluted because the private leagues are incentivized to attract families earlier and earlier.
Now you start to see travel teams and even tryouts for kindergartners, first-graders, second-graders. And what I was hearing from parents over and over again was that there was this fear of missing out: “This isn’t something I would necessarily choose for my kid, but if we don’t get in on the ground floor, the elevator’s going to go up without us and we’re never going to catch up and my kid won’t be able to play and everyone around me seems to be doing this now, so we’re going to do it too.”
What this does to the rec programs is that it dilutes them really early in a couple of ways. One, it just brings the level of play down when kids start leaving in the first and second grade, by third grade. Also, there just aren’t as many kids.
And then the other factor is that kids and parents both notice that these other leagues exist. And so another thing that I kept hearing was, “Well, the rec programs sort of felt second-rate and we’re looking across the field.” There was this one father, he’s a lacrosse coach and he has two children who now play travel lacrosse. And he’s like, “It’s kind of hard when you look across the field and you see the kids with their shiny helmets and their fancy uniforms and their professional coach.”
What did you find all of this money in youth sports is doing to the youths playing the sports?
The benefits of sports have been really well established. Kids who play sports have everything from higher levels of academic achievement to higher self-esteem, better long-term health outcomes.
But ultimately, in their quest to do something good for their kids, the way that the sports ecosystem has changed and is continuing to change can potentially set them up for long-term harm. It can be psychological. So they’re seeing stress and anxiety, burnout, but also physical [harm].
There’s a surge of overuse injuries now in young athletes, especially because the private programs are incentivized again to get kids playing as much as possible. And so what’s happening now is that you have young children playing in this hyper-competitive year-round environment.
Medical advice has said that kids should play all different sports, use different muscles, learn different skills. And that’s what’s appropriate for young developing bodies, not playing one sport 10 to 12 months a year, tournaments on the weekends, six games, practices three or four times a week where then you see these overuse injuries, because kids are just doing that same motion over and over again.
Is there any movement among parents to stop this, to say, “This has gone too far, let’s not do it anymore.”
This is a collective action problem. If more parents stayed in the rec programs, then we would have a more robust rec system: more kids play, it’s more accessible, it’s more affordable. It’s also local and fun.
I don’t want to be so naive and think, “Oh, things could go back to the way they were in the ’90s.” I think you can’t put the toothpaste back in the tube entirely. But the good news is that we do have a model for a pathway forward.
Minnesota Ice Hockey is a nonprofit youth sports program, the core of which is 250 public rinks. The cost to play is about $200 to $400. Coaches are volunteers, but they are trained through USA Hockey. And these kids play more in that rec model where they play with other kids from their community.
This is showing real results. You look at this program and there’s 60,000 kids who play Minnesota ice hockey and Minnesota produces more D1 men’s and women’s ice hockey players than any other state in the country.
And really what this comes down to is it’s accessible to everyone. And so it’s more of a meritocracy, right? Everyone gets to play, and everyone gets to have fun. And then the kids who really do eventually show a high level of ability, they still get to play at that really competitive level because it’s not diluted. That has shown that it can produce really amazing hockey players while giving all these kids a good experience.

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed
- Published
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.
Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.
The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.
Playing on through injury could have disastrous consequences for the rest of the season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year.
"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.
"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.
"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.
"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."
Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.
She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.
Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.
"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.
"I still can't believe it."
Composed Rybakina 'like a machine'
Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.
Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.
She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.
Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but Rybakina who dominated the decider.
While the Belarusian grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.
"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."
However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.
At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she cooly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.
The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.
Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.
'She will win many more Slams'
On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.
She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".
"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.
"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.
"It's not going to be easy to hang onto it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."
Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.
After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.
She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.
Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.
"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

Oracle’s proposed investment in 2 gigawatts of renewable energy projects for New Mexico comes as local opposition could delay development of the Project Jupiter data center that Oracle is building for OpenAI.
The two tech companies are developing the $165 billion Project Jupiter data center in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, as part of the broader Stargate AI infrastructure project announced by President Donald Trump in 2025. But Project Jupiter faces local protests and court battles over concerns about its environmental impacts—and the latest Oracle announcement on September 8 seeking proposals for renewable energy projects does not change the fact that the data center will be powered by fuel cells that consume natural gas.
“Like all matching programs, this would be synthetic in the sense that 2 GW of renewables wouldn’t directly power the data center,” wrote Michael Thomas, CEO of the Cleanview data platform that tracks renewable energy and data center projects, in a LinkedIn post.
Oracle and OpenAI had originally planned to build 2.2 gigawatts of natural gas generation that could have resulted in 14 million tons of CO2 emissions per year, Thomas pointed out. That would have effectively “wiped out 20 years of carbon emissions reductions in the state of New Mexico,” he wrote in his post.
State residents and environmental groups have rallied in opposition to Project Jupiter with protests and lawsuits. New Mexico’s Land Office twice blocked requests to run a natural gas pipeline to the data center in New Mexico’s Doña Ana County.
Such opposition likely prompted the tech companies’ Project Jupiter plan to pivot from gas turbines to fuel-cell technology, which produces electricity through an electrochemical process without combustion.

Six Nigerians accused of romance scams to be extradited to the US
- Published
South African police are handing over six Nigerians wanted in the US for alleged online romance scams to FBI agents later on Friday.
The group is accused of targeting over 100 women in the US and defrauding them of more than 100m rand ($6m; £5m), the South African authorities said.
Those being extradited were arrested in 2021 and are believed to be members of crime syndicate Black Axe - a Nigerian mafia-style gang tied to human trafficking, internet fraud and murder.
Some of their reported victims included pensioners and businesspeople "who were targeted through sophisticated online relationships used to defraud them of their money", according to South Africa's elite Hawks police unit.
The group will be "transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town" to the airport on Friday morning, where they will be "handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service", Hawks spokesperson Colonel Katlego Mogale said in a statement.
They would face wire fraud and money-laundering charges upon their arrival in the US, she added.

Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network known for its extreme violence and operates across Africa, Europe and North America.
A BBC Eye investigation in 2021 suggested that the syndicate had become one of the most far-reaching and dangerous organised crime groups in the world.

'Today the game was unprotected' - Arteta fumes but Arsenal survive
- Published
Arsenal's duality was there for all to see in their 2-0 win at Sunderland: gritty defence and moments of genius.
But things could have turned out very differently had a crucial 121-second period gone the other way.
After close to an hour of physical, full-blooded football, Sunderland were given a penalty when Ezri Konsa fouled Dan Ballard at a corner.
It proved the turning point - David Raya tipped Enzo le Fee's spot kick on to the post, and just over two minutes later, Arsenal substitute Bruno Guimaraes crashed in the opener off the underside of the crossbar.
Arteta's side left the north-east of England with their ninth successive Premier League victory. Not since the days of the Invincibles, in 2003-04, have the Gunners done that.
Yet Arteta was furious about the Sunderland penalty that could have cost his side.
"It's a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri [Konsa] does nothing. Just watch it," Arteta told BBC Match of the Day.
"We have a lot of cameras and VAR, we have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the game and the momentum which is a really, really serious thing."
Referee John Brooks took a few seconds to point to the penalty spot after Ballard and Konsa hit the ground, but once he did the VAR stuck with his decision.
Konsa was certainly committing a foul, though Ballard did appear to have a hold of the Arsenal man.
"This should never happen, it's not fair, and I am sad, very sad, in that sense," said Arteta, who was booked in the first half for repeatedly leaving his technical area.
"I'm making it very clear publicly because it's for the game, it's not only for Arsenal, this cannot happen at this level.
"It's not acceptable, I've watched it 20 times and can't think of why it was given."
This season, Premier League referees have been instructed to clamp down on grappling at corners, something that became a big talking point last term.
"With the new laws trying to get rid of the grappling, Konsa is all over Ballard. You have to be looking at the ball," former England midfielder Karen Carney said on TNT Sports.
"Ballard was holding Konsa's arm but you run the risk," added former Arsenal defender Martin Keown.
"They want to stamp down on it so there is no point arguing about it."
However, Arteta was not alone in questioning the decision.
"It's absolutely not a penalty. He has got it completely wrong, Konsa's shoulder is pulled down by Ballard and he lands on top," former Wales defender Ashley Williams said on BBC Match of the Day.
"It's like a perfect toss in judo. It's very clever by Ballard but in no way is it a penalty."
'Magnificent' Raya and defence survive 'chaotic' moments
Though Arteta spoke more about the awarding of the penalty rather than Raya's saving of it, there is no denying that the Spanish goalkeeper's intervention changed the direction of the match.
The save - only Raya's second penalty stop in the Premier League - came at a time when Sunderland were putting the defending champions under pressure.
Though Le Fee telegraphed his effort, Raya had to be at full stretch to tip it on to the post. Until that point, the goalkeeper had largely been a spectator.
"He keeps us alive in the game, that unbelievable moment saving the penalty," Guimaraes told TNT Sports.
"I think after this moment we [took from it] a big confidence to play forward and score our goal."
"This penalty save is exceptional. He gets out so quick," former Brentford manager Thomas Frank - the man who signed Raya - said on BBC Match of the Day.
"For me he's the best goalkeeper in the Premier League and one of the best in the world."
After building last season's title-winning campaign on a stubborn defence, the Gunners have begun this season with five clean sheets in six matches in all competitions, including in all three away matches.
"It is a fantastic win and the ground work was done by the defence. They have weathered the storm and the goalkeeper steps up and makes a wonderful save," Keown said.
"He is very important to Arsenal and what they achieve. He was magnificent and doesn't get the credit he deserves."
Though seething about the penalty, Arteta took the opportunity during his post-match media conference to praise his side's defensive efforts.
"We knew we would have to go through some difficult and chaotic moments to have the right to win this game," he said. "But we have done it."
Guimaraes makes his mark
On a night when Arsenal were not at their fluid best, one hero was not going to be enough.
Guimaraes stepped up with a goal of the season contender, a curling effort from the edge of the penalty area.
The Brazilian midfielder has had a tough start to life at Arsenal since his £75m summer move from Newcastle, failing to start a match since the Community Shield.
Now recovered from a minor hamstring injury, he showed exactly what he can offer.
"That goal is about personality and character. It was him saying: I am going to make my mark at this football club," Keown said.
"He has been watching on the sidelines, but has said: 'Take a look at me - this is what I can do.'
"Boy did he shut the crowd up. A class player, going to the next level."
Of all the teams to announce himself against, Guimaraes chose the arch-rivals of his former employers Newcastle.
"It was a beautiful goal. Everyone knows my past, I had an amazing history at Newcastle," Guimaraes told TNT Sports.
"But now I'm trying to create a new history here and I start with the right foot."
This match could have turned out very differently for Arsenal, but in the end, it was heroes old and new that got the job done.

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.

Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return gets a very British roast in Saturday Night Live UK sketch
The 4-minute bit took aim at Netflix deal, Markle's lifestyle empire and Royal Family tensions
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan's highly publicized return to England got the full Saturday Night Live UK treatment — and in true British fashion, the welcome was served with a distinctly chilly reception.

The four-minute, 52-second bit took aim at, among other things, the couple's deal with Netflix, Meghan's television and business ventures, and the Royal Family's long-running controversies surrounding race.
The cold open began with Harry and Meghan, played by Jack Shep and Ayoade Bamgboye, visiting King Charles and Queen Camilla, portrayed by Larry Dean and Emma Sidi, at a sketch-set version of Balmoral Castle — the Scottish estate where Charles traditionally spends his summer retreat.
"Daddy, I'm home!" Harry proclaims to his father as he walks through the doorway. But the make-believe monarch seems less than pleased to see his son.
"Harry, what are you two doing here?" he scowls. "This castle is for royals only."
The fictional couple reveal that they are moving back to the U.K. "and need your help."
That sets the stage for Charles's withering indictment of the couple's finances and post-royal ventures.
"Don’t tell me you spent all your Netflix money already," Charles bemoans, referring to the multi-year production deal the couple signed with Netflix after they left the U.K. and stepped down as working royals in 2020. According to People, the five-year contract came to an end in 2025 after Netflix chose not to renew the deal under the same terms.
"Daddy, it was $60 million. How long was it meant to last?" Harry responded, drawing laughs from the studio audience.
Under the Netflix deal, the Sussexes produced several projects, including the wildly popular docuseries Harry & Meghan and Meghan's upbeat lifestyle and cooking program, With Love, Meghan.
Meghan used the latter Netflix series as a promotional platform for her lifestyle brand, As Ever, featuring jams, teas and honeys on the show. That, too, became fodder for Saturday's sketch, which didn't miss the opportunity to poke fun at her attempt to position herself as a lifestyle guru.
"Hey, step-queen, I brought you a gift ... it's ice ... I made it myself," the fictional Meghan told Camilla. "I'm kind of a whiz in the kitchen."
"It's true," Harry added. "She hires the best cooks."
Among the sketch's other biting moments, the writers appeared to reference Harry and Meghan's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, during which they discussed controversial comments allegedly made within the Royal Family about what colour their son Prince Archie's skin might be.
During Saturday night's cold open, when Camilla greeted the couple, she began by saying, "Hello, sweet Harry," while kissing him on the cheek. Then, turning to the fictional Meghan, she said: "And beautiful Meghan, as brown as ever."
The segment then transitioned into a spoof of Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, after SNL UK breakout star George Fouracres — portraying Burnham — burst into the room. The remainder of the skit focused on teasing Burnham's perceived obsession with being viewed as a "regular guy" while Prince Harry and Meghan ignored him and canoodled in the background.
The Duke and Duchess returned to the U.K. from the United States with their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, late last month. The family is expected to live privately outside of London.
No official reason has been given for the relocation. The couple's children have been enrolled in British schools and reportedly started classes this month.

‘Murdered’ woman in Bihar turns up alive in Jharkhand, was living with lover
The body of an unidentified woman was recovered from a canal near Khanda village. The woman’s brother identified the body as his sister’s.
A woman believed to have been murdered in Bihar’s Rohtas district 12 years ago and whose husband, father-in-law and six relatives were sent to jail for the crime has been found living with her paramour in Jharkhand’s Garhwa district, according to police officers aware of the development.
“The woman, Saraswati Devi alias Kanti Devi, was produced before a court in Sasaram on Saturday following a case registered against her for misleading the police,” Rohtas SP Raj said.
According to the woman’s father-in-law, Dilip Mehta, his son Arun Mehta of Balrati Bigha, married Saraswati Devi, a resident of Pirauta village in Aurangabad district, in 2002. The couple had a son after two years into the marriage. Twelve years later, in 2014, Devi ran off with Rattu Singh, a fellow villager without the family’s knowledge.

(Bloomberg) -- Every year, a summer lull in the United Arab Emirates gives way to a September rush. Offices fill up, school buses ferry children through city streets once again, hotels prepare for tourists chasing winter sun while professionals swarm to conferences across the country.
This year, the ritual will test the resilience of the UAE’s post-pandemic boom and whether low taxes and an attractive lifestyle can keep drawing people and capital amid a war that’s showing few signs of resolution. For now, its business as usual in parts of the economy.
Abu Dhabi’s wealth funds are still putting billions to work, encouraging Wall Street banks to add more Gulf staff, while the rush of hedge funds continues. Malls across Dubai and Abu Dhabi are packed with residents chasing “back to school” offers, and restaurants have remained busy.
Still, challenges remain as the regional conflict stretches into its seventh month. Continuing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has raised import costs and fuel prices, while disrupting supply chains. Airport traffic, hotel occupancy and property sales have dropped, and recruiters say they are having to adjust packages to keep attracting the best talent.
Though the intensity of hostilities has abated since the peak of the war, when the Gulf country successfully fended off thousands of projectiles from Tehran, attacks on shipping and Gulf nations continue. The UAE said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters as recently as Aug. 31, prompting a senior adviser to decry “the state of neither war nor peace” and call for a sustainable solution.
Yet hours after that attempted attack, roads around schools in Dubai and Abu Dhabi were jammed with cars as children streamed in for the first day back — an example of how the most significant shock in the country’s history has, so far, not fundamentally disrupted many routines underpinning its economy.
At Brookfield-backed GEMS Education, about 1,800 students relocated when the war began and roughly 700 have returned, Chief Executive Officer Dino Varkey said. He expects 147,000 enrollments this year, 2,000 more than 2025, but cautioned growth may be softer than historic levels.
Dubai-listed Taaleem Holdings PSC has seen enrollment across its private schools rise roughly 7% from the previous academic year to about 19,500. CEO Alan Williamson said its schools were “still seeing demand outstripping supply even in what we would all agree has been a very challenging period.”
Tellingly, seven new private schools opened in Dubai this year, adding 17,000 new places, including branches of international institutions where fees can run as high as about $42,000 a year. Britain’s Harrow and Rugby School have unveiled Dubai campuses this year, while Harrow has plans for an Abu Dhabi branch next year.
There are also signs of broader economic momentum. While the central bank expects GDP growth to slow to 1.7% this year, economists surveyed by Bloomberg now anticipate a rebound of about 7% in 2027.
The UAE’s financial hubs continue to grow, even as competition for global capital intensifies. Singapore and Hong Kong are offering incentives to hedge fund managers, while Greece has recently attracted some big names. Still, Dubai International Financial Centre crossed 10,000 active companies, while Abu Dhabi’s ADGM issued almost 2,000 licenses and added 4,700 workers in the first half of the year.
But the influx appears to be broader than finance. Dubai’s population hit 4.58 million at the end of 2025, and the city added around 200,000 residents this year, according to government figures.
Also Read: London and Dubai Wealth Concerns See Turkey Make a Play for Rich
That increase is showing up in traffic. Activity near DIFC recovered to about 90% of pre-war levels before slipping in August during the school break, according to mobility analytics firm xMap. The rebound was slightly more muted around Palm Jumeirah and Dubai Marina, likely because those areas are more dependent on tourism.
Abu Dhabi’s $2 trillion in sovereign wealth and deep pools of private capital in Dubai have underpinned the relative strength. Officials have rolled out incentives for sectors like tourism and housing, while an uptick in dealmaking from sovereign entities is prompting firms that work with them to add headcount. Many have started offering more generous allowances for housing, return flights and family travel.
“Employers would rather offer a one-off guarantee or relocation protection than bake a temporary geopolitical risk into permanent compensation,” said Greg Agius, Switzerland-based CEO of the eponymous recruitment firm specializing in finance and private banking.
Demand for artificial intelligence talent also remains strong, though international candidates are doing more due diligence before relocating to the region, said Dan Wardle, a recruiter at tech recruitment firm Discovered.
Elsewhere in the Middle East’s fourth-largest economy, growth in parts of the real estate sector is softening. Sales have slowed relative to the boom years that followed the pandemic and some rents have eased. Still, sellers have largely held off on price cuts. Governments have introduced programs to support residents, including flexible monthly rent payments in Dubai and a rent freeze in Abu Dhabi.
Inflation remains a concern, in line with most other economies contending with the global jump in energy costs and disrupted trade. The UAE’s gasoline prices have climbed about 60% since the war began, though they remain significantly below levels in the US and UK. Growth in the UAE’s consumer price index will accelerate to 3.2% in 2026 before easing to 2.3% in 2027, according to the median of 11 economist estimates compiled by Bloomberg.
Ahmed Galal Ismail, the CEO of Dubai-based Majid Al Futtaim, said the conglomerate is navigating a “challenging operating environment,” with hospitality dented by a pullback in tourism and non-food retail facing product availability issues. The group is passing on some higher costs to shoppers, while consumers are delaying big-ticket purchases, he told Bloomberg TV.
Those strains are most acute at Jebel Ali Free Zone and its port, which together account for at least a fifth of Dubai’s GDP. The UAE is now trying to rejig supply chains and develop new export routes, while outlining a multibillion-dollar infrastructure push as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to bypass the waterway.
The conflict has also impacted traffic at Dubai International Airport, which fell by almost a third in the first six months of the year. The hub expects demand to recover later in 2026, but has pushed back its target of 100 million annual passengers.
Dubai hotel occupancy fell to about 64% in August from 76% a year earlier, while room rates dropped about 10%, according to Philip Wooller, Middle East and Africa director at CoStar. “That, considering the reduction in international business, is still a remarkable result,” he said.
That’s due in part to a range of incentives on offer, including campaigns offering free medical insurance and visa-free travel for international visitors. Many hotels and restaurants have also targeted residents with staycation deals and discounts to weather the slowdown.
On a late August weekend, the Atlantis hotel’s Aquaventure water park, built on an artificial palm-shaped island, was packed with people enjoying a reprieve from the desert heat. Upmarket restaurants in the city’s DIFC have remained bustling even during the traditionally slow August.
A stronger recovery may partly depend on the full return of international airlines. Most global carriers remain suspended, with Turkish and Indian airlines among the exceptions.
Hotel operators are already seeing signs of improvement. Philippe Zuber, CEO of Kerzner International, which operates the Atlantis hotels and One&Only Resorts, said regional demand is being bolstered by a gradual return of international travelers, pushing occupancy across its Dubai properties over 80% for the year-end festive period.
Occupancy will likely get a further boost from conferences rescheduled for the final months of the year after being postponed during the conflict. The period is also typically the UAE’s busiest for tourism, with several high-profile restaurants slated to open in Dubai and Abu Dhabi ahead of the expected pickup.
December will bring a slate of major events, including the Formula One Abu Dhabi Grand Prix and the opening of the Guggenheim museum. Abu Dhabi Finance Week has also lined up some of the biggest names in global finance for its annual gathering that month.
Beyond the year-end calendar, the UAE’s traditional advantages should continue to draw expatriates, according to Monica Mali, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank.
“The various indicators point to the UAE’s population as remaining,” she said. “A favorable business environment, including low taxes, world class infrastructure and access to labor will continue to stand out in the medium term.”

Months after Turning Point USA CEO Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, a rumor circulated online that his widow, Erika Kirk, had announced she was pregnant shortly after her husband's death.
The claim about her supposed pregnancy resurfaced (archived) about a year after Kirk's killing, with many people online noting that the baby should have been born by then.
Some social media users speculated it was an example of the "Mandela Effect" — a phenomenon that occurs when people collectively misremember reality.
"Wait wasn't erika kirk supposed to be pregnant or is that some kind of mandela effect?" one TikTok user asked in July 2026. The post (archived), which received more than 4.2 million views as of this writing, was captioned: "It's been well over 9 months."
Dozens of Snopes readers searched searched the site for answers.
While Erika Kirk has repeatedly talked about the two children she had with Charlie Kirk, there's no evidence that she announced she was pregnant again after her husband was assassinated. The rumor has persisted since the shooting took place. We first looked into it in September 2025 and found no evidence that it was true.
In November 2025, during an interview with conservative commentator Megyn Kelly, Erika Kirk said that she and Charlie Kirk had wanted four children.
"I was praying to God that I was pregnant when he got murdered," she said. "I was like, oh goodness, that would be the ultimate blessing out of this catastrophe."
She did not confirm she was pregnant at any point during the interview.
Despite dozens of false claims — often generated using artificial intelligence tools — that Erika Kirk announced she was pregnant after her husband died, Snopes found no evidence in publicly available sources that she made such an announcement.
For further reading, we previously investigated claims that Erika Kirk lost her children in a custody battle and that she had an affair with U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

Mario-a-Lago Kart, Anyone?
The White House made a bunch of parody video games. We have more suggestions.
This week, the White House removed a Tetris-inspired game called Build the Wall from its recently launched arcade website after the Tetris Company publicly warned that it takes copyright law “very seriously.”
Here are a few options the White House might consider to replace the game:
Super PAC-Man
Players direct a round creature with a constantly moving mouth through a maze as he munches on tiny coins. Meanwhile, the ghosts of financial lawsuits past pursue Super PAC-Man—but consuming excerpts from favorable Supreme Court rulings allows him to temporarily devour these ghosts, too. Once Super PAC-Man collects all the coins, he progresses, unsatiated, to the next level, where he sends out a single text and all the money starts flowing directly toward him.
Words With Enemies
Players form new, hateful attacks in this Scrabble-like multiplayer game using letters cut from public-school textbooks, removed museum displays, and maps depicting the former Lake Ontario. Highest-scoring insults include: SCUZZY, ZANY, and LOW-IQ JOKER. Extra points are awarded for letters placed on various Random Capitalization Squares.
Mario-a-Lago Kart
Up to four players race golf carts around a cartoonishly decorated beach club, crashing through boxes of classified documents to unlock power-ups including nuclear footballs and black markers for unlimited redactions. Between races, players can refuel at the gas pump, assuming they have collected the requisite 175,000 coins per gallon. The winner receives a golf trophy; second, third, and fourth place—as well as any observers or people simply standing nearby—get access to state secrets.
Grand Theft Crypto
This game is all in the timing: Players must market their own cryptocurrency, then wait until just the right moment to cash out, crashing the currency and tanking other players’ life savings.
The Oregon Data Center
Modern-day pioneers move into a covered wagon after an eminent-domain order for the construction of a data center displaces them from their hometown. Drinking water is scarce, noise pollution is earsplitting, and morale is low as players try to survive the perilous journey to one of the few remaining corners of protected parkland. Inevitably, all players die when artificial general intelligence bioengineers a new form of dysentery.
Goldeneye
In this first-person interior-design game, players gild every nook, cranny, and free patch of wall space in their virtual home office.
Coal Minecraft
No longer beholden to child-labor regulations, players ages 6 to 8 design their own pickaxes before descending 1,500 feet down a shaft to mine bituminous coal. Open-world play means that the only limit is kids’ imagination and black lung and tunnel collapse.
Super Smash the Kennedy Center
Players battle conservationists, historians, and patrons of the arts atop a revered memorial building, destroying it in the process. Downloadable content expands play to the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, and the East Wing of the White House.
Candy Crush the American Dream
Players rearrange foods that were once safe to eat into matching groups to make them disappear as part of an FDA recall. But miss just one, and players will contract a parasitic infection that sends them to the hospital, where they will incur astronomical medical bills, which will prevent them from qualifying for a mortgage, which will force them to move back in with their parents.
President Evil
A zombie occupies the most powerful office in the world. At the conclusion of Level 2, President Evil might insist that the game isn’t over, but so long as it works as intended, someone else will finally get a turn to play.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Camila Valim. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I spent two decades in corporate as head of marketing for an entertainment group. I left that job due to burnout. I pivoted to becoming a professional organizer and started a successful Instagram account and business.
Then I got divorced five years ago and had to return to the corporate world.
I went back to what I knew, working as a marketing consultant. My contract ended eight months ago. I expected it, but the job search to find a new marketing client has been tough.
I've only had 2 interviews
In eight months, I've only had two interviews. I've been carrying my whole household as a single parent and sole provider for two kids, ages 9 and 12.
I got very far in an interview process a few weeks ago for a head of brand and communications position. It felt like my last lifeline. I told myself, "OK, when I get this job, I'll be able to keep my lifestyle as it is; I won't have to sell my house." I was picking my kids up at school when I got the call that they loved me, but someone else got the job.
I knew then I had to make really serious decisions and take steps that weren't going to be fun.
My food delivery job is flexible
A cousin suggested I do meal deliveries on my e-bike while I searched for a new corporate job.
The process was very quick, and I got approved to deliver in no time. It's flexible and fits with my single-parent schedule. I can be there for my kids, still look for a job in corporate, and create content and rebuild my organizing business at once.
I've learned a lot on the bike, such as punctuality in a way I've never had to deal with before. I'm bringing food and smiles to people at their doors, and I love the freedom of being on the bike. It's a rush, and it gives me time to think. I have lots of insights and ideas on the bike.
The freedom has helped me create healthy space in my mind and take my creativity places it hasn't been before. For example, while on the bike, I had the idea to print out my story and CV and hand them out to people. I deliver to a lot of people who work for big businesses.
I will take income in any form I can get and do whatever it takes. I'm working on growing my Instagram account again. I know I have to sell my house, but I'm grateful I have it as a backup plan to put more money on the table to put food on the table.
I think people recognize themselves in me
This is a bridge for me until my house sells. I cannot live off of delivering food, and I am still pursuing the next chapter of my career.
I posted an Instagram reel about how this is not how I saw life at 45. It went viral. It has almost 900,000 views. I think it went viral because I was refusing to feel ashamed, and I hopefully gave other people permission to stop feeling ashamed, too.
I expected it to resonate with women, but it resonated with men as well. I have women and men messaging me, saying they've never told anyone they're in the same position. I think that tells you how much silence there is around this for everyone.

Uganda set to bury onetime 'boy king' whose death has sparked a succession battle
The funeral is underway in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34
KAMPALA, Uganda -- The funeral was underway Saturday in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34, triggering a succession dispute that has rocked the royal family and gripped the entire nation.
The funeral of Tooro's King Oyo Nyimba in a cathedral in the remote city of Fort Portal, near the Congo border, concludes a nine-day mourning period that was blemished by an increasingly acrimonious dispute over who should succeed him. He will be buried next to his ancestors later on Saturday.
King Oyo, as he was best known to his subjects, was unmarried when he died late in August after suffering from cancer. Elders with the kingdom’s ruling clan, known as the Babiito, said he never declared an heir to them, disputing the account of others in the kingdom who said he left behind a son born out of wedlock. The son has not been publicly identified, leading to sensational claims on social media of at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo’s children.
On Wednesday, a committee of Tooro elders announced that they had chosen a prince working as a journalist to succeed Oyo, earning praise from traditionalists who want an adult on the throne and rebuke from the king’s closest relatives.
Oyo’s sister, Ruth Komuntale, said the announcement sought to “bring division and turmoil.” Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death. “I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.”
Traditional monarchs are beloved but don’t wield any formal power in the East African country.
Oyo was crowned in 1995, at the age of 3, after his father’s death. He was a curious child in colorful robes and an object of adoration for his hundreds of thousands of followers.
At his coronation, he went through a series of tribal rituals and was led into the royal cemetery to perform a coming-of-age ceremony: successfully tossing nine coffee beans into his father’s tomb.
Amid the ongoing succession dispute, it was not clear who would perform this rite. The matter of Oyo’s successor could go to the courts, after his family said he left behind a will that had been ignored by Tooro elders.
Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king, a mesmerizing figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela. Oyo was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom until he became an adult at 18.
“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X. “Not Oyo; not that likeable young man; not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.”
The late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi befriended the Tooro royal family as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011.
Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country, but they were restored in 1993. Although they have no political authority and are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics, monarchs wield authority as guardians of tribal culture.

Ronaldo calls for lifetime bans after 'Jota' chants aimed at Neves
Sept 13 : Cristiano Ronaldo said on Sunday that fans who appeared to make chants referencing former teammate Diogo Jota at Ruben Neves during a Saudi Pro League match should be banned from football stadiums for life.
The chants occurred on Saturday during a fixture between Al-Taawoun and Neves' side Al-Hilal in Buraidah, Saudi Arabia.
Jota died on July 3, 2025, in a car crash in Zamora, northwestern Spain, along with his brother Andre Silva. A close friend of Jota, Neves was a pallbearer at his funeral.
Footage filmed from the stands during the match and circulated on social media appeared to show supporters chanting 'Jota'.
The shouts attracted the attention of Neves, who pointed to his eye and then up to the sky in response.
Passing through the mixed zone after the game, Neves commented, "I hope they don't go to pray afterwards."
In response to an Instagram post showing the footage, Ronaldo commented from his personal account.
"The league must take action and punish this kind of fan behaviour," said Ronaldo.
"This is no longer football, and there have to be limits. People who behave like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again."
The game finished 6-0 to Al-Hilal, with Neves playing 75 minutes before being substituted.
Reuters has contacted Al-Taawoun and Al-Hilal for comment.

The use of coal to generate electricity on the US grid has been plunging for nearly two decades, and the first Trump administration was unable to affect the trend. So his second administration has attempted more aggressive interventions to prop up coal use. One of its most direct means of doing so is to order coal plants that were scheduled to close to remain open, even if there is no need for them.
The administration’s justification for these orders is a statute that allows the Department of Energy (DOE) to declare an emergency in the case of wartime or a sudden shortfall in generation. A number of parties, including states where coal plants have been slated to close, have challenged this declaration. And on Friday, in the first of these cases to make its way through the courts, the declaration was judged to be contrary to the statute. While this only affects a single coal plant in Michigan, the reasoning of the decision will apply to every coal plant closure that has been blocked by the DOE.
No emergency
The decision was issued by a unanimous three-judge panel from the DC Circuit’s Court of Appeals. It focuses on the J.H. Campbell Generating Plant, which was scheduled to close last year but has been kept open by a total of five emergency declarations by the DOE, each limited to 90 days by the Federal Power Act. At issue was section 202(c) of that Act, which allows the DOE to declare emergencies when the US is at war or when “an emergency exists by reason of a sudden increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy.”

American Ryan Garcia defended his World Boxing Council welterweight title on Saturday with a second-round stoppage of Britain’s Conor Benn in Las Vegas.
Garcia delivered a hammering right hand to the chin that dropped Benn to the canvas 45 seconds into the second round and followed with punishing flurries of punches until referee Thomas Taylor stopped the fight after one minute and 25 seconds of the second round.
Garcia improved to 26-2 with his 21st victory inside the distance and denied Benn, in his first world title bout, a chance to become a world champion like his father, England’s Nigel Benn.
The fight was at T-Mobile Arena, where Garcia won the crown in February with a unanimous decision victory over US countryman Mario Barrios.
The 28-year-old American was defending his 147-pound (66.7kg) division title for the first time.
Benn, a 29-year-old Englishman, is the son of a former middleweight and super middleweight world champion. He fell to 25-2 after coming off an April unanimous decision victory over American Regis Prograis at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
That’s the same venue where last November, Benn avenged his only prior loss by taking a unanimous decision from England’s Chris Eubank Jr.
Both fighters were moving quickly and intensely trading punches from the start until Garcia landed his stunning blow. Benn rose but was battered for the fight’s final few seconds.

Brics Summit: PM Modi’s bilateral talks put security, trade in focus
Modi and Marcos agreed to enhance India-Philippines cooperation in defense, trade, and security at the Brics Summit, addressing regional issues together.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Philippines President Ferdinand R Marcos Jr agreed to expand cooperation in defence, security, trade and investment during a meeting on the margins of the Brics Summit on Sunday.
The Philippines participated in the summit as the current chair of Asean, providing an opportunity for the two leaders to review bilateral ties. The Philippines is a key partner for India in the Asean grouping and shared concerns over China’s actions across the region have fostered closer strategic and security cooperation between the two countries.
The leaders expressed satisfaction at progress in bilateral cooperation across all areas and agreed to deepen and expand collaboration in defence, security, trade, investment, space, railway infrastructure, fintech, education, tourism, technology, and people-to-people ties, the external affairs ministry said in a readout.
Deep Dive
Modi and Marcos also discussed regional and global issues and reiterated their commitment to strengthen cooperation across all areas of the bilateral strategic partnership.
“We reviewed the growing momentum in the India-Philippines strategic partnership,” Modi said on social media, adding that focus areas in the discussions included economic linkages, technology, trade and space.
Modi held a separate meeting with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and reviewed cooperation in diverse areas. They also exchanged views on global issues and agreed to maintain close coordination at multilateral forums, the ministry said.
Modi said on social media that he and Ramaphosa reviewed the India-South Africa strategic partnership, including the India-SACU trade agreement, mining and critical minerals, infrastructure, food security, digital public infrastructure and emerging technologies.
“We will work closely for Africa’s progress, the priorities of the Global South and a more balanced global order,” Modi said.
Modi also held meetings with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Ugandan vice president Jessica Rose Epel Alupo, Nigerian vice president Kashim Shettima Mustapha, Burundi President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who is also chairperson of the African Union, and reviewed bilateral ties.
Modi and Tokayev reviewed bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, security, connectivity, energy, critical minerals and emerging technologies, and exchanged perspectives on regional and international developments.
They agreed to strengthen the bilateral strategic partnership for peace, stability and development in the region.
Modi and Alupo reviewed ties between India and Uganda and emphasised the need to enhance cooperation in priority areas through technology partnerships, investment facilitation, and private sector collaboration. They also called for closer bilateral engagement to champion the voice of the Global South.
Modi and Mustapha reviewed the India-Nigeria relationship and discussions focussed on key areas such as trade, investment, defence, energy partnership, agriculture, health and digital technologies. Modi and Mustapha also discussed regional and global matters, including priorities and concerns of the Global South.
They emphasised the importance of strengthening cooperation in multilateral forums and working together for a more representative, inclusive and multipolar global order. Modi highlighted India’s commitment to deepen engagement with Africa, and Mustapha appreciated India’s contribution to capacity building and economic development in Nigeria.
Modi and Ndayishimiye stressed that the India-African Union partnership is a key pillar of cooperation within the Global South. They discussed the early convening of the India-Africa Forum Summit.
Modi commended the African Union leadership for combating the Ebola outbreak, and Ndayishimiye appreciated New Delhi’s medical support to Africa CDC to help in mitigating the outbreak.
