Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers opening remarks at the Brics Summit Session on 'Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth' at Bharat Mandapam, on Day 2 of the 18th BRICS Summit, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Sunday. (@MEAIndia X/ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: The 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi brought together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for two days of high-level diplomacy, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding key bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.The summit saw a renewed push to stabilise India-China ties, a reaffirmation of the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussions on the West Asia crisis, Ukraine, maritime security, trade and energy. Alongside formal negotiations, images of PM Modi with Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian projected a strong message of engagement and unity within the expanded grouping.The summit also featured informal diplomatic moments, including PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex, leaders attending a gala dinner featuring a specially curated Indian menu, and a symbolic Banyan tree plantation highlighting India's emphasis on sustainability and interconnectedness.The two-day summit also produced a series of initiatives covering agriculture, health, technology, startups, energy, urban mobility, supply chains, skilling and global governance. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted after intensive negotiations, provided the summit's principal political outcome, covering terrorism, conflicts, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi meeting signals push to stabilise ties
PM Modi and Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, with both leaders stressing the need to view India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.
The two sides expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and said the relationship should be guided by mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The leaders also discussed maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border, economic and trade relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. Both sides underlined the need to address each other's concerns and facilitate meaningful and predictable market access.Also read: 'Have opportunity to discuss cooperation': PM Modi welcomes Xi; bilateral talks beginPM Modi also thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairship and conveyed best wishes to China as it prepares to assume the Brics chairship next year.Xi said China and India should continue to approach their relationship from a strategic perspective and keep long-term bilateral development in mind. He also stressed the importance of cooperation between the two major Global South countries.
Modi-Putin talks focus on Ukraine, West Asia
PM Modi and Putin held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing major regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist peace efforts.Also read: Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeawaysThe discussions covered defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia also agreed to work towards increasing bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030 and discussed implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030.Putin invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, with dates to be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Putin car ride becomes summit highlight
One of the most closely watched visual moments came after the Modi-Putin meeting, when the two leaders travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The image underlined the longstanding India-Russia relationship at a time of continuing geopolitical tensions surrounding Moscow and highlighted India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.Also read: PM Modi, Putin share car ride again in Delhi, weeks after traveling together in Bishkek - watchPM Modi also presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.
Kremlin says PM Modi, Xi offered help on Ukraine
Russia said PM Modi and Xi offered their "good offices" to help find a solution to the Ukraine conflict during their separate interactions with Putin on the sidelines of the summit.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin welcomed their readiness, saying: “During their bilateral meetings, Modi and Xi took a keen interest in the Ukraine settlement and actively offered their good offices to help find a solution,”.The development came amid continuing international efforts to find a settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks centre on West Asia
PM Modi also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the discussions focusing on India-Iran ties, Brics cooperation and the escalating conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's consistent position that disputes should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region. The two leaders also discussed freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers amid disruptions to shipping routes.The meeting followed their earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India has also stressed the need to expand and diversify bilateral trade channels with Iran.
Iran-UAE engagement amid regional tensions
Pezeshkian also held talks with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit.The meeting was significant as Iran and the UAE have had differences over regional security, while Gulf states maintain varying degrees of security cooperation with Western powers.Their interaction highlighted the diplomatic space created by Brics, which brings together countries with competing interests and positions on major geopolitical issues.
Modi-Xi-Putin-Pezeshkian project Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals involving PM Modi, Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, PM Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The visuals projected unity among members despite differences over conflicts and other major geopolitical issues.The interactions were particularly significant for India as it sought to use its Brics chairship to build consensus among countries with sharply different political and strategic priorities.Also read: PM doubles down on friendship with Iran, seeks win-win strategy; hope mounts for BRICS declaration
Gala dinner adds cultural dimension
Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner during the summit, providing an informal setting for interaction among heads of state and government.The specially curated Indian menu showcased regional flavours, traditional recipes and contemporary interpretations of Indian cuisine. The menu included Khandvi Mille-Feuille, Khumb Galouti, Paneer Lababdar, Gucchi Marmik, Carrot Bean Poriyal, Thakkali Belle Saaru, Millet Pulao, Beetroot Raita and assorted Indian breads.Desserts included Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi and Shahtoot Phirni.The cultural evening added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by negotiations over conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy and global governance.
Banyan tree plantation highlights sustainability
A symbolic Banyan tree plantation ceremony was also held during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the initiative.The Banyan tree, with its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The plantation also reflected India's effort to connect the diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum pushes trade, investment
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders for discussions on trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying Brics countries account for 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date,” the Prime Minister said.Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing. Putin stressed that business-to-business ties and economic partnerships could help build more resilient international economic relations.
PM Modi pushes people-centric Brics
India's chairship sought to connect Brics cooperation more directly with ordinary citizens while focusing on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.Addressing the summit, PM Modi said, "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach."He said resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability had remained India's priorities, with special emphasis on connecting Brics cooperation with common people."Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."India organised more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements across around 30 cities during its 2026 chairship. The programme covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Agriculture and healthcare get major push
Brics countries advanced cooperation in sustainable agriculture through Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology, a Digital Agriculture Network and the Brics AGRIN framework covering agricultural inputs, genetic resources and information.The Digital Agriculture Network is intended to expand the use of AI, geospatial technology, Internet of Things-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics to support farmers.In healthcare, the Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle and a roadmap for joint cooperation on healthy lifestyles were launched. Members also agreed to strengthen cooperation in traditional, complementary and integrative medicine.A greater focus was placed on mental health through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India serving as the coordinating centre.
Energy, climate and urban cooperation expanded
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The grouping also established a Brics Urban Mobility Hub to promote knowledge sharing and technical cooperation on sustainable urban transport. Members adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure and established an Urban Research and Knowledge Network.PM Modi also emphasised the importance of balancing development with environmental protection and said technology and critical minerals should not become instruments that hinder shared progress.
Startups, MSMEs and skilling receive boost
India advanced cooperation among small businesses and startups through a Brics MSME Cooperation Portal designed to connect MSMEs, financial institutions, technology centres, trade associations and policymakers.The Brics Incubator Network will connect startups and incubators across member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.The Brics Science and Research Repository was also welcomed as a platform for scientific knowledge sharing.Through Brics CONNECT, members also advanced cooperation on skills, employability, women's workforce participation, social security and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation, while sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a dedicated working group.
Supply chains and global value chains strengthened
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.Members also gave in-principle approval to an agreement on cooperation and mutual administrative assistance in customs matters, aimed at facilitating trade, reducing transaction costs and improving border security and trade facilitation.
Global South gets stronger voice
PM Modi used the summit to push for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making institutions.He argued that the Global South should move from being a rule-taker to a rule-shaper and called for reforms in global governance, including greater representation in the UN Security Council.Brics also reaffirmed support for comprehensive UN reform and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
New Delhi Declaration: 140 points, 45 pages
The Brics countries adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, a 45-page document containing 140 points, after intensive negotiations that continued into the early hours of Saturday.The declaration brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.Its adoption was particularly significant because the expanded Brics includes countries with differing positions on major geopolitical conflicts, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. India worked to bridge differences and secure consensus among members.
Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and called for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemned the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemned the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards adopting the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Restraint, ceasefire and diplomacy
The declaration expressed deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stressed dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and called for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for upholding a ceasefire, ensuring unhindered humanitarian assistance and ending the forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral military action condemned
The declaration condemned unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts in West Asia and the wider divisions within the expanded grouping.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to reconcile competing positions and produce a common statement.
Trade, tariffs and sanctions
Brics expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.The grouping reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and called for restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.Brics also voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, calling for such measures to be eliminated.
Local currencies and financial resilience
The declaration backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using Brics members' local currencies while respecting national priorities.Members acknowledged work on the interoperability of payment and messaging systems and discussions on facilitating trade settlements and investment using local currencies.The push forms part of a broader effort to strengthen financial resilience and reduce vulnerabilities in international economic relations.
Critical minerals and energy security
The declaration stressed the importance of reliable, diversified, resilient and sustainable supply chains for critical minerals.It called for benefit sharing, value addition and economic diversification in resource-rich countries while recognising their sovereign rights over mineral resources.Brics also stressed the importance of critical minerals for zero and low-emission technologies, energy security and resilient energy supply chains.On energy, the declaration called for diversified sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets. It recognised that fossil fuels would continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies, while backing equitable and inclusive energy transitions.
Health and universal health coverage
The declaration reaffirmed Brics' commitment to universal health coverage and resilient, inclusive and people-centred health systems.Members emphasised the coordinating role of the World Health Organisation and backed continued multilateral cooperation on global health.The declaration also covered the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing negotiations, efforts to end tuberculosis, strengthening the health workforce, digital health and integration of traditional medicine.
Women, development and global governance
Brics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.The declaration stressed women's participation in governance and economic life, financial and digital inclusion, skill development, entrepreneurship and climate action.The grouping also reaffirmed the importance of reforming global institutions to reflect contemporary economic and political realities and strengthen the voice of developing countries.
The New Delhi Summit came as Brics entered its third decade with 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.India's 2026 chairship was its fourth after previous presidencies in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The latest chairship sought to build on those earlier efforts while adapting the grouping's agenda to its expanded membership.In his concluding remarks, PM Modi said the discussions had strengthened the view that Brics had evolved beyond a traditional grouping and could function as an ecosystem for practical solutions."Our discussions over the past two days have further strengthened our conviction that BRICS is not merely a grouping of nations, but an ecosystem of solutions. We hope that the New Delhi Declaration adopted at this summit will provide a clear direction for our shared vision and future cooperation. We must translate all outcomes into time-bound actions that deliver last-mile impact. We will work together to ensure that our framework moves beyond mere documentation and creates a tangible impact in real life," he said.PM Modi also said the world now expected concrete results from Brics rather than only ideas and commitments, as the grouping prepares to enter its third decade.

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the world’s vital shipping routes.
The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.
The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.
Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.
Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.
Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.
British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.
The surge in fighting in the past week had sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.
The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.
The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.
On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.
Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.
On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.
Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.
There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.

I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.

Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 25 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1, USB-C audio, USB-A, 3.5-mm aux input, two 6.3-mm mic inputs |

| Weight | 25.79 pounds | 
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
- Published
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.
The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.
Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.
BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.
The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.
Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.
If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.
However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.
With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.
Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.
She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.
The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.
London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.
Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.
When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.
"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."
Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.
"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."
Inspired by Ronaldo, dancing her way to the top - analysis
Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.
She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.
By October of that year, Luvanga headed for Saudi Arabia to join Al-Nassr, a move that would prove transformative for her career.
Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.
Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.
"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.
There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.
Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.
Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.
Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.
She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.
For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

WASHINGTON – A lightning offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis has put the militants in a position to control a crucial Middle East waterway, creating a major new problem for U.S. President Donald Trump as his war with Iran grinds on in its seventh month.
Widening the Middle East conflict, Houthi fighters have advanced south along Yemen’s coast, increasing their ability to choke off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the “Gate of Tears” at the mouth of the Red Sea — giving Tehran potential leverage over both of the region’s main oil-shipping corridors.

Kathmandu, Sep 13: The death toll in Nepal flash floods climbed to 1,388 on Sunday as more bodies were recovered from the eight affected districts, authorities said.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.
According to the latest data released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 364 bodies were recovered from Chitwan district, 230 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West, and 199 from Nuwakot.
Similarly, 185 bodies were recovered from Rasuwa, 77 from Gorkha, 71 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahun.
Two others died while undergoing treatment in Kathmandu.
Only 104 of the recovered bodies have so far been identified and handed over to their families.
The joint command of security personnel has continued its search and rescue operations, with the number of missing people estimated to be 5,130.
A total of 13,728 people have been rescued so far, officials said.

Assam man, 23, held for rape, murder of woman over alleged affair: Police

A 23-year-old tea garden worker from Assam’s Dibrugarh district was arrested for allegedly raping and strangling a 22-year-old woman over an alleged illicit affair, police said on Sunday.
The woman, who went missing on Friday morning, was recovered from an abandoned pit in Chabua area on Saturday afternoon, and police detained the accused later.
“As per the initial investigation, the woman was sexually assaulted and strangled to death before her body was thrown into an abandoned pit,” officers said, adding that the accused was known to her and they were allegedly having an affair.
The woman, a mother of a two-year-old boy, separated from her husband nearly a year ago and was staying separately in the Chabua area of Dibrugarh.
Police said she had been missing since Friday morning and her family members reported it at the Chabua police station the same day. “A search operation was launched based on the complaint and her body was found on Saturday,” officers said.
Victim’s family members later lodged a first information report (FIR) against Sumit Kalandi (23), who according to them was in contact with her for several months.
“He was forcing her to stay with him but she was not ready because she had just separated and was raising a little kid. They used to fight and when she went missing, we informed the police about it,” family members said on Saturday.
Police said they detained Kalandi after recovering the body, and he later confessed to the crime. “He said they were having a relationship but she was also keeping contact with others, which is why he killed her,” a senior police officer said.
He said that Kalandi has been arrested for rape, murder, kidnap and other charges and the matter is under investigation.
The officer said that victim’s body was sent to Assam Medical College and Hospital (AMCH), Dibrugarh for postmortem on Saturday and they are waiting for the report.

Games may be life with all the hard bits removed, but they provide a way to study why people make the choices they make. Traditional games are usually played against a static background: the rewards per outcome are constant. That limits their relevance to behavior because, in real life, the rewards and consequences of strategic choices are ever changing. Now, researchers have used a mathematical model to study a series of games that include evolving strategies and randomly varying returns.
A bit of history
Perhaps the most famous game-theory contest is the prisoner’s dilemma. In the prisoner’s dilemma, a pair of thieves have been captured and are being separately interrogated by the police. If both clam up, they will be punished for a lesser crime. If one prisoner makes a deal (defects) then that prisoner gets to go free and the other gets a heavier sentence. If both make a deal, they both get an in-between punishment.
The person running the game can start it with different rewards for cooperating and defecting to explore how the optimum strategy varies with reward and risk, which the players can figure out by varying the strategies across multiple rounds. Depending on the balance between the reward for staying silent (cooperating) and betrayal, the game stabilizes with everyone betraying everyone. In this simple situation, everyone loses.
Similar dynamics can be found in games of chicken, rock-paper-scissors, and more. The evolution of strategies can lead to stable populations, bistable populations (where the population flips between two stable strategies), or limit cycles, where the population shifts continuously among multiple strategies.
There is also a rich history of changing a game as it is played. Usually, these are within-game variations. For instance, you can set a limit on the amount of reward available, so strategies evolve to take into account increasingly limited resources as the number of rounds goes up. In other words, most of this older work studied situations where the player’s behavior in the current round changed the resources or rewards available for the next round.

A day after an all-vegetarian spread was served at a BRICS Summit gala dinner, the Congress on Sunday said the BJP was now imposing its "deeply problematic" dietary preferences on dignitaries from across the world, with Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi pointing out that 80% of Indians are non-vegetarian.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosted the dinner for the leaders and delegates of the BRICS Summit at the Bharat Mandapam on Saturday (September 12, 2026).

In a post on social media platforms X, Facebook and Instagram, Mr. Gandhi wrote, "For the record: 80% of Indians are non-vegetarian. Indian non-vegetarian food is delicious. As are my sister's chole bhature." He also posted a picture of chole bhature on a dining table.
While Mr. Gandhi made no direct reference to the BRICS dinner, Congress's media and publicity department head Pawan Khera shared the screenshot of the menu from the dinner and attacked the BJP.
"The BJP's habit of imposing its dietary preferences on fellow Indians is already deeply problematic. Now, they have taken it a step further by imposing their own choices on dignitaries from across the world," Mr. Khera said on X.
“India is a rich, diverse, multi-cuisine country, home to some of the finest non-vegetarian delicacies that people across the world relish and enjoy,” he said.
“So why did the Modi government choose to hide this part of India's culture,” Mr. Khera asked."Is it ashamed of the diversity that makes India what it is," the Congress leader asked.
Rijiju slams Congress
BJP leader and Union Minister Kiren Rijiju lashed out at the Congress for its criticism. "I can't believe that the Congress party is making politics even on the food menu served to the leaders of BRICS nations. Our guests relished Indian vegetarian cuisine which are rich in flavour and nutritional variety with diverse regional traditions," Mr. Rijiju said.
BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said, "When the Opposition has nothing except the food menu to criticise about the summit, it tells you how successful BRICS has been." "Congress is sulking to see India emerge as a global consensus builder," he wrote on X.
Congress' social media head Supriya Shrinate hailed Mr. Gandhi's post and said it defines who he is.
"It stands out for two things: respect for India's diversity; respect for people's choices including what they eat," she said on X.
"That apart, what is a Sunday without yummy lip-smacking chola bhatura?!" she said.
Congress spokesperson Shama Mohamed shared the screenshot of the menu and took a swipe at the government over the issue.
"No wonder Xi Jinping went back to his hotel for dinner. I would do the same!" she said on X.
Srivatsa, a close aide of Mr. Gandhi, said foreign dignitaries would have to wait till 2029 to have delicious Indian food of all kinds. "Sabka Khana, Sabke Saath," he added.
In another post, Mr. Srivatsa said one post from LoP Rahul Gandhi — one fact, one photograph of his lunch and the entire discourse had moved from where the BJP wanted it to where Mr. Gandhi put it.
"And it's a debate this country has needed for a long time. For over a decade, a manufactured vegetarian orthodoxy has been imposed on a nation by the BJP where 80% of people eat meat. Look at what they are doing in States like Bengal and Bihar recently," he said.
Mr. Gandhi has "exposed, with one fact and a plate of food, not a debate about diet, but a debate about who gets to decide how 150 crore Indians live, and what they choose to eat", Mr. Srivatsa said on X.
Earlier, in a post on X on Saturday night, Mahua Moitra said, "Would I be a bad MP if I advised the visiting BRICS leaders to give this menu a miss & get security to nip down to the nearest Karims & bring back some Burrab Kababs." The gala dinner featured an elaborate all-vegetarian menu. 'Khandvi mille', a feuille steamed gram-flour roll, and 'khumb galouti', pan-grilled mushroom kebabs with mint pearls, were served as starters.
The main course offered 'paneer lababdar', 'gucchi marmik' — Himalayan morel mushrooms and tender asparagus — and 'carrot bean poriyal'.
The other items on the menu included 'thakkali belle saaru' — light lentil broth, millet pulao, beetroot raita and assorted Indian breads.
For the desserts, 'Old Delhi fruit cream with jalebi' and 'shahtoot phirni' wrapped up the menu for the VVIP guests.

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

In a letter to the state Chief Electoral Officer, Shaikh said several errors had surfaced during the revision exercise, with names of eligible voters missing from the draft rolls despite their having submitted registration applications and valid documents and received acknowledgment receipts.
He said applications for new voter registration (Form 6) and corrections or change of address (Form 8) were still pending at the Booth Level Officer (BLO) level. He also alleged that voters affected by discrepancies or “no linkage” had not received notices, SMSes or phone calls from the election authorities, leaving them uncertain about whether their names would figure in the final rolls.
The issue, he said, was particularly evident in Bhiwandi, Madanpura, Mankhurd and Govandi.
Shaikh also cited repeated server-related problems on the Election Commission’s website and mobile application, which he said were making it difficult for citizens to submit forms or track applications. He added that BLOs were reluctant to work during the festival holiday period.
He has demanded that voters possessing SIR acknowledgment receipts be included in the final rolls, pending applications be disposed of immediately and an offline, in-person application drive be conducted to address problems with the online system.

Trump says 'very negative forces' raising exaggerated concerns over AI
The public debate about AI has heated up in the US after two Anthropic researchers issued warnings that the rapidly progressing technology could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
DOONBEG, Ireland: US President Donald Trump on Sunday (Sep 13) likened critics of artificial intelligence to "very negative forces" bringing up scenarios that will not happen, and said he wanted to make sure that the US remains the industry leader.
"We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins," Trump told reporters at his Ireland golf course, when asked if the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated.
"We could put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up, and they're bringing up things that won't happen."
Trump has resisted stirring concerns about AI.
The public debate about AI has heated up in the US after two Anthropic researchers issued warnings that the rapidly progressing technology could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
In his second term, Trump's administration has largely embraced AI firms. These AI leaders and other technology companies have also supported Trump's initiatives.
AI executives have poured money into the midterm campaign ahead of the Nov 3 election that will determine control of Congress. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's super PAC, America PAC, has already spent millions backing Republican candidates and is expected to play a major role in voter turnout efforts this fall.
The Pentagon this year warned of risks from Anthropic's model.
After the researchers' warnings, some AI CEOs are pushing for slowing advancement of the models.
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei outlined a three-step framework intended to pace development and create more time to manage its risks. The proposal immediately received endorsements from several other executives at major AI companies, including Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
In an interview that aired Sunday on the CBS program "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan", Amodei said the competition between US and Chinese AI companies was the "toughest dilemma" in trying to establish a "speed limit" on the rate of AI development.
"We shouldn't kid ourselves, because the incentives to pull ahead and the military advantage that you get from that are so large that the ability to check that the other side isn't cheating has to be ironclad," he said. "So I think that's going to be the work of years, and honestly, I don't know if it's possible."
Jacob Coxon, one of the Anthropic researchers who resigned and then issued the warnings, pushed for the US to work with other countries to ensure pace.
"I feel we need international coordination, or else we risk running the same race with China, which could be equally dangerous," Coxon said on NBC's Meet the Press.

Lyricist Sameer had a conversation with Komal Nahta, where he revealed about his struggles before getting a break. He revealed that he almost was a part of Aamir Khan-Juhi Chawla starrer Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak (1988) and that he was dropped at the last minute.
Sameer REVEALS he was DROPPED from Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak at the last minute “Majrooh Sultanpuri came on board as the lyricist. Aur main kat gaya!”
Sameer said, “I became good friends with Anand-Milind. This is when they were offered Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak. Sameer added, “Finally, they reached a middle ground – ek tera, ek mera. In the process, Anand-Milind were retained as the music directors while Majrooh Sultanpuri came on board as the lyricist. Aur main kat gaya (smiles). Meanwhile, Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak became a blockbuster.”

US-Israeli failure to bomb Iran into submission was preordained
From Nazi Germany to Vietnam, history is rich with examples of countries that simply refuse to surrender to bombing
Winston Churchill famously praised the resilience of the British people during the Blitz, describing the nightly bombings of London as a “cruel, wanton, indiscriminate” attempt by Adolf Hitler to break the spirit of a tough “island race”.
He was not wrong about the toughness and courage of his fellow citizens. But as one of the United Kingdom’s greatest leaders and historical writers, he created a false impression of the uniqueness of the British wartime experience.
Strategic bombing alone, without the reinforcement of ground troops, almost never achieves its purpose. British resistance was not the exception but the rule.
Just by surviving, Tehran is winning. He said that “the Iranians have really survived an attack that almost no other country in the region would be able to survive”. He added: “They have been attacked by two nuclear-weapon states and they have essentially come out on top… As a result, their deterrence [against] the other states has increased, and their leverage has increased internally.”
That seems obvious. Yet leaders such as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have boasted that they could bomb their adversary into submission and that its people would rise up to overthrow their government. In his latest escalation, Trump called on the Iranian people to rise up: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” Aside from the criminality, that way of thinking seems absurd.

On April 12, 1955, America threw a vaccine party.
That morning, Thomas Francis Jr. — who had overseen trials of polio vaccines developed by Jonas Salk — held a press conference to announce the results.
Only it wasn’t a press conference. It was an event.
Reporters packed the room. Tens of thousands of physicians gathered in movie theaters to hear the broadcast. Millions of Americans huddled around their radios.
The verdict: The vaccine worked. A disease that had devastated families for decades had finally met its match.
A documentary describes the reaction: “Factory whistles blew, school children cheered, parents wept.” Newspapers ran headlines like “POLIO IS CONQUERED” across their front pages. Store owners wrote “Thank you, Dr. Salk” messages on their windows. Salk took the stage at the press conference to a prolonged standing ovation, on his way to becoming a living legend.
Fast forward 71 years, to 2026.
On Sept. 2, major medical societies released an independent research evaluation covering flu, Covid-19, and RSV shots. There was another press conference, and more good news: These vaccines are still safe and continue to provide strong protection against death and severe illness.
But this was no event.
Experts talked about “informed decisions” and “shared commitment” and “restoring trust.” The American Medical Association launched a new website with JAMA articles and PDF charts, but no real people or stories. The tone was somber, the mood dour.
So much for a party.
As a communications consultant, I have spent years supporting vaccine advocates. Every conversation right now feels bleak. Measles has come roaring back. Vaccination rates keep dropping. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is a wreck. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the ringleader of the country’s vaccine critics, is somehow still in charge of the Department of Health and Human Services.
For the pro-vaccine side, this is all excruciating. We spend our days debunking and fact-checking. We debate repeatedly whether to confront wellness influencers or engage them. We search endlessly for just the right analogy or metaphor to reach the hesitant parent.
We take vaccines really, really seriously. As we should. It’s a matter of life and death.
Somewhere along the way, though, we forgot how to celebrate. We are sorely lacking in optimism and excitement. There’s no sense of togetherness or belonging. We’ve gotten wound up so tightly that there’s no joy in what we’re doing.
We need to remember how to have fun again.
Consider how Children’s Health Defense, the organization Kennedy previously led, rallies people to its cause. This group is deceitful and dangerous. But it knows how to build a movement.
They fight for “health freedom.” Their volunteers are “defenders” who join an “army of truth.” They hold banners and make street signs. They host book clubs and movie screenings. They sell merch. They encourage people to “grab a couple friends” on the first Saturday of every month and go around debating opponents.
Right now, no pro-vaccine equivalent comes close to matching that energy. Which is a crying shame, because that’s exactly what’s worked for us in the past.
Francis’ press conference in 1955 was the culmination of a movement that had been building for years. More than 1.8 million children participated in Salk’s vaccine trials. They were known as “polio pioneers.” Each received a keepsake card, which many kept for decades. Moms and dads across the country rallied Americans to contribute research donations. Millions did so.
The campaign paid off. Less than a decade after that national vaccine party, cases of polio in the U.S. dropped by 97%.
We experienced a similar surge in vaccine enthusiasm during the pandemic. I received my first Covid vaccine in the parking lot of a Six Flags amusement park; everyone honked their horns after getting a shot. On social media, people posted vaccine selfies and wore “I got vaccinated” stickers. States got creative with all sorts of financial incentives, from million-dollar prizes to college scholarships. Major League Baseball offered free tickets to games.
Once again, the campaign paid off. Covid vaccines saved millions of lives.
Of course, this time, the enthusiasm didn’t last. The ensuing backlash to Covid vaccines seems to have convinced the pro-vaccine side to become more cautious, more restrained, and more clinical in our approach.
Problem is, we’ve learned the wrong lesson.
To increase vaccination rates, we need to match our seriousness of purpose with a renewed spirit of possibility. We need to give people who support vaccination — and those who aren’t sure — something to get excited about and a team they feel good about joining.
That should start with how we talk about vaccines. One thing I never see in any vaccination messaging guide is an exclamation point. Vaccines are incredible! They do amazing things! Let’s try getting people fired up for a change!
It should also include incentive programs for vaccinations. Evidence from the pandemic was mixed, but these programs showed more than enough potential to warrant additional exploration.
But the biggest opportunity lies in building our team. Think of everything we could do with just one vaccination clinic. Much as election officials recruit volunteer poll workers, health departments could recruit volunteers to staff information tables. Cities could match volunteers with older residents who need rides. Civic groups could “adopt” a clinic and bring food and swag. Schools could provide service learning hours to students who lend a hand.
Our side will always stand up for science, data, and facts. But some of the best vaccine pushes in history were marked by factory whistles blaring, car horns honking, and people cheering for a cause bigger than themselves.
It’s gotten far too quiet on the pro-vaccine side. Let’s start making some noise again.
Adam Zimmerman is a public health communications consultant.

Mamata reaches out to TMC veteran Akhil Giri as it weighs local face for Nandigram bypoll
The move comes at a particularly difficult juncture for the TMC, which lost power to the BJP in the May assembly elections after 15 years in office.
TMC supremo Mamata Banerjee's outreach to party veteran Akhil Giri has set off fresh speculation that it may be weighing him as a candidate for the Nandigram bypoll, as it seeks to reclaim political ground in a constituency that has come to define both its rise and subsequent decline.
The former chief minister spoke to Giri over the phone and later asked him to meet her at her Kalighat residence on Saturday, according to a TMC leader from the Mamata Banerjee camp.
Also Read | TMC factions gear up for Bengal bypolls amid fight over symbol
The development has fuelled speculation that the TMC is considering Giri for the October 6 bypoll, although the party has made no formal announcement in this regard.
The move comes at a particularly difficult juncture for the TMC, which lost power to the BJP in the May assembly elections after 15 years in office, with saffron party leader Suvendu Adhikari now occupying the chief minister's post. Adhikari also defeated Banerjee in Bhabanipur in the assembly polls, after having beaten her in Nandigram in 2021.
Giri said Banerjee had sought his opinion on the bypoll and that he had conveyed his suggestions. He also said he had sent his views to the party over WhatsApp.
"I am a loyal soldier of the party. If the party gives me any responsibility, I will carry it out," Giri said, while making it clear that the final decision on the candidate rests with Banerjee.
Giri also argued that preference should be given to a local candidate, but said he would abide by any decision taken by the party leadership.
His name doing the rounds is significant, but does not by itself establish that the former minister will be the TMC nominee. It rather indicates the options being explored by a party attempting to rebuild the organisation after an electoral rout, and amid an unresolved fight over its very identity.
Nandigram is a particularly loaded territory for the TMC.
The constituency was the epicentre of the 2007 anti-land acquisition movement that helped catapult Banerjee and the TMC to power in 2011, ending 34 years of Left Front rule. But 14 years later, it became the stage for one of the party's biggest political reversals when Banerjee chose to contest there against her former lieutenant Adhikari, who had joined the BJP.
Adhikari won that contest and went on to become the BJP's principal challenger to the TMC in the state. In May this year, he defeated Banerjee again, this time from Bhabanipur, as the BJP swept to power in Bengal.
Adhikari contested both Nandigram and Bhabanipur in the 2026 assembly election, won both, and then chose to retain Bhabanipur and resigned from Nandigram, which is what necessitated the October 6 bypoll.
The Nandigram bypoll, therefore, carries significance far beyond the vacant assembly seat. For the TMC, it is an early test of whether the party can begin rebuilding its electoral machinery in a region that once formed the bedrock of its political narrative.
However, the party is entering the contest amid an unprecedented organisational crisis.
The TMC's name and twin-flower-on-grass symbol is the subject of a dispute before the Election Commission, with the Mamata Banerjee-led camp and the rebel faction headed by Ritabrata Banerjee staking competing claims over the party's identity, symbol and funds.
The EC held discussions with the rival camps on Saturday, but its decision is awaited.
With nominations for the October 6 bypoll already open, both sides are preparing their electoral strategies, creating the possibility of rival groups seeking votes while claiming the TMC's political legacy.
The Ritabrata-led faction has said it will continue to claim the TMC name and symbol, but is prepared to contest as independents if the poll panel does not decide in its favour before nominations close.
The rebel camp has also put Mamata Banerjee in a politically awkward position by saying it will not field a candidate against her if she herself contests Nandigram.
That challenge has found an echo from within the TMC's old Nandigram network.
Senior party leader Abu Taher, one of the prominent faces of the 2007 anti-land acquisition movement, has already questioned why Mamata Banerjee should not return to Nandigram rather than ask a local leader to fight the battle.
Taher has said he would decline if asked to contest, arguing that he had remained with the party during its years in power, but was repeatedly overlooked when candidates were chosen.
"Mamata Banerjee should come and fight in Nandigram," Taher had said, questioning why he should contest now when she herself had chosen the "trophy seat" in 2021.
Also Read | Abhishek Banerjee's PA Sumit Roy arrested by CID in Salboni land grab case
Taher had also pointed to his role in the 2007 movement, and said he did not want to be made a "scapegoat" after being overlooked by the party for years.
Giri has served as a minister in the erstwhile TMC government and remains a significant figure in East Midnapore politics. But for now, his name remains part of the speculation rather than a declared candidature.
For Adhikari, meanwhile, Nandigram is a personal and political territory. The BJP government he heads has already assigned him organisational responsibility for Tamluk, the district that includes Nandigram, ahead of the bypoll.
The contest, consequently, is shaping up as a test of more than individual candidates. It could become an early measure of whether the TMC can retain its old political vocabulary in Nandigram after losing power, while the BJP seeks to consolidate the gains made by Adhikari in a constituency once synonymous with Mamata Banerjee's political ascent.
The irony will not be lost on Bengal's political observers; the land that once helped Mamata Banerjee dislodge the Left is now the arena in which her party must begin the fight to recover from its own fall from power.

CBS News is getting employees hyped about the first full season of "60 Minutes" under top editor Bari Weiss, months after a string of high-profile exits.
"We don't often send notes to the whole newsroom. But today calls for it. It's a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS," newsroom leaders, including Weiss, wrote about the new "60 Minutes" season in a memo sent to staffers on Sunday.
The memo teases an interview — that "everyone has been chasing" — with a US Air Force officer who was rescued from Iran in April.
The 59th season of "60 Minutes" will have 10 regular contributors, including five correspondents: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Jon Wertheim, Norah O'Donnell, and Ross Douthat, who joined CBS from The New York Times in July.
"60 Minutes" is kicking off its highly anticipated season following a turbulent early-summer stretch for the storied news program.
Lead producer Nick Bilton, who was handpicked by Weiss in May, started his tenure by firing longtime correspondent Scott Pelley after a noisy confrontation in front of "60 Minutes" staffers.
Pelley had publicly questioned Bilton's qualifications, pressed his new boss on why fellow correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were let go, and accused Weiss of "murdering" the iconic Sunday night telecast while trying to "kill" CBS News.
Weiss later addressed the firing, telling staffers she's "only interested in working in a newsroom that is built on trust and mutual respect." Bilton told "60 Minutes" employees that his first week had been "a trying and difficult few days."
Veteran correspondents Whitaker, Wertheim, and Stahl — who's been with "60" since 1991 — decided to return to the program, saying that they "don't want to see 60 Minutes die." They said they're "working to build trust" with Bilton and "heard all the right things" in his memo.
"If we can continue doing the work that made this show what it is — committing acts of independent, fearless journalism and storytelling — we're here for it. If not, we leave," Stahl, Whitaker, and Wertheim wrote in their memo.

All --
