Rules Designed to Create Chaos
The Trump administration is hoping to put so many restrictions on mail-in balloting that people simply won’t be able to vote that way at all.
Donald Trump hates mail-in voting. He has described it as “dangerous,” “corrupt,” “horrible,” and “a fraud.” Last year, in a Truth Social post festooned with capital letters and exclamation points, he announced that he would be signing an executive order to do away with mail-in ballots entirely. That order never materialized, possibly because the president has absolutely no legal authority to carry out such a ban. The federal government plays only a small role in administering elections, and the Constitution locates those authorities with Congress, not the president.
But now, with some ballots already heading to voters as the midterms draw near, the Trump administration is waging another fight against voting by mail, this time through its control over the U.S. Postal Service. Trump’s plan wouldn’t outright prohibit mail-in voting but would throw so many wrenches into the machinery that it could grind to a halt. Federal courts at both the district and appellate levels have blocked the rule, and now the Supreme Court is in the process of weighing whether to allow this effort to move forward before the midterms; it could make a decision as soon as later today. If the justices let USPS take these steps in the coming weeks, the risk, the election-law expert Rick Hasen told me, is “mass disenfranchisement.”
Historically, the Postal Service has simply mailed every ballot provided by state and local election officials. But in a March executive order, Trump directed USPS to develop a new plan that would erect a series of hoops for election workers to jump through before a ballot can be sent to an expectant voter. If the rule goes into effect, USPS will require state and local jurisdictions to obtain federal sign-off on the design of the envelope and then mark each ballot envelope with barcodes. States must also upload a full list of every voter receiving a mail ballot to a so-called federal ballot mail portal. Only then, once USPS cross-checks the barcodes with the voter list in the portal, will the ballot be delivered.
In the abstract, this might sound inoffensive. But the process is so hopelessly tangled that it seems almost designed to fail. Take the portal, which is still not online. On September 3—a week ago—the Postal Service stated in a court filing that the website would be ready “by sometime next week.” Even if the portal were functional, it might not operate fairly. A whistleblower recently filed a disclosure warning that the Postal Service is planning to use the system with a “zero percent failure rate.” USPS will scan ballots in large batches, the whistleblower says, and if a single ballot fails to match the uploaded list of voters, none of the ballots in the batch will be mailed.
Election rules take a long time to change, and states begin preparing the polls long before Election Day. When Trump announced the order, in March, experts did not immediately think that the midterms would be affected. “I had assumed that this was going to be put on hold” until after November, Hasen said. But USPS quickly began putting together the detailed plans requested by the White House, even though the order itself faced multiple legal challenges and was racking up court judgments against it. (Another section of the executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to produce a mechanism by which states can review “citizenship lists” of potential voters. DHS has yet to provide these lists, and the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center recently sued to block the agency from compiling and distributing them.)
The Supreme Court ruled on August 24 that the executive order’s challengers had gone to court too soon, before USPS’s plans were far enough along. Now the Postal Service claims that its work is ready—mostly—to be rolled out, if the justices will let it.
The court dockets are crammed with statements by election experts and state and local officials explaining all of the different problems created by the rule. In their breadth and variety, these declarations are a reminder of just how big the United States is, and how many people must work together across multiple states and levels of government to pull off a successful election season. Hawaii has spent more than $79,000 printing ballot envelopes, the state’s chief election officer wrote in one filing; he worried that if officials need to order new envelopes, they may not arrive from the continental U.S. in time for the election. Rhode Island’s deputy secretary of state explained that the state’s laws regulating ballot-envelope design effectively prohibit officials from affixing the two barcodes required by USPS. In Wisconsin, some rural jurisdictions may not have the ability to print the required barcodes, the chair of the Wisconsin Elections Commission said. The elections director in Oregon, which conducts all of the state’s elections completely by mail, worried that the state’s “aging” computer systems are not equipped to efficiently upload 3 million voters’ personal information into the USPS portal. “If the system fails,” she wrote, “Oregon may be unable to mail ballots to voters at all.”
Election officials who have long relied on the Postal Service are now thinking through alternatives. Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state, told me that he has reached out to private mail carriers about delivering ballots in a pinch. “We got a quote from UPS of about eight bucks per ballot, which is about three dollars more than we pay the Postal Service,” he said. “With 2.1 million ballots in Nevada, that’s a pretty significant expense.” Nevada sends mail-in ballots to voters by default, and mail-in voting is popular: 60 percent of Nevadans voted by mail in the state’s primary elections, Aguilar said. Now his office is figuring out how to communicate clearly with voters who may be alarmed or confused if USPS refuses to mail Nevada’s ballots. “Do we just start to message, Hey, just skip the mail ballot altogether and show up in person?”
Experts are hoping that the Supreme Court takes these concerns seriously. Because of the emergency status of the litigation, the justices can consider not just the legality of the federal government’s actions but also the “equities”—that is, the potential harms suffered by each side depending on how the Court rules. There are strong legal arguments that the administration has no authority to put such a program in place. (Perhaps tellingly, the federal government has been reduced to arguing that the Post Office can impose requirements for mailing ballots in the same way that it can put safeguards in place for mailing cremated human remains.) On the equities, though, the matter seems particularly stark. If the Supreme Court allows the policy to go into effect, the outcome could be catastrophic. But if the policy remains blocked, what is the harm to the federal government? The administration’s briefs make little attempt to answer this question other than vague insinuations about voter fraud.
Then again, a victory at the Court wouldn’t appear to gain much for the administration, either. If the goal is partisan sabotage, there is little reason to think that the USPS plan would help Republicans. “If this actually happens, the burden is going to fall hardest on the most vulnerable of our voters—the elderly, the disabled, rural voters, voters on reservations, voters in the military,” Hasen said. Older voters and rural Americans have tended to be reliable GOP constituencies, and in a season when the Republican Party is struggling to build up voter enthusiasm, there is a real risk that inconvenienced voters who never receive a ballot will simply stay home. Democrats furious with Trump, meanwhile, may be more motivated to find a way to the polls.
Still, the widespread confusion that the USPS rule would inevitably create may have its own appeal to the White House. A group of election officials, including several Republican secretaries of state, warned in an amicus brief before the Supreme Court that “a chaotic election erodes confidence in the result.” For a president long obsessed with undermining Americans’ trust in elections, perhaps that’s victory enough.

The Best Mushroom Coffee
Featured in this article
The world has been addicted to caffeine for centuries, and in the year 2026, the scientific argument over whether coffee is good or bad for you remains unsettled. One might believe the lack of consensus is a Mainstream Media™ psyop to keep people scrambling for marketable solutions to a problem that’s completely made up, but the cottage industry of coffee alternatives that’s proliferated during this endless tug of war is an interesting outcome regardless of which side you’re on. This is where mushroom coffee makes its inevitable entrance.
Some quick googling revealed the known players in the game, all of which offer their own riff on a common base formula of dried mushrooms–usually a combo of lion’s mane, chaga, and cordyceps—boosted with buzzy add-ons like probiotics and nootropics. I spent a week with each, including our top pick, Atlas Coffee Club’s Latte Superblend ($26), swapping out my morning coffee for each brand's recommended dose of powder and hot water. After day five I allowed myself to experiment with sweeteners and milks, which you’ll need with almost all of these to get through the entire cup without gagging.
Some hit like a mild cup of coffee, some were actual coffee, and others were uncanny concoctions no normal person would ever crave unless they were fully indoctrinated in the heady lifestyle this unique alt-beverage industry revolves around. I laughed, I cried, I got the runs, and I crashed on my couch in the early afternoon more times than I could count, all for science, and all so you don’t have to try this on your own.
Be sure to check out our other coffee and caffeinated coverage, including the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Makers, Best Energy Drinks, and Best Electric Kettles.
Updated September 2026: We've added new mushroom coffees from Wunderground, Bullet Proof, and Vahdam; moved some previous picks to honorable mentions; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Others Tested
Lifeboost Mindflow for $45: The flavor of this instant powder is snappy and astringent at first, then it mellows into a warm middle ground after a few sips and a short cooling period. By the middle of the cup I forgot I was drinking something other than coffee, and the mild acidity on the finish–likely a product of the CognatiQ Coffee Fruit Extract that’s lauded on the back of Mindflow’s mylar pouch–tastes similar to a nice cup of Ethiopian or Rwandan coffee if you close your eyes and pretend for just a moment. Regarding its potency, if mushroom supplements were attendees at a state college keg party, Lifeboost would be the unremarkable guy pacing himself in the back while everyone else is getting blitzed like the world is ending. It’s unassuming yet self-assured, patiently waiting for all other entrants to crap out so it can make its move. I copped a mild buzz just a few sips in, and I felt alert and wide-eyed for a good two hours after the silty final sips of the cup were consumed. Electrolytes are uncommon in this space, which means this is a rare entry in the mushroom supplement world that purports to be a good pick if hydration is a trivial concern.
Four Sigmatic Organic Coffee for $20: Four Sigmatic’s Focus blend is labeled as a dark roast, but it’s missing the cigarette-butts-and-bowling-alley aftertaste that looms on the finish of similar blends. Despite my preference for lighter beans, this hit like a hug from an old friend after weeks of sipping murky silt. The caffeine buzz normalized after two days of using Think in lieu of more standard shroom-based coffee replacements, so I added a three-quarter-teaspoon hit of the powdered Focus blend to my daily cup to see what would happen. Within 10 minutes I felt an overwhelming urge to sort my finances spreadsheet in preparation for tax season, then I set up a new template in Loopy Pro to accommodate a friend who planned to join my basement jam session that evening. He bailed, but I was jacked on Genius Adaptogens so I played all the instruments myself into the wee hours of the night.
Terrasoul Superfoods Sun Alchemy Cognitive Coffee for $15: Sun Alchemy plays directly to the interests of busy professionals who only recently stopped using the #riseandgrind tag on their LinkedIn posts, with a greatest hits collection of buzzy adjuncts punctuating the top of its ingredient list. Fans of the bulletproof coffee craze will love the addition of MCT oil and organic coconut milk powder, while mushroomheads of all stripes will find the blend of mushrooms in the sachet to be standard and proper. The package recommends a frothing wand for stirring, but I tried whipping this up in a Wawa with hot water and a stir stick to see if it might be a good fit for a haggard road warrior like me. A fair amount of sediment remained in the bottom of the cup in both scenarios, rendering the last sip or two basically undrinkable. Until that point, this is a totally fine drink, with prominent notes of medium-roast pre-ground grocery store coffee, a light tickle of coconut on the finish, and a sharp, mildly bitter nose a newbie might dislike but a lifelong coffee addict will find endearing.
Everyday Dose Premium Adaptogenic Mushroom Coffee for $40: One month of this fantastical dust promises better sleep and boosted mood. Two months promises a healthy gut, and three months promises glowing skin and boosted immunity. It’s easy to acquire three months of Everyday Dose because its subscription-only model is damn near impossible to cancel. It’s difficult to drink this daily for even a week, though, but best of luck if a guy with an alpha jawline and yacht full o’ thots in Croatia told you otherwise! Unlike MUD/WTR (below), which seems to be the closest analog as far as aesthetics and cheekiness go, Everyday Dose boasts a wee bit of caffeine, which is appealing for coffee addicts like yours truly. I first mixed 1 tablespoon of the powder with 8 ounces of hot water and drank it straight up, which yielded an unappetizing liquid that tasted like a mix of Chex Mix and bong water. Some frothed oat milk and a squirt of simple syrup turned out to be the most drinkable form, but I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed any of it.
Om Master Blend Organic Mushroom Powder for $20: The bulk of Om’s catalog is billed as “dietary supplements,” so its Master Blend is not exactly the kind of thing you’ll want to drink on its own. I tried this for science, of course, and it wasn’t terrible! There’s a vegetal flavor on the sip that tastes like potato water, and the finish has an astringent tingle that’s akin to the tiniest dose of Sichuan peppercorns steeped in hot water. Om really shines when it’s added to a cup of coffee brewed with beans from the Global South. One teaspoon of this sand-colored dust added a savory pop that smoothed out the brightness of my favorite Colombian Supremo beans from Costco, and the requisite jitters that usually kicked in after three cups of the brew felt mellower than usual with Om mixed in. The silty residue at the bottom of the cup is best avoided, but it won’t harsh your vibe too much on the whole.
North Spore Functional-5 Mushroom Coffee for $18: Most mushroom-infused ground coffee blends are filed under the “Medium Roast” category, which is typically a safe catch-all that grocery store brands and discount purveyors describe their preground product as to avoid pissing off discerning light-roast aficionados such as yours truly. Nine times out of 10 they hit like a dark roast, with an ashy taste and a healthy dose of the oil that seeps out of the beans during the elongated roasting process, shimmering and swirling around the top of your cup like a puddle in a parking lot. This coffee from North Spore, which makes our favorite mushroom-growing monotub and spray-and-grow mushroom kit, lacks all of those off notes while still retaining a sturdy, earthy flavor that’s far enough removed from the citric and buttery notes I love most about classic high-end light roasts to stand up as its own unique thing. There’s a hint of mushroom flavor on the swallow if you really look for it, but you could easily swap this in for someone's morning cup of Folgers or Illy medium roast and they’d be none the wiser.
Ryze Superfoods Mushroom Coffee for $75: One could consider two different approaches to how purveyors of mushroom coffee dial in the flavor profile of their product: They can go all in with a bombastic brew filled with spices and overtones, or they can play it safe and concoct the base of a beverage that tastes more like memories of other drinks than a beverage with an identity of its own. The underwhelming flavor of Ryze falls in the latter camp. In fairness, there are plenty of folks who have no interest in savoring their morning beverage and instead need to put the liquid inside them as fast as possible so they can “adult” that day. Twenty-one-year-old Pete thought people who claimed to enjoy espresso were insane, yet here I am, two decades later wishing I could sip bitter bean water instead of this sour cup of forgettable swill that curdled the whole milk I tried to cut it with. A week with Ryze did little to boost my mood, focus, or energy. It mostly made me cranky and sad.
Cuppa Medium Roast Mushroom Coffee for $30: Like the friendly foreigner who calls his daily cup of tea or coffee his “cuppa,” this newcomer is polite, congenial, and inoffensive. The first sip brought to mind a really good cup of coffee at a nameless diner, with a light body and very mellow acidic notes on the swallow. The small dose of ruddy powder pulled from the bag with the included plastic scoop dissolved thoroughly with a few stirs, and the pristine lack of sediment in the cup was exactly as advertised. The boost of energy is also unassuming and easy to relegate to the background, which could be a welcome respite from the blast of caffeine many coffee addicts think they need right when they wake up every morning. After a week with Cuppa I started to enjoy easing into my daily brain vibrations rather than white-knuckling it off the rip at 7 am on the dot every morning.
Not Recommended
MUD/WTR Original Blend for $60: The packaging of MUD/WTR isn’t quite as unhinged as a bottle of Dr. Bronner's, but it’s definitely in the same realm. The spicy dust inside the can is a maximalist circus of weirdness as well, with herbaceous stalwarts like turmeric and masala chai holding it down alongside the usual shroom suspects. It took me a few days to realize that properly emulsifying this ruddy power per the suggested instructions—1 tablespoon with ¾ cup of water, battered thoroughly with the included handheld immersion blender—is an impossible task, so I started experimenting with supplemental ingredients in hopes that some blend of milk, fat, and sugar would minimize the gritty aftertaste that overwhelms the palate. I landed on 1 tablespoon of simple syrup and 4 ounces of whole milk frothed in my trusty Subminimal NanoFoamer Pro. The final result hits somewhere between a chai latte and the kind of hot cocoa you’d order at a coffee shop with boring ’90s music, mean baristas, and a dirty bin full of stale vegan + gluten-free snacks next to the register. I didn’t hate it, but the bottom quarter of the cup is an undrinkable gunky mess. And don’t get me started on the chunky brown lacing that clings to the edge of the cup. The physical and mental effects of MUD/WTR felt more like a facsimile of a boost than a visceral kick in the pants, but a placebo high is better than nothing, right? Combine that with the amount of adjunct ingredients required to make this drinkable and I ended up with a beverage I would only drink every now and then as a treat on a chilly day rather than a daily sipper I can rely on for increased focus, energy, virility, and the million other things this product promises within the wall of text that adorns its packaging.

The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the Tamil Nadu Government’s announcement of a salt reduction campaign in the Assembly on Tuesday.
Reducing salt intake could help lower the burden of hypertension, stroke, heart attacks and kidney disease. In a press release, the foundation cited the UK’s salt-reduction campaign, initiated in 2005 by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health (WASSH), which resulted in a reported 30% reduction in salt in bread.
The Foundation’s salt-reduction campaign began in 2010 with a walkathon at Marina Beach, followed by similar events in Tiruchi and Puducherry and awareness programmes in colleges. In 2014, its founder-chairman Rajan Ravichandran received the Notable Achievement Award from the World Hypertension League for the campaign.
The Foundation has written to more than 300 food manufacturers seeking reductions in salt content and cited reductions in salt in noodles by Nestlé and Hindustan Lever as examples of industry response. It also organised international conferences on salt and health with IIT-Madras and IIT-Bombay in 2017.
The Foundation has conducted salt and health workshops for more than 500 physicians in Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Vijayawada. It also welcomed the growing focus on front-of-pack food labelling and said the State’s decision to take forward the campaign will be an important step towards improving population health.

Minor abducted, sexually assaulted; accused attacks cop with machete, gets shot
A Coimbatore police probe into the alleged abduction and sexual assault of a 14-year-old turned violent when an accused allegedly attacked Inspector Suvarnavalli with a concealed machete. Police said they opened fire in self-defence, while the investigation and further legal action continue.
A police investigation into the alleged abduction and sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl in Tamil Nadu's Coimbatore takes a violent turn after one of the accused allegedly attacks a police inspector with a concealed machete and is shot in the leg in self-defence.
The two accused, identified as Santhosh, 24, and Thavasi, 28, were arrested after allegedly abducting the minor on a two-wheeler and sexually assaulting her at a house in Kanjikkonampalayam.
The case was registered by the All Women Police Station (South) following a complaint. During the investigation, police allegedly found that the two men had abducted the girl and taken her to the house, where she was sexually assaulted.
The survivor was subsequently sent to hospital for a medical examination.
ACCUSED ALLEGEDLY ATTACKS POLICE INSPECTOR
After the arrests, police took Thavasi to a location where he had allegedly hidden a machete that was used to threaten the girl.
A police team led by Inspector Suvarnavalli went to the location to recover the weapon.
According to police, Thavasi suddenly took out the concealed machete and attacked Suvarnavalli, injuring her.
Police then opened fire in self-defence, hitting Thavasi in his left leg.
He received first aid at the spot before being taken by ambulance to the District Government Medical College Hospital, where he is undergoing treatment.
INSPECTOR ALSO HOSPITALISED
Inspector Suvarnavalli, who was injured in the alleged machete attack, was also admitted to hospital and is receiving treatment.
Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the alleged abduction and sexual assault as well as the subsequent attack on the police team.
Further legal action is being taken against Santhosh and Thavasi.

25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim
The GOP wants America to fear Muslims.
Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11. In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks.
Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies.
Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice-disbarred, disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.)
But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11. One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it.
As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry, explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month: “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today. And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.”
The GOP is running on Islamophobia in 2026
The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn.
On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.”
At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
As Christian reports, Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia.
Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”
And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month, Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state.
El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”
Without much else to run on, though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia.

Surrey man awarded $275K in defamation suit after months-long protest in front of his home
Protestors gathered in front of Bing Chen Gao's Surrey house for 77 days straight in 2020
A B.C. journalist has won a defamation lawsuit after a 77-day-long protest in front of his Surrey house in 2020.
In a Thursday decision, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Richard Hewson awarded Bing Chen Gao $275,000, finding defendant Yun Fei Zhu had published defamatory statements about him.
Gao testified that Zhu and others protested outside his home daily, starting Sept. 15, 2020, until Dec. 1, 2020.
Crowds ranged from about 10 to 60 people and the protests were livestreamed, mostly by Zhu, who was treated as a "leader," for about five hours a day to an online audience.
More protests and livestreams took place outside his house in 2023 from Jan. 20 to 25, according to the court document.
Gao said the protesters called him a Chinese Communist Party (CCP) spy, distributed pamphlets disclosing his home address, and played funeral music outside his house.
Guo Wenghui supporters
The protestors were supporters of Chinese tycoon Guo Wenghui, a public critic of the Chinese Communist Party. He started the New Federal State of China (NFSC), a political movement dedicated to replacing the CCP in China.
Two months ago, Guo was sentenced to 30 years in a U.S. prison for fraud.
"Some viewed Guo Wengui as a courageous dissident exposing corruption, while others regarded him and the NFSC as unreliable, conspiratorial and cult‑like," said Hewson’s decision.
It said Gao, who worked as a journalist, was an outspoken critic of Guo.
Gao was also a critic of the CCP — he was involved in the pro-democracy movement in China before he moved to Canada in 2004 — but those who protested outside his house accused him of being "a professional agent long trained by the CCP."
Some of the distributed pamphlets read:
"Gao disguises himself as an anti‑communism activist and has set up a special YouTube channel to spread false information on behalf of the CCP, steer public opinion, and defame real anti-communism activists and the Canadians who are against the CCP."
They also accused Gao of taking money from the CCP.
Throughout the livestreams, protestors could be heard chanting in English and Mandarin "CCP spy," "stinky dog poop," "trash," "we all hate your guts," and "everybody on this cul-de-sac hates you."
Zhu testified he stopped taking part in the demonstrations after an assault took place in the cul-de-sac, but returned for the protests in 2023.
Gao testified the assault was against a friend of his. He said protests affected his wife, young daughter, and elderly mother-in-law.
Hewson found Zhu was liable for defamatory comments made by himself and other speakers during the livestreams that he published.
Gao was awarded $250,000 in general damages and a further $25,000 in aggravated damages.
Hewson also ordered an injunction prohibiting Zhu from repeating defamatory statements and ordered him to pay Gao $5,000 in court costs.

'I've never seen anything like this' — A U.S. doctor treats Ebola's youngest victims
An Ebola treatment unit in the city of Butembo, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, has 30 beds. Tonight, they're all full.
"I don't know how this is going to slow down," says Dr. Rupa Narra, a U.S. pediatrician who arrived in August to work for Doctors Without Borders. "It's the most devastating thing I've ever seen in my life."
With at least 6,800 confirmed cases and more than 3,310 deaths since May, the latest outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is on track to be the worst on record. Last week, Narra's unit lost eight patients — all under the age of 5.
The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain of ebolavirus; which has no approved antiviral medication or vaccine. Without these medical options, about 30% of adults who are diagnosed with the virus die within two weeks. The death rate is even higher for children, whose immune systems are less developed. For newborns, the virus is almost always fatal.
While children have made up 1 in 4 confirmed cases in this outbreak, they represent 1 in overall 3 deaths.
Narra and her colleagues spend their days providing supportive care: running fluids through an IV, giving oxygen or blood transfusions. Treating hypothermia, fever or secondary infections as their patients' bodies try to fight the virus. Part of her role is helping train about a dozen doctors and nurses in Butembo on how to adjust this care for pediatric and newborn patients.
"I had to change my mindset, that we were going to save kids," Narra says. "Now, it's — we're going to minimize suffering, and we're going to let the Congolese staff know that they did everything they could to save that baby's life."
The Bundibugyo strain can often begin with symptoms similar to malaria, so 15 of the beds in the unit are for sick patients who are waiting on test results. The other 15 beds are for confirmed Ebola patients. But in recent days, Narra says, there are so many people coming to the clinic that they have begun using quarantine beds for confirmed cases.
"It's still not enough," Narra says. "I know everyone is trying to scale up as fast as possible, but it's moving at a rapidity that never was the case."
There's a tricky thing about taking care of kids in an Ebola unit. Because there's no approved vaccine — it's hard to find someone already immune to the virus, from a prior infection, who can watch over the smallest patients. Narra and her colleagues are limited to about an hour at a time due to the difficulty and risks of working in protective gear.
Shortly after she arrived in Butembo, Narra says, a young mother died in the Ebola unit soon after giving birth. Her newborn daughter was entirely alone.
"I didn't know what we were going to do with this baby, because there were no other family members who had been exposed, and there was a high likelihood for this child to have Ebola," Narra says.
But when she entered the baby's room — there was a woman there, holding her in her arms.
"Actually, she was an Ebola survivor," Narra says. "She did not know the family and agreed to take care of this baby."
The baby lived for 10 days — but eventually succumbed to the virus. Her caregiver never left her side.
Narra is no stranger to crisis. She worked as an epidemiologist in 2014, responding to the West Africa Ebola outbreak that killed 11,310 people. She was a pediatrician in an emergency department in Brooklyn when COVID-19 hit the United States. She worked for Doctors Without Borders in Haiti.
"I've never seen anything like this," she says. "The speed of transmission, along with other aspects of a fragile healthcare system."
The latest Ebola outbreak is concentrated in the eastern border region between the DRC, Rwanda and Uganda, where fierce clashes between the Congolese army and Rwandan-backed paramilitary forces have forced families to find refuge in cities like Butembo. Meanwhile, the region's healthcare system is already stretched thin, treating children with malnutrition and outbreaks of malaria or measles on a regular basis. The conflict, and cuts to foreign aid have disrupted routine vaccinations and other assistance.
As a pediatrician, there's little Narra can do to help a kid feel a little less scared.
Every day, before she sees her patients, she puts on a fully disinfected hazmat suit. Only her eyes are visible.
"You're 5 years old, and these people walk in with what looks like a spacesuit. Of course you're going to scream!" she says.
She can't bring in a toy to distract them, wear a funny hat. Pick them up and show them around the clinic, bouncing them on her hip. She can't hold their hand through the night, when they get really sick.
"That's been the very difficult part for me — is I can't be at the bedside of this critical child," she says.
She remembers one 5-year-old patient in quarantine, waiting on test results, whose father would sit with her, letting her watch Bollywood movies on his smartphone. Narra, whose family is from southern India, recognized one of the songs — a number from the romantic comedy, Desi Boyz.
After her shift that day, Narra took off her gear and ran outside to her patient's window. She knocked, this time looking like herself –- and did her best Bollywood dance moves from the film.
"And then, she was smiling, laughing and clapping," Narra laughs. "I was like –- I don't even know these moves but I will make them up for you!"
A few days later, the test results came back for the little girl: negative. One bright spot, in Narra's painful summer.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

A video showing a woman being brutally assaulted by a man in an open field is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it depicts a real incident involving the assault of a primary school teacher in Maharashtra. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a primary school teacher being brutally assaulted in Maharashtra.
Fact: The video does not show an assault on a primary school teacher in Maharashtra. Instead, it shows a scripted fight video posted by a user who regularly shares similar staged fighting videos on his page. Hence, the claim is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the video posted on an Instagram account named ‘Vipin Chauhan’ on 11 August 2026. One of the hashtags in the video’s description was #acting. We also found that multiple videos in similar attire were shared, with captions indicating that the man was assaulting the woman after she allegedly cheated on him (here, here, here). The fact that the video was circulated in parts, along with these captions, suggests it was a scripted act rather than a real incident.
The same video was reposted in September 2026, and the description stated that it was a planned video and warned viewers not to try it at home.
Further, the page bio stated that the user was available for WWE-style videos. We also reviewed other content shared on the profile and found multiple videos featuring the same duo seen in the viral video in similar fight scenes (here, here, here). This further indicates that the viral video depicts a staged act rather than a real incident.
To sum up, a scripted fight video is being falsely shared as an assault on a primary school teacher in Maharashtra.

How to adjust the Liquid Glass effect on your iPhone with iOS 27
Apple's new controls make it easier to set things just how you like them.
Apple's Liquid Glass interface doesn't appeal to everyone. Some people love the glossy look, while others criticize it for reducing readability. Apple quickly became aware of this after it launched and introduced new ways of adjusting the Liquid Glass effect in iOS 26.1. Dubbed Tinted Mode, the feature reduces the opacity of Liquid Glass and increases its contrast. Still, that wasn't enough to satisfy frustrated users who continued to complain about Apple's modern design language.
An even bigger update to Liquid Glass arrived with the release of iOS 27. If you've never been satisfied with the Tinted or Clear options on your iPhone, then you'll probably like Apple's latest update. It adds a much-requested slider for making Liquid Glass more readable and customizable, putting you in more control over how iOS looks and feels.
It begins with a slider
In order to customize how Liquid Glass presents on your phone, you'll first need to go into your iPhone's Settings app. From there, look for the Appearance section and select the Liquid Glass menu. Instead of the old rigid toggles, you'll now see a slider. Dragging it to the left will make the glass look more like, well, glass. Dragging it to the right gives it that more opaque look from earlier versions of iOS.
If you want something that does a little bit of both, just leave the slider in the center. Apple gives you a quick preview of the effect right on that same screen, so you don't have to keep switching between apps just to see the changes in action. It should be noted that the option to adjust the intensity of the glass effect on the Lock Screen remains separate from the slider in the Settings app.
Of course, this option is only available in iOS 27, so you'll have to update your iPhone if you want to tweak the appearance of Liquid Glass. Fortunately, Apple has made iOS 27 compatible with iPhone 11 models and upwards, so your old iPhone likely won't be stuck with a limited version of the UI.
How to turn off Liquid Glass completely
If you don't like Liquid Glass and want to disable it almost completely, there's a way to do just that in the Accessibility settings. There, look for Display & Text Size and enable the Reduce Transparency toggle. This option is much more aggressive than the Liquid Glass slider, but it works best for those who really don't like the glassy effects in iOS.
iOS 27 updates have been accessible to developers and beta testers for a little while, but the public release rolled out in September. If you're willing to get the beta version on your iPhone, then you won't have to wait for future updates to Liquid Glass and other iOS features: Just sign up for the Apple Beta Program, and be aware there could be a few bugs here and there.

GOP congressman from Wisconsin swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in a lake
A Republican congressman from Wisconsin says he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday
A Republican congressman from Wisconsin said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday.
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport. The pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau. They both ended up in the water and swam to safety.
"After landing, we called 911. As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," he wrote on X.
The Marathon County Sheriff's Office said in a statement that the emergency landing happened just before 9 p.m. Saturday. Tiffany and the pilot, Leonard Boltz, got out of the plane and called 911. They were rescued by emergency responders in a fire department airboat just after 9 p.m.
Both men were taken to a nearby hospital, where they were treated for minor injuries and released. Tiffany suffered a cut above his right eye that required stitches, his campaign said in an emailed statement.
A no-wake buoy was placed near the plane, which remained in the lake, and boaters were being asked to avoid the area until the plane can be removed, the sheriff's office said. A Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson said the agency would investigate the incident. A National Transportation Safety Board spokesperson said that agency is waiting for the FAA to assess the plane as to whether the damage was substantial enough for it to get involved.
Tiffany is running for governor on the Republican ticket in Wisconsin and has been endorsed by President Donald Trump.
David Crowley, the Democratic candidate, wished Tiffany a “quick recovery” in a post on X and lauded the “heroism of the pilot.”
The plane Tiffany was traveling in was a single-engine, four-seat Beechcraft Bonanza aircraft.

BRICS leaders meet in India as wars and US tensions test the bloc
Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and counterparts from the other eight BRICS members. The summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising U.S.-China tensions, test the bloc's ability to find common ground among countries with competing geopolitical interests.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the summit venue and other parts of New Delhi, with traffic restrictions and diversions in place.
BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2010. It has since expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world's population and a significant share of global economic output. The group has increasingly called for greater representation for developing countries in global institutions.
The leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, energy, food security, technology, supply chains and reforms to global institutions. Reducing reliance on the U.S. dollar will also be a priority, with members promoting greater use of their own currencies in trade and payments, as well as pushing for alternatives to Western-dominated financial institutions.
Russia and China seek to expand influence
China and Russia see BRICS as a way to reduce Western dominance, particularly that of the United States, while strengthening cooperation among emerging and developing economies.
Putin, in a speech at the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi on Friday, said the grouping was not against anyone and Moscow was open to cooperation with countries around the world
"We are in favor of our interests," he said.
Iran has also pushed for mechanisms that could reduce the bloc's reliance on Western financial systems and shield members from economic pressure, as Tehran faces sweeping sanctions and a U.S. blockade.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian backed expanding trade in national currencies among BRICS members.
"One of the most important steps is to expand the use of national currencies in trade among the members," he told reporters on Friday.
China, meanwhile, is leveraging the grouping to deepen its influence within the bloc and position it as a counterweight to U.S. power.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday that Xi was expected to discuss major international issues and ways to deepen cooperation among BRICS members.
India balances strategic partnerships
For India, the summit highlights its effort to maintain strategic ties with Russia and Iran while deepening relations with the U.S. and Europe. New Delhi has sought to balance its longstanding partnerships with Moscow and Tehran with efforts to expand economic, defense and technology ties with Washington and other Western nations.
India has maintained close ties with both Moscow and Tehran despite the war in Ukraine and tensions between Iran and the U.S., while calling for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts. Modi met Putin and Pezeshkian separately in New Delhi on Friday ahead of the summit.
India is also hoping the forum will help ease its longstanding strained ties with China. Modi and Xi are expected to hold talks later Saturday, a meeting that could help consolidate a diplomatic thaw between the two countries after border tensions escalated in 2020.
A key test for India will be whether it can secure a joint statement from leaders at the summit. Those divisions were evident in May, when BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement over the Iran war, forcing India to issue a chair's summary instead.
The summit convenes as fears grow that the Iran war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, may expand amid escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels. The bloc's unity under pressure is expected to be tested as its members navigate differing positions on the conflict and relations with the U.S.

Paediatric heart surgeries that can cost families anywhere between ₹5 lakh and ₹20 lakh each at private hospitals, were provided free of cost to children at the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad. As part of its fifth paediatric cardiac surgery camp, NIMS performed 19 complex heart surgeries on a cashless basis on children aged between two months and 13 years. The week-long camp concluded on Saturday (September 12, 2026)
The surgeries were carried out by the NIMS Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery in collaboration with Healing Little Hearts, with a specialist team led by paediatric cardiac surgeon Ramana Dhanapuneni from the UK. The NIMS team was headed by M. Amaresh Rao, Head of Cardiothoracic Surgery.
From screening to surgery
The camp’s impact extended well beyond the 19 operations. Around 1,000 children were screened as part of the programme. Of these, few were found to require minimally invasive intervention rather than open-heart surgery. The surgical team, meanwhile, selected a mix of complex congenital heart cases for the camp, prioritising children who required specialised cardiac surgery. More than 100 children who require surgery are still waiting, with dates already allotted for their procedures, said Dr. Amaresh.
“Congenital heart disease is common and the cost of paediatric cardiac surgery in private hospitals can be prohibitive for many families, ranging from ₹5 lakh to ₹20 lakh. Hope for the poor is public sector hospitals like NIMS,” said Dr. Ramana.
80 surgeries through five camps
The latest camp is the fifth such programme conducted through the collaboration between Dr. Dhanapuneni’s team and NIMS. The partnership began in 2023, when two camps were conducted. One camp was held in 2024 and another in 2025.
NIMS Director Rahul Devraj said the five camps had resulted in about 80 surgeries so far. “NIMS would like Dr. Ramana and his team to visit twice a year, assuring continued institutional support to the visiting specialists and the cardiac department,” he said.
Around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases
Dr. Amaresh said there are around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases, while NIMS currently performs around 400 paediatric cardiac surgeries annually. The department needs to reach 1,000 surgeries a year, he said.
ECMO support under Aarogyasri
Another significant development pertaining to the camp was the availability of ECMO services at NIMS under the Aarogyasri scheme for the first time. “No patient needed it during this camp,” Dr. Amaresh clarified. However, he said the significance was that ECMO would now be available to eligible patients free of cost for as long as it is medically required, subject to the scheme’s provisions.

India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
- Published
In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations.
Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.
Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.
But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.
In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.
In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.
For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.
A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented.
The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.
Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.
BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible.
"Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC.
"We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."
But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says.
Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government.
"When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains.
Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.
Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.
Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says.
"Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.
Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.
India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University.
"This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.
For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.
Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak.
"It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.
The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures.
"The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."
Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.
The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.
Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September.
"I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"
Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.
Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.
The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator.
"A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.
Rao agrees.
"It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.
What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.
Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.
Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.
The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."
Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.
Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.
But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see.
"I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student.
"In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

Meta has removed several Instagram and Facebook accounts and content related to the Jantar Mantar protest that Alt News had flagged as AI-manipulated visuals.
On September 2, a Meta spokesperson confirmed to Alt News that following a review, all the accounts and content were found to be violative of the platform’s policies and had been removed.
These posts included several AI-generated and AI-manipulated photographs and videos of women protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest in July. Alt News flagged Instagram and Facebook accounts and posts to Meta, in which real visuals women had been altered using AI, purportedly in an attempt to outrage their modesty.
In these posts, women’s clothes, bodies and poses had been altered in such a way that they looked starkly different from the original videos or photographs. Alt News’ investigation found that many such visuals were either entirely AI-generated or altered using AI. In some cases, techniques such as face swaps or body swaps were used.
Targeting Women CJP Protesters
Women protesters who participated in the CJP protests in Delhi were particularly targeted on social media. For several days, women faced online harassment and trolling, doxxing, rape threats and the public disclosure of personal information. These AI-visuals formed part of this larger pattern of attacks against female protesters.
These fake visuals were shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, among other platforms, claiming that they were real footage from the Jantar Mantar protest. Users then mistook the AI characters for real women partaking in the protests which was followed by objectionable and misogynistic comments targeting their identities, physical appearance, clothes and character. A few of those comments are displayed below:
Alt News identified several Instagram accounts which circulated such malicious content, including @kauronfire, @sirfseerat, @tia_kaurr, @hey.siya_2.0, @kavya_homevibes, @annika0022, @divyankaha and @its_anushkaa69.
Right-wing Users Share AI Image
During the protest, several right-wing users, including RSS supporters Acharya Ankur Arya and Vikram Pratap Singh, shared an AI-generated image claiming that it was a real photograph from the Jantar Mantar protest.
The purported image showed a young woman wearing a crop top and jeans. Users who shared the post made objectionable comments about the woman’s clothing and character. Alt News fact-checked this viral image and found that it was entirely AI-generated.
However, in some cases that surfaced on social media during the final days of the protest, besides entirely AI-generated images, real photographs of women were being altered, making it difficult to determine its authencity.
Visuals Of A Woman In White Saree
An user, @divyankaha, shared a photo and video on their Instagram account and YouTube channel respectively. These showed a woman wearing a white saree and navy blue blouse, linking her to the Jantar Mantar protest. (Archive link-1, Archive link-2)
Alt News found the original video of the post uploaded on an Instagram page @khoji_reporter24news.
Comparing the viral clip with the original video, we found that the body and clothing of the woman were entirely different, thus confirming that the image had been altered using AI. The background and original footage of the viral video remained the same, but the appearance of the woman had been completely manipulated. After Alt News flagged this to Meta, they removed @divyankaha‘s account.
We found several such posts and videos on @divyankaha‘s page. In another post, a woman wearing a white saree is seen sitting on the road wit posters infront of her. Alt News found this photo was also an AI-deepfake. (Archive link)
Several different versions of the viral post, with a woman in a white saree, were also found circulating widely on social media. All of these were AI-deepfakes.
Visuals Of A Woman Standing With A Poster
Another photograph went viral showing different women near the stage at the Jantar Mantar protest, holding posters that read “Resign De De Bhai PUNE SE Aai hu..and Hum jeet gaye”.
In the different iterations of this photo being shared, the woman as well as the design of the poster kept changing. These photos were shared by right-wing handles and those opposing the CJP protest, with objectionable comments and captions. (Archive Link-1, Link-2, Link-3, Link-4)
We found that this photo had been altered using AI. The original photoe was posted on July 22 by an Instagram account named @nanddhini.
A comparison of the original and viral photos clearly showed the difference in the woman’s face and body. The design of the poster also appears to have changed across different viral versions. Thus, the face and body of the woman in the original photo were swapped using an AI editing tool.
Similarly, several AI-generated and manipulated photos and videos were shared on the Facebook and Instagram accounts of @sirfseerat. These posts either altered real visuals related to the Jantar Mantar protest or created entirely new AI visuals. Some of these posts, displayed below, were later deleted.
Woman Speaking To Journalist
An Instagram AI-digital creator page named @kauronfire shared a video on July 23 in which a journalist can be seen interviewing a woman participating in the protest. (Archive)
We found the original video posted on journalist Muskan Bhagat’s Instagram account. (Archive)

Woman Raising Slogans
@kauronfire shared another video showing a woman protester wearing a yellow crop top and shorts, raising slogans during the protest. (Archive)

Indore Video Falsely Circulated
In another video, a woman wearing red and black gym clothes was shared with the claim that she was distributing sharbat (juice) to people at the Jantar Mantar protest site. (Archive)
We found the original video on the Instagram account of content creator Himani Chawla, who can be seen wearing a blue suit in the video. This video is actually from Indore, Madhya Pradesh, where Chawla and her companions were serving sharbat to passersby. Thus, the video had absolutely no connection with the Jantar Mantar protest. These accounts misused AI, not only as a means to spread misinformation, but also to depict women in an objectionable manner, exposing them to online, and even real life harassment and abuse — all of which amount to punishable offences under the IT Act and the IT Rules of India.
On August 25, after receiving confirmation from Meta regarding the action taken, Alt News rechecked those accounts and posts, and some accounts and posts appeared to be available. Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”
